# Sūrah al-Nisāʾ (Chapter 4) — Expanded Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Introduction to the Sūrah

Sūrah al-Nisāʾ — "The Women" — is the fourth chapter of the Qur'an and the second longest of the Madinan sūrahs, comprising one hundred and seventy-six verses. It was revealed in Madinah in the years immediately following the Battle of Uḥud (3 AH / 625 CE), when the young Muslim community was confronting simultaneously the wounds of that defeat, the treachery of internal hypocrisy, the open hostility of certain Jewish tribes of Madinah, and — most pressingly for this sūrah's distinctive subject matter — the social wreckage war leaves behind: widows without provision, orphans without guardians, households fractured along lines of loyalty and belief.

The sūrah takes its name from the prominence of its legislation concerning women — their marriage rights, their bridewealth, their inheritance shares, their protection from the predations of guardians — the first corpus of revealed law in history to establish, categorically and by divine command, the independent legal personality of women in property, marriage, and succession. Alongside this, however, the chapter builds an equally weighty architecture on other foundations: the sanctity of family relations and the duty of parents and children to one another; the administration of justice and the obligation of equity even against one's own soul; the crime of usury and the ethics of commerce; the status of the People of the Book — their distortions of scripture, their rejection of the Prophet ﷺ, their claims concerning Jesus son of Mary — culminating in the Qur'an's definitive address of the crucifixion question (vv. 157–159); the exposure of the hypocrites and the mechanics of their double-dealing; the laws of war, of the fear-prayer, of emigration, and of the protection of the weak; and, woven through every section, the demand that faith be complete — that entering Islam means entering it wholly, in conduct as in creed.

Commentators have long noted the sūrah's architectural symmetry: it opens with an address to all mankind — *Reverence your Lord, Who created you from a single soul* — placing the entire human family under one Creator and one womb, and it closes, at verse 176, with a question asked and answered about inheritance, so that the chapter that begins with the origin of human kinship ends with the law that governs kinship's final earthly transaction. Between these poles stands one of the most consequential bodies of legislation and exhortation in the Qur'an: family law, commercial law, penal law, the law of war and peace, and above all the law of the heart — reverence (*taqwā*) — commanded at both the sūrah's first verse and repeated through its course as the single thread binding every statute to its Lord.

## The Occasions of Its Revelation

The Battle of Uḥud (Shawwāl, 3 AH) looms over this sūrah as the Shadow over its opening sections. Seventy Muslims had been martyred; households were suddenly headed by grieving widows raising fatherless children; and the question thrust upon the community — *who now stands guardian over the orphan's property and the widow's future?* — is answered in the sūrah's celebrated opening pericope (vv. 1–14), where the orphans' sacred trust, the women's marriage rights, and the inheritance ordinance are legislated together in a single sweep. The Prophet's ﷺ own era of consolidation in Madinah — the expulsion of Banū al-Naḍīr after their treason (4–5 AH), the crisis of the slander against ʿĀʾishah and its exonerating revelation, the expeditions of the middle Madinan years, and the Jews of Khaybar and Madinah contending with the new polity — supplies the occasions for verse after verse recorded in the works of al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Suyūṭī, many of which are noted in the commentary that follows.

## Distinguished Contents

Among the matters for which Sūrah al-Nisāʾ is especially renowned:

- **The inheritance code** (vv. 7–14, 176) — the revealed mathematics of succession that founded the science of *ʿilm al-farāʾiḍ*, which the Prophet ﷺ urged his companions to learn and teach, calling it "half of knowledge."
- **The women's charter** (vv. 3–4, 19–25, 34–35, 127–130) — bridewealth as the woman's own property, prohibition of inheriting women against their will, the obligations of maintenance and kindness, and the machinery of arbitration in marital discord.
- **Justice as testimony to God** (v. 135) — *O you who believe! Be custodians of justice, witnesses for God, even if against yourselves* — a verse the scholars have called the supreme statute of judicial integrity.
- **The verse of universal trust** (v. 58) — *God commands you to deliver trusts to those entitled to them* — which the commentators, citing the Prophet's own precedent at the conquest of Makkah, have made the charter of all governance and office-holding in Islam.
- **The crucifixion passage** (vv. 157–159) — *They did not slay him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so unto them* — the Qur'an's own account of the end of Jesus's earthly mission, around which the whole theology of the People of the Book section (vv. 44–55, 153–173) is arranged.
- **The hypocrites' anatomy** (vv. 60–63, 78–83, 137–146) — the chapter's systematic diagnosis of the double-hearted: their speech, their hesitation, their terror, and their end.
- **The fear-prayer** (vv. 101–104) — revealed for the battlefield's exigency, and the divine condescension of shortening prayer in travel.

## Structure of the Commentary

What follows is a verse-by-verse expanded commentary in which every one of the one hundred and seventy-six verses receives its own complete treatment, in the manner of the earlier volumes of this series on Sūrah al-Fātiḥah, Sūrah al-Baqarah, and Sūrah Āl ʿImrān. Where the source groups verses together (as with vv. 13–14, 27–28, 57–58, and others), the verses have been separated and treated individually, as the method of this series demands. Each commentary draws upon the Arabic language and its roots, the transmitted views of the classical commentators — al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī, and the reports of Ibn ʿAbbās among them — the authenticated words of the Prophet ﷺ with their collections identified, the occasions of revelation where they are soundly transmitted, and the living reasoning that connects this Madinan legislation to the households, marketplaces, courts, and battlefields of every age that inherits it.

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:1

> **O mankind! Reverence your Lord, Who created you from a single soul and from it created its mate, and from the two has spread abroad a multitude of men and women. Reverence God, through Whom you demand your rights of one another, and family relations. Truly God is a Watcher over you.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Yā Ayyuhā al-Nās: The Address That Enfolds Every Human Ear**

The sūrah of legislation par excellence opens not with *"O you who believe"* — the address that will recur nearly a dozen times within its own pages — but with the widest summons in the Book's repertoire: *yā ayyuhā al-nās* — "O mankind." The distinction is the first lesson of the chapter's jurisprudence: the laws about to descend upon women and orphans, spouses and heirs, guardians and wards, are not tribal customs binding one polity but ordinances addressed to the entire human family — for their foundation, laid in this very verse, is the kinship of all flesh. Ibn Kathīr notes that this opening returns the Madinan community — and every community after it — to the primordial fact: before there were Muslims and non-Muslims, there was one soul and its mate, and the multitude scattered from them both. The legislation of the family must therefore begin with the origin of the family; God legislates for households as their Creator, not as a foreign lawgiver.

**Ittaqū: The Shield-Verb at the Head of the Law**

The first imperative of the sūrah is *ittaqū rabbakum* — "reverence your Lord" — from the root *w-q-y*, to guard, to shield: taqwā is the heart's buckler against the displeasure of its Lord, raised through obedience and maintained through vigilance. That the longest body of social legislation in the Qur'an should be prefaced by taqwā is no ornamental juxtaposition: al-Rāzī draws the connection plainly — law without God-consciousness degenerates into technique, manipulated by the clever against the weak; the orphan's rights, the widow's share, the wife's bridewealth are defended in the last instance not by courts but by the watcher-consciousness named at the verse's close. Ibn Taymiyyah's celebrated definition gathers the thread: *taqwā is acting in obedience to God, upon light from God, hoping for God's mercy; and abandoning disobedience to God, upon light from God, fearing God's punishment.* The light comes first in both clauses — for the sūrah that follows *is* that light, statute by statute.

The community's worship enshrined this very verse in the canonical sermon of need (*khuṭbat al-ḥājah*) — the Prophet ﷺ taught ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd the opening with which he commenced every address, and the jurists fixed it as the introduction to the marriage sermon:

> *"Truly the best speech is the Book of God... O mankind! Reverence your Lord, Who created you from a single soul... O you who believe! Reverence God as He deserves to be reverenced... O you who believe! Reverence God, and speak a word directed to the right..."* (Abū Dāwūd 2118; al-Tirmidhī 1105; al-Nasāʾī 3279)

Three taqwā-verses — 4:1, 3:102, and 33:70–71 — open every wedding in Islam to this day: the sūrah of the family, the sūrah's first word, spoken first over the family's founding.

**Nafs Wāḥidah: The Single Soul and the Grammar of Reciprocity**

*Khalaqakum min nafsin wāḥidatin* — "created you from a single soul" — is the chapter's founding anthropology, affirmed across the Book: "He it is Who produced you from a single soul" (6:98); "It is He Who created you from a single soul, and made from it its mate, that he might find comfort in her" (7:189); "your creation and your resurrection are only as a single soul" (31:28). The single soul is Adam, upon him be peace; *minhā khalaqa zawjahā* — "from it He created its mate" — and the commentators of every century have inquired into the *min*: from it, or of its kind? The transmitted report of the rib — "treat women kindly, for woman was created from a rib; and the most curved part of the rib is its topmost part" (al-Bukhārī 3331; Muslim 1468) — underwrote the Genesis-echoing reading favored by al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī: made from Adam, for Adam. Al-Rāzī, reasoning from the Arabic *min* of kind (as in "mates from among yourselves," 30:21), argues the woman's creation *of the same nature* — and the two readings shelter beneath one canopy: same substance, same dignity, no second clay. The Shiʿi tradition transmits from Imam Muḥammad al-Bāqir that she was formed of Adam's own superior clay. And the verse's own grammar gossips its secret to the attentive: *nafs* is feminine, *zawj* masculine — soul and mate trading grammatical gender in the single sentence — which the rhetoricians, and al-Zamakhsharī among them, took as the text's own signet of reciprocity: each sex carries the other's form within the language itself, as 2:187 declares of the spouses, "they are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them."

**Baththa: The Scattering That Became the Nations**

*Wa baththa minhumā rijālan kathīran wa nisāʾ* — "and from the two He spread abroad a multitude of men and women": the verb *baththa* is the scattering of seed into prepared earth, deployed here for the human sowing that populated the earth. From two — to "a multitude," uncounted and uncountable — runs the genealogy of every reader; the verse quietly razes every aristocracy of blood: all lineages terminate at one pair, so *boasting of fathers is boasting of nothing* — the very lesson the Prophet ﷺ pressed at the Farewell Sermon's plum-line: "No Arab has superiority over a non-Arab... all of you are from Adam, and Adam is from dust." Ibn Kathīr and al-Rāzī both detect in the clause the sūrah's abiding social command: universal siblinghood is not a metaphor but a pedigree — the orphan of v. 2 is your brother's child; the widow of v. 3 is your father's daughter. Kin is not sentiment; it is fact.

**Tasāʾalūna Bihi wa-l-Arḥām: The Oath and the Womb**

The verse's second taqwā-command is aimed at two objects joined in one breath: *wa-ttaqu Allāha alladhī tasāʾalūna bihi wa-l-arḥām* — "reverence God, through Whom you demand of one another, and the wombs." The Arabs of paganism swore their claims *by God and by kinship*; revelation did not strike the custom but re-consecrated it: the God invoked between claimants is watching the claim, and the kinship invoked is a trust with rights of its own. *Raḥim* — womb — shares its root with *raḥmah*, mercy, and with the Divine Name *al-Raḥmān*, the Compassionate — the Book's etymology made audible in the ḥadīth qudsī the community has never ceased repeating:

> *"God created creation, and when He had finished, the womb (al-raḥim) rose and took hold of the waist of the Compassionate. He said: What is it? It said: This is the station of one who seeks refuge with You against severance. He said: Are you not content that I should connect whoever connects you, and sever whoever severs you? It said: I am content, my Lord."* (al-Bukhārī 5988; Muslim 2554, from Abū Hurayrah)

The womb's own name is thus a fragment of the Name of the Compassionate; to sever it is to tug at what hangs from His Throne. This is why the sūrah of women and orphans opens with arḥām: every statute that follows — the shares, the gifts, the guardianships — is an application of *do not sever.*

**Raqīb: The Watcher Above Every Court**

The seal — *inna Allāha kāna ʿalaykum raqībā* — "truly God is ever a Watcher over you" — supplies the sūrah its great enforcement clause. *Raqīb* (root *r-q-b*, the stationed lookout) is the sentinel who neither blinks nor is bribed: over the guardian tempted by the orphan's estate, over the husband weighing equity, over the executor dividing shares, over the judge and the witness — the Book posts, before any human inspector, the divine Inspection itself. Al-Qurṭubī remarks that the chapter's threats to embezzlers and its commands to judges all budget with this attribute; and the believer reads the seal the way the chapter intends: the Lawgiver who teaches the law in the assembly is the Watcher who keeps its ledger in the privacy of every heart. Law opened by kinship is closed by surveillance — not of men, whose watching fails, but of the Lord who made us of one soul, and watches what we do one with another.

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:2

> **Give orphans their property, and exchange not the bad for the good, nor consume their property with your own. Truly that would be a great sin.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Uncle and the Orphan: The Case That Opened the Law**

The commentators of the occasions of revelation bring us into a Madinan courtyard: an orphan, come of age, demanded his inheritance from the uncle who had held it in trust; the uncle refused. The young man carried his complaint to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and heaven's answer descended — *ātu al-yatāmā amwālahum* — "give the orphans their property" (al-Wāḥidī; the report is preserved by al-Qurṭubī and underlies the whole pericope ff. in Ibn Kathīr's collection). The related case in al-Ṭabarī's transmission — a man of the tribe of Ghaṭafān who held a great sum belonging to his orphaned nephew and withheld it when the boy reached maturity — shows the temptation in its classic form: not naked theft but *prolonged custody*, the guardian's gradual inability to distinguish between what he administers and what he owns. Revelation's response cuts at exactly that confusion, which is why the imperative is *give* — *ātu* — and not "return": the property was the orphan's all along; the guardian's vault never altered the title. Custody is administration, not possession — the first axiom of the whole law of wards.

**Yatāmā: The Word of the Fatherless**

*Yatīm* (plural *yatāmā*) derives from a root of singleness and bereavement: in the usage of the Arabs and the law alike, the orphan is the child who has lost his father before reaching maturity — for the father was, in that world as in most worlds of provision, the roof of the household. The Book's own biography of the word reaches its tenderest point in the Prophet's ﷺ person: "Did He not find you an orphan and shelter you?" (93:6) — God reminding His Messenger of his own fatherless boyhood, and thereby consecrating orphan-care as an act performed upon the Prophet's own childhood in every later child. His ﷺ famous gesture, made with two fingers, fixed the station of the guardian for all generations:

> *"I and the one who sponsors an orphan will be in Paradise like these two" — and he raised his index and middle fingers together.* (al-Bukhārī 6005; Muslim 2983, from Sahl ibn Saʿd)

Proximity to Muhammad in Paradise measured by two adjoining fingers — such is the estate held out to the guardian who fulfills this verse.

**Exchange Not the Bad for the Good: The Embezzler's First Skill**

The first prohibition anatomizes the craft of subtle robbery: *wa lā tatabaddalū al-khabītha bi-l-ṭayyib* — "do not exchange the bad for the good." Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr define the classic operation: the guardian, distributing the orphan's estate, returns it in debased coin — the emaciated camel for the fat one, the moth-eaten cloth for the bolt of fine weave, the inferior land-parcel for the prime — valuing each substitution at the value of what it replaces, and calling the ledger square. The verse names the practice *tabdīl* — swapping — because its essence is not confiscation but substitution, robbery wearing the mask of accounting. A second reading, transmitted from the early exegetes, widens the clause: do not exchange the *bad practice* — consuming the orphan's wealth — for the *good practice* of preserving it. Both readings stand, for both are one sin seen from two sides: the debasing of a trust.

**Consume Not Their Property with Your Own: The Dangerous Illness of Mingling**

*Wa lā taʾkulū amwālahum ilā amwālikum* — "nor consume their property with your own": the preposition *ilā* (with/alongside) is, Ibn Kathīr points out, deployed in the sense of *ka* — *as* — as though the orphan's estate were a mere extension of the guardian's own table. The danger it names is the most realistic in all fiduciary law: not the dramatic embezzlement but the daily confusion — one purse, one pot, one account — out of which wrong invisibly grows. So searching was the command upon the first community that the Companions went to extremes of separation: al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī report that after this verse, guardians would keep the orphan's water apart from their water and his flour from their flour — until God relieved their hardship with the revealed concession of 2:220: "if you intermingle with them, they are your brothers" — communion permitted where *iṣlāḥ*, betterment, governs the household. The two verses together draw the permanent map: separation is the safe default; mixing is lawful only under proven good intent and scrupulous accounting, for "God knows the corrupter from the improver" (2:220's own protocol clause).

**Ḥūb Kabīr: The Naming of the Sin's Weight**

The verse's verdict — *innahū kāna ḥūban kabīrā* — "truly that is a great *ḥūb*" — selects one of the gravest nouns in the Book's lexicon of guilt. *Ḥawb* denotes a sin of crushing weight — al-Qurṭubī glosses it as the mighty transgression that burdens its bearer until it bears him down — and its pairing with *kabīr* (great) heaps emphasis upon emphasis: this is no peccadillo of accounting but a destroyer. The Prophet ﷺ enrolled the deed in his census of the fatal seven:

> *"Avoid the seven destroyers (al-mūbiqāt): ascribing partners to God; sorcery; killing the soul God has sanctified except by right; consuming usury; consuming the property of the orphan; fleeing on the day of battle; and slandering chaste, heedless, believing women."* (al-Bukhārī 2766; Muslim 89, from Abū Hurayrah)

Between idolatry and murder sits the embezzlement of a child — the Lord of the orphan counts His ledger in the company of the gravest crimes. The sūrah will deepen the sentence at its tenth verse into the fires of the belly; and the Muslim of every age inherits the warrant plainly: the wealth of the fatherless is guarded from the strong by a Guard stronger than them all, and the two fingers raised beside the Prophet in Paradise await only those who gave *all*, on time, untouched.

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:3

> **If you fear that you will not deal fairly with the orphans, then marry such women as seem good to you, two, three, or four; but if you fear that you will not deal justly, then only one, or those whom your right hands possess. Thus it is more likely that you will not commit injustice.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**ʿĀʾishah's Key: The Orphan Girl Behind the Marriage Verse**

No verse of the sūrah has been so misread at a distance — and so precisely explained at its source — as this one. The mother of the believers, ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, preserved its occasion and its logic for all generations, in the very verses' own custody-chain:

> *She said: "It concerns the orphan girl who is in the care of her guardian, and her property is joined to his; her wealth and her beauty please him, and he wishes to marry her with less than the standard bridal gift that any other would give her. So they were forbidden to marry those orphan girls unless they did them justice and gave them the highest bridal gift of their peers — and they were commanded to marry, apart from them, whatever women pleased them."* She said: "The people then asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the matter after this verse, and God revealed: *They ask you for a ruling about women. Say: God gives you the ruling about them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning orphan girls to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, yet you desire to marry them* (4:127)." ʿĀʾishah added: "God's saying about 'other women' shows that they were forbidden to marry them merely because of their beauty and wealth — unless they treated them justly — on account of their being drawn to them by beauty and wealth." (al-Bukhārī 4573; Muslim 3018)

The verse's architecture is thereby made clear: it opens exactly where v. 2 left off — the guardian's conscience — and diagnoses the next abuse after embezzlement: the *marriage of exploitation*, the ward married by her own warden for her own money, at a discounted dowry no outsider could write for her. God's ordinance: *keep away from the vulnerable; if your fear of God cannot secure even their dowry, go to the open market of marriage where women can bargain full.*

**Mathnā wa Thulātha wa Rubāʿa: Restriction, Not License**

*"Then marry such women as seem good to you, two, three, or four"* — and here the whole scholarly tradition speaks with one voice, from al-Ṭabarī to al-Qurṭubī to Ibn Kathīr: this clause did not open polygamy; it *closed* it at four. Pre-Islamic Arabia knew no ceiling — men circled women as wealth allowed and conscience permitted, and the early community included companions with many more than four wives upon Islam; the reports are famous that Ghaylān al-Thaqafī and others embraced Islam with ten wives, and the Prophet ﷺ commanded: *"keep four, and part from the rest"* (reported by al-Tirmidhī 1128 and Ibn Mājah 1953 from several channels; the ruling unanimous in the books). The revealed number-words — *mathnā* (two by two), *thulāth* (three by three), *rubāʿ* (four by four) — thus fixed a maximum where none stood, bound to a clause the legislatures of the age never dreamed of: *but if you fear that you will not deal justly, then only one.* Divine law capped the custom, then chained the cap to justice — and chained justice to the husband's own fear of inability. The license has a guardian: conscience measured against capacity — financial, physical, moral.

**ʿAdl: The Justice the Marriage Market Owes**

*Fa-in khiftum allā taʿdilū fa-wāḥidah* — "but if you fear you will not deal justly, then one": the justice stipulated, explain al-Qurṭubī and the jurists with him, is the *measurable* equity: maintenance at like standards, lodging, clothing, and the nights' rotation — the outer ledger every wife can audit. The inner ledger — love's tilt, the heart's lean — the sūrah itself exempts at v. 129: "you will never be able to deal fully equitably between your wives, even if you strive" — the Prophet ﷺ himself living under that dispensation and teaching his ummah its prayer:

> *"O God, this is my allotment in what I control; so do not hold me to account for what You control and I do not control"* — meaning the heart's inclination (Abū Dāwūd 2134; al-Tirmidhī 1140, who graded it ḥasan; from Abū Hurayrah).

And his ﷺ sternest warning stands sentinel beside it:

> *"Whoever has two wives and inclines to one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side of his body hanging down paralyzed."* (Abū Dāwūd 2133; al-Tirmidhī 1141; al-Nasāʾī 33942 — from Abū Hurayrah)

The leaning side drags into the next life: so precisely does the verse's justice-verb weigh husbands who multiply vows.

**Adnā Allā Taʿūlū: Tilting Away from Justice**

The seal — *dhālika adnā allā taʿūlū* — "thus it is likelier that you will not incline [to injustice]" — closes the statute with the Book's precise jurisprudential idiom: revelation aims at the *likelier* justice, legislating probabilities into structures. *ʿŪl*, from the root of inclination and deviation, is the tilt of the scale-beam; the verse's entire edifice — cap of four, condition of equity, retreat-option to one — is an instrument for keeping the beam level. Al-Rāzī observes that the legislation thereby binds the marriage law to the orphan law by a single thread of *preventive* wisdom: a man overburdened with mouths he cannot honestly feed is a man driven toward the orphan's vault; house-laws that keep his dependents within his honest means are orphan-protection by another door. The sūrah's pericope is thus one fabric: ward the orphan's property (v. 2), ward the orphan girl's dowry and person (v. 3), ward the wife's gift outright (v. 4) — three fences around one garden, whose gate is taqwā and whose watchman is the Raqīb of v. 1.

**The Post-Uḥud Prudence and the Modern Reading**

Read against its battlefield background — seventy widows made in a single morning, their daughters of marriageable age — the verse performs one more office: it makes room, within strict equity, for the sheltering of the war's surplus of women, a sociological mercy the European wars of later centuries would render unintelligible and necessary alike. The scholars therefore refuse both distortions: the zealotry that reads v. 3 as a standing encouragement to multiply households, and the apologetics that erase its license altogether. It is, say al-Qurṭubī's words, a law of *permissibility within bounds, conditioned by justice, measured by fear of God* — marriage, whatever its number, remaining what the whole sūrah declared it: a trust before the Watcher, in which the woman's rights are as revealed as the man's, and likelier to be defended by heaven than by any human court of her age.

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:4

> **And give the women their bridewealth as a free gift, but if they are pleased to remit unto you any part thereof, then consume it with wholesome enjoyment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ṣaduqāt: The Gift Called Truth**

*Wa ātu al-nisāʾa ṣaduqātihinna niḥlah* — "and give the women their bridewealth as a free gift": the Book names the dower *ṣadūqāt* (singular *ṣadūqah* or *ṣidāq*) from the root *ṣ-d-q*, truth and sincerity — a bride-gift stamped by its very name as the *proof* of a covenant-claimant's sincerity, not a purchase-price nor a toll. Al-Qurṭubī lingers on the fit between name and thing: the Arabs said *ṣadaqa al-khāṭib* for the suitor who honored his proposal with substance — and the Qur'an ratified the idiom into statute, making the gift the husband's first installment of truth in the marriage-files. And *niḥlah* — the glossators dispute its etymology between *naḥl*, unconditioned largesse, and the bee's poured-out honey — fixes the manner: given outright, without strings, without "loan" or "return on divorce," a transfer of ownership as clean as the word itself. The Book's choice of *give* (*ātū*) against Jāhiliyya's vocabulary of buying and selling announces the reclassification: the woman is no chattel priced between men; the gift is *hers*, flowing past her father, past her warden, to her own hand.

**Breaking the Chain of the Fathers**

For the statute abolished an economy: in pre-Islamic Arabia the *mahr* of daughters and wards was customarily pocketed by guardians as a house-revenue, and the *shighār* marriage — exchange of daughters between two men in lieu of any dowry at all — had built the practice into a system, which the Prophet ﷺ struck with a single prohibition:

> *"There is no shighār in Islam"* — the shighār being that a man marries his daughter to a man on condition the other marries him his daughter, with no bridal gift between them (al-Bukhārī 5112; Muslim 1415, from Ibn ʿUmar).

Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī enumerate the abolished forms re-appearing in later ages under new etiquette — the guardian taking his daughter's mahr "for her own keeping," the uncle marrying off the orphan for her gift, the father-in-law consuming the payment as "compensation for raising her" — and the verse's own sealings forbid them all, with v. 19 and v. 20 soon reinforcing its fortress from two more sides. Under heaven's charter, title vests in the bride at contract; her lien against a deferred remainder ranks before the husband's estate's other debts.

**Ṭibna Nafsan: The Soul's Signature on Every Remission**

The verse's second clause governs the delicate case of the bride's own generosity: *fa-in ṭibna lakum ʿan shayʾin minhu nafsan fa-kulūhu hanīʾan marīʾ* — "if they are pleased to remit to you any of it, with a willing soul, then consume it in wholesome enjoyment." Three verbs and two adverbs stand guard around her consent: *ṭāba* — to be goodly-willing at heart's ease; *nafsan* — the accusative of state, "with her soul" — stipulating that the soul itself sign the waiver, not the browbeaten face; and the paired *hanīʾan marīʾan* — roots of sweet digestion and nourishment — the Book's own culinary idiom for lawfulness enjoyed without hidden rot (as at 2:168's ḥalālan ṭayyibā). Al-Qurṭubī records the juristic distillate: the remission extracted by shame, family pressure, or the husband's sulk is *null beneath the verse's condition* — and judges have annulled waiver-receipts signed under the father-in-law's roof ever since. God's registry refuses phantom gifts, for the same Watcher of v. 1 stands over the signing.

**The Dower's Measure: Between Extravagance and Miserliness**

How much, then? The Prophet's own household marked the middle path: the mahr of his daughters and most of his wives stood near five hundred dirhams — the silver of a working man's year — and he would bless the contracted pairs with *"may God bless you both, and bless upon you, and unite you in good"* (Abū Dāwūd 2130; al-Tirmidhī 1091), calling likewise for the feast of walīmah even with a single sheep (al-Bukhārī 5167; Muslim 1427). Yet he refused to fence out the poor: when a suitor owned nothing — not even an iron ring — he accepted the farthest descent of the scale:

> *"Seek something, though it be an iron ring."* He could find none; so the Prophet ﷺ said: *"What have you of the Qur'an?"* He named certain sūrahs. *"I marry her to you for what you have of the Qur'an"* — that he should teach it to her (al-Bukhārī 5149; Muslim 1425, from Sahl ibn Saʿd).

Against the other extreme, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's platform from the caliphal pulpit — "do not overmultiply the women's bridewealth, for if it were an honor in this world or taqwā with God, the Prophet ﷺ would have been first to it" (al-Tirmidhī 1114; Abū Dāwūd 2106 — and the report continues with the woman who answered him with 4:20's *qintār*, whereupon he conceded: "the woman is right and ʿUmar is wrong") — fixed the jurisprudential prudence of the community: neither impoverishing suitors nor selling daughters, the gift measured by *ability, custom, dignity* — but given, in every case, as *niḥlah*: a free truth-token into the bride's own treasury, written in the Book beside the orphan's vault and the widow's share, within the sūrah's uninterrupted argument: *the weakest signature in the marriage-file shall be guarded by the strongest seal in the heavens.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:5

> **And give not the feeble-minded your property, which God has placed in your hands to manage, but provide for them and clothe them from it, and speak unto them in an honorable way.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Sufahāʾ: Incompetence as a Legal Category**

After the orphan and the bride, the sūrah's guardianship-litany reaches its third protected class: *al-sufahāʾ* — the feeble-minded, from the root *s-f-h*, lightness, the lightness of a judgment that cannot hold weight. The Arabs used *safīh* for the man of unstable reason, and the revealed law adopted the idiom as a precise juristic category: the person incapable of preserving property — the child before discernment, the insane, the chronically profligate who consumes capital as though it were appetite — is placed under *ḥajr*, interdiction, his signature suspended to spare him and society his own hand. The learned disciples of Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted his wider flavor of the term — every persistent sinner has a *safah* of soul — yet the verse's legal register is firm, and al-Qurṭubī polices its boundaries with particular care against the misreading that would enroll *women* among the sufahāʾ: the noun stands in the masculine plural covering both sexes, and the sūrah itself has already commanded that women and orphans be *given* their property (vv. 2, 4); Islamic law vests women with complete financial competence in dower, inheritance, gift, and earnings. The incapacity intended is demonstrable, functional, and individual — not assigned by gender or class, but proven by conduct, exactly as the courts of Islam have administered it, from the interdiction registers of Kūfa to the hospital-adjacent guardianships of our own day.

**Amwālakum Allatī Jaʿalahā Allāhu Lakum Qiyāman: Property as Standing-Provision**

*Wa lā tuʾtu al-sufahāʾa amwālakumu allatī jaʿala Allāhu lakum qiyāman* — "and give not the feeble-minded your property, which God has made for you a means of standing": the possessive *your* with money is swiftly reinterpreted by the clause following: this wealth is *qiyām* — the thing by which a society *stands*, its provision-structure, its standing-energy — "made for you" as stewardship, not as desert. Al-Rāzī notes the profound reclassification hidden in the phrase: property is here defined *functionally* — by the support it renders to persons and orders — so that handing it to one who cannot preserve it is an offense against the wealth's own purpose, not merely against the ward. The Book repeats the doctrine in its management-verses (57:7's "He has made you trustees in it [khulafāʾa fīhi]"; 24:33's "give them of the wealth of God which He has given you"), and al-Qurṭubī records the jurists' corollary: this verse is among the foundations of the law of *ṣulḥ*, *waqf*, and interdiction together — the legal machinery by which wealth is preserved for its qiyām-function across generations incompetent or unborn. God calls the community's patrimony *its standing*; the hand that squanders or endangers it saws at the beam beneath the whole house.

**Provision, Clothing, Speech: The Triple Charge of the Guardian**

The ward under interdiction is not thereby reduced to a ledger entry. The verse assigns his guardian three offices in one breath: *wa-rzuqūhum fīhā wa-ksūhum wa qūlū lahum qawlan maʿrūfan* — "provide for them from it, and clothe them, and speak to them in an honorable way." The first two discharge the body's account: the feeble-minded person eats *from his own property* — *fīhā*, "from it" — by the guardian's administration, housed and clothed at the standard of his peers. The third guards the subtler treasury: *qawlan maʿrūfan* — speech *maʿrūf*, known-good, recognizable-to-the-heart as kindness — the standard the sūrah fixes again at v. 8 for the indigent at the division, and the Book rings wherever power towers over weakness: "say to My servants that they speak what is best" (17:53); "kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury" (2:263, *qawlun maʿrūf* in the same formula); culminated in the parent-clause of 17:23, where even *uff* is barred. The jurist-theologians — al-Rāzī among them — remark that incompetence to handle property never suspends the right to be addressed as a person: wealth can be interdicted; dignity cannot. The mad, the simple, the spendthrift son — all remain *mukallaf* of respect: every forbiddance that shields their purse concludes, in the same verse, with a commandment for their ears.

**The Fiduciary Mind as a Religious Formation**

The sūrah's triad across three verses — orphan (v. 2), sufahāʾ (v. 5), and the absent heirs of v. 8 — assembles Islam's complete wardship-ethic: hold; do not consume; administer; provide; clothe; and *speak honorably*. The Muslim societies arrived early, through these verses, at the mature legal institution the later ages would call fiduciary duty: the guardian bound to the ward's interest as though it were his own, audited by heaven where no earthly auditor sits. The Prophet's own teaching set the same standard for trustees of every description — guardians of estates, executors, treasurers of mosques, deputies of absent persons:

> *"Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock: the ruler is a shepherd and is responsible for his flock; the man is a shepherd of his household and is responsible for his flock; the woman is a shepherd of her husband's house and children and is responsible for her flock."* (al-Bukhārī 893; Muslim 1829, from Ibn ʿUmar)

The shepherd-law of v. 5 thus trains the believer in the disposition the whole sūrah demands: wealth is qiyām entrusted; mouths under one's authority are trusts in kind; and speech — the cheapest good and the easiest wrong — is *maʿrūf* or it is sin. Between these three, guardianship becomes what the verse-medicine intended: not power over the weak, but a pastors' office under the Watcher's post.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:6

> **And test the orphans until they reach the age of maturity; then if you perceive in them sound judgment, deliver unto them their property, and consume it not wastefully and in haste before they come of age. Whosoever is rich should abstain, but whosoever is poor should partake thereof in an honorable way. And when you deliver unto them their property, bring witnesses on their behalf, and God suffices as a Reckoner.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa-btalū: The Guardianship as Examination**

The verse's first verb sets the whole pedagogy of the trust-years: *wa-btalū al-yatāmā* — "and test the orphans": *ibtilāʾ*, testing, for once here a trial administered *by the guardian* to the ward. God's law does not permit the vault's key to pass on a birthday's dusk; the estate of the fatherless is released only upon *measured* competence. Al-Qurṭubī preserves the classroom of the salaf: the testing included advancing the young heir small sums of his own money and watching his commerce — whether he bought and sold with judgment, preserved his capital, paid his workers, kept his accounts. The verse thereby founded, centuries before its appearance in the codes of other nations, the transitional instrument of supervised financial apprenticeship: guardians had been told at v. 5 not to hand wealth to the incompetent; v. 6 now teaches them *how competence is manufactured* — by degrees, with the child inside the household's commerce long before the vault is his.

**Balughū al-Nikāḥ... al-Rushd: The Two Credentials of Release**

The two gates of release stand in sequence: maturity and rectitude. *Ḥattā idhā balaghū al-nikāh* — "until they reach marriage-age" — the idiom for puberty, set by the majority of the jurists between fifteen and eighteen years for males; and *fa-in ānastum minhum rushdan* — "then if you perceive in them sound judgment": *rushd*, the guardian's certification, defined by al-Ṭabarī's authorities as the compound of a functioning rational faculty, upright religion, and proven property-sense — the three of which a guardian has been observing at close quarters since the parent's grave. The schools sharpened the clause: the Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs require both rushd in religion and rushd in wealth; the Ḥanafīs allow additional time — to twenty-five in Abū Ḥanīfah's ceiling — where financial ripeness lags the body's; the reports of Ibn ʿUmar capture the practice: his father ʿUmar was tested by the Prophet's own household-principle that the youth who shows judgment early may be handed his charge early. The law's architecture is merciful realism: puberty opens the *possibility* of release; rushd alone *commands* it — *fa-dfaʿū ilayhim amwālahum* — "then deliver to them their property."

**Wastefully and in Haste: The Guardian's Two Temptations**

Against the relapse into consumption, two adverbs seal the statute: *wa lā taʾkulūhā isrāfan wa bidāran an yakbarū* — "consume it not wastefully nor in haste, anticipating their coming of age." *Isrāf* — waste — and *bidār* — hurried squandering — each name a distinct sin of the trustee: the slow bleed of the careless administrator, and the sudden gutting of the one who hears the heir's majority approaching like a bailiff and spends the trust before the audit. Al-Qurṭubī's masters read the second with special poignancy: the verse anticipates the oldest maneuver of corrupt custodianship — the end-of-term raid — and forbids it in its own name. Between v. 2's *do not exchange* and v. 6's *do not waste and do not rush*, the Book closes every valve by which trusts leak into guardians' pockets before their owners' hands are strong enough to hold them.

**The Rich Abstains, the Poor Eats Honorably: The Wage of Care**

The guardians themselves are next admitted into the statute's justice: *man kāna ghaniyyan fa-l-yastaʿfif, wa man kāna faqīran fa-l-yaʾkul bi-l-maʿrūf* — "whoso is rich, let him abstain; whoso is poor, let him partake honorably." The rich guardian — abstinence as his honor-budge — keeps his hands wholly off the ward's estate, his service counted to God. The poor guardian's licensed share the commentators disciplined by two lights: Ibn ʿAbbās and the strict school — a loan repayable, food of necessity only; the majority of the jurists — a wage measured by his labor upon the estate, *bi-l-maʿrūf*: as the shepherd of another's flock drinks of the milk and rides no beast to its hurt, the administrator of property draws reason's fee. Al-Qurṭubī, answering the charge that v. 10's hellfire abolishes all consumption, distinguishes with the register of all the schools: dishonest consumption is the fire of the tenth verse; *maʿrūf* compensation earns the guardian's bread — the law that forbids embezzlement likewise refuses to make charity compulsory of the poor who serve orphans.

**Witnesses at the Hand-over, and the Reckoner Above**

The statute's closing machinery is procedural and theological in a single seal: *fa-idhā dafaʿtum ilayhim amwālahum fa-ashhidū ʿalayhim, wa kafā bi-Allāhi ḥasībā* — "and when you deliver to them their property, take witnesses over them; God suffices as Reckoner." The witnesses (two, per the courts' extending of the law of testimony) protect both parties forever after: the guardian against the grown heir's later charge of shortfall, the heir against the guardian's false claim of delivery — the ancestor of every inventory-and-receipt practice in Islamic probate. Then the verse lifts the room: *ḥasīb* — the Reckoner — the same root-word Lady Mary's mother used presenting her newborn ("God is my Reckoner," in the ḥadīth of the name-recital), the same audit-attribute sealing the borrowed-property verses: *custodies end in witnessed papers on earth, but the audit that cannot be bribed is kept Above*. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's saying, treasured by the commentators in this pericope, lays the guardian's working creed in one line: *"the orphan's property is fire, and the poor man's consumption from it is per God's measure"* — between the two clauses the orphan-law of Islam stands complete, and the Watcher of v. 1 adds at its gate His final title: Reckoner over the reckoners.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:7

> **Unto the men a share of what parents and kinsfolk leave, and unto the women a share of what parents and kinsfolk leave, be it little or much—a share ordained.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Umm Kujjah at the Prophet's Door**

The scholars of the occasions of revelation — al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Suyūṭī in their registers — carry us to the Prophet's ﷺ assembly for the case that forced the legislation: Aws ibn Thābit al-Anṣārī died in Madinah, leaving a widow, Umm Kujjah, and three small daughters. His two cousins — Suwayd and ʿArfajah, men of the martial generation — took the estate entire, and left the mother and her girls nothing. She came to the Messenger of God ﷺ with her complaint; he said, *"go home until I see what God reveals about you,"* and summoned the two men. They answered with the creed of the old world:

> *"O Messenger of God — her children cannot ride a horse, nor bear arms, nor gain booty!"*

— that is, they are not *heirs*, by the only definition pagan Arabia knew: heirs were those who bled for the tribe. God's answer descended: *li-l-rijāli naṣībun... wa lil-nisāʾi naṣībun* — unto men a share, and unto women a share — and with it the whole cavalry-theory of inheritance fell; the specific apportionment followed in v. 11, and the cousins' temporary possession was reversed by the Prophet's command. In one Madinan morning, the sword forfeited its seat at the probate table.

**Naṣīb: The Appointed Portion as a New Legal Idea**

The word around which the statute turns is *naṣīb* — from the root *n-ṣ-b*, to set up, appoint, fix — a portion *installed* by authority, not wrested by strength. Al-Ṭabarī's gloss is doctrinally exact: a share *mafrūḍ*, made binding by God — the verse's own final word — so that no agreement of the clan, no custom of the century, no affection or aversion of the dying could add or erase an ounce. The weight of this idea upon the history of law can hardly be overstated: inheritance ceases to be the tribe's redistribution of the strong man's gear and becomes a *revealed right* vesting automatically in named persons — in *women* as a listed class, in children, in the old. The sūrah's whole architecture of succession — the science the Muslims would name ʿ*ilm al-farāʾiḍ*, "the knowledge of the ordained portions," from this very verse's *mafrūḍan* — rises on the foundation laid here: the grave opens a court; the will of God is its code; the heirs walk to fixed seats.

**Mā Qalla Minhu aw Kathura: No Estate Too Small for Justice**

*Mimmā taraka al-wālidāni wa-l-aqrabūn mā qalla minhu aw kathura* — "of whatsoever parents and near kin leave, be it little or much": the clause forecloses the lawyer's first loophole before it opens — that trivial legacies fall beneath the law's regard. Al-Qurṭubī's scholars understood: one palm-tree distributes its shares as exactly as one oasis; a widow's needlework inheritance obeys the same fractions as a merchant's caravan-stock. The universality extends equally to the lecturers' other point: neither does greatness exempt — no estate is so vast that the heirs may convene and, by *consensus*, vary the ordinance. The clause thereby teaches the community its first lesson in the precision-fiqh of family property: revelation measures justice not in totals but in *ratios*, and the written shares hold in the cottage as in the castle — the arithmetic of the Unseen falling the same everywhere, the sixth to the mother, the residue to the sons of the house, in every tent from Yathrib's walls to the ends of every later empire.

**Half of Knowledge: The Prophet's Blessing on the Fractions**

The Prophet ﷺ singled out this body of law with an honor he gave few subjects — counting its very transmission among the trusts of the nations:

> *"Learn the ordained shares (al-farāʾiḍ) and teach them; for they are half of knowledge, and they will be forgotten, and they are the first thing that will be taken from my community."* (reported by Ibn Mājah 2719 and al-Ḥākim from Abū Hurayrah and Ibn Masʿūd — much-cited by the jurists as the charter-tradition of the science, though some of its channels were disputed)

— and at his direction the commanders of the early generations set the teaching of the shares in the mosques beside the teaching of the prayer itself. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib would address the people from the pulpit: *"whoever among you can recite the Qur'an, let him recite — and let him learn the laws of inheritance"* (al-Khaṭīb's transmission from the caliphal registers), and ʿUmar's school counted the computist of farāʾiḍ equal to the scholar of memorization. From that pulpit-climate descended the science's wonders: the algebra-works of al-Khwārizmī — the man whose own name became the modern world's word for the algorithm — opening his treatise with the inheritance-problems as their natural first client; the great registers of *farāʾiḍ* rulings beside every qāḍī's seat in every Islamic century; and the quiet persistence, in every Muslim funeral till today, of the distributors working the shares pen-in-hand at the graveside, lest the burial sun set on an unsettled estate.

**And the Women a Share: The First Statute of Female Property in History**

The clause itself is the marvel, read against its century: *wa lil-nisāʾi naṣībun* — "and unto the women is a share." The legal systems of the age — Roman patria potestas, near-eastern custom, Arab tribalism — treated women variously as dependents transmitted *with* estates rather than recipients *of* them; and here, by revealed statute, the female heir walks into fixed, enforceable, unmediated ownership — *her* name, *her* portion, *her* disposal thereafter; for what a woman inherited became, like her dower of v. 4, her sole property, to sell, endow, or bequeath. Al-Qurṭubī's remark captures the verse's placement logic: separated from v. 2's orphan-protection only by the guardianship-chain, the law here places its second fence — the *mothers* of the orphans are themselves propertied, so that widowhood cease to mean destitution. A commentary tradition of women commentators through the ages — from the learned ladies of Ṣafiyyah's circle reading *farāʾiḍ* to the female muftis of later capitals — springs directly from this sentence: the Woman's Charter began, in the Qur'an's own chronology, with the grave and the ledger: *unto the women a share — be it little or much — a share ordained.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:8

> **And when kinsfolk, orphans, and the indigent are present at the division, make provision from it for them and speak unto them in an honorable way.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ḥaḍara al-Qismah: The Gallery at the Probate Table**

The Book moves from the fixed seats of v. 7 to the gallery of the excluded: *wa idhā ḥaḍara al-qismata ulū al-qurbā wa-l-yatāmā wa-l-masākīn* — "and when the near kin, the orphans, and the indigent are present at the division": the funeral division was a *social* event in Madinah as in every society since — the kin gathered, the neighbors watching, the poor attracted by the rumor of distribution — and the revealed law refuses to disperse that gallery with empty hands. *Ulū al-qurbā* here denotes the kin *outside* the ordained shares — the aunt, the cousin, the kin-disabled — for the named heirs have already found their seats in v. 7 and vv. 11–12; alongside them stand the two standing clients of the sūrah's whole economy: the orphans and the *masākīn*, the indigent, from the root of motionlessness — those whom want has stilled. The command: *fa-rzuqūhum minhu* — "make provision for them from it" — clothe the excluded from the same table at which the heirs now sit.

**Abrogation's Dispute: A Statute the Scholars Refused to Bury**

The commentators' debate over this clause is one of the elegant cases in the science of *naskh*, and al-Qurṭubī presides over it with his usual fullness. Three opinions came down from the early generations: (1) the verse is *binding* (muḥkam) — the very position of Ibn ʿAbbās, who the report says used to recite it and declare it never abrogated — a gift owed at every division, its measure at the heirs' discretion; (2) it was *abrogated* by the fixed shares of vv. 11–13 — the economy of distribution henceforth exhausted by the ordained seats; (3) it governs the *bequest-third* — the dying person's disposable third, from which the unseated may be remembered. Ibn Kathīr marshals the witnesses and inclines, with characteristic balance, to the first: the verse addresses the *living* division-ceremony as a standing courtesy-obligation, one the community often neglects — his own era already lamenting it — without its law-claim ever being formally lifted. The Shiʿi tradition through the Imams of the Prophet's house reads the same: al-Bāqir taking the *provision* as recommended in every case, greatest where the division is public. The lesson beneath the disagreement is permanent: whether as duty or as generosity, revelation insists that the room of distribution never void of kindness — the excluded watch God's portions dealt, and they are fed with the dealing itself.

**Qulan Maʿrūfan: Speech as the Second Alms**

The clause's twin-command is the verse's charm and its severest instrument: *wa qūlū lahum qawlan maʿrūfan* — "and speak to them an honorable word." For the Book knows the economy of funerals: the poor who linger around probate tables carry the *double* burden — want of the hand and lowliness of the eye — and a distribution that feeds no palms can still wound them at the tongue's edge. The maʿrūf-command, the same speech-standard as v. 5's to the feeble-minded, addresses the second wound *as law*, and al-Rāzī pauses on the structure: the verses' pairing of *provision* and *honorable speech* — material gift and verbal gift — instructs the house of Islam that charity corrupts into insult wherever its manner forgets its soul: the Book itself has already laid the principle across the entire economy of giving — "kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury" (2:263) — and the Prophet ﷺ extended it to the smallest coin of dignity:

> *"Do not belittle any good deed — even meeting your brother with a cheerful face"* and *"Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him speak good or keep silent."* (Muslim 2626, 48; al-Bukhārī 6018 — from Abū Dharr and Abū Hurayrah)

At the probate table, the polite sentence is counted among the shares distributed.

**The Funeral-Table as a School of the Afterlife**

Why should a *law* reach so far into the etiquette of the death-chamber? Because, the commentators answer, the division-scene is *the one hour* in which the clan beholds the whole motion of wealth openly: the owner gone, the estate lying in the tray, the heirs approaching with their names. It is the hour of maximal greed — and therefore revelation's chosen classroom. By commanding provision-for-the-excluded and beautiful speech *at precisely that table*, God plants His remedies where the disease flowers, and models forever what the Prophet's house practiced: ʿĀʾishah's report of the Prophet's own dividing of what arrived — *"he would take a portion and say: give this to so-and-so"* — immediately accessible to those at the door. The verse closes its case gently, without a seal-clause — no Watcher, no Reckoner named this once — as though the Lord of the arḥām knew that the gallery at the division needs no threat: the orphans there are the very ones whose trusts the previous six verses have ringed with fire, and no reader of the sūrah's opening page will look at a poor child's face across the tray and need the tenth verse explained to him. Provide them from it; speak to them beautifully; the court is in session and the Reckoner is still in the room.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:9

> **Let those who would dread if they left behind their own helpless progeny have fear; let them reverence God and speak justly.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Dread Transposed: Empathy Written as Statute**

The sūrah's orphan-pericope closes its opening movement with one of the Book's most beautifully engineered clauses: *wa-l-yakhsha alladhīna law tarakū min khalfihim dhurriyyatan ḍiʿāfan khāfū ʿalayhim* — "let those fear, who, had they left behind weak offspring, would have feared for them." The construction performs its own meaning: it takes the deepest animal terror in any parent — *what becomes of my little ones when I am gone?* — and transposes it, by grammatical sleight, onto everyone standing in an orphaned child's vicinity. Al-Ṭabarī's transmission-grid catches the clause's two complementary readings from the Companions' school: it addresses the deathbed's *witnesses and counselors* — those who gather round a dying man with advice about his estate — bidding them fear for his helpless children the very fear they would feel at a like scene over their own deathbeds; and it addresses every guardian and *trustee* — deal with this ward as you would pray that a strange guardian deal with *your* child, in the morning after your grave. Ibn Kathīr, gathering both threads, makes of them one rope: the verse is the orphan-law's *empathy-engine* — for law's clauses can be gnawed by clever counsel, but conscience armed with a father's own dread does not misread a child's face.

**Saʿd's Hospital-Chamber: The Third That Is Much**

The verse's companion in the Prophet's practice is the celebrated bedside of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ at the conquest-illness of Makkah — the chamber that fixed forever the limits of generosity over inheritance:

> *Saʿd said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ came to visit me in my illness, the year of the Conquest. I said: Messenger of God, I am wealthy, and my only heir is one daughter — shall I bequeath two-thirds of my property in charity?" He said: "No." I said: "A half?" He said: "No." He said: "A third — and a third is much. To leave your heirs wealthy is better than to leave them destitute, begging of people; nor will you spend anything, seeking God's face, but that you are rewarded — even the morsel you put in your wife's mouth."* (al-Bukhārī 2742, 2745; Muslim 1628)

The ceiling of the bequest-third, fixed in that chamber, is v. 9's law in action: deathbed-counsel cooled to protect the small; the dying told, with prophetic gentleness, that their heirs' bread outranks their worries about the surplus man's applause. Al-Qurṭubī obliges the connection expressly: the verse was sent for every comforter who whispers to a wasting man *"give, give, and empty the tray before your sons arrive"* — let such counselor fear for the children as for his own; and the pious press the same clause upon the executor at the desk of the legacy, and the notary at the pen.

**Dhurriyyatan Ḍiʿāfan: Weakness as the Measure of Duty**

The verse chooses its noun with precision: *dhurriyyah ḍiʿāf* — offspring *weak* — the plural *ḍuʿafāʾ* of the helplessness-class the Book names in every protection-verse (the weak of the earth at 4:75 and 8:26; the formerly-weak of Pharaoh's Egypt made heirs themselves at 28:5) — because duty is measured in the Book by the very variable the strong erase: the *weakness* of the dependent. The more helpless the progeny, the heavier the obligation-onlookers bear; and God's citation of *ḍiʿāfan* at exactly this clause fixes the calibration-rule of the entire orphan-pericope: the presumption is always of the child's incapacity, never of the trustee's benignity — an inversion of presumption, al-Rāzī notes, from the Jāhiliyya order in which the minor's *defenselessness* was the reason to consume his estate. Under the sunna's architecture, vulnerability is not opportunity but summons: the weak one's weakness is read as the strongest mandate for his protection.

**Qawlan Sadīdan: The Just Word at the Death-Chamber**

The seal joins fear of God to speech — *fa-l-yattaqu Allāha wa-l-yaqūlū qawlan sadīdā* — "let them reverence God, and speak a word that hits the mark": *sadīd*, the arrow-word (its root giving the archer's *straightness* — the shaft that reaches its target), a speech that neither deflects toward flattery of the dying nor curves toward interest of the counselor; the same word God will bind to taqwā for our very public tongue at 33:70–71 — *"reverence God, and speak a directed word; He shall set right your deeds for you."* The commentators of the pericope hold the meant *word* to include the entire service-language around the succession: what the counsel says at the bed, what the guardian tells the child, what the executor reads in the assembly — each word weighed against what its speakers would ask, at their own beds, of the same functionaries. And the sūrah will now pass, the verse having planted empathy at the heart of its orphan-law, to the inheritance-code's own mathematics — as if to say: the shares that follow are not arithmetic merely but the very answer, by statute, to every fearful prayer a dying father offered: *God, keep my little ones in feeding and in dignity after me* — to which heaven's reply comes mandatory, in numbers.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:10

> **Truly those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire in their bellies, and they will burn in a blazing flame.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Meal That Is Already Fire**

The orphan-pericope reaches its terrifying culmination with the Book's most incinerating metaphor of consumption: *inna alladhīna yaʾkulūna amwāla al-yatāmā ẓulman innamā yaʾkulūna fī buṭūnihim nāran* — "truly those who devour the orphans' wealth unjustly are only devouring fire into their bellies." The grammar is itself the sentence: not *will* devour but *yaʾkulūna* — the present-continuous of an eating already imaged at its end — and the restrictive *innamā* — *only* fire — hollowing the meal's every pretense of nourishment: what passes their throats is not provision but fuel, stored. Al-Rāzī anatomizes the trope with the coldness it warrants: fire is the perfect sign of this robbery because it is invisible-in-potency at the meal and total-in-act at the end — as the consumed dinars warmth the tyrant's table through years without a visible flame, so the sin burns him nowhere until, in one unveiling, its whole hidden inventory ignites. Al-Qurṭubī registers the scholars' consensus location of the verse in the scale of crimes: no lesser sin than the gravest class — *kabīrah* of the kabāʾir — shares its imagery; and its neighbor across the Book is only one: the ribā-consumer's arising like one demon-maddened (2:275), the two satans' banquet-halls of the orphan-vault and the usurer's table furnished with one kind of furniture.

**The Ghatafānian's Morning: When the Sentence Walked into Madinah**

The verse was no abstraction to its first hearers; the transmitters record the famous awakening of its occasion-case. Ibn ʿAbbās's pupil-generation report — treasured in al-Ṭabarī's chains and echoed by al-Tirmidhī's tafsīr of the passage — tells it: a man of Ghaṭafān had held in trust a great fortune belonging to his orphan nephew, and when the youth came of age the uncle denied him; the case reached the Prophet ﷺ — and the fire-verse descended. Whereupon, the reports complete:

> *The man came at daybreak carrying the wealth entire, and said: "I deliver to my nephew his property — and I seek refuge with God from the blazing flame (al-saʿīr)."*

The whole pericope's court-procedure thus closes with a real repentance: trust disgorged, sentence escaped, on a Madinan morning where the words had scarcely finished reciting. The jurists and preachers have taught from that morning ever since: the fire-image is not rhetoric to be admired but *a verdict to be exited* — and the exit-door is exactly what the uncle found: restitution, in full, while the hour of return still stands open; for the verse's tense-structure leaves no other negotiation: the eating continues as long as the eaters continue, and its end is named in the seal.

**Saʿīr: The Furnace-Word of the Sentence**

*Wa sa-yaṣlawna saʿīrā* — "and they shall roast in a burning blaze": the Book's *saʿīr* is Hell as furnace-kindled, its fuel stoked (the verb *saʿʿara* — to set blazing — standing behind the noun), reserved in this sūrah's own registers for the severest addresses (4:55 and 4:56's kafā bi-jahannama saʿīrā for the Book-people's obstinacy; 48:6's for polytheists and hypocrites; 76:4's prepared-for-the-ingrates chains and yokes and blaze). The Prophet ﷺ was shown their working-dress in the vision the mufassirūn cite beneath this verse — Ibn Kathīr adduces it from the Musnad of Aḥmad, from Abū Hurayrah:

> *"On the Night of the Ascent I passed by people whose lips were like the lips of camels; and their lips were clipped with scissors of fire — then cut pieces of fire were thrust into their mouths, and they came forth from their rear passages."* He asked: *"Who are these?"* — Gabriel said: *"Those who consume the property of the orphans unjustly."*

The image fulfills the verse's arithmetic exactly: mouths that consumed at Madinah's quiet tables are fitted at last with the cuisine of their diet, the shears of flame standing to the severing-spades the taklif of just guardianship had once made needless. And the seal's future-particle *sa-yaṣlawna* keeps the appointment fixed: roasting-in-blaze is scheduled, not suggested: *ṣalāya*, the broiling of direct flame-contact, unnamed but one day away from each belly that loaded it.

**The Door That Remained Open: Repentance with Restitution**

Yet the sūrah, having burned the pericope's circle closed, leaves by its own larger architecture the one crevice of hope it always leaves — the chapter's own general absolution-regime at vv. 17–18, 27–28, and 146-148, and the standing rule the scholars drew from the Ghatafānian's own morning: the fire of v. 10 is escaped *the way it was entered — through the property*: return the estate, seek forgiveness for the delay, and the meal is voided at the ledger where it was loaded. Ibn Kathīr quotes the salaf's equivalent at this clause: *"repentance from the consuming of orphans' wealth is in giving back; there is no dua-substitute."* A believer reading v. 10 therefore reads precisely as its first defendant read: inventory first — what is in my house of another's weakness? — restitution second; and the pericope's full court may adjourn in the Ghaṭafānian's own words, which should belong to every trustee's dawn: *here is all that was entrusted — and refuge is sought from the blaze. The Lawgiver, having guarded the meekest vaults in the earth, now turns to the double-sided mirror of the grave's other room: the division where the fire never approaches — the fractions of vv. 11–13.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:11

> **God enjoins upon you concerning your children: unto the male a share equal to that of two females; but if there are only daughters, two or more, then unto them is two-thirds of what he leaves; if only one, then unto her a half. And unto his parents—each of the two—a sixth of what he leaves if he has a child; but if he has no child and his parents are his [only] heirs, then unto his mother a third; and if he has brothers, then unto his mother a sixth, after paying any bequest he may have bequeathed or any debt. Your parents or your children—you know not which of them are nearer to you in benefit. [This is] an obligation ordained by God. Truly God is Knowing, Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Yūṣīkumu Allāh: The Testator Is God**

The inheritance-code opens in a construction of singular majesty: *yūṣīkumu Allāhu fī awlādikum* — "God enjoins upon you concerning your children": *yuṣī* — He testates, He gives the final charge — the same root as the dying man's *waṣiyyah* (bequest). The rhetorical reversal is the entire doctrine: the dead neither own nor allocate anymore; upon decease the estate reverts to the real Owner — "We it is Who give life and death, and We are the Inheritors" (15:23) — and God now *makes His own will known* concerning His returned property. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr both mark how the *faṣl*, the legal clause, arrives therefore without negotiation-address: not "O you who believe, apportion thus," but a declaration over the dead man's most sensitive dependency, his children: the Lord of the family legislates direct. The occasion-reports set the scene back in the wake of Umm Kujjah's complaint: when this verse descended confirming the daughters' portions, the shock ran through even the Companions' assembly, long habituated to cavalry-law — the women and minors allocated the lion's share — until the Prophet's teaching habituated them to the arithmetic of mercy.

**Li-l-Dhakari Mithlu Ḥaẓẓi al-Unthayayn: The Ratio and Its Rationale**

The first ratio, most quoted and most polemicized of the code's clauses, assigns son over daughter at two-to-one: *li-l-dhakari mithlu ḥaẓẓi al-unthayayn* — "unto the male the like of the allotment of two females." The commentators fix the ratio's logic within the law's own architecture, for it is *cost-accounting, not honor-accounting*: upon the male heir, revealed law lays the total financial burden of his household — the bridewealth he must pay to marry (v. 4), the maintenance he owes his wife and children wholly (v. 34's *because they spend of their property*; 65:6–7's nursing-houses and wage obligations), his unmarried sisters' and widowed mother's support — while the female heir bears *none* of these, her own mahr, earnings, and inheritance locked to her sole name (al-Qurṭubī's spelling out of the design, with the full juristic register). Ibn Taymiyyah's summary is the schools' common one: Islam assigned each sex a financial *role* and funded the role: the man is made provider at law — his double portion is his equipment, carried in trust for dependents — the woman is relieved of provision-duty — her single portion is *freehold*, hers to keep or spend. The same Book that distributed mahr entirely to the bride and maintenance wholly to the husband made the probate shares balance the ledger: two-to-one measured against lifetime liabilities, not against souls, whose full equality the Book seals at its standing address: "whoever works righteousness, male or female, being a believer..." (16:97).

**The Daughter-Shares: Half and Two-Thirds at Law**

The verse's middle clauses give the single daughter half, two-or-more daughters two-thirds — and here the commentators record the first-era's astonishment this way: in a world where daughters inherited *nothing*, God's probate handed them the estate's largest ordinary fractions — half and two-thirds — and then *completed* their advantage through the residue-rules the jurists opened from the verse (with a son, she shares as one-of-two-parts; with no sons, the sole daughter takes half and the residue reverts by established maxims — Ibn ʿAbbās's school confirming the majority's rule in a maxim the masajid still teach: *a daughter is never without her fixed chair*). ʿUmar's caliphate already witnessed qāḍīs processing daughter-estates by the verse exactly; the Shiʿi transmission through Imams al-Bāqir and al-Ṣādiq affirms the same clauses (with their own doctrine on the daughter's return of residue where no father-brother competes); and the clause *fa-in kānat wāḥidatan fa-lahā al-niṣf* — "if one, to her a half" — is the single sentence by which, thirteen centuries ago, the world was informed that a lone girl-child is *heir of half a man's wealth*, full and personal.

**The Parents' Third and Sixth: Filial Debt Paid at the Grave**

The parents' clauses — *wa li-abawayhi li-kulli wāḥidin minhumā al-sudus* with child-heirs; the mother's *third* where no children and no crowd of siblings; her *sixth* under the brothers' reduction (the celebrated *ʿawl*-adjacent question for which ʿUmar, in the case known as *al-ḥimāriyyah*, consulted the assembly before conceding the siblings-rule) — enact, at the point of deepest test, the Book's one abiding symmetry: the parents who spent are *repaid at last from their own child's grave-goods*, the mother with her named chair in every scenario, the father riding his named-sixth plus his residue-position as ʿaṣabah (nearest male kin — the majority's reading). Al-Qurṭubī's inheritance chapters and Ibn Kathīr's tafsīr beneath these clauses stand as the direct fountainheads of the entire Muslim probate-practice — and the structure is transparent about its pedagogy: "your parents *or* your children — *lā tadrūna ayyuhum aqrabu lakum nafʿan* — you know not which of them are nearer to you in benefit": benefit in this world and the next, unknown to dying men; hence the shares were left *revealed*, not elected — so that where affection misjudges, and cost miscalculates, the fraction from the Knower's hand stands correct. The verse's seal ascends therefore to its proper attributes: *farīḍatan min Allāh* — an obligation from God — *inna Allāha kāna ʿalīman ḥakīman* — Knowing, Wise: Knows what men owe; is Wise in what men cannot see; and settles, between the mother and the child of every dead householder, the estate's story without passion, error, or greed.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:12

> **And unto you a half of what your wives leave, if they have no child, but if they have a child, then unto you a fourth of what they leave, after paying any bequest they may have bequeathed or any debt. And unto them a fourth of what you leave if you have no child, but if you have a child, then unto them an eighth of what you leave, after paying any bequest you may have bequeathed or any debt. If a man or woman leaves no direct heir, but has a brother or sister, then unto each of the two a sixth; but if they are more than two, they share equally a third, after paying any bequest he may have bequeathed or any debt, without harm to anyone—a duty ordained by God, and God is Knowing, Clement.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Marriage-Bond at the Probate Table**

The revealed arithmetic now seats the two spouses at the grave-side: the husband receiving half his wife's estate childless, a quarter where children exist; the wife a quarter of his childless, an eighth with children. The asymmetry — half/quarter answered by quarter/eighth — distills in miniature the code's whole logic laid bare at v. 11: the husband, bearer of mahr and maintenance through life, is likewise the closer claimant in death; the wife, never charged to provide, steps back one rank — and al-Qurṭubī is careful, as at v. 11, to keep the table's philosophy in view: the entire scheme is the *cost-ledger of the family*, distributed across two sexes the law has made financially asymmetric by deliberate mercy, not any scale of souls. That the wife's bond is named *in* her death as well as his teaches the code's own doctrine of marriage: the house that was two governments for the budget — his for spending, hers for holding — is nonetheless *one* corporation before God in both graves. The reports from the days of the statute's descent tell of the Anṣār's wives receiving what pagan Islam's own mothers never dreamed: a pitched, written share of the husband's caravan and palm-grove, no fraction removable by the sons of his brother.

**Each Clause a Shelter: The Double-Repetition of Debts and Bequests**

Twice in the verse the apparatus-clause is rung — *min baʿdi waṣiyyatin yūṣīna bihā aw dayn* — "after the bequest they made and debt": again the code's unvarying sequence: funeral-claims (under jurists' extension), then creditors, up to the bequest-limited third, and only then the seats. The doubling is itself a guardianship of the dying: the Book refuses to let the grieving glance skip the settled order — each party's share is calculated on the net, every loan of the two lifetimes honored before a single heir is served, as the Prophet's own teaching had cemented the rule in tthe assembled dictum of the law: *debts to God before debts to men, and debts to men before bequests, and bequests before shares* — the Prophetic consensus-sequence as al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr register as unanimous in the law-books. The clause stands likewise as the law's first anti-fraud fence: *no* inventing generous "bequests" at the bedside to starve specific heirs, no conveniently remembered "debts" — subjects the *without harm* clause comes, at the verse's end, to seal with a special lock.

**Kalālah: The Word ʿUmar Carried to His Grave**

The verse introduces the code's famous difficulty — *wa in kāna rajulun yūrathu kalālatan aw imraʾatun* — "if a man inherits by kalālah, or a woman": *kalālah*, the deceased *without parent or child* — the descendant-chain snapped at both ends, the estate left looking sideways to siblings. The word weighed upon no one more than the second caliph; the compilations of the *Sunan* and the Musnad-gatherers preserve his pulpit-grief:

> *"There are three matters — I would rather that the Messenger of God ﷺ had left us a decisive word upon them than that I should possess this world entire: the kalālah, the grandfather [in inheritance], and of ribā certain dealings."* (transmitted by ʿUmar's son and others — its substance running through al-Bayhaqī's Sunan, al-Tirmidhī's registers on the grandfather, and the tafsīr-collections at this verse)

And it was for kalālah alone that God would send a *second* seat of legislation — verse 176's closing statute of the sūrah, answering ʿUmar's own envoy with the Prophet himself months before his ﷺ death, "Have the summer's verse not come, with the sūrah's own end?" — the completion which set maternal and paternal siblings in distinct seats: this verse, per the consensus of the law's doctors from Ibn ʿAbbās forward, addressing the *maternal* brothers and sisters (sixth each; more than two sharing a third *equally*, male and female — tied at the womb's own tie), and v. 176 the *full or paternal* (male two-to-one over female), the difference itself teaching the two ships' names the Arabs kept distinct: a brother of one mother shares the kinship of the birth-waters alone, ranked with women equally as children of one merciful channel — a brother of one father shares the father's line, riding the v. 11 ratio.

**Ghayra Muḍārr: The No-Harm Lock on Every Testament**

Then the seal with which no other statute in the Book's corpus closes: *ghayra muḍāran bi-waṣiyyatin* — "no bequest-worked harm" — with its Prophetic hardening into statute:

> *"No bequest to an heir"* (Abū Dāwūd 2870; al-Tirmidhī 2120, graded ṣaḥīḥ; al-Nasāʾī 3639, from Abū Umāmah — the ruling of the conquest-year pilgrimage-address)

and with the Prophet's separate maxim — *"harm is not permitted in Islam"* (Ibn Mājah 2340) — sealing the same gate.
