The clause thereby posts at every dying man's desk the law's anti-malice rule: one may love whom one likes, and owe whom one lists — *but the probate floor is God's; no last letter may kick seats away.* Al-Qurṭubī's masters classify the harms the clause blocks: bequest to one heir above others (the express Prophetic bar), false debt-acknowledgments on the deathbed, and bequests just under the third worked with an accomplice-heir. The verse then takes its attributes: *farīḍatan min Allāh* — an ordinance from God — *wa kānā Allāhu ʿalīman ḥalīman* — Knowing, Clement: the Knowing-of-estates couples here with forbearance-toward-the-faulty — and the probate's two offices are complete, one verse for children and parents, one for spouses and siblings, all calculated under heaven's own patient, sinless accountancy: death unties every purse-string except these.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:13

> **Those are the limits set by God: whosoever obeys God and His Messenger, He will cause him to enter Gardens with rivers running below, abiding therein. And that is the great triumph.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Tilka Ḥudūd Allāh: Boundaries Named for the Ledger**

The crowding pronoun *tilka* — "those" — gathers six verses of statutes — orphan-trust, wardship, the men's and women's shares, the provision-word, the arithmetic of children, parents, spouses, and siblings — into a single legal noun: *ḥudūd Allāh*, the limits of God. *Ḥadd*, plural *ḥudūd*, is before all else a *boundary-line*: the hedge, the pale, the fence-post at the field's edge — named in God's law therefore *both* the ordained penalties and every ruling placed like a marker between lawful and unlawful (2:187's twin-clause: "those are God's limits; so approach them not"). Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr lean on the clause's majesty quietly: the Book could have summed vv. 1–12 as "the inheritance rules"; it chose *the limits of God* — elevating the family's ledger into sacred geography — so that a man moving a sixth to a seventh feels it in his bones as *moving a fence*, the oldest violation in every covenant of God (with 58:4's consequence for posts removed: a clod's weight of wrong to the clan, the full law-claim of heaven). The distribution-paper becomes thus as grave as the temple-stone: boundaries are boundaries, in pastures or percentages.

**Man Yuṭiʿi Allāha wa Rasūlahu: Obedience Again at the Ledger**

Then the promise: *wa man yuṭiʿi Allāha wa rasūlahu yudkhilhu jannātin tajrī min taḥtihā al-anhāru khālidīna fīhā* — "whoso obeys God and His Messenger, He admits him into Gardens, rivers flowing below, abiding therein." Commentators of the schools — al-Qurṭubī pre-eminently at this clause — have always paused at the *placement*: the paired obedience-command — God and Messenger, in the creed's binding-canonical form, the very formula of 3:32, 4:59, 5:92 — is issued here *not at prayer or pilgrimage but at a probate schedule*. The lesson stands as one of the sūrah's quiet definitions of Islam: obedience is not a liturgy-department but a way of answering a revealed ratio — the sixth given as sixth, the eighth as eighth, the widow seated, the orphan full-handed — whole religion at work in pen, ink, and scale. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's school pressed exactly such pointings from this verse-family: these are limits *carried out*, not merely recited — for the promise's verb, *yudkhilhu* — "He will cause him to enter" — is awarded to the *doer*. The garden-rivers' image — water under the pavilions, permanence above the water — answers the grave's drying: *dividing duly in death's chamber, the believer hires rivers for eternity's chamber.*

**Al-Fawz al-ʿAẓīm: Triumph's Superlative on a Probate Line**

The verse's seal — *wa dhālika al-fawzu al-ʿaẓīm* — "and that is the great triumph" — takes the Book's supreme success-title and nails it to inheritance-obedience. The phrase *al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm*, with its fixed throne in ten verses across the Book (5:119's "God content with them... that is the great triumph"; 9:72's again above the Gardens; 44:57's and 64:9's "that is the great triumph"), names the *summit* of every divine scale — and here furnishes the clause the scholars bundle with the sūrah's chapter-meaning: God's ledger of triumph numbers honesty-with-shares among its peak-pass entries. Al-Rāzī's note in the companions' spirit: the greed that guards dinars at probate and the glory-love that guards fame in speeches are *one* interior foe; letting go at God's named fraction is fawz of the exact sort because it is the here-located victory over that foe. The community's practice answered with its feet: Islam's first centuries read v. 13 in the mosques at the teaching-circles of farāʾiḍ — teachers of fractions beginning lectures with the *ḥudūd*-recitation, a habit al-Qurṭubī's own age still kept — as if to teach every student of the reckoning-science: the syllabus's stakes are *garden and fire*; the ratios are a pilgrimage; the pen that writes them right walks, its holder with it, *into the garden where rivers run below — the triumph beside which the estates men died for are nothing, and beside which nothing else is anything.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:14

> **But whosoever disobeys God and His Messenger, and transgresses His limits, He will cause him to enter a Fire, abiding therein, and he shall have a humiliating punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Yaʿiṣ and Yataʿadda: The Twin Verbs of the Crossed Line**

The complement-verse arrives with the chilling symmetry of the Book's paired promises, distinguishing itself from v. 13 by the additional verb: *wa man yaʿiṣi Allāha wa rasūlahu wa yataʿadda ḥudūdahu* — "whoso disobeys God and His Messenger, and *transgresses His limits*": the first verb names the direction of the heart — *maʿṣiyah*, disobedience, the will's turn; the second names the accomplished deed — *taʿaddī*, crossing-over, from *ʿadw*: overstepping, intrusion past the boundary — and the commentators' pairing holds them in sequence: v. 13's obedient walks *within* the posts; v. 14's adds to refusal the *achieved trespass*, the sixth reduced, the widow's seat commandeered, the bequest's floor broken. Al-Ṭabarī marks the fiqh-note the law schools drew at this exact doubling: *taʿaddī al-ḥudūd* became the standing idiom for transgression against every divine statute whatsoever — coined from this verse's own mint; every fence-post cut down thereafter in estates, in blood, in chastity-laws is described in the fiqh-registers by v. 14's verb.

**Yudkhilhu Nāran: Entrance Mirrored, Destination Reversed**

*Yudkhilhu nāran khālidan fīhā* — "He will enter him into Fire, abiding therein": the terrible mirror to v. 13's *yudkhilhu jannātin*, same verb — *He will cause him to enter* — same construction, hell's gate now the threshold; the Book forcing the eye to compare the two admissions side by side, as an estate's two roads fork from a single gate-clerk. *Khālidan fīhā* likewise repeats, and the repetition is itself the shudder: permanence was the garden's crown; it is the fire's despair — the same word, *abiding*, blessing one course and sealing the other. Al-Qurṭubī's transmission of the salaf-reading keeps the clause soberly general: whoever disobeys the Lord's limits *in this way* — consuming trusts, falsifying shares — stands exposed to the verse's full threat; and the majority read the khulūd-of-the-disobedient-sinner per the Book's own exempting-window (God forgives other than shirk whom He wills, v. 48 below) as the Hereafter's threatened consistency: *the fire-admission is the limit-crosser's earned lodging until God's pardon or the intercession-term* — with the verse's own disaster *complete* for the denier, who has no exit at all. Either way, no reader of vv. 10–14 is left unadvertised: the arch of the orphan-pericope closes at fire for embezzlers and at fire for boundary-breakers, and the middle path of obedience walks straight.

**ʿAdhābun Muhīn: Punishment's Disgrace-Accent Stipulated**

The final clause appoints the punishment's particular flavor: *wa lahu ʿadhābun muhīn* — "and his shall be a punishment of humiliation": *muhīn*, from *hawn* — the low, the stripped of all standing — the Book's terminal insult-level (its cousins: 3:178's *ʿadhāb muhīn* awaiting liars on God, 3:192's Fire-enterers' disgrace, 22:9's "his in the world is disgrace..."), deliberately added where the offense's root was *pride over property*: he who reached across God's line to *magnify himself* against weak mouths receives, as custom-fitted requital, humiliation — the aggrandizement burned off him the way the forged-amended page is burned off its ink. Ibn Kathīr's note is austere: the muhīn-epithet fits v. 14's crime precisely because the estate-cheat is almost always a *face-crime* — the strong disdainful of tables where orphans sit — and God's sentence answers disdain with its own coin magnified to permanence. The warning thus ends the legislative overture of Sūrah al-Nisāʾ on the Book's by-now-declared principle: *the limits are the Lord's; the auditor He posts is His own; the two gates of v. 13 and v. 14 stand open at every probate, every trust, every ledger — and what men enter through their pens, they shall abide.* From here the sūrah turns from the dead's property to the living's purity — to the ordinances of chastity, where the same *ḥudūd*-words preside over the beds of the community as they now have over its graves.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:15

> **As for those of your women who commit an indecency, call four witnesses among you to bear witness against them. And if they bear witness, then confine them to their houses until death takes them, or until God appoints for them another way.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Fāḥishah: The Named and the Unnamed**

The sūrah's journey from the graves of property-law to the bedrooms of chastity-law begins with the Book's grave-euphemism: *fāḥishah* — indecency, monstrosity, from the root of the *fāḥish*: the act that exceeds all bounds of the seemly. The transmitted consensus of every school names it precisely, as Ibn Kathīr records from the first exegetes: *zinā* — adultery and fornication — the sin the Book assaults with the peculiar ferocity of a legislator defending two sanctities at once: the bed and the pedigree, since by this one breach both the spouses' covenant and the children's lineage are effaced. The community's memory has preserved the Prophet's own ranking of the crime among the destroyers — his list of the seven mortal sins binds *zinā with the neighbor's wife* beside idolatry and murder (al-Bukhārī 2766; Muslim 89) — and among the three at whose account there is no chance of acceptance, his searching of the ummah's conscience: "three with whom God will not speak on the Day of Resurrection... nor purify them: the aged adulterer, the lying king, and the arrogant poor man" (Muslim 107). In the present verse the assault begins with the process of proof — and proof here is armor for the town, not artillery against the woman.

**Four Witnesses: The Near-Impossible Standard**

*Fa-stashhidū ʿalayhinna arbaʿatan minkum* — "and summon against them four witnesses from among you": four — not two, not three — eyewitnesses to the act itself, in a unanimity no other crime in the Book requires. Al-Qurṭubī's jurist-reasoning: the legislator thereby armored domestic rumor, woman's honor, and the household's peace simultaneously — for adultery, the injury that unbloods the most households, is also the charge most ruinously cheap to allege. Islam's law made the charge *expensive*: eyewitness-quartet or nothing, with 24:4's complement striking the other side — the unproven *accuser* is himself flogged eighty and his testimony voided forever: *"those who accuse chaste women, then do not bring four witnesses — flog them with eighty lashes, and do not accept their testimony ever after."* The Prophet's own invocation in the hadith that defines the standard confronts the accruer's hunger plainly, Māʿiz's case being the great witness alongside: Māʿiz ibn Mālik came confessing, again and again, the Prophet ﷺ turning away from him, sending him back — "perhaps you only kissed... perhaps you only touched" — until the fourth time of insistence, and then only upon confession unforced (al-Bukhārī 6824; Muslim 1691). Proof of dishonor, in this law, is walled about with the utmost difficulty; confession is refused thrice before heard — for what is at issue is not the sin's excuse but *its holiness-guard* of the social fabric: God veils; the fourfold door stands between His veiling and men's exposure.

**Confinement Until Death: The First Ruling, Meant to Be Replaced**

The first-appointed consequence is domestic: *fa-amsikūhunna fī al-buyūti ḥattā yatawaffāhunna al-mawtu aw yajʿala Allāhu lahunna sabīlā* — "confine them in houses until death takes them, or God appoints for them a way." The clause holds, inside itself, the philosophy of gradual law, which the commentators — Ibn Kathīr with his usual clarity — draw in two strokes: (1) Islam found chastity-law in a society to whom its stringency was unknown; the discipline began with confinement matched to no public execution, no bloodstream — the sinner *warehoused* until straightening, until God's "other way"; (2) and that *way* arrived on the Prophet's own lips, in the celebrated subscription through ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit:

> *"Take from me, take from me: God has now appointed a way for them: the unmarried with the unmarried — a hundred lashes and exile for a year; and the married with the married — a hundred lashes and stoning."* (Muslim 1690; al-Bukhārī 6827 — at whose wording jurists founded the ḥadd of 24:2 in the Book and the stoning in the Sunna)

— *"a way"* the earlier verse had left deliberately unnamed. The verse is thus read today, across the entire tradition, as preserved text and archived ruling — its recitation cautioning ages how mercy-of-process is *had while waiting for justice*: the household's honor was repaired domestically first; the state's sword-arm unsheathed only at the last revelation.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:16

> **And if two of those among you are guilty thereof, punish them both; but if they repent and make amends, then let them be. Truly God is Relenting, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Alladhāni: The Dual Pronoun and Its Reading**

Where v. 15 addressed the women with its plural feminine, v. 16 arrives with the dual masculine: *wa-lladhāni yaʾtiyānihā minkum fa-ādhūhumā* — "and the two among you who commit it — punish them both" — and the pronoun's gender has occupied every school of tafsīr. The great current of transmitted reading — al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr with them — resolves the masculine dual by the Arabic rule of *taghlīb*, the predominant gender's covering of the mixed pair: the verse takes the two of the act, male and female together, and appoints them one penalty in common, closing the asymmetry the female-singular of v. 15 might have allowed. A second reading binds the verses as distribution — v. 15 married adulteresses, v. 16 the unmarried fornicators, male and female both (a reading al-Qurṭubī traces to the Companions' generation) — and a third, preserved with the source-reporting it requires, takes the masculine dual *of males with males*, al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī noting the opinion with the doubt-marked distance the chains impose. The settled register of the schools cleaves to the first; and the load of the verse rides on the clause at its close, which does not vary between readings.

**Ādhūhumā: Harm Appointed, Then Softened to a Word**

The penalty-word is *ādhū* — the imperative of *adhā*, harm, injury — light in etymology, stern in law: *fa-ādhūhumā* — "hurt them both" — the harm the commentators discipline into its era: the *taʿzīr*, rebuke-and-scold, of the early dispensation, speech cutting where nothing yet cut flesh — al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr both naming the public tongue-lash and the assembly's rebuke the core of it, with some of the Salaf adding chastisement mild as an option beneath the fuller ḥadd then unrevealed. And it was, again, *temporary*: 24:2 cancelled it into the hundred lashes for the free fornicator of either sex, so that v. 16, like v. 15, stands as a station of the revealed pedagogy — the community's training in stages — al-Rāzī's perpetual lesson on the sequence: Islam's penal law was not flung whole upon a desert habit, but struck step upon step, each station real until the next arrived. What never lapses in the verse is its other half, which no abrogation has ever approached, since it is the chapter's unexpiring door.

**Tābā wa Aṣlaḥā: The Two Verbs of the Door**

*Fa-in tābā wa aṣlaḥā fa-aʿriḍū ʿanhumā* — "if the two repent and make amends, then turn from them": the pardon-clause appoints its two joint-credentials, *tawbah* the inward turn — remorse, resolve, abandonment — *iṣlāḥ* the outward amendment of life, and then binds the *community* itself: *aʿriḍū* — withdraw from them; let them be; re-open their names. The commentators dwell tenderly upon this: repentance in God's law does not only erase the higher register; it commands society's register to close, the tongue to stop, the file to be boxed. Ibn Masʿūd's oft-quoted maxim at this clause, cited by Ibn Kathīr and the commentators after him — *"one who repents from a sin is as one who never sinned"* — stands inseparable from a hadith precise to the scandal-management of the verse — the Prophet's reported word when the case of the confessed woman al-Ghāmidiyyah reached its bloody end and a man reviled her after death:

> *"Had you reviled her? She has repented a repentance that, were it divided among seventy of the people of Madinah, would suffice them all. Have you found better than that she gave her soul to God Almighty?"* (Muslim 1695, from Buraydah)

**Tawwāb Raḥīm: The Seal That Names the Habit of God**

The verse closes with the Name-pair the sūrah's repentance-files will claim as their own: *inna Allāha kāna tawwāban raḥīman* — "truly God is ever Relenting, Merciful": *tawwāb*, the intensive-pattern of turning-back — the One whose habit is to turn again and again toward who turns — matched against man's single turn; *raḥīm*, the Merciful-in-effect, the mercy not merely owned but *run down* upon the forgiven like the rain that runs down walls. The attributes' placement in this exact verse is medicine measured: between v. 15's dreadful process and v. 16's rebuke-office, sinners might despair of return; the seal informs the fearful that the court of return belongs not to the harsh but to *the Relenting-Merciful* — that Abd Allāh ibn Masʿūd's fellow, asked why God bothered to command the repenting sinner new works, answered in the old Talmud-spirit of the Madinan schools: *because only preachers of despair call repentance enough without a changed life.* Reversed lives, sealed names, pardoned storyboards — these are the wares of Tawwāb-Raḥīm; and the sūrah's repentance-arch will now open fully at vv. 17–18, whose clauses fix exactly *who* may pass this door, and *how late* is too late — the twin questions of every sinning reader since the morning the verses were spoken.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:17

> **God only accepts the repentance of those who do evil in ignorance and then turn quickly in repentance: these are the ones unto whom God relents, and God is Knowing, Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Tawbatan min ʿIndi Allāh: Repentance as Divine Promise**

The verse opens with a possessive construction that recasts the whole enterprise: *innamā al-tawbatu ʿalā Allāhi li-lladhīna yaʿmalūna al-sūʾa bi-jahālatin* — "repentance is upon God — an office He owes Himself — for those who work evil in ignorance": rendering literally, repentance is *binding* on God toward a described class — the phrase the commentators incline to unpack as His self-written pledge: God has *kept repentance upon Himself* for such people, as He has written mercy upon Himself (6:12, 54). Al-Qurṭubī gathers the theological care this clause required: no creature can *obligate* God — ʿqawm al-wujūb* (the Muʿtazili doctrine of rational duty upon God) al-Qurṭubī answers with the Sunnah's own dictum: the obligation here is *promise*, laid on God by God — *"He is too truthful for His promise to fail"* — so that repentance-forgiveness is as certain as a covenant, yet remains *grace* in kind, because no hand but His bound Him. The door-post of v. 17 therefore stands inscribed with two truths: the acceptor of tawbah is the Lord who *swore it open*; its opening is to a described people — and the description follows.

**Bi-Jahālatin: Ignorance Widened to the Whole Colony of Sin**

*Those who do evil in ignorance* — and the clause worried the early centuries, for sinners frequently know exactly what they do. The tradition's answer, recorded in its full gallery from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās through ʿIkrimah and Qatādah and received by al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, and al-Qurṭubī as the majority's resolution: *jahālah* here is the Book's own widened ignorance — the ignorance-in-act of every disobeyer, who at his sin's moment stands fully ignorant of God: of the punishment the thing entails, of the Witness then present, of the wages of the one he wrongs — so that "whoever disobeys God is jāhil, knowingly or not" runs Qatādah's maxim. The Book's own precedent is two-sided and decisive: Joseph cries *"unless You turn their guile from me, I shall incline toward them and be among the ignorant"* (12:33) — the solicited man, well-aware, pleading against entry into *jahālah*; and Zulaykhā's own excuse — *"I was of the ignorant ones"* (12:89's context of her confession) — while yet everything about her intrigue was intended. Al-Rāzī adds the argument's neat inversion: sins can *only* be repented from if they were *in some measure* voluntary; the unwitting error needs no tawbah at all — ergo the ignorance the verse owns must span intention itself. The clause is thus a promise wide as the whole fallen colony: any son of Adam who wronged, even while seeing, was in the Book's deep sense *not-seeing* — and for every such, God's pledge of acceptance stands.

**Thumma Yatūbūna min Qarīb: Quickness Before the Veil**

*Then they repent quickly* — *min qarīb*: "from near" — and the commentators divide its nearness across three refiners: repent while in *health and capability*, before the sick-bed writes evidence of delay; repent before the *death-foretoken* locks certainty; repent simply *before death* — and the law-books keep all three in view, since each sternness levels consoles a different procrastinator. The tradition marshalled its two appointment-verses for the outer walls of the delay-permitted:

> *"God accepts the repentance of His servant so long as the gurgling (al-ghargharah) has not come"* — the spirit's rattle at the throat (al-Tirmidhī 3537, grades ḥasan; Ibn Mājah 4253, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar)

and the cosmic shutter's hour:

> *"The door of repentance stands open until the sun rises from its west."* (Muslim 2703 — also Abū Dharr's long form at Muslim 2758–59 bis.)

Between ghargharah and the western sunrise, *min qarīb* stretches — but only across the daylight of a life that can still act, for tawbah, the doctors insist, includes amendment and amends, neither of which a throat-gurgle performs. And the seal *wa Allāhu kāna ʿalīman ḥakīman* — Knowing, Wise — shows God, at the door's very lintel, policing the thing the clause could be misread into: He *knows* the ignorance from the engineered "ignorance"; is *wise* in delimiting the promise — lest the pledge of forgiveness, made unconditional, become the charter of the deliberate.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:18

> **And repentance is not accepted from those who do evil deeds till, when death confronts one of them, he says, "Truly now I repent," nor from those who die as disbelievers. For those We have prepared a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ḥattā Idhā Ḥaḍara Aḥadahumu al-Mawt: The Last Call That Comes Too Late**

The partner-statute to v. 17 maps the terrain where the door stands shut: *wa laysa al-tawbatu li-lladhīna yaʿmalūna al-sayyiʾāti ḥattā idhā ḥaḍara aḥadahumu al-mawtu qāla innī tubtu al-ān* — "and repentance is not for those who work the evils until, when death has arrived to one of them, he says: I repent now." Two portraits are denied: the *deathbed-late*, tawbah at the arrival — root *ḥ-ḍ-r*, presence — of death itself, and the *death-dwellers in kufr*, those who *die while disbelieving*. Al-Rāzī marks the semantic division precisely: the defect in the first is *time*, not class — the same sinner who might be embraced at morning is rejected at the gurgle — turning a promise-of-acceptance into the sharpest alarm of all; the defect in the second is *state* — death seals as it finds, belief or unbelief, and unsealed thereafter no more. The commentators of the occasions link the first clause to the old ones who spent a life in evil and, sighting the angel, scrambled for the formula; Ibn Kathīr places beside it the Pharaoh of the Book's memorial — "until, when drowning overtook him, he said: I believe there is no god but He in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the submitters" — met with heaven's one-word courtroom: *"Now? — and you had disobeyed before, and were of the corrupters"* (10:90–91) — the standing precedent that the acceptance-gate outruns exactly one hour of sighted proof.

**Why Now Is Not Now: The Logic of the Shut Gate**

Al-Rāzī, whose kalām-precision summons the theological question (why should the latest honest turn be refused?), renders the school's answer in layers: (1) tawbah under God's rule is *a trust made credible by freedom*, and the death-arrival is freedom's terminus — hence no faith at that hour counts, "for faith profits not a soul which had not believed before, nor earned good in its faith" (6:158's full clause); (2) the late-turner's every earlier hour had the chance, so the refusal is the logical last mercy: had God ratified the death-minute conversion, *every* scoffer could license himself; the one denied hour guards the sincerity of all the earlier ones — (3) and the *why can't He?* answer is simply: He can; the verse records what He has *willed* — and appointed that the Book announce the rule universally so that no one can claim surprise at the border. The tradition adds the soul's own eyewitness-condition from the ḥadīth of the sun-and-breath already noted — while the spirit remains unravished, the sun unrisen-in-the-west, and the ghayb (unseen) unseen — the door stands "outstretched as the Lord stretches His hand by night that the sinner of the day may repent, and by day that the sinner of the night may repent, until the sun rises from its setting-place" (al-Tirmidhī 3379 to this effect; the *night-and-day hands* of Muslim 2759, from Abū Mūsā, is the standing text).

**The Disbeliever's File: Death as Binding Verdict**

The second portrait — *wa-lladhīna yamūtūna wa hum kuffār* — "those who die while they are disbelievers" — carries the seal that needs no clock because the file itself is closed at the divider: death-in-kufr — and for these the verse pronounces the prepared room: *ulāʾika aʿtadnā lahum ʿadhāban alīman* — "for those We have prepared a painful punishment": *aʿtadnā* — the verb of prepared-readiness, as of banquet or army laid out before the guests arrive — reserved in this chapter (vv. 37, 93, 151, 161, 167) for the case of disobedience-filed-at-death. The commentators register the parallel of the last-hour seeker cited by Ibn Kathīr with the Book's own light on the death-criers: "when they see Our punishment, they say: I believe... their faith availed them not when they had seen Our punishment — the wont of God that has passed among His servants — and there the disbelievers lost" (40:84–85) — sunnah-of-God being the tradition-term for unalterable precedent. The chapter's adjacent theology is in plentiful supply: 2:161–162's died-kuffār-abiding; 3:91's earth-ful of gold refused; 4:97 below blaming angels' questioning the self-harmers — *in what condition were you?* The teaching stands through them all: the grave is an appointment with a verdict matching the condition died-in; and no horizon-prayer after fixes it.

**The Two Doorside Lamps for the Living**

With v. 17's open door beside v. 18's shut one, the sūrah has set the two lamps under which every sinner-plan forms — and the commentators bundle them as one counsel: count no hour yours; the door's open date is unpublished. The salaf's devotional practice lived the order literally: Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's well-known exchange with a youth who postponed — *"when my beard is white, I shall repent"* — answered in the spirit of these two verses with one question: *"and who promised you that you will grow a beard?"* The community is thereby trained into the verse's own arithmetic: *min qarīb* (v. 17) is the genuine *now*, and any later *now* dreamed of is, by the grammar of the refuse-clause, v. 18's *innī tubtu al-ān*. The pericope therefore ends exactly as the orphan-pericope began — at watchfulness: keep accounts short; repentance done *quickly* is the only repentance promised; the quick one is the promise; the postponed one is the gamble against the gurgle and the sun.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:19

> **O you who believe! It is not lawful for you to inherit women through coercion, nor to prevent them from marrying [again], that you may take away some of what you have given them, unless they commit a flagrant indecency. And consort with them in a kind and honorable way; for if you dislike them, it may be that you dislike a thing in which God has placed much good.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Stepson Who Draped His Cloak: The End of Wife-Inheritance**

The verse struck at one of pagan Arabia's strangest customs, and the reports of its occasion — preserved by al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī in their several chains — bring it before us: a Madinan man died; his stepson walked to his stepmother — the famous case attaching to the household of Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat's son — and threw his cloak over her, the tribe's own ceremony of claim: *by this draping I inherit her as I inherit the camels.* Thereafter she was his chattel: married to him unconsulted, or married off at bridewealth he consumed, or confined a widow till death so that her wealth fall where he wished. And the woman came to the Messenger of God ﷺ: *"I am inherited, Messenger of God — neither married nor left alone."* Heaven answered: *lā yaḥillu lakum an tarithū al-nisāʾa karhan* — "it is not lawful for you to inherit women *against their will.*" Ibn Kathīr takes the clause's full measure: the verse abolishes at a stroke the woman-as-estate — with one clause transferring her from the *inventory* of inheritance to its *registry of heirs*, as vv. 11–12 have since sealed: she is seated at the table now, no longer laid upon it. The *karhan* — by coercion — is itself a second teaching: where heiresses' consent might have sanctified *nothing* in the old law, in Islam marriage never exits consent's door — the Prophet's own documentation standing in the celebrated report of Khansāʾ bint Khidhām, given by her father against her liking, whereupon the marriage was invalidated and the maxim descended to the entire law: *"the previously-married woman has more right to herself than her guardian"* (al-Bukhārī 5138; Muslim 1421 — from Ibn ʿAbbās, who told of the case directly).

**ʿAḍūl and Mīmār: The Two Ways of Stealing Back a Gift**

The statute's second arm — *wa lā taʿḍulūhunna li-tadhhabū bi-baʿḍi mā ātaytumūhunna* — "nor bar them [from remarriage] in order to take back part of what you gave them" — forges the two locks of the ancient dowry-theft. *Taʿḍilūhinn* — the verb of obstruction — names the Jāhili weapon exactly: the heir barring the widow's remarriage until she ransom her freedom from her own dower; and the companion-form, the husband's *hostility-tactic*: the man who sours against a wife — beating, starving, humiliating — not to divorce but to *force her hand* at the return of her bridewealth for release. The exception-gate — *illā an yaʾtīna bi-fāḥishatin mubayyinatin* — "unless they come with a flagrant indecency" — the commentators distribute with care: for those who read *fāḥishah* as adultery, no gift-recovery is re-licensed thereby, since the public ḥadd answers the public wrong; for those receiving *nushūz* — the wife's declared defiance, perpetual abandonment — the clause opens the road to the khulʿ proceeding of 2:229, in which *she*, uninjured yet seeking release, may buy her exit with what she freely returns. Al-Qurṭubī's juristic sum: no taking-back may begin in a husband's force — the one legal channel is her un-coerced wish.

**ʿĀshirūhunna bi-l-Maʿrūf: Companionship as Worship-Grade Conduct**

Then the verse's positive heart, which generations of preachers have made the charter-verse of Muslim marriage: *wa ʿāshirūhunna bi-l-maʿrūf* — "and consort with them in the honorable way": *ʿashara* — to consort, to keep daily company, from the root of *ʿāshirah*, intimate clan — names marriage not as contract-law but as *companionship*, a shared living; and *bi-l-maʿrūf* — by the known-and-recognized good —delegates its content to the moral conscience of every age and house while setting its direction infallibly. The commentators fill the clause with the Prophet's own household as its prime gloss — he ﷺ the "best of you to his wives, and I am the best of you to my wives" (al-Tirmidhī 3895, ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ) — serving in his house, mending, listening long into night at Ḥudaybiyyah-eve to ʿĀʾishah's tale of the eleven women, racing with her on the road. From God-and-angel-witnessed sermons the same command went down the Farewell Pilgrimage's standing tiers: *"Fear God concerning women! You have taken them as a trust from God... and they have rights over you that you feed them and clothe them honorably"* (Muslim 1218, the ḥajjat al-wadāʿ sermon-text) — and in the equity-counsel preserved against the strong-willed: *"the best of you is the best to his family."* Muʿāsharah bi-l-maʿrūf is thus no decorative mercy but the household's own *act of worship*, the dawning discipline by which the sūrah's whole women's-charter becomes a lived interior.

**ʿAsā an Takrahū Shayʾan: The Inscrutable Good Hidden in Dislike**

The verse seals with one of the Book's deepest counsels on endurance, repeated to warriors at 2:216 and now issued to husbands: *fa-in karihtumūhunna fa-ʿasā an takrahū shayʾan wa yajʿala Allāhu fīhi khayran kathīrā* — "if you dislike them, it may be you dislike a thing in which God has placed much good." Al-Rāzī loves the clause's psychology: the dislike here is the uncaused kind — no cruelty, no defect — the itch of *nafs* before God's verdict has matured; the command stands against divorcing-in-haste against v. 20's own calumny-trap; and the consolation-word *ʿasā* — "perhaps, it may be" — in God's dialect is near-promise: *he waits, and finds the good.* The school of patience drew from the clause its marriage-rule of thumb: the unblamed wife often bears children who become blessing, supports at hours history later reveals, builds patience itself — the patience of the #1 household virtue — and that houses survived by one partner's forbearance fill God's reading with *khayran kathīran*, much good. The whole verse thus runs the gamut of a woman's passage: no inheriting of her; no obstructing of her; no clawback of her gift; companionship with her in kindness; and in the last refinement — even where nature recoils — a standing invitation to *look again at what God has hidden in the disliked*, the same surprise reserved for every saddled patience in the Book: *"bear patiently, that God may bring after the hardship ease"*.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:20

> **If you desire to take one wife in place of another, even if you have given to one of them a great sum, take back nothing from it. Would you take it by way of calumny and manifest sin?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Qinṭār: The Hundredweight You Cannot Carry Back**

The law of the irrevocable gift is now fixed at its maximum setting: *wa in aradtum istibdāla zawjin makāna zawjin wa ātaytum iḥdāhunna qinṭāran fa-lā taʾkhudhū minhu shayʾan* — "if you wish to exchange one wife for another, though you had given one of them a *qinṭār*, take not back anything of it." The Quran borrows the weight-word deliberately: *qinṭār*, of foreign extraction, the merchant's hundredweight — commentators calculate it variously between forty and twelve hundred ūqiyyah, and a host of silver over a man's two hands — chosen so that no husband could plead *smallness*: the gifts between man and wife are no reclaimable deposits, once given at any scale. Al-Qurṭubī's axiom from the clause runs into every code of the schools: the bridewealth has *vested*, contract-delivered, remainder a debt divorce cannot void — so that in the lawbooks of every century the mahr stands in the wife's estate ahead of wills, ahead of creditor-jostlings, where even the husband's poverty pleads in vain. The occasion-frame shows the law taming a tactic: the downtrodden "replacement-marriage" circuit — soured husband, fresh bride-interest, engineered recovery of the old's dower as the new's stake — named here and retired at the full force of the concluding clause.

**Calumny and Manifest Sin: The Two Enemies of the Cold Husband**

*A-taʾkhudhūnahu bi-buhtānin wa ithmin mubīn* — "would you take it by calumny and manifest sin?" — and the commentators expose the mechanism: to claw the mahr back lawfully, the husband needed a crime — hence the manufactured one. *Buhtān* — calumny-astonishing, the lie that stuns the hearer, from its root of dumbfounding — is here, per al-Ṭabarī's authorities and al-Qurṭubī's juristic eye, the fabricated charge of the *fāḥishah* or of *nushūz*: accusations alone opening v. 19's little exception-gate; *ithm mubīn* — clear sin — is the rest of the toolkit: cruelty staged so she might *offer* the ransom herself. That the Book should speak in this interrogative-mocking register — *would you take it?!* — seizes every generation's attention from al-Rāzī on: revelation adopts the bench-sarcasm of judges who have watched it all, the crooked petition named before it is filed: *the clause which could legalize the theft is here declared the theft.* And 2:229 — the Book's twin ruling at divorce — completes the statute from the other side, with its khulʿ-mercy alone held out for the *wife's own* unhurried choice: the husband can never even *ask back*; she alone, and only freely, may offer.

**ʿUmar's Pulpit and the Woman Who Knew Her Verse**

The community's proudest vignette of *female* competence in the Book centers precisely on this verse's hundredweight-word, in the story the commentators — Ibn Kathīr first among them — pass down from the days of the Caliph ʿUmar: he stood at his minbar regulating a society swollen with bride-price bargains, and moved to cap the mahr at four hundred dirhams — whereupon a Qurayshī woman got to her feet and recited: *"though you had given one of them a qinṭār — take nothing of it back"* — and added, in a session every century after has quoted: *"Umar, God has given us more and you would lessen? Forbid men from nothing that God has permitted!"* The Caliph's retraction was historic courtroom-dictum:

> *"The woman is right and ʿUmar is wrong — everyone is more knowing than ʿUmar."* (variant readings of the retraction run through the Sunan-compilations and the tafsīr of 4:20, being among the most quoted aṣḥābi-precedents of the shariʿa)

The jurisprudential treasure of the tale — that even a caliph's *public-welfare* ordinance perishes against a woman's recitation of her revealed share — is weighed as heavily by scholars as its social treasure: the first marriage-gift statute of Islam did not merely *defend* the woman's bounty; it *taught her* to defend it, pulpit against pulpit, the Book in her mouth and the Caliph bowing to it.

**Istibdāl Zawj Makāna Zawj: Beneath the Swap-Word, the Whole House**

Beneath the legal surface the verse's own choice of phrase — *istibdāla zawjin makāna zawjin*, "exchanging a spouse in place of a spouse" — exposes the act's deeper nature: the verb *istabdala* is the Book's word for swaps and trade-ups (2:61, 61:11's *do you prefer the world's life?*) — marriage-cycling drawn for once in the idiom of *merchandise* — and legislators in every school have read the noun-swap as the verse's interior rebuke: the renewed bride at the old dowry is a discount-store marriage, and God forbade its discount. The Muslim household has retained the verse's lesson at two poles ever since: men *may* divorce — the gate is not barred — but they may never *mine* a marriage; and a woman's dower is hers as the sight in her eyes is hers — transfer absolute, un-cancelable by his weariness, his newer love, or his economizing intent. The hundredweight the Arabs knew well: God's measure of *irretrievability*. A man delivers it in the wedding — he hears, at the parting, in the same chapter, the only reply of heaven: *take back nothing. Nothing. Though it be a qinṭār.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:21

> **And how can you take it back, when you have lain with one another and they have made with you a solemn covenant?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Kayfa Taʾkhudhūnahu: The Question That Silences the Courtroom**

After v. 20's waving hundredweight, God's voice closes around the plaintiff-husband with one of the Book's most intimate rhetorical devices — *wa kayfa taʾkhudhūnahu?* — "and how could you take it?" — the *kayfa* of scandalized impossibility (its sisters: 2:28's *how do you disbelieve in God?*, 3:101's *how could you deny?*) — a question asked not for lack of mechanism but as exposure of *moral impossibility*: the thing can be imagined, and the question denies it could be *imagined without shame*. The two grounds the verse lays out follow into the heart of the marriage-mystery: one of the *body*, one of the *word*: proximity past undoing, pledge past recalling. Between them God answers — no juristic heavy-studied code — with the simple amazement of decency: *how, with what face, at which reckoning?*

**Qad Afḍā Baʿḍukum ilā Baʿḍ: The Closet Congress of Two Lives**

*Qad afḍā baʿḍukum ilā baʿḍ* — "you have already gone in one unto another" — the commentators take in the full company of its shading: from *ifḍāʾ*, arriving unto, emptying into, coming upon — a phrase including the directest meaning the law-speech of the Arabs permitted the Book to use without loss of its veil: lying together (Ibn Kathīr's authorities, with immediate juristic explication: full entitlement of the wife's mahr on consummation drops clear of every schools' dispute), stretched by others of the Salaf, al-Ḥasan at their front, to *khalwah* — privacy accomplished, door-shut alone-ness — a reading by which Abū Ḥanīfah rested full dower-title upon the proven privacy alone (al-Shāfiʿī allotting half — the disputation al-Qurṭubī transcribes at full scope with the reasoning of both schools). The argument of the verse either way overwhelms by delicacy: *yours was the secret sharing that emptied her before you* — the Book mindful of everything public society cannot see, demanding at bar the memory of what each husband saw. The law's protection of the *used* relationship is thereby founded upon its protection of shared *memory*: what you alone knew cannot be un-known for a price.

**Mīthāq Ghalīẓ: The Covenant Word That Marriages Share with Prophethood**

*Wa akhadhna minkum mīthāqan ghalīẓan* — "and they have taken from you a weighty covenant" — is, in the company of the women-commentators' treasuries, the most celebrated grammatical gift of the verse: the covenant exacted is said to be taken *from you, by them* — the wife and her house standing at contract as *requirement-issuers* over the groom — and the weight-word *ghalīẓ*, thick and grievous, is otherwise reserved in the Book for God's own bonds: the covenant of the prophets (33:7), the covenant of Israel (4:154), the believers' works-side of heaven's contract. Marriage alone among human compactions enters that register — al-Rāzī documenting theologians at this sharpened point: the nikāḥ is *ʿaqd* — binding — not bargain: its desk is the mosque's, its witnesses God's, its unpicking mortally serious. Ibn Kathīr's transmitters give the *mīthāq* its content from the Prophet's own formula in the farewell year's company-instruction: *"You have taken them as a trust from God, and intimacy with them was made lawful to you by the word of God"* — the amānah-word and the kalimah-word together forming, in the scholars' later development, the precise instruments of every nikāḥ-khuṭbah before every qāḍī's assembly to our time: the mannered *ʿaqd* every Muslim still hears read from this verse's lineage: *"give her unto me upon the Book of God and the way of His Messenger."*

**The Three-Sentence Citadel: Vv. 19–21 as the Wife's Bill of Rights**

The cumulative fortification of vv. 19–21 stands measured at its third wall: *consort honorably* (v. 19), *take nothing back though a qintār* (v. 20), *remember what you shared and swore* (v. 21) — the Muslim woman defended at law by affection's memory, by gift's permanence, and by covenant's gravity in one breath. The Prophet's own record in such causes sealed the principle in courtroom-flesh: the reports stand in the books — the accuser-husband of the liʿān cycle asking the restitution of his mahr after the curse-divorce, answered by the verdict he heard rendered from God's message: she keeps it (Ibn Kathīr relates beneath these clauses) — and the new groom whose bride was found gravid by another, likewise fined no recovery of his gift. In all three history-forges the statute holds: the mahr never rides back; the covenant never thins; the *how can you?* of v. 21 remains unanswered by any husband in thirteen centuries of qāḍīs' courts — because no answer could be framed that respects either of the verse's two unanswerable witnesses: the body that was trusted, and the word that was bound.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:22

> **And marry not those women whom your fathers married, save for what is past. Truly it was indecent and loathsome, an evil way.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Lā Tankiḥū Mā Nakaḥa Ābāʾukum: The Forbidden Enterprise of the Sons**

The prohibition arrives with terrible plainness: *wa lā tankiḥū mā nakaḥa ābāʾukum min al-nisāʾi illā mā qad salaf* — "and marry not such women as your fathers married — except what has passed": the statute of the stepmother, closing the door the plume-and-cloak code of v. 19 had left ajar: for whereas wife-inheritance *by coercion* had been banned at v. 19, some of the early Madinans continued seeking the father's widows *with consent* — the cloak-claim run under new gentleness — until this verse gave the practice its absolute burial. The transmitters of its occasion (al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr in their magisterial chains, with the fullest narrative in al-Qurṭubī) attach it to the four sons of the to a cluster of four questions of the same kind — the crystal-case being the son of Abū Qays ibn al-Aṣlat, seeking marriage with his father's widow, who herself found the trade unseemly and carried it to the Prophet ﷺ; God's answer removed the matter from desire altogether. And the law's precision knows its own fences: the prohibition holds whether the father's marriage was consummated or not (al-Ṭabarī's register); the jurists extend it likewise to any woman of the father's private intimacy (marriage-form or not, per the per the broader reading of the verb *nakaḥa*); while *illā mā qad salaf* — "save what is past" — covers the pre-Islamic estate of everything: the God of the new community does not unpick the pagan past, He interdicts the future.

**Innahū Kāna Fāḥishatan wa Maqtan: The God's Own Insult-Vocabulary**

The sentence God renders on the practice is composed of His strongest censure-language, three nouns deep: *fāḥishatan* — flagrant indecency, the name already established at vv. 15–16 as the category of maximum sexual breach; *wa maqtan* — *maqt*, loathing, abomination-one-hateful — the Book's rare grave-accent (used for God's loathing of the disobedient at 40:10 and 35:39, for the sabbath-breakers' apportionment at 2:65) — and *wa sāʾa sabīlā* — "evil as a way," the malway-word the Book bestows on courses in entirety evil. Al-Rāzī dwells on the communion of the three: the practice is censured intellectually (*it repugns the nature of fatherhood*), legally (*it intrudes the son into the father's chamber-past*), and customarily (the God's-made fiṭrah of the Arabs of the Arabs themselves already knew its shame in parts, as their own poets reviled the one dubbed the *dayzan* — and Islam made universal what instinct half-knew). The theologians of the schools note the weight of *maqt* in God's own mouth: when loathing is attributed to the Creator of souls, the practice is bound to an an interior horror deeper than community-custom — fathers' chambers are not inheritable goods because fatherhood is one of the human estates that survive the grave.

**Mā Qad Salaf: The Habit of God with Dead Pasts**

The little saving-clause — *illā mā qad salaf* — deserves its own dignity in the map of revealed forgiveness: it is the Qur'an's standing refusal to prosecute yesterdays under today's statute (paired threefold with its sisters in these very verses: v. 23's *illā mā qad salaf* on the two-sister marriages and v. 24's similar framing), and the commentators lay down from it one of the great principles of conversion-jurisprudence: Islam accepts the person *in the condition Islam finds him* — Ghaylān with ten wives choosing four (the reports of al-Tirmidhī 1128 already noted), the two-sister husbands choosing one — because accounting begins at hearing, not at birth. Al-Qurṭubī's jurist-pastoral note generalizes still more softly: the clause also teaches *how revelation legislates continuity*: its bans are not certificates against ancestors — the fathers of the first Muslims had lived under no dispensation known to them — but *frontier-posts*, beyond which the new road runs. So, too, the family of Islam instructs every convert, every young Muslim confronting family history: the practice of forefathers belongs to their own ledger; what is *ours* to choose is the road from here — and in the matter of fathers' wives, that road closed at this verse for every generation to come: *evil as a way.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:23

> **Forbidden unto you [as wives] are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your fathers' sisters, your mothers' sisters, your brothers' daughters, your sisters' daughters, your milk-mothers and milk-sisters, the mothers of your wives, the stepdaughters in your care—born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage, but if you have not consummated the marriage with them, then there is no blame on you—and the wives of your sons who are from your loins, and two sisters together, save for what is past. Truly God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ḥurrimat: The Table of the Seven Bloods**

The verse finally unrolls the marriage-map's dark side — *maḥārim*, the prohibitions-of-nearness — in the statute-form *ḥurrimat ʿalaykum* — "forbidden to you are..." — a roll-call the jurists memorize as seven blood-ties: mother (and through her every grandmother upward, al-Qurṭubī's hereditary rule without gaps), daughter (and every granddaughter downward), sister (full, paternal, maternal alike), the two aunts of both parents, and the two lines' nieces — brother's daughters, sister's daughters — *both downwards and backwards, the tree's rings barricaded in all directions*. The commentators pause over the map's own *philosophy of blood*: the prohibited seven are exactly the degrees in which Islamic society is commanded *unveiled intimacy* — the circle within which a woman may relax her dress, travel with a male, and live in household freedom — so that the single statute draws both the safe-room and its boundary at one stroke: those forbidden in marriage are, by the same text, the permitted of domestic trust (24:31's paired roster proving the correspondence). God closes what He opens: the nearness-love was never meant to complete itself in the bed; the household's sanctity is built precisely on the union it forbids.

**The Womb-Match of Milk: Raḍāʿah, the Suckling Prohibition**

Then comes the statute that most displays revelation's independence of biology alone: *wa ummahātukumu allātī arḍaʿnakum wa akhawātukum min al-raḍāʿah* — "and your milk-mothers who nursed you, and your milk-sisters": the bond of nursing raised to the full rank of the bond of blood — five sucklings in the leading legal schools (al-Shāfiʿī fixing the count from the traditions; the Ḥanafīs content with one; ʿĀʾishah's report marking the earlier ten-then-five stages of the ordinance), and the mouth stretched to the breast within the first two or three years of life. The Prophet's own code was enacted in court-scenes the age memorized: Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ's brother ʿUtbah's the Prophet instructing ʿĀʾishah's nephews through Sahlah bint Suhayl against Salīm the freedman (that particular case the special exception the books preserve), and the general maxim of Islam writing the statute in his own mother's voice:

> *"What is forbidden through milk-kin is as what is forbidden through blood-kin."* (al-Bukhārī 2645, 5102; Muslim 1444–45 — the milk-law's corner-hadith)

— a maxim its teachers and mothers still hold before every every suckling-arrangement in every Muslim home: wet-nursing is a legal act, binding houses together as surely as marriage, confining them therewith as surely as blood.

**Rabāʾib and Daughters of the Son: The Affinity-Chain**

The statute then turns to the *in-law* degrees — maṣāhir — with the care of a lawyer of families: the mothers of wives — forbidden by the very contract, consummation or not (the consensus the schools affirm against the minority read); the stepdaughters — *rabāʾibukumu allātī fī ḥujūrikum min nisāʾikumu allātī dakhaltum bihinna* — forbidden where the mother's marriage was consummated, *fa-in lam takūnū dakhaltum bihinna fa-lā junāḥa ʿalaykum* — otherwise no blame — the accompanying gloss of *fī ḥujūrikum* ("in your care") read by most as description of the household's closeness, not a condition of the ban (al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, Z); and the wives of loins-sons — judgment eternally separated from the Prophet's Zayd-affair's shadow through 33:37, since adoptive sons are no loins-sons — *ulāʾika banūkum min aṣlābikum* deliberately qualified, the commentators reminding every generation the statute fenced the son's divorcée from his *father*, as the son's mother had been fenced at v. 22 from her *son*: the house of Muhammad, al-Rāzī remarks, *needed the clearest statute-book on this planet, for his own doors were its object-lessons.*

**And Two Sisters Together: The Verse's Closing Combination**

The table's last clause bars the *combination*: *wa an tajmaʿū bayna al-ukhtayn illā mā qad salaf* — "that you take in wedlock two sisters together, save what is past" — and the jurists' reasoning completes its wisdom with its its sister-clause: aunt-with-niece, by the Prophet's still-extant courtroom-ruling — *"God and His Messenger have forbidden a woman and her father's sister together, and a woman and her mother's sister together"* (al-Bukhārī 5109; Muslim 1408; al-Tirmidhī 1157; Abū Dāwūd 2066). Jealousies at the blood-line of sisters was the commentators' standard note; furthermore the Book's seal — *inna Allāha kāna ghafūran raḥīman* — Forgiving, Merciful — stretches over the whole table of of prohibitions-of-marriage its own grace-banner: what was crossed before hearing falls under the old *illā mā qad salaf*; what is crossed after, under repair-of-repentance — for the statute-draws of God are matched, line for line, by mercy measured for the man who weeps. Thus the *maḥram*-table stands finished — one of the oldest intact marriage-maps of mankind — and every Muslim wedding since that Madinan noon has been walked through it, ring by ring.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:24

> **And married women [are forbidden unto you] save those whom your right hands possess; thus has God prescribed for you. Lawful unto you are all others whom you would seek in marriage with gifts from your property, in honest wedlock and not in fornication. And those women whom you enjoy thereby, give unto them their bridewealth, as an obligation; but there is no blame on you for what you agree to after the obligation. God is Knowing, Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Al-Muḥṣanāt: Fortress-Women and the Rule of Another's Covenant**

The verse resumes the marriage-map at its largest perimeter: *wa-l-muḥṣanātu min al-nisāʾi illā mā malakat aymānukum* — "and the fortress-women among women are forbidden — save those your right hands possess": *muḥṣanāt*, from *ḥiṣn*, fortress — the women made inaccessible by standing covenant — married women, according to the consensus of the tradition, as are the nearest words of al-Ṭabarī and the great congregations of schools after him: another man's wife is forbidden absolutely, her covenant his *ḥiṣn* about her; the Book's own protected integrity thereby advanced from blood (v. 23) to parchment-and-honor — the marriage-bond itself entered into the list of holies. The reports of its comprehensive occasion — women of Ḥunayn's battlefield within this within the statute's ancient exception — boxed provisionally within the then-standing law of captives, which the law later disciplined afresh; but the mosque-law scholars of every generation have kept first its standing clause: *no man may approach, flirt with, or negotiate around the covenant of another* — the law of brotherly reverence at the last door, where every house is a fortress against every hand save the one the door was built for.

**An Tabtaghū bi-Amwālikum: Marriage by Gift-Money, Not by Whim**

The verse then re-opens the lawful wide world with a complete methodology in a single sentence: *uḥilla lakum mā warāʾa dhālikum an tabtaghū bi-amwālikum muḥṣinīna ghayra musāfiḥīna* — "lawful for you is all beyond that, to seek with your property, as chastity-keepers, not as fornicators." The clause instructs *how* one marries, threefold: (1) *an tabtaghū bi-amwālikum* — seek *by means of your property* — the mahr-way, public, priced, documented — against the Jāhili roads that cost no one anything: al-Qurṭubī reading the reference to property as demanding quantifiable bridal-gift, not vague service; (2) *muḥṣinīna* — *as chaste ones* — the man himself fortress-warded *within* the taking, the ḥiṣn built this time round the seeker: marriage as the chastity-instrument, its own contract a a wall; (3) *ghayra musāfiḥīna* — not *sifāḥ*-practicers: *sifāḥ*, the poured-out way — pouring seed into unguarded channels — the Book's own image for fornication-as-spillage: against every "connection" the age invents, God contrasts a house keyed with property, witnesses, naming, and the bride's own treasury. The *muḥṣanīn / musāfiḥīn* polarity is exactly the Qur'an's double-register of marriage against every since: *chastity-builders against spillers*: where chastity holds, contract and payment; where spilling rules, no contract, no account.

**Fa-Mā-stamtaʿtum Bihi Minhunna: The Bridewealth-Anchor and Its Echoes**

The verse's crown-clause — *fa-mā-stamtaʿtum bihi minhunna fa-ātūhunna ujūrahunna farīḍah* — "so those whom you enjoy thereby, give them their rewards, an obligation" — resumes the sūrah's central women's-right (v. 4's *ṣaduqāt*; v. 20's qintār) with its juristic synonym *ujūr* — wages/fee — set in the divine-payroll voice. The eternal the eternal statement: her due is a *farīḍah*, statute-assigned — distant now from the dispute of later centuries over the clause's over the famous *mutʿah*-question, on which the tradition itself preserves the entire debate honestly: the memory of Ibn ʿAbbās's reading *"ila ajalin musamman"* — "for a term appointed" — the Shiʿi schools cleaving to the verse as mutʿah's own text, the Sunna-schools holding to the Prophet's final prohibition at Khaybar and Mecca's year — "God and His Messenger forbade the mutʿah to the Day of Resurrection" — with the ruling of the Caliph ʿUmar sealing the community's operational consensus since. The honest exegete transcribes both — as al-Ṭabarī himself does in his catalogs — and the believer notices that where tradition broke, the *verse's own central content* stands identical in every school: *whatsoever be the creature's contract, the woman's gift is God's statute, never the man's benevolence* — upon which note all sects and centuries still unite, the wage-word *farīḍah* striking the same settled chime it did at the grave's ledger: marriage without the farīḍah is a denied marriage here.

**Wa Lā Junāḥa ʿAlaykum Fīmā Tarāḍaytum Bihi: Freedom After the Obligation**

The statute then closes — exquisitely — with a liberty: *wa lā junāḥa ʿalaykum fīmā tarāḍaytum bihi min baʿdi al-farīḍah* — "no blame upon you in what you mutually consent to, after the fixed obligation": after the farīḍah is *safely fixed* — registered, owed, sealed — the spouses' consenting commerce of increase or remission lies open: he may add; she may yield (v. 4's ṭibna); installments may be reshaped — the law stepping out of a bedroom it has furnished with rights. Al-Qurṭubī draws the seal-wisdom of the sequence: Islam writes marriage as *statute-floor plus consent-ceiling*: the floor is immutable — God-forged: mahr, consent-of-brides-past, prohibited degrees; above the floor, two adults live as free souls under God. And the verse's attribute-closure gathers the whole pericope again — *inna Allāha kāna ʿalīman ḥakīman* — Knowing, Wise — Every exception weighed against every house: the He knows what marriages build and what marriages conceal; He is wise in what He closed and what He left open; and the family of believers, its map now complete within the pericope vv. 22–25, may walk from the statute-table into the courts and bedrooms of the world carrying, like a passport, the signature of the Knowing and the Wise.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:25

> **And whoever of you has not the means to marry believing free women, then [let him marry] from among those believing slave girls whom your right hands possess. And God knows best your faith. You are of one another. So marry them by the permission of their people, and give them their bridewealth honorably, as married women, not as fornicators, nor as takers of paramours. And once they are married, should they commit an indecency, then upon them is half the punishment of free married women. This is for those among you who fear hardship. But to be patient is better for you. And God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Man Lam Yastaṭiʿ: The Poor Man's Door God Himself Cut**

The verse answers a distressed question of the new community's young men — its occasion standing in the Companion-reports as the plea of those without property for marriage, falling to desire's danger — with an escorted alternative: *wa man lam yastaṭiʿ minkum ṭawlan an yankiḥa al-muḥṣanāti al-muʾmināti fa-min mā malakat aymānukum min fatayātikumu al-muʾmināt* — "whoever of you lacks the amplitude (*ṭawl* — wealth's stretch) to marry free believing women, then from among your right-hand-possessed believing slave-girls." The clause erects upon the ancient world's most hardened status-wall — the slave's body as commodity — a wholly new estate of humanity: the slave-girl is *mu'minah*, a believer — marriageable by God's law, dowered by statute, wed by ceremony — entering marriage not as used goods but as bride. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī labor the significance in every matter the verse furnishes: the Prophet's own the Prophet's own counsel over the class had set the theology: Abū Dharr's report of the prophetic instruction — *"your brothers whom God placed in your hands: feed them of what you eat, clothe them of what you wear, and do not burden them with what overwhelms them"* (al-Bukhārī 30, 2545; Muslim 1661) — and the emancipation-hedges of the Book in every expiation verse — from this statute the believers learned slavery was a temporary legal estate of persons, never a metaphysics of persons, with the bridal-verse its first and loudly humanizing proof.

**Allāhu Aʿlamu bi-Īmānikum / Baʿḍukum min Baʿḍ: The Great Leveling Sentence**

Then the verse reaches what its commentators have repeatedly called its social trump: *wa-Allāhu aʿlamu bi-īmānikum, baʿḍukum min baʿḍ* — "God knows best your faith; you are of one another." *Baʿḍukum min baʿḍ* — a clause of three Arabic words voluminous as a manifesto: *each of you is from the other* — free and slave from a single clay, a single nafs wāḥidah of 4:1 — spiritual status never purchasable and never chattel-ized, for the title-deed of worth is the faith God alone measures. Al-Rāzī takes it to its full consequence: outward inequalities are the world's business; inner rank is God's; and the slave-wife's soul may stand, at Judgment, rows above the free woman's. The clause stands at the summit of those compressed Qur'anic sentences in which a social system is quietly annulled: between v. 1's one-soul and v. 25's *you are of one another*, the sūrah's whole anthropology of women-and-wards comes to speech.

**By the Permission of Their People, Muḥṣanāt: The Slave-Bride's Full Honors**

The statute then reproduces, for the slave-bride, every safeguard the free bride received: *fa-nkiḥūhunna bi-idhni ahlihinna wa ātūhunna ujūrahunna bi-l-maʿrūf muḥṣanātin ghayra musāfiḥātin wa lā muttakhidhāti akhdān* — "marry them with their people's permission, and give them their rewards honorably: fortress-women, not pourers-out, nor takers of secret lovers." Three honors, bestowed in sequence: hers is a wali-witnessed contract (the *ahl* — her legal holders, the jurists refining how much passes to her and how much to the estate); hers is her own *ujūr*, her *mahr*, in the Book's same wage-word measured to rank; hers *also* is the conduct-word *muḥṣanāt* — the fortress-title once married: once wed she is *fortress-woman*, and marriage is to be built against both ancient shapes of the pour (the open *sifāḥ*-fornication and the secret *khidn* — the paramour kept hidden) — the Book barring both its ages' two exits from covenant-honor: public shamelessness and private arrangements. The commentators' distinction — *musāfiḥāt* as the open marketplace-women and *akhhdān*-takers as veiled alliances (Ibn ʿAbbās's full triad-description: marriage public, fornication open, paramours hidden, as Ibn Masʿūd-explicated — in al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr's preservation) — has become a paradigm for later marital law-book: Islam recognizes the *announced* house alone.

**Half the Punishment of the Fortress, and a Concluding Mercy**

The verse's legal tail — half the free woman's penalty upon the slave-wife's proven offense — the jurists read within God's distributive realism: the slave-wife's walls stood lower, her protection thinner in the world's actual sociology; so her accountability is mercifully measured, while (33:30) the Prophet's own household stands its inverse: double for doubling of station: heaven's equity runs both directions of status. The verse then seals, against the pressure-brooding man himself: *dhālika li-man khashiya al-ʿanata minkum* — "this is for him who fears hardship (al-ʿanat — the crush of desire-hardship)" — *wa-an taṣbirū khayrun lakum* — "but that you be patient is better for you": release provided, patience crowned — God's law easing and exhorting in the same paragraph — with the twin-attributes of the marriage-pericope returning at the close: *wa kānā Allāhu ghafūran raḥīman*: the living God of this entire legislative block, forgiving the lapses of the law's subjects, merciful in the tailoring of the law itself — statutes sewn, from orphan to slave-bride, to the measurements of mercy.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:26

> **God desires to make [this] clear unto you, and to guide you to the traditions of those who went before you, and to relent unto you. And God is Knowing, Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Yurīdu: The Legislator Who Announces His Desires**

The great marriage-pericope — prohibited degrees, dower-statutes, the slave-bride's charter — closes with a curtain-speech the commentators hold among the tenderest in the codex: *yurīdu Allāhu li-yubayyina lakum wa yahdiyakum sunana alladhīna min qablikum wa yatūba ʿalaykum, wa-Allāhu ʿalīmun ḥakīm* — "God wills to make clear to you, and to guide you in the ways of those before you, and to relent toward you; and God is Knowing, Wise." The Book rarely unveils the lawmaker's *intention* at the moment of the lawmaking — and here it unveils three, in succession, as lamps over the just-finished statutes: *clarification*, *guidance*, *relenting* — so that the household of faith understands its new laws not as decrees descending from a sealed heaven but as chapters in a companionship the Lawgiver Himself explains. Al-Rāzī marks the stylistic tenderness: the discourse had been *command-and-forbid*; the curtain is *desire-and-promise* — as though God, handing the marriage-map to a nervous community, kneels to say what He was *doing for them* the whole time: unveiling their confusion, walking them down roads walked by prophets before them, and keeping the return-door of repentance behind them at every experiment of their implementation.

**Li-Yubayyina Lakum: Clarification as Worship's First Need**

The first divine desire is clarification — *li-yubayyina lakum* — and the commentators' theology of the clause runs wide: no religion of God has ever asked *blind* obedience — the statutes must be settled first in the understanding (*bayān*), then enacted — with the precise content of the clarification here being the whole just-finished pericope: which women stand prohibited and why, what belongs to the bride and what may be remitted, how the marriage is contracted and how it is honored, how much depends on *consent* and how little on *custom*. Al-Ṭabarī reads *li-yubayyina* — "to make clear" — against the *opposite* competitive practice of revelation's enemies at 3:78 and 2:75–79: God *clarifies*; the corrupting among the ancients *twist*; the community of Muhammad thereby receives its constituting epistemological grace — the Book closed in their hands with nothing reserved for a priestly caste, the degrees of marriage advertised to every suitor, the dower-law placed in the bride's own memory. Clarification-outsourced ends here: henceforth the creed of Islam knows no mystery the layman may not read.

**Sunanan Alladhīna min Qablikum: The Old Roads, Now Lit**

The second desire is guidance into the roads of the ancients — *sunan alladhīna min qablikum* — the trodden ways of the prophets and their faithful before Islam — and the mufassirūn of the early generations read the clause as the marriage-map's *pedigree*: the degrees now forbidden in Madinah were forbidden of old to Abraham's house and the purified among the nations; the the marriage-covenant with its truth-gift descends from the primordial law; so that in receiving vv. 22–25 the Muslims are not enrolled in novelty but *re-enrolled* in an ancient sunnah of God with mankind (7:38's "our wont of those whom We sent before you"; 17:77's "no change in Our wont" — in the sunans of God), and the pagan charge of innovation against the Prophet's community is answered from within its own legislation: *your-forefathers', too, was this constitution; you are but its latest court.* Ibn Kathīr's anchoring of the clause goes to its first-teacher: the prophets' communities are held in v. 26 as one continuous brotherhood walking *one* road of God in institutions and ethics — a claim the chapter will pick up again in its great census of prophets at vv. 163–165 — with the family-law now joined to faith, creed, and monotheism as one unbroken chain.

**Tawbah Behind Every Statute**

The third desire is relenting — *wa yatūba ʿalaykum* — and its placement *behind* the laws is the Book's preventative against the legalistic despair of the sinning implementer: knowing the statutes, these Muslims would break them often enough (vv. 31, 48, 110 below will keep the subject), so God announces the compliance-safety: repentance keeps working during implementation — God's triple intention never forgets its third lamp. Ibn ʿAbbās's celebrated selection — preserved in al-Rāzī's own transmission at this verse — counts vv. 26–28 among the *eight verses of mercy in this sūrah* (with vv. 31, 40, 48, 110, 147) that should be of the Muslim's treasures — evidence the first disciples themselves treated the trilogy as a jewel-engraving on the legislative block. And the attribute-seal — *wa-Allāhu ʿalīmun ḥakīman* — crowns the ceremony dogmatically: the Clarifier is Knowing of all the statute-hidden temptations; the Guide is Wise in what He uncovers and what He leaves to reason; the Merciful One has appointed repentance with knowledge of the with knowledge of how much mud the feet that walk His roads will gather. Laws were revealed; the heart of their Reveler is now read — and the Muslim comes out of vv. 22–26 with both in hand: a marriage-map, and a Companion upon it.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:27

> **God desires to relent unto you, but those who follow lusts desire that you go tremendously astray.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Yurīdu Allāhu an Yatūba: The Will of God Above the Wills of Men**

The verse plants the two contesting wills side by side — *yurīdu Allāhu an yatūba ʿalaykum, wa yurīdu alladhīna yattabiʿūna al-shahawāti an tamīlū maylan ʿaẓīmā* — "God wills to relent toward you, while those who follow passions will that you incline with tremendous inclination" — and the juxtaposition is the whole conflict-file of revelation: above every soul hover two designs, one from the Lord building the return-road toward Him (tawbah as His willed gift, repeated from v. 26's third lamp in emphatic foreground now), the other from the passion-merchants angling to *tilt* the soul (mīl, from the weighing-scale's lean) — not merely an inch into sin but *maylan ʿaẓīman*, a great career-deviation. Al-Ṭabarī and the early school named the tilting-party from the occasions: sections of the People of the Book, whose own scriptures showed tolerances the new law now abjured, pressing the Madinans to take the easier marriage-contracts and slackened morality-roads — whether the verse's arm reaches exactly them (the common reading) or the whole species of corrupters whose trade is comfort-sin licensed (the majority's wider take: al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī) — the lesson stands twofold: (1) religious relaxations pressed with fervor are rarely neutral — each has a *design* behind it; (2) God's design answers, and His is *acceptance of the repenting*: God desires your *return*, not your ruin.

**Yatūb: The God Who Turns — Before You Do**

The verb the sūrah assigns God is from the same root as the servant's repentance — *tāba / yatūb* — but turned: God *turns-toward the turning*, and in the Arabs' great philosophical coincidence the two verbs mirror: man returns to God; God returns *to* man — the Holy One also "repenting," in the only sense that honors Him: mercy coming out to meet the approacher. The Prophet's report on this verse's theme — that God stretches out His hand through the night and the day for the day-sinner and the night-sinner — runs beneath it (Muslim 2759, Abū Mūsā's standing hadith, as at v. 17-18): the readiness precedes the repentant, which is precisely the difference from *the other will* — desire-partisans' welcome comes *after* you tilt, to keep you tilted. Your allies shape your direction, Ibn Kathīr's commentators return constantly: the first will-embraced is usually the will owned — and the verse puts both hands before you at the same signage: *God's: turn; theirs: tilt.*

**Maylan ʿAẓīman: No Small Tilt in the Desires-Plan**

The measuring-phrase deserves its exact reading: not merely that men "sin" but that the tempter's industry pushes *to a great inclining* — *a catastrophic career of the soul*, the commentators glossing the ʿaẓīm along a spectrum from the technically theological (deviation into disbelief itself, by the road of licensed sins) to the morally social: licensed looseness never stops at Zulaykhā's porch; looseness granted becomes looseness organized — until marriage-maps crumble, pedigrees wobble, and the orphan-files of vv. 2–10 are re-opened by the back way: everything the sūrah legislated against expands through the passion-road. That is why the Book's wariness of loose license is structural, and seen across the whole chapter: God fortifies *the law's locks* (prohibited degrees, dower-seatings, shares) while the tempters market *the keys* — and one more theological subtlety the schools noted: God's "will" here (*yurīdu*) is His prescriptive will — His command and His love of obedience-repentance — not necessitating: man remains addressed, fearing, choosing — lest anyone read the desire-clauses as fate.

**The Contest of the Two Intendants at Every Door**

The believer's daily spiritual intelligence derives directly from this verse: before each open doorway of ease-and-license there stand invisibly *two Intendants* — one who desires your relenting, another who desires your tilt — and the religious life consists substantially in reading which attendant holds which invitation. The followers of desires may be flesh-people — seducers, corrupters, profiteers of laxity — or market-ideas, fashions, cutting-edge permissions, "everyone does," "times have changed" — but their will is the same: *maylan ʿaẓīman*, always the farther-than-you-meant, never the small drop. The Muslim's own position under v. 27 is therefore surveillance over his own concessions: at each relaxation, ask the verse's question: *whose desire is this?* — if it inclines massively, its author is not God. Thus the sūrah's mercy-verses (Ibn ʿAbbās's eight) protect the *sinner-penitent* from despair of God's door — and this companion-verse protects *the waverer-tempter's prey* from entry into sin in the first place, the scheme uncovered at the threshold and named *by desire*.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:28

> **God desires to lighten [your burden] for you, for man was created weak.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Takhfīf: The Lightened Law as Divine Design**

The trilogy of divine desires finds its third lamp in the statute-book's own easy chair: *yurīdu Allāhu an yukhaffifa ʿankum* — "God wills to lighten for you": *takhfīf*, the taking-off of weight, announced here not as concession reluctantly granted but as legislated *purpose* — and the placement seals the lesson of the whole pericope: when the law allowed the poor man the slave-bride's marriage (v. 25), when it received the repentant sinner mid-law (vv. 17, 26, 27), when it opened khulʿ beside ṭalāq (2:229's symmetry remembered at vv. 19–21), it was not patching weakness in religion but *revealing* the religion's own economy: *its Maker intends it portable*.
