The verse hangs therefore beside the Qur'an's greatest declarations of statutory mercy — "God wills for you ease, and wills not for you hardship" (2:185); "He has chosen you, and has laid no hardship upon you in religion" (22:78); "We shall ease you to ease" (87:8) — beneath which al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr situate the entire ramadan-concessions code, the combats' reduction at Badr-era from one-against-ten to one-against-two (8:66's "now God has lightened for you, knowing there is weakness in you"), the tayammum of v. 43 below, the five prayers descended from fifty at the Night Journey (the Muslim 162 report from the Prophet's own narrative), and the traveler-and-a's concessions throughout the books of fiqh — a full doctrine in a single clause: God builds His law *around human scale*, not around angelic.

**Wa Khuliqa al-Insānu Ḍaʿīfan: Weakness in the Blueprint**

Then the reason-clause, one of the Book's most quoted anthropology-items in every pulpit since: *wa khuliqa al-insānu ḍaʿīfan* — "and man was created weak": *ḍaʿīf*, weakened-made — the passive of createdness itself, the weakness planted *at formation*, not acquired — covering, per the commentators' anatomy, the full sweep of human fragility: resolve weak before desire (the occasion-context: sexual appetite's long endurance breaking down, per al-Ṭabarī's explicit occasion-reading), patience thin under burden, memory slipping the covenant (20:115's "he forgot, and We found no firmness in him" of Adam the father), the body's own set-limits of hunger, vigilance, hour of sleep and age. Al-Rāzī's crucial theological note stands beneath: the clause *answers* an accusation that would later grow heavy in kalām (how can God command what men sustain not?), by lodging the remedy inside the fact: since weakness is *created*, mercy must be *legislated* — the Lawgiver accounting in advance for His clay's known tolerance — so that at no statute does the God of the Qur'an play the taskmaster who measures timber loads on mice. The Prophet's own legislation-idiom echoed the doctrine in his ministry:

> *"This religion is *yusr* — smooth ease; and no one will do battle with religion but that it will overcome him."* (al-Bukhārī 39: from Abū Hurayrah — the mosque-school's standing maxim)

— his own sūrah of pilgrimage direction, always the gentle gradation: fasting's permissions, witr's lightening, the standing offer of qasr and jamaʿ on roads.

**Between the Two Edges: Ease Without License, Burden Without Crushing**

The commentators are unanimous in fencing the verse from its two misreadings: it is *not* license for the sluggard — God lightens within the statutes' lines, He does not dissolve them: the degree-map of vv. 23–25 stands entire; the prayers were five, not one — nor is it *pessimism* about a contemptible creature: weakness spoken as the *opening* in God's compassion-machine, not as the slur of a creation once more disfavoured. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's school left the twin-edges in proverbs the preachers have kept: *"make religion approachable to us as You have made the fire decreed?"* — no; the line from their pulpits runs rather: *"the people are weak; and God desired ease for them — so do not be harder on them than their Lord."* Every teacher of Islam, jurist-mufti, qāḍī, marriage-counselor and and general caller to God has worked beneath v. 28's directive: measure the load to the back; take the seeker to easy halal-granted rooms before the hard; remember that the Prophet's sunnah taught without all-at-once — "the religion was not revealed in a day" — for the takhfīf was not only in *what* was ruled but in *how* it was handed.

**The Statute-Mercy at the Reader's Own Meal**

The verse finally lands, within Sūrah al-Nisāʾ's architectural design, as the assembly's keystone: the heavy blocks around it — indecency's prosecutions (vv. 15–16), the mother's and daughter's titles at graves (vv. 11–12), wealth and murder's forbiddance (vv. 29–30 below) — all sit *inside* this lightness-clause, so that strictness itself is weighed in mercy's scales. And Ibn ʿAbbās's memory enrolled v. 28, with vv. 26–27, in the sūrah's eight mercy-verses (al-Rāzī's citation of his pupil-chains): *yurīdu*, God's will to lighten, is placed among the community's miḥrāb-anchors — for the Muslim at every ritual and legal fork may say to his soul exactly what the Lawgiver announced to His ummah at its founding: *I was made weak; my Lord knew it; He desired my ease; and in His book there is a lawful door* — so that law falls from above, no more as burden-drop, but as grace carefully measured: line by line, statute by statute, makruh and mubāḥ balancing man's frail palm: the law of a Knowing, Wise, and *lightening* Lord.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:29

> **O you who believe! Consume not each other's wealth falsely, but trade by mutual consent, and slay not yourselves. Truly God is Merciful unto you.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lā Taʾkulū Amwālakum Baynakum bi-l-Bāṭil: The Forbidden Economy of the Stomach**

The sūrah's statute-line resumes with one of the Book's mightiest economic sentences — *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū lā taʾkulū amwālakum baynakum bi-l-bāṭil* — "O you who believe, do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood": wealth harvested by *bāṭil* — by the vain, the void, the title-less — and consumed among the community as though lawful. The commentators enumerate the devouring instruments in the full register, as al-Qurṭubī sets them from the Companions' interpretations through the law-books' maturity: **usury** (ribā — 2:275–278's own war-declaration against its eaters), **gambling** (maysir — 5:90–91's abomination-pair), **fraud and measure-cheating** (the people of Shuʿayb's signature sin: 11:84–85's "give full measure and weight in justice"; 83:1–3's woe upon the *muṭaffifīn*), **theft, embezzlement, bribery** (2:188's direct command from the same divine mouth: "do not consume your wealth among yourselves falsely, nor proffer it to judges, that you may devour a known portion of people's wealth sinfully"), and every contract whose consent has been tricked, coerced, or misinformed. The offense is measured at the *eat*: *akl al-māl* — consumption of property — because the Book's moral eye fixes wealth's telos: provision; the false-taken dinar feeds its taker only as illusion — khabīth — and the Prophet's own inventory seals the file:

> *"The flesh grown from the unlawful — the Fire has first claim to it."* (al-Tirmidhī 616; from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah — among the standing hadiths of the market-sermons; and Muslim's parallel from Jābir on the supplicant with disheveled hair: *"his food is unlawful, his drink unlawful... how then shall he be answered?"* — Muslim 1015)

**Illā an Takūna Tijāratan ʿan Tarāḍin Minkum: Consent, the Soul of Lawful Trade**

The verse then answers its own ban with the lawful road in five words — *illā an takūna tijāratan ʿan tarāḍin minkum* — "except that it be commerce by mutual consent among you": *tijārah*, open trade, *ʿan tarāḍ* — *upon mutual contentment* — the word tarāḍī from *riḍā*, the pleasure of consent — the commentators deriving from this tiny circumstantial clause the entire law of valid sale: offer-acceptance without coercion, fraud-free, substance-known — al-Ṭabarī's authorities — Ibn ʿAbbās' school at their head — took *tarāḍ* as the sine qua non that *bāṭil* lacks: what is wrested, swindled, or concealed-defective never met *riḍā*. Al-Qurṭubī hereby grounds pillars of the fiqh of transactions — gharar's reduction, option-cooling (*khiyār al-majlis*, from the hadith: "the two parties of a sale hold option until they part" — al-Bukhārī 2119; Muslim 1531/1532), and the Prophet's blessed dua for the honest trader:

> *"God has mercy on the man who is easy when he sells, easy when he buys, and easy when he claims his due."* (al-Bukhārī 2076, from Jābir)

And beneath *consent* the Book plants a soul *within* trade that law alone cannot manufacture: marketplace-love — commerce between people who deal as brothers — as the hadith again shaped it: the two traders are the two friends till they separate honestly.

**Wa Lā Taqtulū Anfusakum: Self-Killing and Brother-Killing in One Command**

The verse's second prohibition — *wa lā taqtulū anfusakum* — "and slay not yourselves" — the commentators read in its blessed breadth, three mutually-supporting senses standing in the tradition from Ibn ʿAbbās's school on: (1) *slay not one another* — your *anfus* comprising your own community-body, so that the murdered Muslim's blood is *self*-blood of the ummah (al-Ṭabarī's first reading, coeval with vv. 92–93's with vv. 92–93 on the believer-slayer's doom and 17:33's "slay not the soul God has forbidden except by right"); (2) *slay not your own souls* — suicide flatly — directly barred: the life-breath is God's deposit, unlawful at one's own hand as at another's — and the hadith-collection stands terrifyingly explicit here: Thābit ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk's treaty-story: "Cursed is he who kills himself with iron — his eternal punishment at Hell with iron forever in his hand" (al-Bukhārī 1363, Muslim 110 — the standing text); and the wounded man of the Khaybar-campaign who impatient of pain finished himself with his sword: *"God said: My servant hastened before Me to his soul; I have forbidden him Paradise"* (al-Bukhārī 1363; Muslim 111, from Abū Hurayrah — the exact wording of the qudsi sentence); (3) the subtler derivative the the ascetics treasured from the Sufi commentators: do not *kill your souls* through sin's slow strangulation — sin also a self-killing (the killing of the spirit), like ākil-māl, the inward consumption — three warnings drawn in one phrase.

**Inna Allāha Kāna Bikum Raḥīman: Why the Severe Sentence Ends Soft**

Then the mercy-seal whose deep placement the commentators never stop wondering at: *inna Allāha kāna bikum raḥīman* — "truly God has ever been Merciful toward you" — following bans as grave as fraudulent eating and bloodshed: the mercy is *in the forbidding* itself — for a community permitted to eat each other and slay each other consumes itself. Al-Qurtubī's own summary holds the theological register precisely: God's statutes around wealth and blood are mercy-architecture; the verses immediately adjacent (v. 30's fire-warning to the defiant; v. 31's absolution-promise to the avoiding) complete the mercy-proof-balance — covenant-limits *itself* being divine care. Thus the marketplace and the blood-price were placed, by this twenty-ninth verse of the chapter, forever inside the shrine of mercy: for the honest traders and alive bodies of an ummah that stops eating each other, life itself becomes a masjid-canopy — *wealth neither devoured nor devourer; souls neither killed nor squandered; and over both, the Merciful watching His own mercy at work in His law.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:30

> **And whosoever does that in enmity and injustice, We shall cause him to burn in a Fire; and that is easy for God.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Man Yafʿal Dhālika: The Sentence Clause That Follows the Mercy**

The law of v. 29 — wealth not consumed falsely, souls not slain — ends in that verse's astonishing mercy-seal, *God is ever Merciful toward you*; and the very next sentence stands in the deliberate anatomy of legislation: *wa man yafʿal dhālika ʿudwānan wa ẓulman fa-sawfa nuṣlīhi nārā* — "whoever does that, in enmity and injustice, We shall roast him in a Fire": the promise of mercy guarded by the sword-edge of threat, so that the lightened law of v. 28 would never be read as fiction or the mercy of v. 29 as license. Al-Ṭabarī's register of the pronoun *dhālika* — "that" — is decisive for the whole juristic architecture: it reaches back to the verse's *two* great prohibitions together — the false-eating of property and the slaying of souls — and many commentators extend it further to *the sum of the established forbiddance in the pericope* (v. 29's two majors, with the orphan-embezzlement and indecency chapters still neighbor-standing) — the verse thus functioning as the seal of penalty upon the entire first legislative slab of the sūrah, from orphan to marketplace-marriage, an architecture no attentive reciter can miss.

**ʿUdwānan wa Ẓulman: The Pair That Doubles the Indictment**

The two accusatives of manner — *ʿudwānan wa ẓulman* — "in enmity and injustice" — rank among the Book's formula-pairs of aggravated guilt, and the commentators parse the doubling with the precision its Lawgiver demands: *ʿudwān*, enmity-transgression — overstepping into the property and blood that another also breathes behind, the trespass *against the neighbor*; *ẓulm*, injustice — the misplacement of thing from its right, trespass *against the order* — so that the verse damns the deed under two arraignments: aggression against persons, disorder against God. Al-Rāzī's reading of the pair is worth its courtroom care: *ʿudwān* is the *intention-in-motion* — the hostile spirit that *meant* the crossing — *ẓulm* the deed *as legally misordered* — so that no defense survives the pair: neither "I never meant" (the enmity supplies the meaning), nor "it was accidental" (the injustice fixes the deed). The commentators of the occasions found the pair exact to the first audience's behavior — the the Ansari faction-disputes and the Jāhiliyya blood-tempers, wealth-grudges waked at every distribution — the verse teaching them in one breath: God seals His law's door with the the with both the motive and the measure.

**Sa-Nuṣlīhi Nāran: The Fire-Clause of Specific Application**

*Fa-sawfa nuṣlīhi nāran* — "We shall broil him in Fire" — the verb *aṣlā*, to roast against flame-direct, from the same image-set as v. 10's orphan-eaters' broiling and 4:56's skins renewed for flaming — chosen for the sharpest tactile force: not merely entering fire but roasting at it — the verb of spit-contact that nothing in the Book mitigates afterward. And the the law's wisdom in appending the clause just here, the commentators of the schools observed through generations: *threats of specific fire-clauses attach traditionally to gravest sins* — Ibn ʿAbbās's kabaʾir-counting principle stands this way: whatever God threatened with His fire, cursed, or apportioned a fixed doom, belongs to the majors — so that v. 30 itself is listed among the evidences the early doctors used to catalog the kabāʾir: consuming-by-fraud, slaying, and orphan-devouring all grade within the seal's range.

**Wa Kāna Dhālika ʿAlā Allāhi Yasīran: The Ease of Omnipotence as Deterrent**

The verse's darkness-clause closes at last on the terrifying theology of *ease*: *wa kāna dhālika ʿalā Allāhi yasīrā* — "and that, for God, is easy": the deterrent-word of the Book's God-address to the armed and the confident: your walls, your cash, your alliances shall not add one atom to the difficulty of your broiling — the doing is *yasīr*, light — and the righteousness-minded commentators (al-Qurṭubī pre-eminently here) hear the clause's counter-melody for the believing pair of ears: *God's ease is also in the reward-gate* — for the faithful guardian and honest trader, heaven is equally effort-free for Him — the chapter's fire-reference recurring at v. 55's *kafā*, where the *sufficiency of Hell* balances balances ablangs of threat and refuge. The Muslim reader exits vv. 29–31's trinity as from a courtroom where all three words were spoken: *fear*, *mercy*, *appointment* — and the statute-table of verses 14–31 stands sealed at its pivot-point: wealth's lanes fenced, lives inviolate, each sealed by broiling and forgiveness — and the hearer relieved into the paired safer door that opens immediately after: the absolution-clause of v. 31, the very next recited sentence, whereby *avoid, and be forgiven* — mercy as always stationed nearest the threat.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:31

> **If you shun the grave sins that you are forbidden, We shall absolve you of your evil deeds and cause you to enter at a noble gate.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Kabāʾir and Sayyiʾāt: The Two Ledgers of the Record-Books**

The adjacent-threat of v. 30 now gives way to one of the Muslim's standing promises-of-relief, and the first sister in Ibn ʿAbbās's canon of this sūrah's eight mercy-verses — *in tajtanibū kabāʾira mā tunhawna ʿanhu nukaffir ʿankum sayyiʾātikum wa nudkhilkum mudkhalan karīmā* — "if you shun the major sins you have been forbidden, We shall absolve you of your evil deeds and enter you by a noble entrance": the Book holding out, to the community it has just finished fencing around with fire-clauses, a treaty-structure of staggering generosity: **avoid the majors, and the minors are struck off**. The commentators at once set about *defining the registers*, for the Book nowhere prints the list — and the tradition's reportage here forms its own garden of studying: al-Ṭabarī records the Companion-generations' differing counts — ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib's list of seven (ascribing partners to God; killing the soul unlawfully; slandering the chaste; consuming the orphan's wealth; usury; fleeing the battlefield; and the peculiar item *returning to Bedouinry after the settlement*, seeing the settled Muslim life as covenant) — with variants adding false testimony, undutifulness to parents, despairing of God's mercy, sorcery; and the Prophet's own census, kept in the two Sittings: the four-catalogue *"the greatest of the great sins (akbar al-kabāʾir): associating with God, undutifulness to parents, killing the soul, and the false oath (al-yamīn al-ghamūs)"* (al-Bukhārī 2511, 6675 many; Muslim 87) beside the and the seven-destroyers canon (mūbiqāt: shirk, sorcery, soul, ribā, orphan, flight, slander — al-Bukhārī 2766; Muslim 89 — attached above at v. 2). The line of doctrine the schools then settled: majors are *whatever God has attached a fixed ḥadd, a threat of fire, a curse, or a closing of the gates* — the sayyiʾāt, the slips-of-day, the lapses of temper and eye — with the with Ibn ʿAbbās' own memorial word giving the believer his perpetual crowbar: *"no sin is minor while persisted in; and no sin is major with repentance following."*

**Nukaffir ʿAnkum: Expiation as the Book's Weight-Word**

The promise-verb — *nukaffir* — is from the Book's great root *k-f-r*: *kaffāra*, the covering-over, erasure — God's own verb for washed guilt — and its role in the verse is structural: the absolution is an *act of God upon the ledger* (cf. 3:193's "expunge our sins"; 2:271's "and expiation of your sins" for open giving; 2:271-2's word) — not the minor-sinner's flimsy earning but a *divine bookkeeping-off*, which is why many commentators — with the deep law-mind al-Qurṭubī on the clauses — taught it as *by His bounty*, the avoidance-of-majors itself no equivalence of worth but *a condition He honored*, like the ḥadīth's prayer-promise it echoes full-circle with echoes full-formed in the Prophet's own mosque-prophesy — Prime among its ḥadīth-sisters:

> *"The five prayers, and Friday to Friday, and Ramadan to Ramadan, are expiations (kaffārah) for what is between them — so long as the major sins are avoided."* (Muslim 233, from Abū Hurayrah — same covenant-formula, same condition)

so that v. 31 is the treaty-text and the several-fasts-and-prayers canons are its named instruments: expiation *runs continuously* through the believing week upon the one stipulation the verse seals in bold — *kabāʾir abstained*.

**Mudkhalan Karīman: The Entrance as Honor-Gift**

Then the clause of destination — *wa nudkhilkum mudkhalan karīman* — "We shall enter you by a noble entrance": the phrase is read in the text's own two channels, both drawn by the commentators forward into Paradise: *mudkhal* as *the gate of entrance* — the gate described as noble: dignified, untroubled filing past the benches of reproach into the Mansions — and as *the entry-state itself* — an arriving honored and unblamed. Both mean one beatitude: the abstainer-of-majors not squeaking past the border but *welcomed* — and the angel-walī testimony from al-Bukhārī's and Muslim's hadiths of arrival — "peace upon you; you were pure; so enter it, abiding" (39:73's peer-verse) — is the day-scene the verse promises the steady. The theologians of the mercy-schools (al-Rāzī the very chapter here) guard carefully the guard carefully the non-arithmetic of the covenant: not that avoidance *buys* the minors — for God's forgiveness is never barter — but that the Lord of the ledger *honors the will of avoidance with the covering of the rest*: *faḍl*, bounty, from start to finish.

**Between Despair and Insolence: Where the Muslim's Fiqh-of-Heart Lives**

The verse's design teaches the believer exactly where to stand: *above despair* (the minors are manageable; God carries them), *below insolence* (the majors are non-negotiable; you have been warned) — the standing-position of the middle community. The Sufi commentators, whose tradition runs long at this clause (al-Qushayrī and the rest of the older masters), carried the clause one layer deeper: the ultimate *kabīrah* is whatever veils from God — shirk's last dress being the self-regarding soul — and the Rābiʿian maxim sounding beneath it: *"your own existence is a sin beside which no sin compares"* — hyperbole of the gnostics, not law — while the street-Qur'an of the verse stays at the register named: grave sins avoided, misdeeds expunged, noble entry achieved. The sūrah from this point moves to internal disputes of roles (vv. 32–36), but the mercy-keystone now stands inspected: the whole of vv. 1–30's severe law closes at v. 31 with an *exit-hall* — the ummah walks into the remaining statutes knowing that the ledger it carries can be washed washed weekly, upon one condition the Lawgiver never blurred: *the majors are not for you.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:32

> **And covet not that by which God has favored some of you above others—unto men a share of what they have earned, and unto women a share of what they have earned—but ask God for His Bounty. Truly God is the Knower of all things.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Umm Salamah's Question: Allowed to Be Asked at Heaven's Desk**

The verse was born of a question the tradition keeps tenderly, a question only a believing woman could ask and only revelation could answer — the occasion-reports (al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr from Mujāhid's chain) fixing it in the Prophet's own house: Umm Salamah, the Prophet's ﷺ wife, reflected upon what the new law and the new army-life had given the men — the double share of inheritance (v. 11), the fortune of the jihād-field, and with them the doubled opportunities for worldly and other-worldly storehouse — and she said in the presence:

> *"O Messenger of God, the men go out to battle and we do not; and they receive two shares of the inheritance — would that we could share in what they obtain of reward!"*

And God answered her with the verse: *wa lā tatamannaw mā faḍḍala Allāhu bihi baʿḍakum ʿalā baʿḍ* — "covet not that by which God has favored some of you above others." The occasion is essential to the verse's meaning: this was no rebuke of an envier's malice — the Prophet's household were not a court of spite — but a *pedagogy over the very question*: the believer, male or female, who notices disparity of *means* is taught where to look instead. Completing it, the companion-revelations — 3:195's *"I waste not the work of a worker among you, male or female"* and 33:35's spread of equal tenfold rewards for each sex's obedience — give Umm Salamah's anxiety the complete divine answer: *spirit wages are paid perfectly; only the instruments differ.* And the wish of the sisters who said "would our burden on the Day be half as theirs, like our share of the estate?" (a saying of the transmitters the Shiʿi collections preserve) received the same lesson: heaven's desk is not a tribunal that takes proportion from commerce in goods.

**Li-l-Rijāli Naṣībun Mimmā-ktasabū: The Earning Arithmetic for Both Sexes**

The verse then re-states the apportioning in the two matched clauses — *li-l-rijāli naṣībun mimmā-ktasabū wa lil-nisāʾi naṣībun mimmā-ktasabna* — "unto the men a share of what they earned, and unto the women a share of what they earned": the *kasb*-word — earning — applied symmetrically to both estates of mankind, ending forever any theory that one sex is the other's is ranked as the other's *share-less* dependent: each *earns*, each is *paid*, by his and her own earning — and the Book's insistence on *mimmā-ktasabū* (from one's earning) turns the discussion from *garments and gold* to *works and wages* — precisely the swap Umm Salamah's question had circled. The commentators (al-Qurṭubī's full tracing) locate the clause's promise: men hear — even your shares must be *earned*; women hear — your works are *seen* in the same arithmetic; and both hear in the wage-theology: no prejudice in heaven's payroll: *mimmā ktasab* — from earnings — not *from sexes.*

**Covet-Not: The Prohibition Targeting the Disease of Comparison**

The command against *tamannī* — wishing, coveting the allotments of others — is the first member of the Book's famous anti-envy corpus, and this verse is its anchoring verse in the law of gendered and provisioned disparity. The commentators identify the disease precisely in the object-form: *mā faḍḍala Allāhu bihi baʿḍakum ʿalā baʿḍ* — *what God Himself has preferred some by* — so the coveting is *a wish against the Distributor* — forbidden because it double-sins: envy of the favored, implicit complaint against the Favorer. Al-Rāzī's kalām-surgical reading carries the carries the clause to the theology of contentment: disparity of provision is *wisdom's artifact*, grounding the world's economy — *by Him are your various grades* (6:165's *darajāt*) — and the believer's task is not to flatten the scales but to sail with his own cargo. The companion-hadith-file of the Prophet's own counsel — the hadith of the envy's ledger:

> *"Be satisfied (iqnaʿ) with what God has apportioned for you, and you will be the richest of people"* (al-Tirmidhī 2305, ḥasan — from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr); and *"Look to those below you [in provision], and not to those above you — it is worthier that you not belittle the blessing of God upon you."* (al-Bukhārī 6490; Muslim 2963 — from Abū Hurayrah)

— these are the verse's two practical rules, standing in the companion-file of the revealed word.

**Wa-sʾalū Allāha min Faḍlihi: The Lawful Desire**

But the statute's mercy holds one desire always open: *wa-sʾalū Allāha min faḍlihi* — "and ask God of His bounty": the door marked *request* is never locked — coveting being barred exactly because asking is available, complaint against distribution being punished exactly by prayer-repair replacing it — the very point the commentators fix: *do not watch your neighbor's tray; lift your hands:* Covet-not belongs to *comparison*; ask-bounty belongs to *petition*. The Prophet's own encouraged formula of this life and the next is the is the brother-reported ḥadīth of general instruction: *"Ask God of His bounty — for He loves to be asked"* (al-Tirmidhī 3384, ḥasan), with groups of the salaf glossing the *faḍl* here as both the provision of of the world and the greater *faḍl* of faith-works in which alone the judgment sits. And the seal — *inna Allāha kāna bi-kulli shayʾin ʿalīma* — Knower of all things — is the court's last stamp on the whole commerce of comparison: He knows *why* each vessel holds its measure; knows how wishes migrate from heart to covenant; and knows the one petition that is always answered at its at its station: ask *Him*, and stop watching the neighbor's plate.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:33

> **To each We have appointed heirs for what parents and kinsfolk leave. Those to whom you have given your oath, give them their share. Truly God is Witness over all things.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa li-Kullin Jaʿalnā Mawālī: Everyone Has His Written Heirs**

The inheritance-architecture opens its last aperture — a verse in the cipher of ancient alliances: *wa li-kullin jaʿalnā mawālī mimmā taraka al-wālidāni wa-l-aqrabūn* — "and for every one We appointed *mawālī* — successor-kin — of what parents and relations leave": *mawālī* — plural of *mawlā*, from the copious root *w-l-y* of nearness, whose branches give the law its vocabulary of heirs, protectors, freedmen, and allies — arrived in this clause at the newest seat of succession: *your heirs are by Us installed*, kin seated by the kinship-bond God assesses — with the commentators of the schools unanimous in the clause's measure: a declarative of the *kin-based inheritance system* now whole — the grave opened, the bonds of blood (and marriage — v. 12's spouses) alone called to the seat — every person born into a written line of succession that no club, no tribe, no friendship-of-oath may rearrange. The al-Qurṭubī's jurists at this sentence never tire of marveling at the clause's floorwork: probate ceased with one line to be a *tribal-revenge* event and became *identity's own settling* — son and daughter, parent and sibling, by God's appointment of each to each.

**Alladhīna ʿAqadat Aymānukum: The Oath-Companies of Ancient Arabia**

Then the verse's difficult second half — *wa-lladhīna ʿaqadat aymānukum fa-ātūhum naṣībahum* — "and those with whom your oaths have compacted — give them their share": the *ʿaqd* of the right-hand — the hand-clasp contract — the pact-brotherhood of the Jāhiliyya and the early days, in which two men — or a man and an an adopted stranger — would swear inheritance-rights mutually: *"your blood is mine, your estate is mine, your avenger is my sword"* — the ḥalīf-inheritance institution, standing beside the Prophet's own *mu'ākhāh*, the brothering between Emigrant and Helper in Madinah's first year (the brothering-reports of al-Bukhārī and Muslim in many channels: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf paired with Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ and refusing Saʿd's offer of half his household, "may God bless you in your family and wealth, show me the market" — al-Bukhārī 2049 — the mu'ākhāh had at its first stage carried a real succession-claim). The commentators of the occasions agree that this verse addresses those *oath-inheritances*, and its ruling depends upon when it fell beside 8:75's *ulū al-arḥām*:

**From Sworn Shares to Blood Shares: The Sunna's Sealing of the Grave's Ledger**

The most weighed doctrine — al-Ṭabarī's and Ibn Kathīr's consolidated voice — holds v. 33 *superseded* in its oath-clause by the definitive ring of 8:75 — *"possessors of wombs are nearer among them in the Book of God"* — inheritance finally confined to the relatives-by-blood: the pact-inheritance of the early brotherhood lapsing with the community's consolidation, so that Saʿd's brother ʿAbd al-Raḥmān took no estate at his death but what kin-law gave. The bridge-readings the tradition also preserved stand beside: (1) the *old* pacts made before the sealing are *honored* — the verse commanding fulfillment of the prior compacts while new ones are barred (Ibn Kathīr's balance-note, with the Shiʿi authorities likewise distinguishing past-honor from future-license); (2) the *share* assigned the oath-companions is read as a share *from the bequest-third* — the testamentary free-third any man may still volunteer to non-heirs — or else as the blood-brotherhood's duties themselves: *support, counsel, vengeance*, the *naṣīb* of alliance honored now by things richer than gold (al-Qurṭubī's reconciliation, the road by which the schools interpret the verse among the *muḥkam* verses while the exact money-right sleeps). Either way the moral-order announced by verses 33-and-8:75 stands forever: *at death, kin come before companions*; at life, the oath-brother was brother indeed. The emigrant-binding did not disintegrate with the grave-law: it became *honor without probate*, affection and *naṣr* without title, the purest brotherhood-money free.

**Inna Allāha Kāna ʿAlā Kulli Shayʾin Shahīdan: The Last Seal of the Grave-Arch**

The verse closes the whole probate-arch (vv. 7–13's seats, v. 33's alliances) with the same Witness-attribute the marriage-pericope's clauses also carried: *inna Allāha kāna ʿalā kulli shayʾin shahīdā* — "God is ever Witness over all things": the Shahīd-seal where the sūrah's recurring *shahādah*-vocabulary enforces an audit of the very materials this law cleans: *kinship*, the making of whose claims is a thing only God sees whole: actual mothers' lineage, the family-tree of men, whether the hidden claimant grieves or the cloak of the pact-brother has been honored true. The commentators of the pericope remark that no other *attribute* could better close the marriage-plus-inheritance complex than the attribute of *witnessing*, for both bodies of law live and die by what occurred in *un-filmed* rooms — the wedding bed, the deathbed — thin as walls that only God sees through. In this the reader now stands at the sūrah's great hinge: the *family's* inner laws (vv. 1–33) have been sealed; the *household's* daily weather — the qawwāmūn-universe of breadward duty, arbitration, and iḥsān (vv. 34–36) — comes forward next, precisely in the same spirit: laws that must be *lived, unseen*, under the eye of the Watching One.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:34

> **Men are the upholders and maintainers of women by virtue of that in which God has favored some of them above others and by virtue of their spending from their wealth. Therefore the righteous women are devoutly obedient, guarding in [their husbands'] absence what God has guarded. As for those from whom you fear discord and animosity, admonish them, then leave them in their beds, then strike them. Then if they obey you, seek not a way against them. Truly God is Exalted, Great.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Qawwāmūn: The Leader-Steward of the Household**

The most debated sentence in the sūrah begins with the Book's own loaded participle: *al-rijālu qawwāmūna ʿalā al-nisāʾ* — "men are *qawwāmūn* over women": *qawwām*, the intensive of *qāma ʿalā* — standing over, standing *for* — the one who stands guard, administers, and above all *stands the cost*: the standing-provider, standing-guardian, standing-bearer of the family's affairs. The whole classical tradition from al-Ṭabarī through al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr reads the word at the *household* level — the man as the accountable head of his family — with the two grounds the verse itself immediately pledges: *bi-mā faḍḍala Allāhu baʿḍahum ʿalā baʿḍin wa bi-mā anfaqū min amwālihim* — "because of what God has favored some of them over others with, and because they spend of their wealth." The two grounds divide precisely: the *first favor* — the greater estate assigned men in the inheritance-architecture of vv. 11–12 — and the *spending* — the mahr of v. 4, the nafaqah-command of house, food, and clothing — al-Qurṭubī's jurist's-eye fixing the doctrine in the sentence most quoted from his commentary: the qawwāmūnah *is staked to performance* — he who withholds provision has no standing over her (the Shāfiʿīs and Mālikīs binding authority to maintenance the same) — so that the verse reads, by its own syntax, not as a coronation but as *an employment-contract under God*: leadership *because of responsibility*; and the title's much-quoted danger dissolves when the first pillar of the favor-word is genuinely read as *provision*, not person. The learned modern redactions — from the salaf-mindful — therefore never lose the household *function* in the in the now-present debate: the Book made the man*answerable* *for*, not merely *master of*, and tied his claim exactly to his spending-string of law.

**Qānitāt Ḥāfiẓāt: The Righteous Wife Under the Verse**

The reciprocal virtue runs parallel: *fa-l-ṣāliḥātu qānitātun ḥāfiẓātun li-l-ghaybi bi-mā ḥafiẓa Allāh* — "the righteous women are devout-ones, guarding the hidden [in their husbands' absence] by God's guarding": *qānitāt*, standing-devoted — whose every Qur'anic use otherwise points at divine devotion (2:238; 66:12 — Mary of ʿImrān its queen) — the majority of the tradition taking it here as devotion to God flowing into household-faithfulness (Ibn Kathīr's middle-way: *devout to God, therefore dutiful in the house*), and *ḥāfiẓāt li-l-ghayb* — guarding the unseen: the Prophet's own dictum defining the wife who pleased him:

> *"The best of women is she who, when you look at her, pleases you; when you command her, obeys you; and when you are absent, guards you in herself and your property."* (al-Nasāʾī among the Sunan, from Ibn ʿUmar)

— *ḥāfiẓah* defined by the Prophet himself as the keeper of *nafs and māl* — chastity and stewardship in the husband's absence, the exact two treasuries the qawwām bears in presence. The couplet of roles is thus not master and servant but the two-sided guardianship of a house — his outward accountability for provision and protection, her inward guardianship of home, honor, and and assets: each a *ḥāfiẓ* / *qawwām* of the side the other cannot reach — and its aim not hierarchy for its own sake but the tranquility the Book names *sakīnah* at 30:21: *garments to each other* (2:187), *mawaddah and raḥmah* between them.

**Nushūz: The Crisis-Protocol, Fenced at Every Door**

Then the verse's storm-clause: *wa-llātī takhāfūna nushūzahunna fa-ʿiẓūhunna wa-hjurūhunna fī al-maḍājiʿi wa-ḍribūhunna* — "those from whom you fear nushūz: admonish them, then leave them in beds, then strike them." *Nushūz* — rising-up, from *nashaza*, the raised ground — is the state of *declared, ongoing defiance and contempt*: the wife's flagrant rising against the legitimate structure — al-Ṭabarī and the authorities distinguishing it from momentary strife and from any dislike (v. 19 covers mere dislike by *patience*), and the tradition underlining its *relational*, not merely legal, register in 4:128-130's reciprocals where the husband's nushūz opens the wife's own remedies — the protocol's rungs then ascending by obligation-made-mercy: (1) *ʿiẓūhunna* — admonish: counsel and reminder — words, only words, first; (2) *wa-hjurūhunna fī al-maḍājiʿi* — withdrawal *in the beds*: the bed-fellowship's suspension, *inside the house* (the Prophet's own instruction marking its limit: "not leaving the not abandoning her save in the house" — Sunan-reporting's discipline in Abū Dāwūd 2142 at the ḥajj-sermon's series, *"clothe and feed them, strike not the face, do not revile, and abandon not save in the house"*), time and pride both given room to melt; (3) *wa-ḍribūhunna* — and strike: the third rung hedged by the whole law-tradition in hands the in the hedges the tradition never tired of citing: *ghayr mubarriḥ* — non-injurious (the ḥadīth-standard in Muslim 1218's farewell-sermon register); *ghayr muʾaththir* — mark-less (the gloss of the early police of every school); not the face (Abū Dāwūd 2142 again — the face singled out absolutely); al-Shāfiʿī's own maxim counting the step as *makrūh*, near-forbidden by distaste; Ibn ʿAbbās's antique image of the twig-*siwāk* — the token by which severity could never exceed a signal; and the Prophet's own body, the ummah's walking tafsīr — "the best of you will not strike" (Abū Dāwūd 2149's wording), and never in his life did he hit wife or servant (Muslim 2328, ʿĀʾishah's own report). The classical record is unanimous — the tradition never licensed violence: it *narrowed* a violence-ridden world to a no-pain tap, fenced first by sermons and silences and the Prophet's perfect absence of the act.

**Occasion, Wisdom, and the Clause That Closes the Door**

The verse's own occasion anchors this reading in the Prophet's particular mercy: the reports (al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī's chains, Ibn Kathīr with the fullest choreography) remember the woman of the Ansār — Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ's wife, struck by her husband — coming with her people to the Prophet ﷺ; his first instinct was *qiṣāṣ* — retaliation against the husband — and God's verse stayed him: *the Prophet said, "I desired something, and God desired something else, and what God desires is best."* — himself then placing the three-rung protocol, in which the lawyers see the law's own medicine: *remedy, not vengeance* — each rung designed to *stop* before the next (bed-separation re-heals; the tap signals; reconciliation follows) and the whole section aimed at *avoiding divorce* (v. 35's arbitration-system arriving immediately as the institutional pair). The seal then bars the house-door itself: *fa-in aṭaʿnakum fa-lā tabghū ʿalayhinna sabīlan* — "if they obey you, seek no way against them": no resenting-tactics, no reopened files, no accountancy of old wrongs — with the eternal with the attribute-seal *inna Allāha kāna ʿaliyyan kabīrā* — "God is Exalted, Great" — warning the towering husband that his station itself stands beneath a Station higher and greater: strength shown to the weaker is measured by the Greatest of all; and the qawwām's and the qawwām bears his office under that exalted review. The Muslim household read beneath this verse is finally and always a *reconciliation-architecture*: its hinges counsel, withdrawal, and the feigned strike; its summit the arbiters of v. 35; its seal the Knowledge of the Exalted — with mercy laid at every rung, and the Book set over all: *the prophets' house, the swordless house, the listening house.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:35

> **And if you fear a breach between the two, then appoint an arbiter from his people and an arbiter from her people. If they desire reconciliation, God will bring about agreement between them. Truly God is Knowing, Aware.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Shiqāq: The Breach the House Cannot Hold Alone**

The reconciliation-architecture the sūrah built around marriage now adds its final and most somber chamber — for v. 34 treated the wife's nushūz and vv. 128–130 will treat the husband's — and here the case is *between the two*: *wa in khiftum shiqāqa baynihimā fa-bʿathū ḥakaman min ahlihi wa ḥakaman min ahlihā* — "and if you fear a breach between the two, then send an arbiter from his people and an arbiter from her people." *Shiqāq* — the split, the tear — from the root of the from *shiq*: splitting, shearing of a thing once one — names marriage-crisis at the stage where within-household resources are spent, where neither nushūz-rung nor ʿiyāshirunna-counsel can reach across the room anymore: the tear *between* them being itself named, so that the community knows the case now involves *two souls*, two rights, two versions, and can no longer be treated from one side of the bed. And the imperative *fa-bʿathū* — then *send*: the community appoints — the verb a mission-verb — arbitration as the the ummah's *public duty*, not merely a private expedient: the marriage of two believers is *social property*, its repair the assembly's work — and Islamic fiqh built from this tiny verse its family-court system, the qāḍī appointing the two arbiters where families cannot field their own (al-Mālikī and Shāfiʿī placements into the standing marriage-court laws of the mujtahid schools).

**Ḥakaman min Ahlihi wa Ḥakaman min Ahlihā: Two Arbiters from the Two Houses**

The instrument is exquisitely domestic: *one arbiter from his people, and one from hers* — not one impartial stranger, but two *partial* friends, one picked from each clan: and the commentators have always loved the wisdom: (1) knowledge *of* the married pair's natures lives inside each house — where a judge sees papers, the cousin sees the life; (2) each party's advocacy is *secured within the room*, so no one feels massacred by a stranger-ministry; (3) each clan is thereby *invested in the salvage*, since its own honor-bearer sits at the table — and the sentence flows most mercifully toward settlement, since both houses lose face if it fails. al-Qurṭubī's al-Qurṭubī's jurisprudence works the full fiqh from it: the arbiter must be *just, sane, knowing*, and of kin when kin are fit; the two function by *agreement* — and (his registering of the majority's law) may not separate without authorization, while a strong school — with ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib's own early ruling behind it — grants the pair empowering if delegated in advance: the empowered ḥakamayn (two arbiters) may *dissolve* where salvation is impossible — setting the instrument as both *marriage-mechanic and judge of termination* in commission from the pair themselves.

**In Yurīdā Iṣlāḥan: The Condition of the Two Wills**

Then God's remarkable promise, attached to the arbiters' own intention: *in yurīdā iṣlāḥan yuwaffiqi Allāhu baynahumā* — "if the two desire reconciliation, God will bring about agreement between them": the conditional points at the arbiters' wishing alone in one reading (al-Ṭabarī's register), at the spouses' too in its balanced extension (the mainstream take) — and either way heaven's law of the of mediation is disclosed: *God's own help (tawfīq) rides with the honest intention of making peace*. The clause thereby constitutes one of the Book's perpetual graces for every ministry of people in crisis — two persons sit as healers of a marriage and God's aid descends upon the session *according to intention*: God joins the mending; God un-joins the farce — the commentators' treasury of cases gathering the evidence: spouses brought to arbitration expecting tragedy leaving reconciled where the arbiters believed the two in wills as much as their own. The *in*-conditional is a whole doctrine in itself: *God does not endow success to someone who to one who undertakes what his heart does not want.*

ʿAlīman Khabīrā: Knowing and Aware, at the Arbitration-Room's Doors**

The seal comes with the attribute-pair the sūrah has already used at v. 26 — at this seal — *inna Allāha kāna ʿalīman khabīran* — Knowing, Deeply-Aware — and the marriage-crisis section cannot in fact imagine a more fitting gatekeeper's double-title: *ʿalīm*, knowing the inside-of-natures — which party is truth-cloaked, which grievance just; *khabīr*, aware of what chambers hide — the skillful accuser, the tearful manipulator, the *private* nushūz that never reaches policemen — and the attribute-pair thereby posts heaven over the arbitration-room itself: the human arbiters may be tricked, but the God of the crisis-verses is not — every speech-cluster of a warring pair is filed in the open book of His khabr. The readers, man and woman, then read the whole v. 34–35 institution in the direction the seal orders: the qawwāmūn's discipline, the arbiter's office — all are watched all are watched; and the last hope for the house at war is also God's own attendance upon the honest conciliating intent, so that any family perishing around us may yet be rescued by the un-hidden labor of two sincere arbiters — beneath the eye of the Knowing, the Aware, and behind behind it the promise: *if they desire reconciliation — God will bring agreement.*


---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:36

> **Worship God, and ascribe not partners unto Him. And be virtuous toward parents and kinsfolk, toward orphans and the indigent, toward the neighbor who is of kin and the neighbor who is not of kin, toward the companion at your side and the traveler, and toward those whom your right hands possess. Truly God loves not one who is a vainglorious boaster,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa-bʿudū Allāha wa Lā Tushrikū Bihi Shayʾan: The Vertical Axis First**

After the household-architecture, the sūrah plants its creed-pillar mid-l mid-law with the grand * with the two commands that govern every clause that follows: *waʿbudū Allāha wa lā tushrikū bihi shayʾan* — "worship God, and ascribe nothing as partner to Him": *ʿibādah*, total devoted service — from *ʿabd*, servant, the self-surrender that is worship's root — and the absolute *shayʾan*, *a thing* — nothing, however small: no icon, no saint-share, no self-share, no star. The commentators note the verse's placement: it is the sūrah's central axis (the ~72nd verse of 176), and, and the two half-surahs of law turn upon it — for without tawḥīd all the orphan-statutes and justice-commands would be *ethics*; with it they are *worship*. Al-Rāzī draws the structural the thread: what God commands next (iḥsān through seven human classes) flows *from* worship of Him, for service to people is here declared the immediate exterior of service to God — the second clause obeyed *because* of the first, the whole Book resolving its law into the two imperatives of 4:36 — worship the Creator; beautify conduct to the created — the same twin-pillars the Prophet's own compressed: *"the best of you is the best to his family"* extended at last to all mankind.

**Wa bi-l-Wālidayni Iḥsānan: Immediately After God, the Parents**

The first addressees of the iḥsān-command are always the parents — *wa bi-l-wālidayni iḥsānan* — and the Book's architecture of the clause is itself an unbroken sermon assembled from its five parallel planks (2:83; 6:151; 17:23–24; 31:14; 46:15): *right after the shirk-prohibition, the parents* — no other creature ever placed between these two clauses, not prophets, not angels. Ibn Kathīr's commentary at this verse's sister (17:23) carries the tradition's deepest note, the celebrated report of Ibn Masʿūd:

> *"I asked the Prophet ﷺ: which deed is most beloved to God? He said: prayer in its time. I said: then which? He said: goodness to parents (birr al-wālidayn). I said: then which? He said: striving in the way of God. He (Ibn Masʿūd) said: these he told me, and had I asked more, he would have given more."* (al-Bukhārī 527; Muslim 85)

— *iḥsān*, from *ḥusn*, beauty — naming thereby not mere non-harm but *beautiful conduct*: gentled speech, lightening of their affairs, patience with their age, and remembrance of their dead with prayer and release of their debts — all this the Book then binds with half a with the List it now spreads around the compass — *kinsfolk; orphans; the indigent (masākīn, the stilled-by-want); the near neighbor; the distant neighbor; the companion beside; the wayfarer; and the owned*: a concentric outpouring of charity from the nearest blood to the uttermost dependent — so that no human being on earth falls outside its arc.

**The Two Neighbors, the Companion, the Wayfarer, and the Owned**

The compass-points deserve their separate naming, for the Prophet expanded them into standing libraries of instruction: *the near neighbor* — al-jār dhī al-qurbā, kin-neighbor, holding thereby *three* rights (neighbor, kin, co-religionist per the finest gloss) — and *the far neighbor* — al-jār al-junub, distant or alien — on whom the hadith of this office is unrelenting:

> *"Gabriel kept counseling me about the neighbor until I thought he would make him an heir; whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest; whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him not harm his neighbor."* (al-Bukhārī 6014–16; Muslim 2624, from Abū Shurayḥ and Abū Hurayrah)

*the companion at your side* — al-ṣāḥib bi-l-janb — the seated partner, the travel-mate, the wife at the commentators' chief reading (al-Qurṭubī's remembering the married life after the whole pericope), and any beside-one in the company or the road; *ibn al-sabīl*, the son of the road — the stranded traveler, whose hunger and distance make him God's special ward (the Prophet's repeated practice, lodging strangers at the mosque's suffah-benches as the standing office of Islam) — and *mā malakat aymānukum*, those your right hands possess — the owned of the old world, over whom the sūrah ended every hierarchy with iḥsān, the Prophet's own last-days admonition still hot — *"your brothers whom God placed in your hands... do not burden them with what overwhelms them, and if you do, help them"* (al-Bukhārī 30; Muslim 1661). Across the whole register runs one engine: *iḥsān* — beauty without account-book — unaccountable kindness flowing down every gradient of power.

**Man Kāna Mukhtālan Fakhūrā: The Two Nouns of the Self-Viewer**

The seal names the character God does *not* love, in two antique nouns of intensity: *mukhtāl* — from *ikhtiyāl*, strutting, gait-arrogance — the one puffed by his own self-assessment; *fakhūr* — the loud self-celebrator, from *fakhr*, boast, vaunting over others with the goods of his hand — the pairing deliberate: concealed swagger of the interior, public swagger of the tongue — both God-loathed in the Book's long roster (57:23's *God loves not any vainglorious boaster* — same doublet; 31:18's "do not turn your cheek from people..."). The commentators connect the seal to the verse's own logic of placement: iḥsān-downward — kindness exactly into the weaker classes — is the precise antidote of the two named diseases: for strutting and boasting both feed on withholding before inferiors, on the posture of *looking down* at orphan and wayfarer and slave — hence the Book ordered its care-register *descending*, and closed with the two sins that that grade exactly power abused: *arrogance of heart, boasting of mouth.* The believer has now his full map in one verse — worship God alone, and beautify toward everyone beneath beneath his reach — and divine love is withheld from one character only: the man who made his rank a mirror. *That alone God does not love.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:37

> **Those who are miserly and enjoin miserliness upon the people and conceal what God has bestowed upon them of His bounty — We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment,**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Yabkhalūna wa Yaʾmurūna al-Nāsa bi-l-Bukhl: The Double Miserliness**

The previous verse's iḥsān-compass meets its inverted portrait in two antique greed-words: *alladhīna yabkhalūna wa yaʾmurūna al-nāsa bi-l-bukhl* — "those who are miserly and enjoin miserliness upon the people": *bukhl*, from *b-kh-l*, withholding what is due — the closed hand — and its first category is plain enough, the stingy man; but the second is morally darker and much rarer in any scripture: *the miserliness-propagandist* — the man who admires his own vice so much that he makes a school of it (the Prophet's two-eyed diagnosis standing beside:

> *"Beware of stinginess, for stinginess destroyed those before you: it commanded them to miserliness so they were miserly; it commanded them to sever the womb-ties so they severed; it commanded them to obscenity so they committed it."* (Abū Dāwūd 1698 — narrated by Abū Hurayrah)

— the chain the hadith uncovers precisely our three: personal greed clenched fist; the teaching of greed severing kin; and obscenity as its third its summit-offshoot). Al-Rāzī's psychology of the double sin notes the ruin's structure: the ordinary miser harms only himself, and the preache d-miser corrupts the world — for the vice *transmitted* becomes a custom, the custom a culture, culture a doom; consequently the therefore the Lawgiver's vice-list is ascending here — individual theft punished less than the theft-schools of men; and the miser-preacher, by recruiting others into his closed circle, is judged as causing the as causing the stifling of iḥsān across generations, guilt multiplying in chains without increase of his burden *beyond* likeness (cf. 16:25 — they bear their burdens in full together with the burdens of those they misguide).

**Wa Yaktumūna Mā Ātāhum Allāhu min Faḍlih: Concealing the Bounty — Wealth or Word**

The third clause — *wa yaktumūna mā ātāhum Allāhu min faḍlih* — "and conceal what God has bestowed on them of His bounty" — drew the tradition into its own two classical excavations: (1) the immediate-context excavation (al-Rāzī's context-rule: verses thirty-six through thirty-nine are *spending-talk*, one unbroken treasury-sermon) reads the concealed bounty as *wealth* — the hoarded fortune, the deductible-right never told, the poor-neighbor kept from every ledger — and al-Qurṭubī's law-eye deriving the whole zakāh-machinery behind it: *whoever holds wealth has God's bounty; whoever conceals it has joined the miser-ranks* — with the wealth-flow's the wealth-flow's theology unpacked at 9:34–35 (hoarders' gold branded to their foreheads in Fire) and 3:180's collar of collar readied for the Day of Resurrection: *let not those who are miserly with God's bounty think it is better for them*; and (2) the report-backed excavation (al-Ṭabarī's chains, al-Zamakhsharī's register) reads bounty as *knowledge* — the verse an early Madinan arrow at the scripture-concealers among the People of the Book who hid what their Torah told of the Prophet ﷺ: *they concealed their bounty* in the very sense 2:42, 140 and 2:159 charge against them — God inscribing both treasuries in the single faḍl-word since Heaven's logic made no distinction: *goods given are a trust; knowledge given is a greater one; and both perish only in concealment.* The two excavations do not quarrel — each is the Book's plenary style, treasures of hand and treasures of tongue taxed under the same Name.

**Li-l-Kāfirīna ʿAdhāban Muhīnan: Why the Misers Enter Under "the Disbelievers"**

The seal's horror, on first glance, overshoots its target: *wa aʿtadnā li-l-kāfirīna ʿadhāban muhīnan* — "We have prepared for the *disbelievers* a humiliating punishment" — where the verse spoke of misers — and the commentators drew the single entire doctrine the sūrah repeatedly encodes: *bukhl at its root-state is kufr* — stinginess perfected amounts to disbelief, for the miser has made the gold his trusted god (the seven-destroyers hadith of v. 31 already placing *stinginess with what God gave* — * the *shuhḥ* exactly beside sorcery and blood). The Prophet's widow-report ties even ordinary petty greed to faith-exit in the famous indication indicated beneath this clause's branch: *"the miser does not enter the Garden"* (a report circulating in the Musnad channels), and al-Bukhārī's great theology-book (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 11 — the Kitāb al-ʿIlm related register) echoing from the companions' tongues the doctrine's understanding: sins sins of *that seed* — stinginess, deception, betrayal — were ranged under * their doom the doom of the kāfirūn because their root is the same — *dis-trusting God's provision: the miser refuses to believe that what goes out of his hand returns seventy-fold from God's* (2:261); so the withholding hand is, inside, an unbelieving heart: hence Hell-ward twin to God's statute for partner-setters. *Wayl to him who died owning* — the old proverb of the salaf — and the Garden belongs to the open hand.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:38

> **And those who spend their wealth in order to be seen by the people and believe neither in God nor in the Last Day. Whosoever has Satan for a companion, what an evil companion has he!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Riyāʾ: Spending for Eyes, Not for God**

The sūrah's treasury-sermon passes from the hoarders to their polished twins: *wa alladhīna yunfiqūna amwālahum riʾāʾa al-nās* — "and those who spend their wealth to be seen by the people": *riyāʾ*, from *ruʾyah*, sight — the alms aimed at eyesight rather than heaven, a coin traveling upward that is deflected down by the almsgiver's own by the almsgiver's own aim: given *for* the onlooker, so the First Witness gets no claim in it. The Prophet's own deepest warnings converge on this single line:

> *"What I fear most for you is the lesser shirk." They said: What is the lesser shirk, Messenger of God? He said: *Riyāʾ*. God the Exalted will say on the Day rewards are meted out for deeds: Go to those for whom you made a show in the world and see whether you find with them any recompense."* (Musnad Aḥmad 23528 — from Maḥmūd ibn Labīd)

— *shirk aṣghar*, the junior idolatry: the deed's *destination* switched while its outward form remained — the Messenger thereby showing how the sin is at root a misdirected worship, and its carrier's wages therefore claimable only from the audience itself, at that Day *nothing* being transferable from men's hands. The three-stage knowledge of riyāʾ that the salaf preserved (ʿAlī's triple in the sayings-collections: baseline riyāʾ spoils the root; riyāʾ midway, the tree; third-stage riyāʾ — *al-shahwah al-khafiyyah*, the hidden appetite, needing the Prophet's prescription — "the hidden riyāʾ is subtler than the ant's crawling," Abū Dāwūd's wording attached to the sigh of the early saints) — has filled a thousand treatises with the one unkillable question it plants at the center of the deed: *whose eye?*

**Wa Lā Yuʾminūna bi-Allāhi wa lā bi-l-Yawmi al-Ākhir: The Creed-less Charities**

The second clause does not enlarge the circle but deepens the charge: *and believe neither in God nor in the Last Day* — and the reading divides tradition draws the clause two ways both indispensable: (1) joint sense — the spending-show *proves* the unbelief (al-Ṭabarī's logic: one who truly believed in the Rewarder above would never settle for the witnesses below; riyāʾ is therefore unveiled kufr, the actor disclosing he has no inland God); and (2) distinct circle — the verse charging the *hypocrite* class made famous in Madinah (the nifāq-portraits built up in 2:8–16, 4:142, and 63:2–7, their works * laundered displays over hollow hearts: *"they only spend unwillingly"* — 9:53–54) — the Madinan double-life intersecting the plain wealthy-show of the old society in this one verse so that *both* outward charity of the open pagan and hollow charity of the pious-faced parasites of faith stand condemned by the one clause: charity *without* creed is not charity at all. The light of the Last Day frames especially the horror — for one who believed the whole record opens then would carry coin into the after-balances, not into the not into the eyes of today only; riyāʾ thus testifies, as the commentators put it, to *short-termism as creed* — preferring what the day can spend to what eternity asks — *hasbunā* never widened — *the poor man of the nex-t day swapping the Lord's Treasury for the eyes of his neigh-borhood*.

**Man Yakuni al-Shayṭānu lahu Qarīnan Fa-sāʾa Qarīnan: The Companion-Transfer**

The seal, most the seal lifts the whole paragraph into a spirit-map: *man yakuni al-Shayṭānu lahu qarīnan fa-sāʾa qarīnan* — "whosoever has Satan for a companion — what an evil companion has he!": *qarīn*, the fellow-sitter, travel-partner, appointed shadow — the Qur'anic given that every heart walks with a traveling-spirit (the notion running from 41:25 — "We have appointed for them companions who made fair to them what was before them" — through 43:36 — "whoso blinds himself to the Merciful's Remembrance, We appoint for him a Satan who is his companion"; and the Prophet's own register on the constant companion in the human frame:

> *"There is not one of you but has been appointed his companion from among the jinn." They said: Even you? He said: Even me — except that God has aided me against him, so he submits and bids me to nothing but good."* (Muslim 2814)

— *aslama*, the the submitted companion of the Messenger). Riyāʾ's place on this map is exact: the the showy coin already has its assigned qarīn — every look-up of the alms to a crowd is the Devil's own *seat* taken at the table of the deed — and what the Devil seats himself into never arrives never arrives above: what an evil traveling-fellow he is, for he *rides* the charity home and leaves the man destitute of it on the Day of Account. The antidotes the tradition therefore pours into the heart of the spending-moment: quiet hands: the right hand so in secret that the left knows not (Bukhārī 1423 — the the seven shaded classes, class five: a man who gives charity secretly until his left knows not what his right gives), and the fire-tested habit of the honest ledger — give as one who has checked his companion, stared down his companion, and answered with *ilā Allāh* (to God, for God), for an evil qarīn is the price of every of every deed of every deed performed for men's eyes, face-to-face before the Face that alone remains.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:39

> **What would it have cost them had they believed in God and the Last Day and spent from that which God has provided them? And God knows them well.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mādhā ʿAlayhim: The Question of the Impossible Bargain**

The sūrah's treasury-sermon closes its block of greed and display with one of the Qur'an's gentlest and most cutting rhetorical forms: *wa-mādhā ʿalayhim law āmanū bi-Allāhi wa al-yawmi al-ākhiri wa anfaqū mimmā razaqahumu Allāh* — "and what would have been *upon them* — what would they have lost — had they believed in God and the Last Day and spent of what God provided them?": *mādhā ʿalayhim*, literally "what would it have been against them?" — the interrogative of the free benefit, God's invitation phrased as *cost-accounting*: the whole proposal laid out — believe, and spend — and the absurdity of refusal laid bare by the arithmetic of loss: *nothing* would have been lost; everything would have been gained. Al-Rāzī treasures this mode as one of the Book's reasons-with-man — the arguer who is made to carry his *own case*, the divine reasoner showing that faith's price is *zero* while its return is immeasurable — and al-Ṭabarī's note notes the form's continuity with the Qur'an's whole evangel of *cheap godliness*: *forgive and be forgiven* — 24:22's own logic; *spend and be repaid* — 34:39's; *fear God and He will teach you* — 2:282's: nowhere does obedience cost a single thing that was not better spent. The doctrine-of-spending verse that 4:39 delivers from this shape is therefore double: its sting for the miser (you lost *nothing* — you only lost your loss) and its balm for the giver (nothing you spend actually departs — it *transfers*: from the perishing wallet to the everlasting ledger).

**Mimmā Razaqahumu Allāh: Out of What *He* Provided**

The qualifying phrase is the entire theology of Islamic wealth: *of that which God provided them* — the money being invited out was never theirs: it is it is *rizq*, provision, God's continuous act of supplying (the Book's omnipresent name for the flow: 2:3's initial character-quark of the God-ware: the God-fearing spend *from what We provided them*), and the possessive grammar itself thus patents the indictment: the *donor's* capital being quarreled over by the *trustee's* fist. The tradition folds the whole thing into a single coupon—hadīth the commentators never tire of laying beside it:

> *"The son of Adam says: My wealth! My wealth! Do you possess of your wealth anything but what you eat and consume, what you wear and wear out, or what you give in charity and send forward?"* (Muslim 2958 — Kitāb al-Zuhd)

— the human wallet audited down to three offices — stomach, back, ledger — of which only one survives the funeral. From that audit, stinginess reads at last as the *category error* it deep-down is: guarding in the name of "mine" what remains, at last accounting, either eaten or buried-in-cloth — with the charity-column alone carrying forward; rizq-theology makes makes treasuring the spending-stream not merely piety but sanity; hence the sūrah's earlier command to gift the asylum-seekers from it (v. 8) now becomes here the whole economics of existence: keep flowing what is flowing — trust's own conduct for what was never ceded to you — and the escrow of the world hands over on the Day when the only *owned* wealth is the forwarded.

**Wa Kāna Allāhu Bihim ʿAlīmā: And God Knows Them — A Double Seal**

The seal steps softly and lands dreadful lands heavy: *wa kāna Allāhu bihim ʿalīman* — "and God is knowing of them": *ʿalīm*, knowing-entire — the clause at first sight a mild statement of omniscience, but in the rhetoric of the Book the *awareness-seal after an offer refused* is a veiled alarm (al-Rāzī's standing observation for this style: when God closes an entreaty with His knowing-name over people, it signals that every hidden motive behind the refusal is unhidden from Him — the avarice that masqueraded as prudence; the unbelief that masqueraded as policy); and it equally seals *comfort* for every reader who complies: of such too God is knowing — the heart's purity in the unrecorded gift, the wife's private coin, the servant's coin-halved al the servant's split coin — reaching the Knower with no other witness — so the clause completes the register of v. 38's riyāʾ-hell with the knowledge-heaven opposite: *what eyes never saw, ʿAlīm saw.* The sūrah's little treatise of wealth — custody in vv. 5–6, share in v. 7, kind-word in vv. 8–9, fear of unjust eaters in v. 10, and now the anti-twin of greed and display in vv. 36–39 — is thereby sealed as the ummah's permanent finance-charter: worship God alone; beautify downward along the seven-class compass of v. 36; withhold nothing at most that flows; spend toward none but the Face; and know — in both warning and and in mercy — that the Knower of the servants is the auditor of the is He who audits the closed seals, the fountains never exhausted, the ledger already written: *you could not have given away a single grain without Him knowing it from before the worlds were made.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:40

> **Truly God commits not so much as a mote's weight of wrong; if there is a good deed, He will multiply it and grant from His Presence a great reward.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mithqāla Dharratin: The Weight-Ward of the Infinitesimal**

The sūrah's justice-register, having sealed treasuries, orphans, oaths and households, now plants its mathematical center on the smallest unit the poetry of Arabic could name: *inna Allāha lā yaẓlimu mithqāla dharratin* — "God does not wrong — not the weight of a *dharrh*": *mithqāl*, weight-measure; *dharrah*, the particle — mote, atom, speck — that the old commentators glossed as the tiniest red ant or the least fleck glazing gliding in the sunbeam (10:61 and 34:3 using the same unit for what misses His hearing; 99:7–8 setting it as Judgment's smallest sentence-item: *whoso does a dharrah-weight of good shall see it*). The rulers-of-measures structure is thereby the Book's own answer to every suspicion the sūrah's hard laws would invite: over orphans and wives and servants God does not wrong — not the photon-weight — so any injustice any reader might ever allege against statute or decree has been mathematically excluded in advance, infinitesimally bounded at *zero*; and the whole function of the verse within the pericope is what al-Ṭabarī names it: reassurance after a long compliance-train — the duties of vv. 32–39 made heavy precisely because the Arbiter is infinitely exact.

**The Impossibility-of-Injustice: Kalām's Two Doctrines Upon One Verse**

The classical theology-schools built their statutes of divine justice upon this clause, and their two great postures remain the architecture of Sunni kalām: (1) the *intrinsic* doctrine — al-Rāzī's own record record here — injustice is *impossible to God by concept*, for injustice means transgressing another's right, and rights exist only by God's own establishment; nothing outside His grant, hence nothing to wrong against — the House *there is no house to rob when every house is His*: the Ashʿarī mainstream thus tying *wronglessness* to authorship itself (cf. 6:12 & 54 — "He has prescribed mercy upon Himself" — even mercy, in the same words, *self-prescribed*); and (2) the *voluntary* doctrine — attributed in the same commentaries to other theologians (al-Qurṭubī's careful parenthesis records the school-split): injustice lies within sheer power, but it is self-forbidden by His wisdom and mercy — the position pressing that *imposed-by-nature nonwrong* would subtract from His praise, since one praises a *choice*. Both doctrines agree on the operative floor of faith: *there is never in God's dispensation a real victim.* The Muʿtazilī's corollary (which al-Rāzī reports as the as the earlier-horse corollary of the verse) — that since God does no injustice, evil *doings* emerged from man (man the author of his acts) — is the parting-point of kalām — with the Ashʿarite counter (from the same commentary-page) reminding that His *renunciation of wrong never exhausts His rule* — that wronglessness is equally the measure of all qadar, the decree beneath which even the atom-scale rests under perfect rule.

**Yuḍāʿifuha: The Multiplied Good and the Ibn Masʿūd Ledger**

The mercy-side follows the justice-side in one breath: *wa in taku ḥasanatan yuḍāʿifhā wa yuʾti min ladunhu ajran ʿaẓīman* — "and if there is a good deed, He multiplies it, showing and out of His own to Him gives a tremendous reward": *yuḍāʿifhā* — multiplies it, as 6:160 fixes the baseline ("tenfold the like"), and as the multiply-unspecified opens it beyond counting (the alms-plant of 2:261 — seven hundred grains, and God multiplies *whom He wills*). The celebrated eschatology that that al-Ṭabarī attaches to this verse is in Ibn Masʿūd's register: on the Day all interpersonal claims are settled first — *good deeds transferred from debtor to wronged claimant* — and then comes the particle-moment the verse declares: whatever dharrah-weight of good yet remains to a man after all transfers, *God multiplies it and by it admits him to the Garden* — the audit settling not by arithmetical survival but by overflow; conversely the man whose claims-overhead outruns his dharrah-per no — outruns any remainder perishes — the teaching thereby fixing Judgment's two-process structure known as the known to Islam as *settlement* — *and* *multiplication*: strict rectification among creatures, followed by pure bounty from the Creator, with even *His own* creditors-debts sorted in righteous order before the mercy-cascade falls (cf. the hadith-qudsī of Muslim 2581 — "if the whole of you were as pious as the most pious heart... that would add nothing to My dominion" — showing bounty is of *Him* and not of ledgers).

**Min Ladunhu: Al-Rāzī's Two Rewards**

Al-Rāzī closes his eye upon the last distinction — the verse's two recompenses: *yuḍāʿifhā* — multiplied return for outward deeds, and *ajran ʿaẓīman min ladunhu* — a "great reward from His very Presence" — read by him as the soul's as the *beatific* order — the reward that comes not for limbs-obedience alone but for the soul sanctified and illumined, the reward of vision-love-knowledge — matched against the merely bodily registers of delights: al-Rāzī never letting the pleasure of paradise's flesh stand alone, teaching instead the many-leveled Garden — bodies feasting, souls seeing — and he assigns the twofold grammar of v. 40 as its charter: multiplication for the deed; the *ladunnī* bounty for the purified seat of the soul. The salaf understood in simpler language but the same depth: *from His Presence* means the reward is *personal* — the Giver Himself the recompense (the Exalted's *riḍā* being greater than the Garden itself — 9:72 sealing it: "God's approval is greater"). And so in a single verse the sūrah bequeaths both anti-anxiety and anti-complacency: no weight of wrong shall ever be found on God — no soul need fear audit farce — and no weight of good shall ever be lost in Him — no miser need fear the the vanishing of his alms: the scales wherein even a dharrah is kept are *His own* — *no one walks away robbed of anything except his own refusal.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:41

> **How will it be when We bring forth a witness from every community, and We bring thee as a witness against these?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Fa-Kayfa Idhā: The Opening Cinematic of the Reckoning**

The sūrah pivots from reckoning-arithmetic (v. 40: no wrong of a dharrah-weight) into the very theater of the Reckoning itself, opening with its with the Qur'an's stock scene-verb of awe: *fa-kayfa idhā jiʾnā min kulli ummatin bi-shahīdin wa jiʾnā bika ʿalā hāʾulāʾi shahīdan* — "How then shall it be, when We bring from every community a witness, and bring thee against these as a witness?": *kayfa* — *how shall it be!* — the interrogative-without-answer whereby the Book inducts its reader into an event no description can carry (cf. its fearful siblings: "How shall it be when We gather them on a day of no doubt" — 3:25; "How will you guard if you disbelieve a Day that makes children gray" — 73:17): imagination itself tasked, since the scene is too large for stages. The specific assembly-line is unveiled in one clause: from *every ummah* of history a designated *shahīd* — testimony-bearer — is brought forward, and that bearer is its prophet (al-Ṭabarī's unanimous verse-chains: each community's own messenger testifies over his people — acceptance or refusal — with 16:84's parallel summons and 16:89's double of our exact clause; 4:159 adding that even Jesus witnesses upon the people of the Book given him; 28:75 folding the same draw-from-each-community into judgment-day liturgy). The Lucan The Rule stands established: *prophethood shapes itself finally as testimony* — every messenger's whole career summed up, on the Last Day, as a witness-stand deposition for or against the ones he was sent among.

**Jiʾnā Bika ʿalā Hāʾulāʾi Shahīdan: Muhammad Over the Middle Proof-Community**

The second summons is the verse's drama and its crown: *and We bring thee against these as a witness*: the last Prophet's case is singled-out not merely as one shahīd among the shahīds (his would be sequential) but as the culminating witness over *"these"* — the demonstrable the demonstrative pointing variously read: over *his own ummah* (the plainest line, matching 2:143 and 22:78 — "We made you a middle community that you may be witnesses over mankind *and the Messenger a witness over you*": the elaborate architecture wherein the Muslims themselves function as witnesses over the earlier communities — on the ground that they acknowledged the earlier prophets whom their nations denied — and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is witness *over the Muslims*, the great circle closing with the ummah's accreditation under its own master) — and, in al-Qurṭubī's amplified sense, over *the foe-pagans of his of his day* whose wars and sneers fill this very surah (the clause a quiet dread-exact a quiet threat to the men then legislating prayer-drunkenness and mocker-imprecation around his mosque: you will stand opposite him at that bar). Either way the table-order is transcendent: prophets as evidence-bearers, communities as cases — and above all the and at the zenith the seal of prophets given his double commission: witness over the believers, intercessor between them and wrath (al-Qurṭubī's window on the ummah's comfort — he who must testify against is likewise he by whose appeal they may be freed).

**The Weeping Prophet: When the Verse Was Recited to Its Owner**

The tradition preserved at this verse belongs to the highest clas s of Prophet-psychology disclosures — the verse was a burden-felt, not an honor-boasted: Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī both anchoring the celebrated scene of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd (in al-Bukhārī 4582 and Muslim 800):

> *"The Messenger of God ﷺ said to me: Recite to me. I said: Messenger of God, shall I recite to you when it was revealed to you? He said: I love to hear it from other than myself. So I recited Sūrah al-Nisāʾ until I reached: *How will it be when We bring forth a witness from every community, and We bring thee as a witness against these?* He said: Enough now. I looked at him, and behold, his eyes were flowing with tears."*

— the Prophet crying at his own summons to the stand — Abu Abū Hurayrah's nuq for no verse could touch him deeper than the one where *he* was conscripted to bear testimony upon beloved and disobedient alike: the *daʿwah-cost* of prophethood there at its heaviest — to be compelled forever to speak truth against people one ached to save. The wisdom of the weeping long outlasted its scene — the early community recited this verse as their mine as their mirror-house: if its shaft if even its addressee wept at the coming bar, how shall any grafter in orphan-gold or bedroom cruelty not weep who stands numbered among *the witnessed*?

**The Identity Clause of All Witnesses**
