— and the term's placement here is no accident, as al-Rāzī observes with characteristic brilliance: vv. 68–69 comprise *the exact answer of the prayer of al-Fātiḥah* — for 1:6–7 petitions *ihdinā al-ṣirāṭa al-mustaqīm* — "guide us upon the straight path — the path of those Thou hast blessed" — and the sūrah's two apodoses reply clause-for-clause: *guidance upon the road* (v. 68) and *company of those blessed upon it* (v. 69 — prophets, ṣiddīqūn, shuhadāʾ, ṣāliḥūn — the very *anʿamta ʿalayhim* cohort of the Fātiḥah's own syntax) — Sūrah 1's prayer being thereby reprinted inside Sūrah 4's conditional-promise: petition in chapter one; receive in chapter four — and between them stands the standing grammar of compliance.

**Better and Firmer — Then Guided and Companioned**

With the payment-doublet now complete (reward-from-His-Presence at v. 67; guidance-upon-the-road at v. 68), the reader perceives the mounting logic of the trinity: what obedience gains is not merely *banked* (reward) but *navigational* (continuing guidance) — treasury and chart both issued at signing — so that however much the waverer feared losing his way after complying (the nifāq-class's secret fear, whispered at every full-surrender: *if I submit wholly, what shore holds me?*), heaven answers that the road itself comes as part of the wage: *We will show you where to step, every furlong.* The sufi-readers' commentary (al-Qushayrī's line and its descendants) feasted upon the perpetual light of this sequence: submission once made never leaves a man a mapping-orphan — God undertakes the pilgrim's directions inside the bargain — and the Prophet's own daily Fātiḥah-liturgy (seventeen rakʿahs of obligatory prayer, minimum, each containing the petition) stands as the ever-renewing activation of the covenant: each *ihdinā* prayed humbly, each step taken thereafter, answered with guidance anew. And upon the trinity's third rail (v. 69) comes then the final and dearest payment — companionship — for which the road itself was only the preparation: obedience's last dignity being the *fellowship* it acquires, among those whom God has blessed.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:69

> **Whosoever obeys God and the Messenger, they are with those whom God has blessed, of the prophets, the truthful ones, the witnesses, and the righteous. What beautiful companions they are!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Man Yuṭiʿ: Obedience as Citizenship**

The trinity's third payment arrives as the verse the earliest community treasured above all comfort-texts — heaven's own rostral decree upon obedience's full consequences: *wa man yuṭiʿi Allāha wa al-rasūla fa-ulāʾika maʿa alladhīna anʿama Allāhu ʿalayhim mina al-nabiyyīna wa al-ṣiddīqīna wa al-shuhadāʾi wa al-ṣāliḥīn wa ḥasuna ulāʾika rafīqā* — "whoever obeys God and the Messenger — those are with those whom God has blessed: of the prophets, the truthful, the witnesses, and the righteous — and beautiful are they as companions": the double *maʿa* — *with* — the whole verse pivots upon companionship-grammar (obedience no longer merely paid — it *locates* the soul: man = whosoever — general; yuṭiʿ — obeys — the criterion; fa-ulāʾika maʿa — those are WITH — the reward's substance being not what but *where and with whom*) — the asbāb-report the tradition never ever stops retelling (al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabarī, and al-Ṭabrisī's collated rolls): certain Companions — Thawbān of the freedmen in Ibn Kathīr's favorite narration, others of the Anṣār in parallel chains — came heavy-hearted to the Prophet: they loved him so, yet he as prophet would be exalted above them in the Garden by stations they could never reach — *shall we lose your company after death?* — and heaven answered them with our verse: *obedience purchases place-in-common*: the levels differ (prophethood not granted) but the *withness* is conferred wholesale — the fear measured and healed in a single clause, the community learning thereafter that the afterlife's true division is not ranks but *presence*: with the blessed, or outside them.

**The Four Ranks Unfolded**

The blessed cohort gets its four columns, and the commentators have ever loved to march them in order: (1) *al-nabiyyīn* — the prophets — the apex — human speech-jo God's own spokesmen; (2) *al-ṣiddīqīn* — the absolutely truthful — the highest human sub-rank (the tradition's chief examples: Abū Bakr — his very title al-Ṣiddīq minted upon the Night-Journey-morning when he said *"if he said it, it is true"* — al-Bayhaqī's register — and ʿĀsiyah Mary's sawn the Qur'an conferring the feminine the feminine model of it at 5:75 — "his mother was a ṣiddīqah" — ṣidq being trust-speak so perfect that no shadow of speech-dis of mismatched inner/outer remains); (3) *al-shuhadāʾ* — the witnesses — martyrs, but wider (al-Rāzī's luminous breadth: all who bear testimony to religion *by argument or by sword* — the tongue-witnesses and the grave-witnesses both — the Book's own usage at 4:41's prophet-witnesses and 2:143's ummah-witnesses forbidding the narrow sense); and (4) *al-ṣāliḥīn* — the righteous — public and secret rectitude complete (al-Ṭabarī's definition: *those who do right in what is seen and unseen*) — the cohort thereby encompassing the whole pyramid of human sanctity — prophets at the summit, saints beneath, witnesses beside them, the righteous as its broad faithful base — into which cohort the obedient are *written*, even at the lowest floor.

**Wa Ḥasuna Ulāʾika Rafīqā: Beautiful Companionship as Heaven's Close**

The seal does what human astonishment does upon the census: *wa ḥasuna ulāʾika rafīqā* — "and how beautiful are they as companions!": *ḥasuna* — beauty-exclamation (the Book's own startled doxology — it being seconded only by *niʿimma* of v. 58's counsel); *rafīq* — fellow-traveler — from rifāq: gentle companionship (both the company and its *softness*: no rough fellowship — the Prophet's own beat blessing upon the pilgrims' fellowship in the communitas-traditions of the early Muslims being its foretaste: brotherhood on tawbah brotherhood contracted at Madinah in the muʾākhāh, al-Bukhārī 2049's own account of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and Saʿd ibn al-Rabīʿ dividing goods) — and behind it waits the Tradition's own *proof-of-companionship*, the hadith this verse's greatest commentary in viva in living exchange — the man asking the Prophet about the Last Hour and receiving the answer (al-Bukhārī 6168–6171 and Muslim's register 2639–2640 — Anas's celebrated report of the Anṣārī's weeping joy):

> *A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked about the Hour... then said: "Messenger of God! I do not do much prayer, fasting, or alms, but I love God and His Messenger." He ﷺ said: "A man shall be with those whom he loves." Anas said: Never were we so gladdened after Islam as by this word: a man shall be with those whom he loves.*

— love joining obedience as the second key to the same doors (for love is love itself the *fruit* of obedience 3:31-style: "if you love God, follow me — God will love you"), and the pericope therefore closing its whole its whole mediation-drama with the brightest promise-block of the chapter: the triple payments of vv. 67–69 now fully laid out: reward from His Presence *for the ledger*, a guided road *for the walking*, and *for the heart that feared loneliness after death* — to stand in the cohort of prophets-and-witnesses, beautiful companions, forever with.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:70

> **Such is the Bounty from God, and God suffices as Knower.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Dhālika al-Faḍlu mina Allāh: The Inventory Sealed as Grace**

The apodosis-block completes with the ledger-signature of the whole: *dhālika al-faḍlu mina Allāh* — "that is the Bounty from God": *dhālika* — the demonstrative sweeping over the whole threefold payload (v. 67's mighty reward from His Presence; v. 68's guidance upon the road; v. 69's companionship with the blessed — each item now stamped under a single title: *faḍl*, bounty — surplus-grace) — and the root f-ḍ-l already etched in the reader's memory at this point of the sūrah from its many stations (v. 32's "ask God of His bounty" — for wage-claiming instead of envy; v. 37's misers concealing God's bounty; v. 54's bounty-envy of the portion-bearers — so that the word arrives here carrying its full pericope-history: *everything humans fight over — bread, gold, office, prophecy — hangs in this one vault, and here God opens it not by merit but by grace*). The theological sharpness of the seal is the whole Sunni grace-doctrine in miniature — al-Rāzī's comment standing: the triple payment outruns any arithmetic of deed-value — no obedience weighed in scales could *earn* prophet-companionship or Presence-proximity — hence the item's label: it is *bounty*, not compensation; payment received according to service, but measured by the Giver's generosity — a doubl the same twofold accountancy the Book carves upon its wage-verses everywhere (24:38's reward "and more of His bounty" — *min faḍlih* appended beyond the reckoning; 4:173's own parallel ahead: "He will pay their wages in full — and more of His bounty"; 62:4's "the bounty is in the hand of God") — works measured exactly, bounty lavished boundlessly, so the believer receives justice *plus* overflow, and never one without the other.

**Wa Kafā bi-Allāhi ʿAlīmā: The Sufficiency-Knower Behind the Payments**

Then the verse's closing attribute-signature — *wa kafā bi-Allāhi ʿalīmā* — "and God suffices as Knower": *kafā* — the sufficiency-verb fourth-time-deployed in the pericope (God suffices as Helper — v. 45; the manifest sin suffices as proof — v. 50; Hell suffices as blazing at v. 55 — each sufficiency fitted to its own chamber of assurances) — and here its object is *ʿalīmā* — the Quality-Noun of knowledge absolutized (God as as the Knower-Par-Excellence: the verdict certified from omniscience) — its function in the clause being three-deep a triple-barreled warrant, as the commentators array it: (1) *knowledge of who obeys* — the eligibility-verifier of v. 69's maʿa-promise (no false enrollment in the cohort, no lost enrollment either — the sufficiency of the files its office being heaven's perfect HR-record: the obedient all counted); (2) *knowledge as the reward's own witness* — the bounty being indelibly registered (no amnesia-heaven — the promise cannot spoil in record); and (3) *knowledge replacing every human audit* — for men could never measure which obedience was real (v. 60's professed believers among them, recall) — so God's sufficiency as Knower seals over inter seals over man's file-insufficiencies: *His knowing is enough.* The established tradition’s note upon the attribute is hereby again with the whole pericope's: the hypocrite-bloc feared riyāʾ-audits and lost files while the obedient-bloc feared lost wages — and the same attribute waters both anxieties flat: *He who knows cannot be files fooled by the first, nor forgetful of the second.*

**The Trust-Block's Apodosis Completed — and the Hinge Toward the Battle-Calls**

With v. 70 the authority-architecture of vv. 58–70 has run its full circle: duties and trusts (58–59), the tribunal-refusers exposed and admonished (60–65), and the counterfactual payments pledged upon obedience (66–70) — bounty and knowledge sealing it on both ends: grace paying; omniscience certifying — and the believer left where every covenant-exchange leaves him: *with a standing contract*: obedience exchanged for the trinity — Presence-reward, path-guidance, blessed-companionship — God inscribed as the Bountiful-Granter and the Never-Forgetting-Knower upon the document's closing line — with the sūrah's very next verse's picking up next verse (71: "O you who believe! Take your precautions...") now swinging the polity from covenant-comforts into campaign-discipline: the ummah that knows its recompense must also keep its guard — the grace-doctrine never licensing carelessness — for as the pericope has taught from its first clause: trust *carries responsibility* (amānah must be delivered) — and responsibility in Madinah now requires shields: *take your precautions — God watching over all.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:71

> **O you who believe! Take your precautions; then go forth in companies or go forth all together.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Khudhū Ḥidhrakum: Precaution as Command, Not as Cowardice**

The sūrah swings at last from covenant-consolations into campaign-discipline with one of the Prophet's most-lived clauses: *khudhū ḥidhrakum* — "take your precaution": *ḥidhr*, from ḥ-dh-r — caution, guard, the watchful fore-arming — rendered in the traditional explanations as both *armor* (the equipment one wears) and *wariness* (the disposition you carry) — the command unmistakably rooted in Madinah's security-crisis climate (the pericope of vv. 71–104 being the sūrah's battle-mobilization arch, borne upon the breach of Uḥud and the anticipation of the Qurayshian return) — but the commentators cross the whole register for its universalization: arms-bear equipment-assembling (the Arab glossers glossing it *carry your arms*), intelligence-gathering, fortification, formations — every species of prudent anticipation falling under the noun, one of the Ṣaḥabah even reporting bare direct field-memoranda formed around it (the pre-battle wakefulness of the Prophet's own night rounds among the outposts being cited in the Sīrah chronicles as the verse's life-form). Al-Qurṛṭubī's statutes classical comment-crossroads raises at once the theological seam the reader most needs stitched: does precaution contradict reliance (tawakkul) the tradition's permanent answer being the famous two-edged instrument the hadith masters lodge precisely here:

> *A Bedouin came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: Shall I leave my camel and trust in God? He said: "Tether her, and trust in God."* (al-Tirmidhī 2517 — graded likewise in the Musnad-registers)

— *iʿqilhā wa tawakkal*: the camel tied — then the heart made over to God — this pairing thereafter standing as Islam's final word on preparation versus trust: no precaution without faith becomes pagan insurance; no faith without precaution becomes testing-God presumption — the two together constituting responsible tawakkul (the same pair as the sages bound at the hijrah's own ḥadīth-machinery: Abū Bakr's companionship in the cave — the Prophet commissioning all the the whole apparatus — food, mounts, scouts, decoy bedstead — then saying "Do not grieve: God is with us" — 9:40) — so the verse enshrines precaution itself as obedience, thereby outlawing the false piety that parades carelessness as trust.

**Fa-nfirū Thubātin Awi-nfirū Jamīʿā: Two Modes for Every Manner of Mission**

Then the twin deployment-forms: *wa-nfirū thubātin awi-nfirū jamīʿā* — "then go forth in companies, or go forth all together": *nafara*, to surge out, to detach into expedition (the verb of detach of detachment-in-force: 9:122's tafaqquh-delegations built on the same root — *why should not a squadron of each band stay behind to gain understanding in religion?*); *thubātin* — clustered parties — from *thubah*, a knot or separate band — units sent by detachments (raiding parties, reconnaissance columns, successive waves per the glossers' spectrum Ibn ʿAbbās's roll recording "one after another"); *jamīʿā* — all as one — the whole force as single muster (the Prophet's own great expeditions — Hunayn, Tabūk, the conquest column) — so that the command covers *both* order-types permitted to the Commander's discretion: piecemeal operations for harassing-and-probing; full assembly for decisive massings (the juristic commentators using the verse to ground both military law-forms throughout the caliphate-annals: ʿUmar's far-flung army-posts evidence of units; ʿUmar's Fertile Crescent hosts evidence of mass) — and al-Rāzī's wisdom-note agrees stands for all later ages: the military form is left open within *two* because the sūrah's business is *readiness*, not choreography — God legislating the principle of guarded motion while leaving the art to the men of command — a standing teaching thereafter echoed in the sunnah's own tactical pluralism.

**The Readiness-Quadrant: Believers Summoned as a Garrison**

Beneath the two orders stands the verse's civic-sign decreeing doctrine: *the believing community is a permanently-ready force*: the address itself being *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* — O you who believe — faith itself conscripted (the note of the commentators: as this very pericope will before long expose those who claim faith but will not march — vv. 72–77 — the address-form itself is rendered into a morale-test: *come forward sincerely or be sifted*); and the whole chamber sits upon the seal of v. 70 like a red upon like a seal upon a declaration: the mercy-payments have been pledged; the battle-call now summoned now summons — bounty and readiness being the two wings of the same defense-treaty — with al-Qushayrī's spiritual inversion treasured by the sufi-books as the clause's interior chamber: *taking precautions* for the gnostic = to flee from aught but God in the inner field; *going forth* = seizing surging from every created attachment, in detachments if you must, or all-at-once if you can — the external discipline yielding the inner mysth inner thumbnail: *the soul fortifying against false-security just as the garrison fortifies against the night-raid* — so that from desert-warfare into heart-warfare the verse marches unbroken: ḥidhr within, ḥidhr without — and the whole community thereafter formed as Islam's standing glass garrison: *precaution belted on, ranks formed, the Name overhead — trusting and tethered both.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:72

> **Among you indeed is one who would tarry; then, if misfortune should befall you, he would say, "God has blessed me, in that I did not accompany them."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Inna Minkum la-Man la-Yubaṭṭiʾanna: The Lagger Inside the Ranks**

The battle-mobilization arch now trains its lamp upon the reader's closest danger — the straggler *inside*: *wa inna minkum la-man la-yubaṭṭiʾanna* — "and verily among you there is indeed one who would tarry": *yubaṭṭiʾanna*, doubled-emphatic an intensified verbal manṭ an emphatic-der a strong form from b-ṭ-ʾ — to be slow, drag feet — rendered by the commentators through its two calibrations (al-Ṭabarī's chains and al-Rāzī's review): (1) *the mere lagger* — one who simply holds himself back, arriving after the contest is settled (al-Rāzī's own preferred reading — the particles' grammar suggesting the sluggard's simply *avoiding battle*, not a conspiracy to brake the army); and (2) *the brake-man* — one who weighs down the march of others with hesitation-infection (some early glossers tying it to 9:38's "you sink heavily to the earth" — thāqaltum — and the heavy the heavyweight inertia against jihād summons) — either way a portrait of *sluggishness as stance*: the soldier formally enrolled and functionally absent. The occasion-reports the tradition carries to the clause name its archetype in Madinah's deepest stain (al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī's collations): **ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl** — chief of the hypocrites — at Uḥud: marching out with the Muslims until the approaches of the Peak, then peeling off with a third of the host — nearly three? famously three hundred souls — back to the city — pleading grievance that ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy's that his counsel to fight inside Madinah had been rejected — its companion-report marking the exact morale-tax such drag-kings levy upon young converts (some of the Anṣār nearly following him back — Bukhārī's Uḥud-era registers and the Sīrah chronicles recounting the wavering before the hardy stood fast) — the verse's *inna minkum* — verily among you — thereby carrying its cruelest disclosure: the army already compromised not by infiltration, but by *membership*.

**Fa-In Aṣābatkum Muṣībatun: Disaster Photographed by the Absentee's Eyes**

Then the narrative-horror clause: *fa-in aṣābatkum muṣībatun qāla qad anʿama Allāhu ʿalayya idh lam akun maʿahum shahīdan* — "then if misfortune befall you, he says: God has blessed me, in that I was not with them as witness": the lagger's true interior unmasked in a single sentence spoken over fellow-believers' pain — misfortune (the Uḥud reversal being its immediate night-dress — seventy slain Companions among the seventy martyrs arrayed upon that hillside) read by him not as national tragedy but as *vindication*: his absence converted into *divine favor* — *anʿama Allāhu ʿalayya* — God conferred upon me — the pronoun-fixation of the clause (*ʿalayya* — upon *me*) itself a self-analysis the Quran the Qur'an meant for every generation's ears: the hypocrite can speak God's name yet mean *his own safety* — religion vocabulary worn over creaturely self-alarm (the commentators noting the grotesque invertedness the inverted use: the believer too says *anʿama Allāh* — but over hardships shared and martyrs mourned; the tarrier says it over *escaped* hardship and *distant* graves) — and *shahīdan* — as a witness — poignant with the word's double current: witness of the scene, and — the overheard secondary — *shahīd*-martyr — refusal to arrive as witness shading into refusal to *become* one. The Prophet's own Uḥud-hour pronouncements stand beside the clause as its living contrast-picture — the genuine believing brothers mourning at their wounds yet counting martyrdom not loss but success — the Prophet's own words at the slain (Bukhārī 4078's account of the burial-pairings and the tenderness toward Ḥamzah's body; the angel-washed shuhadāʾ reports across the maghāzī) — against which portrait the tarrier's *"blessed me — not there"* chills into one of the Book's coldest character-analyses: *some men convert only in the direction of pain-avoidance*; they are enrolled in religion so long as religion costs nothing — the first misfortune priced into faith, and they cash out — not with apostasy-words (they will never say them plainly) but with a *thanks-giving over their own absence*.

**The Morale-Weapon of the Second Clause — and the Reader's Inoculation**

The verse's diagnosis therapy the tradition's diagnosis was needed as inoculation for the first ummah as much as indictment: the Prophet's community had to be *told in revelation* what the tarrier's speech meant — lest its lest its surface-form of gratitude infect others ("maybe God *does* reward staying home!") — revelation thereby naming the tactic and drawing draining it: the mercy-sentence misused is *not mercy*, only the hypocrite's self-witness (his very testimony a self-disclosure — *idh lam akun maʿahum shahīdan* stands in the criminal-file of the disinclination of the Book's inside-the-psyche reportage as one of its most precise) — and every later reader of military, market, ministry, or family fronts inherits the template: watch the ones whose gratitude blooms only in the shadow of others' wounds — the pericope's diagnostic-arc now proceeding (vv. 73–74) to expose his *other* symptom — jealousy at the returning victors — and then to prescribe the counter-stance: fight for the sale of this world for the Hereafter, where *shahādata being* — presence at the appointment — is itself the blessing, whether of survival or of shahādah — for God is not mocked by absences; He blesses presence — *wa Allāhu yaʿlamu mā fi ṣudūrikum* — and the appointment of the faithful stands always among the ranks.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:73

> **But should a bounty come to you from God, he would surely say—as if there had been no affection between you and him—"Oh, would that I had been with them, so that I had attained a great triumph!"**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Faḍlun mina Allāh: Victory Read as Pay-Day**

The portrait of the backward man of the tarrier completes its opposing second half — for the same heart that blessed God over the Muslims' defeat now mourns its absence from the gate from the gate from their victory: *wa la-in aṣābakum faḍlun mina Allāhi la-yaqūlanna ka-an lam takun baynakum wa baynahu mawaddatun yā laytanī kuntu maʿahum fa-afūza fawzan ʿaẓīman* — "yet if bounty from God befall you, he will surely say — as though no affection existed between you and him — Oh, would that I had been with them, that I might attain a great triumph!": *faḍl* — bounty — here the victory-and-spoils bounty (the qur'anic the Quran's own equivalence of faḍl with both spoils and grace at 4:70, 72 cf. at 8:1's ghanāʾim-discussion and the faḍl-of-conquest tones across the Book) — and the whole sentence built as *forecast*: *la-yaqūlanna* — *he will surely say* — the doubled-lām of prophecy-of-character: heaven foretelling the man's future sentence so that when he finally speaks it the believers will recognize the line as previously scripted in the Book — an exposure-by-preemption, al-Rāzī-notes-style as al-Rāzī notes in such constructions: God *personnel literally writes the villain's dialogue in advance*, so there is in so that nothing in the theater then surprises — the whole drama unfolding under a script already heaven-published.

**Ka-an Lam Takun Baynakum wa Baynahu Mawaddatun: The Parenthesis That Cuts the Heart**

The verse's most devastating clause sits in the simile paused mid-reported-speech: *ka-an lam takun baynakum wa baynahu mawaddatun* — "as though there were no affection between you and him": *ka-an*, as though — the comparison-particle pinning the *shape* of his words — not their literal content but their *quality*: his *yā laytanī* spoken with exactly the ardor of a of an absolute stranger — a man professing regret to share in the comrades? in the companions' triumph while while his own back was turned — *mawaddah* — affection, warmth — from w-d-d itself the root of love's contract-language (30:21: "He set between you mawaddah and raḥmah" — the marriage-rh the covenant-word between spouses) — heaven thereby itemizing what the tarrier *by his showing forfeited*: the mutual warmth of the warband — so the simile cuts two ways: (1) exposure — he speaks like an alien to the cause (his own sentence betraying his non-membership), and (2) bill — the verification that his affection is *appraised declared* absent by his own speech, since who grieves only over *spoils* and never over *graves* proves in two battlefield moments where his treasure lodged — the closest closing there is no fear for God's own house — the *brotherhood* and at stake are graves for the believer's brotherliness is measured at funerals, his tarrier's only at dividends — and the simile thereby left as the universal scanner: *the true measure of mawaddah is what strikes him as loss: is your loss theirs-loss — or only your own missed spoils?*

**Yā Laytanī Kuntu Maʿahum: Regret as Idol of the Absent**

The two sentences now completing the hypocrite's character-file in the purest mirror-form the comparison with the believer's own yā-laytanī the tradition has always made: the world the Book had rendered all mankind's three archetypal regrets — 78:40's *yā laytanī kuntu turāban* — would that I were dust; 25:27's *yā laytanī ittakhadhtu maʿa al-rasūli sabīlan* — would that I had taken a way *with the Messenger*; 89:24's — "oh, would that I had forwarded for my life" — all three vertical, God-ward: *dust, the Messenger's road, death-forwarding* — and beside them the tarrier's yā-laytanī is the only one horizontal: *yā laytanī kuntu maʿahum* — would that I had been *with them* (not with God!) *fa-afūza fawzan ʿaẓīman* — *that I might triumph a great triumph* — the fawz-terminus of his sigh naming spoils, not salvation; al-Qurṛṭubī's line the commentators' needle into the clause being precisely that: the believer's *fawz* in the Book's own mouth is *garden-and-pleasure-of-God* (9:72 — *God's approval is greater — that is the supreme triumph*, al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm — the very compound of our verse — 85:11 re-stamping the heaven-sense) — whereas this man burns only for his share of the spoils-table. The two verdicts of vv. 72–73 then settle as the twin-mirror diagnosis that rauk that outlasted centuries: *the hypocrite at affliction congratulates God on his absence; at bounty, curses God on the same absence* — i.e., *his inner god is at bottom neither victory nor defeat but the avoidance of loss itself*: the whole pericope moving immediately after into its opposite proclamation — *"Let them fight in the way of God those who sell the world for the Hereafter"* (v. 74) — the two economies thereby displayed back to back for every generation's choice: *shahīd-logic* (presence at the appointment, both outcomes gainful — v. 74's "whether slain or victorious — We shall grant him a great reward") and *tarry-logic* (absence at the appointment, both outcomes mournful — blessed at other's wounds, wretched at their spoils) — the reader stopped by the Book and asked in effect: *which voice is your own?*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:74

> **Let them fight in the way of God, those who would sell the life of this world for the Hereafter. And whosoever fights in the way of God — whether he is slain or victorious — We shall grant him a great reward.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Fa-l-Yuqātil fī Sabīli Allāh: The Counter-Muster After the Tarriers**

Immediately after the twin-portrait of absence (vv. 72–73: the man who blessed God over the Muslims' wounds and grew wretched at their spoils), the sūrah issues its counter-call: *fa-l-yuqātil fī sabīli Allāhi alladhīna yashrūna al-ḥayāta al-dunyā bi-l-ākhirah* — "let them fight in the way of God — those who sell the life of this world for the Hereafter": *fa-l-yuqātil* — let them fight, the imperative-lām of commission; *fī sabīli Allāh* — *in the way of God* — the battle-clause the Book forever pins to legitimacy (the commentators' standing law-note, al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī concurring: the way of God is the cause God appointed — the defense of His religion, its upholding, and the call to it — never pride, never clan-glory, never plunder: aim governs act, so that an identical combat severed from this intention loses the sabīl-qualification and reverts to *fī sabīli al-ṭāghūt* per v. 76 immediately below) — and *alladhīna yashrūna* — *those who sell* — the mercantile lexicon the Book reserves for its most radical exchanges (from sh-r-y: to sell and in some registers to purchase, the same market-voice heard at 9:111's celebrated purchase-verse: "God has purchased from the believers their souls and their wealth — for that the Garden is theirs — they fight in the way of God, so they slay and are slain — a promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Quran") — war recast as a *transaction*: the worldly life offered as the sale-price, the heart liquidating everything perishable, with the counter-price everlasting — al-ākhirah — al-Qurṛṭubī's note observing that the two sides of the exchange have no ratio in any finance: the perishable swapped for the Imperishable, a trade conceivable only because the divine Purchaser is generous past arithmetic — the traders' own ledger-clause pinned beside it in the most-cited jihād-hadith of the Sahīh corpus:

> *"Standing guard at the frontier in the way of God for a single day is better than the world and all that is in it."* (al-Bukhārī 2892; Muslim 1880)

— one day of battlefield vigil outweighing the whole commodity of earth.

**Fa-man Yuqātil fī Sabīli Allāh: Win or Die — Both Are Wages**

Then follows the soldier's guarantee — the clause armies of believers have recited before battle release: *fa-man yuqātil fī sabīli Allāhi fa-yuqtal aw yaghlib fa-sawfa nuʾtīhi ajran ʿaẓīmā* — "whoever fights in the way of God — then is slain, or prevails — We shall grant him a mighty reward": the grammar lists both battle-outcomes, no third arm needed — *yuqtal*, he is killed — *aw yaghlib*, or he is victorious — Heaven pronouncing both gain: if he falls, shahādah and its wages; if he prevails, victory and its wages — no battlefield exit goes unpriced; *fa-sawfa nuʾtīhi* — We shall surely give him, the deferred-certain of majesty — *ajran ʿaẓīmā* — a majestic reward — the ʿaẓīm-noun of vv. 40 and 67's promised payments returning as the regular currency of God's own contracts. And over it the tradition suspends the standing qualification — the hadith that has defined "in the way of God" for every campaign of Islamic history, the Prophet's own sieve upon intentions when the asker named the warrior-cases (al-Bukhārī 2810; Muslim 1904 — narrated by Abū Mūsā):

> *"A man said: Messenger of God! One man fights out of bravery, one out of zeal, and one to be seen — which of these is in the way of God? He said: Whoever fights so that the word of God may be the highest — his is the way of God."*

— sincerity of aim being the full enlistment-paper, and the classification of every other combat instantly following: whatever fights for the name of tribe, glory, or worldly gain — lies outside the sabīl.

**The Two Economies Side by Side**

Set against vv. 72–73, the clause is the pericope's great divide (the commentators sensing it as one of the Book's starkest either-ors): the tarrier's economy — abstain; then whether your side bleeds or feasts, you measure your private ledger alone; the seller's economy — enlist; then *either* ledger prints *ajran ʿaẓīmā* — two outcomes, one profit-class: battle robbed by God of its risk-asymmetry — death versus plunder as the world counts it — dissolved into the heavenly arithmetic where death is the *larger* half of success. The sages' summary fixes the verse's historical substance: *Islam needed an army unbuyable by spoils and undissuadable by graves — this clause recruited it*; and the Prophet's own heart gave the doctrine its most human expression, in the famous wish he disclosed at the departure of a detachment (al-Bukhārī 36 and 2797; Muslim 1876–1878):

> *"Were it not that it would grieve some of my ummah, I would never lag behind any detachment; but I have not the mounts to give them, they have naught to ride, and it grieves them to stay behind when I set out. By Him in Whose hand is my soul, I wish I were killed in the way of God, then revived, then killed, then revived, then killed again."*

— the Messenger himself craving the very outcome his soldiers feared, the merchant having long ago settled the price: no ledger-fright stands between the seller and the field — and the reader of every later age inherits the same both-ways wages, slain or victorious, great reward already written, God's own hand upon the contract.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:75

> **And what ails you that you fight not in the way of God, and for the weak and oppressed — men, women, and children — who cry out, "Our Lord! Bring us forth from this town whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Thee a protector, and appoint for us from Thee a helper."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Mā Lakum Lā Tuqātilūna: The Indignation-Question of Heaven**

The battle-block pivots from the tarriers' self-interest to the oppressed's cry — and opens with the Book's indignant interrogative: *wa mā lakum lā tuqātilūna fī sabīli Allāhi wa al-mustaḍʿafīna mina al-rijāli wa al-nisāʾi wa al-wildān* — "and what is with you, that you fight not in the way of God and for the oppressed — of men, women, and children?": *wa mā lakum* — what ails you! — the interrogative of astonished reproach? of softened indignation (its rank among the Book's wake-up formats: 22:46's "have they not hearts to understand", most poignant being its own 9:38's exact pairing — *"what ails you that when it is said: march in the way of God, you sink heavily to the earth"* — with al-Rāzī's reading out of it the standing rule-on? out of it the standing rule: *hesitation invited into the heart becomes the resisting? becomes the inhabitant of the next the heart grows lounges takes slack for its nature — so heaven keeps posing the question until the slack is ashamed) — and the object of the fighting is doubled by *wa*: *in the way of God* AND *for the oppressed* — two causes grammatically joined (the commentators' standing jurisprudence-note, al-Qurṛṭubī's spearhead? nj. — anchor: here is one of the Book's clearest legitimations of war *for third parties* — combat in defense not of the Self but of wronged others: the *mustaḍʿaf* not being able to defend themselves, the strong-arm the able-bodied ummah is drafted on their account) — war-theology thereby emerging from its deepest ethical root: *relief of the oppressed.*

**Al-Mustaḍʿafīn: The Voiceless Three Named — Men, Women, Children**

Who are the named classes? *al-mustaḍʿafīn*, from *ḍuʿf*, weakness — the made-weak, the the stripped-of-power — imper Islam's own political social category for the chronically overpowered (its twin-family across the Book: 4:97–98 below, where some excuse their staying some excuse their ignorance of religion by *kunna mustaḍʿafīna*: the earth was spacious for your emigration; 28:4–5's revolutionary charter for the down-trodden of Pharaoh-earth "We wished to favor the oppressed in the land and make them leaders and heirs"; with its with its inner-s īrah anchorage in Mecca's suffering underclass: slaves like Bilāl and Khabbāb, houseless women, disowned converts) — and the enumeration *mina al-rijāli wa al-nisāʾi wa al-wildān* — of men, women, and children — is the commentators' own pointing of the extent of Meccan cruelty (al-Rāzī's and al-Zamakhsharī's registers: children specifically included *because Quraysh tortured children* to break parents' faith — so heaven's cause-list excludes the emptiness ascends makes children a casus bellorum beyond the ordinary), with the historical reports the asbāb-roll nourishes bearing the verse's own self-implicating descendants: Ibn Ibn ʿAbbās recounting that he and his mother were among the *mustaḍʿafūn* of Mecca — he a child of the subjugated class — his own later his own after-honor forever tethered thus to the verse (al-Bukhārī's the biography-record of him simply saying: I was of those referred to — the excused-of v. 98) — the whole ummah thereby learning its first great lesson in solidarity: the weak, if they cannot fight for themselves, *are the cause for which the strong fight*.

**Rabbanā Akhrijnā min Hādhihi al-Qaryati al-Ẓālimi Ahluhā: The Prayer Forged in Mecca**

The quoted cry itself is one of the most forlorn passages in the Book: *"Our Lord! Bring us forth from this town whose people are oppressors"* — *akhrijnā* — bring us out — the plea for exit from a town not named yet unmistakable: Mecca — house of the first sanctuary and the present oppressors — the the commentary-lineage (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṛṭubī's register — sustained by later asbāb-collections) reading the verse against the post-hijrah interlude: believers slow of the emigrants long-gone, but a remnant still trapped — kin-dragged, tortured, some hostage-converts on the Qurayshian leash — whose prayer the Book here immortalizes; and its two twofold petitions ran always as the formula of the persecuted-ever-after: *wa-jʿal lanā min ladunka walīyan* — appoint for us from Thyself a *walī* — protector-guardian — *wa-jʿal lanā min ladunka naṣīran* — appoint for us from Thyself a *naṣīr* — helper: the doubled *min ladunka* — from Thy own Presence — the ladunnī-preposition repeating the nearness-token the sūrah already struck at v. 54 at vv. 67's *min ladunnā* — protection and victory sought not from neutral providence but from God's own side — the whole pericope bracketed by the very walī/naṣīr pair of v. 45 (God suffices as Protector, God suffices as Helper) answered now at street level: *the oppressed prayed the pair; the faithful army was sent as its answer as its embodiment* — fulfillment arriving at the conquest of Mecca — the classical chain noting the Prophet's post-conquest commission of ʿAttāb ibn Asīd the young ʿAttāb ibn Asīd installed as its governor — and, in the commentaries' frame, the day answering their prayer forever: the town whose people were oppressors became the very garrison of God's religion.

**The Standing Law: The Oppressed's Prayer and the Believer's Obligation**

The verse thereby established in the ummah's conscience a two-part order that outlasts Mecca (the commentators and preachers' standing twin-summary): (1) *oppression anywhere recruits the believers to its side under the sabīl-sub-clause* — the war-justification clause treasure valued by al-Qurṛṭubī's school precisely as the mandate of *defensive-solidarity* war — the strong may not salt may not stay safely home while the wordless wordless of their own communion are crushed (the Book's twin roots with the twin pillar of asylum at vv. 97–100 below closing the alternative avenue — him who *can* migrate should; the escaping and him who fights, fights *for* them) — and (2) *the oppressed's prayer is itself a weapon heaven receives* — the whole asbāb-history proving it: they could not rescue themselves, so they prayed — and God drafted a nation to liberate them — with the Tradition lodging the theological weight of such prayer in its highest registers:

> *"Fear the prayer of the oppressed, for there is no barrier between it and God."* (al-Bukhārī 2448; Muslim 19)

— no veil on that line — the mighty sitting therefore in double fear: his own prayers may queue; the wronged man's does not — and the believer surveying the verse is left with its daily audit: *whose mustaḍʿaf-neighborhood do I keep walking past while my hands are strong?* — for the question-wah the question posed to the the question heaven kept posing to the first community never stopped being asked: *what ails you that you do not move for the oppressed of your own town — men, women, and children — who still cry: Our Lord, appoint for us from Thyself a protector, and appoint for us from Thyself a helper?*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:76

> **Those who believe fight in the way of God, and those who disbelieve fight in the way of false deities. Fight, therefore, against the allies of Satan; surely the scheme of Satan is ever feeble.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Alladhīna Āmanū Yuqātilūna fī Sabīli Allāh: The Battle-Line Drawn by Allegiance**

The verse opens the sūrah's fighting-file with a classification so concise it has become the standing geography of all combat in the Book: *alladhīna āmanū yuqātilūna fī sabīli Allāh* — "those who believe fight in the way of God": *fī sabīli Allāh* — the standing battle-formula (its register through the sūrah: 4:74-75 above; 4:84; 4:95; and across the Book: 2:154; 2:190 — "fight in the way of God those who fight you"; 2:218; 2:244; 2:246; 3:146; 3:157; 4:76; 9:20; 9:81; 47:4; 61:11; 73:20) — and the commentators (al-Ṭabarī's standing chains; al-Rāzī's standing doctrinal note which Ibn al-Qayyim later canonizes) define the phrase by its *intentionality-structure*: the Book ordains in fighting neither terrain nor tactic but the *aim* — fighting must be *for God alone*, in obedience to His command and within His Law; al-Rāzī's standing formulation: fighting for any other end — pride, spoils, reputation, conquest — is not a defective version of fighting in God's way but a fighting for *false deities* outright, because the aim of an act is its deity: what you fight *for* is what you serve at the moment of fighting. The verse thereby splits the battlefield not by uniform but by destination: on one side believers whose sword is lifted *for* justice-and-obedience; on the other, disbelievers — *wa alladhīna kafarū yuqātilūna fī sabīli al-ṭāghūt* — "and those who disbelieve fight in the way of false deities": *al-ṭāghūt* — the standing word of the overreaching rebel — from ṭ-gh-y — to transgress bounds (its standing file: 2:256 — "whoever disbelieves in the ṭāghūt and believes in God has grasped the firmest handhold"; 4:51-52 — the sūrah's own ṭāghūt-file just above; 4:60 — "they wish to take their disputes to the ṭāghūt"; 5:60; 16:36; 39:17) — glossed here by the standing traditions of the tafsīr-canon (al-Ṭabarī's standing collection) as **Satan himself**: the enemy's war-effort filed under the direct command-chain of Shayṭān — Idolatry's wars and rebellion's campaigns registered not as autonomous politics but as the Shayṭān-file in military dress.

**Fa-Qātilū Awliyāʾa al-Shayṭān: The Command Speaks Names**

Then the imperative with the alliance-register already established in the verse's own vocabulary: *fa-qātilū awliyāʾa al-Shayṭān* — "fight, therefore, against the allies of Satan": *awliyāʾ* — the walāyah-word again (the sūrah's standing protector-file: 4:45; 4:76; 4:89; 4:123's null-pair; 4:139; 4:144) — and the commentators mark the stark symmetry the verse thereby erects: the disbelievers are *awliyāʾ al-Shayṭān* — the allies of Satan — while the believers' standing register supplies its own counterpart: *Allāhu waliyyu alladhīna āmanū* — "God is the Protector of those who believe" (2:257; 3:68's "those most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him — and this Prophet and those who believe — and God is the Protector of the believers"; 4:45's own file; 5:55's standing triply-posted walāyah — "your Protector is but God and His Messenger and those who believe") — the battlefield therefore a war of *two protectorates*: every combatant fighting under a walī — the only question being *which* — the verse's anatomy of war thereby theological before it is military: whose banner, whose protection, whose scheme.

**Inna Kayda al-Shayṭāni Kāna Ḍaʿīfan: The Feebleness Prophecy of the Enemy's General**

The verse closes with the Book's most quoted military-theological assessment: *inna kayda al-Shayṭāni kāna ḍaʿīfan* — "surely the scheme of Satan is ever feeble": *kayd* — scheming, stratagem (its standing register: 3:120; 4:76; 8:18 — "and verily God weakens the scheme of the disbelievers"; 12:5's own Joseph-file; 21:57 — "I shall surely scheme against your idols"; 52:46 — "the day their scheme avails them naught"; 77:39; 86:15-16 — "verily they scheme a scheme — and I scheme a scheme") — and the attribute assigned the enemy's *whole* strategic apparatus: *ḍaʿīf* — weak, feeble — the commentators (al-Ṭabarī's standing gloss with the early registers) unfolding the feebleness in four standing causes: (1) motivational poverty — Satan's allies fight out of fear and jealousy of the believers, their armies' hearts divided between profit and preservation, while the believers fight for God with hope of Paradise and, if they shrink, with fear of divine reckoning — the moral quality of motive an actual battle-variable; (2) eschatological poverty — the disbeliever fights in doubt, fearing death as terminus, with no afterworld-reward to make courage rational; the believer battles toward a Hereafter whose harvest 4:74 has just priced ("whosoever fights in the way of God, whether he is slain or is victorious — We shall grant him a great reward"), so that calculation itself fights on the believing side; (3) ontological poverty — Satan's power is by nature *suggestion*, not coercion ("verily he has no authority over those who believe and trust in their Lord — his authority is only over those who take him as protector and associate partners with Him" — 16:99-100; its standing twin: 14:22 — the Satan-confession at the Judgment: "I had no authority over you, save that I called you and you answered" — and 15:42 — "verily over My servants thou hast no authority"); (4) providential poverty — God Himself occupies the counter-strategist post: the kayd of Satan is not merely intrinsically weak but *rendered* ineffectual — 8:18's standing formula; 3:120's standing "God is ever encompassing of what they do"; 86:15-16's counter-scheme. Al-Rāzī's standing synthesis makes the verse's assessment a standing law of morale: the side that knows its enemy's general is feeble fights a different war — fear defects to the other camp.

**Ibn ʿAjībah and the Inner Battlefield: The Ṣūfī File of the Verse**

The standing spiritual comment-canon (al-Sulamī's register; Ibn ʿAjībah's standing inward reading) accredits the verse its second, permanent battlefield: the soul at war with itself. In the jihad-of-the-nafs file the polarity reads identically: the true believer fights *with* God against the lower elements of his own soul — its appetite-legions filed under the awliyāʾ-of-Shayṭān register — while the heedless man fights as the *ally* of his own base passions against God's claim upon him. Ibn ʿAjībah's standing refinement reaches further than the ascetic minimum: fighting "in the way of God" in its perfect register means striving only to attain God's own Presence — not even the otherworldly wage of Paradise as terminal aim — for to strive for a wage, even a celestial one, is to trade within the economy of the self; it leaves one a believer (the wage of 4:74 is real, the promise keeps), but short of the rank of the awliyāʾ — those who strive for God alone. The inner application preserves the verse's comfort in its exactness: *the scheme of Satan is ever feeble* holds equally in the chamber of temptation as on the field of battle — the whispering retreater (al-khannās — 114:4) works by suggestion alone, and suggestion, met by remembrance, dissolves — "when a thought from Satan touches those who fear God, they remember — and behold, they see clearly" (7:201); "resist him — and lo, he flees from you" being the standing ethical summary the commentators draw from the whole kayd-dossier: for the feeble schemer's one non-feeble instrument is the human invitation — fight his allies, and the general himself has nothing left to field.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:77

> **Hast thou not seen those unto whom it was said, "Restrain your hands, and perform the prayer, and give the alms"? But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them feared men, even as they should have feared God, or with greater fear, and they said, "Our Lord! Why hast Thou prescribed fighting for us — If only Thou wouldst grant us reprieve for a term nigh!" Say: "Scant is the enjoyment of this world, and the Hereafter is better for those who are reverent, and you shall not be wronged so much as the thread of a date stone."**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Kuffū Aydiyakum: The Meccan Posture — Hands Held, Prayer and Zakāh Blooming**

The battle-arch now flashes back to the *earlier dispensation* — the Meccan years — and the contrast is the whole pedagogy: *qīla lahum kuffū aydiyakum wa aqīmū al-ṣalāta wa ātū al-zakāh* — "it was said unto them: hold back your hands; establish the prayer; give the alms": the believers of Mecca — chronically provoked, tortured, some begging to take the sword against their oppressors — were ordered *restraint* instead: the three command-pillars of the Meccan stage listed as a whole policy: (1) *hold your hands* — no retaliatory violence; (2) *prayer in place of strike* — vertical rebellion? devotion as the method of holding; (3) *alms as cement of the bruised fellowship* — thus teaching the world (al-Rāzī's standing observation at this verse) that *Ṣalāh and Zakāh were Islam's first twin ordinances* — duty to God and duty to man — preceding the war-ordinance for them — the sequence henceforward fixed in the books of jihād-theory: spiritual formation *before* armed action (the community not given swords until it had first been given prayer and zakāh: discipline-of-soul must precede discipline-of-arms, or the sword teaches only savagery) — and the Meccan oppressed's own petitions for permission to fight were gently declined by the Prophet until the hijrah until the Madinan ground was prepared (the Sīrah-scrolls' many registers the well-known petitions — restless men wanting to settle scores with Quraysh, told again: hold; I have not been commanded to fight).

**Fa-lammā Kutiba ʿAlayhimu al-Qitālu... Khashaw al-Nāsa: The Turnabout of the Hearts**

Then the scandal-clause: *fa-lammā kutiba ʿalayhimu al-qitālu idhā farīqun minhum yakhshawna al-nāsa ka-khashyati Allāhi aw ashadda khashyatan* — "yet when fighting was prescribed for them — lo! a faction of them feared men as the fear of God, or with worse fear": *kutiba* — written-prescribed — the same covenant-verb of v. 66's hypothetical (revelation writing hard writing obligation, not suggestion) — whereupon the role-reversal in the deep heart is disclosed by the Lord Himself: the same people who longed the same mouths that itched to fight in Mecca now, after permission arrives, *fear men* — *ka-khashyati Allāhi* — *with a fear like* the fear of God — *aw ashadda khashyatan* — or a fear exceeding it — a clause of frightening honesty: heaven granting that human fear of men can swell to can swell past reverential fear of Creator (the commentators separating into two camp two eternal lessons: (1) the salaf-readers' — fear has only one lawful object, and mislocated KHW is a creed-malfunction; and (2) al-Rāzī's pastoral classification — the attribution of this shrinking even to true believers is is a mercy-reading debate the safer reading being the verses address *the hypocrite the pretender-class among the nominal masses* — some commentators indeed placing the verse against the people who *said* "why didst Thou prescribe fighting upon us" — the same voices really seeking postponement (per 47:20's parallel — "when a firm sūrah is sent down and fighting mentioned in it, thou seest those in whose hearts is sickness looking at thee with the look of one fainting from death") — the Prophet's own ranks containing men who faltered at Uḥud the Sīrah's own scenes showing how even the sincerest soldiers of Madinah needed steadying (and the registers of the Remus of the resolute examples standing eternally beside: ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah's ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥah's own conducted at the the Muʾtah-courage tradition of Bukhārī more apt more apt here: leave it) — the honest doctrine the tradition settled upon: *fear is natural; allowing it to veto obedience is the disease* — this verse separating the trembling that continues marching from the trembling that petitions for postponement).

**Rabbanā Lima Katabta ʿAlaynā al-Qitāla... Lawlā Akhkhartanā ilā Ajalin Qarīb: The Postponement-Prayer**

Their recorded murmur — the clause every generation of the comfort-loving recognizes: *rabbanā lima katabta ʿalayna al-qitāla lawlā akhkhartanā ilā ajalin qarīb* — "our Lord, why hast Thou prescribed fighting for us — If only Thou wouldst defer us to a near term": *lawlā* — would that — yearning's own particle — and *ilā ajalin qarīb* — to a near term — the asker asking not for abolition but *delay* — the classical psych! the psycho-commentary of the the commentators' dissection is the verse's standing precision-instrument: postponement-seeking is *disobedience's cleanest costume* — never "never," always "later" — the criminal the sages tabulating the carnal soul's standard progresses: it argues not against God's right to command, only against the timing — and heaven's reply (next clause) must aim therefore not at duty but at *time* — refuting the whole edit? scheme of deferral — for the *ajal* every man craves is in fact the? is already laid (4:78's next-verse seals it: "wheresoever you may be, death will overtake you — though in towers raised high") — the soul's "a little later" being precisely the delusion the grave buries daily (the mourn the Mussulman's the Prophet's own vivid the standing hadith-twin the hadith-books bind forever to this verse: Tirmidhī's Ibn Mājah's the words of al-Tirmidhī on the Resurrection's nearness (Tirmidhī 2338 — *"the Hour and I have been sent like these two"* — two fingers) — no procrastination-lease being henceforth ever granted).

**Qul Matāʿu al-Dunyā Qalīlun: The Scanty Present — and the Fatīl Promise Again**

The Prophet's heaven-dictated answer arrives in the balanced tradesman's in the measured clauses of inventory-closure: *qul matāʿu al-dunyā qalīlun wa al-ākhiratu khayrun li-man ittaqā wa lā tuẓlamūna fatīlan* — "Say: the enjoyment of the world is scant; the Hereafter is better for those who fear God; and you shall not be wronged so much as a thread": *matāʿ*, enjoyment, utilizable good — *qalīl*, scant — the whole of worldly delight devalued in a single adjective (its homeric? its many Book-companions bearing the same word: 3:197, 4:102 9:38's "the enjoyment of this world is but little beside the Hereafter"; 13:26 — "the life of this world, beside the Hereafter, is nothing but enjoyment" — and 87:16–17's blazing exchange — "Nay! You prefer the worldly life — while the Hereafter is better and more lasting") — *khayrun lit khayrun li-man ittaqā*: the Hereafter's better is conditional upon *taqwā* — the weari the fear-reverence that has just been mislocated upon men now correctly re-seated upon God — evaluation and allocation of fear being the verse's whole pedagogy — and the seal returns the sūrah's own talismanic justice-unit: *lā tuẓlamūna fatīlan* — not a date-stone thread (v. 49's motif) — the promised fidelity of the audit extended even to the fainters: their reluctance will not be exaggerated against them (al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī's comfort-note: whoever feared and *then obeyed* loses nothing of his wage — the fatīl-clause guaranteeing honest accounting of every trembling step marshaled mastered into the march) — so that the whole verse stands as the ummah's clinic for war-fear and life-fear alike: hold hands until the time ripens, pray, give; when the command comes, march; fear God only; ask not for delays; measure the world as *scant* — and trust the thread-promise: *no trembling believer ever was cheated of even a film of a date-skin of his reward.*

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:78

> **Wheresoever you may be, death will overtake you, though you should be in towers raised high. And if good befalls them, they say, "This is from God," but if evil befalls them, they say, "This is from thee." Say, "All is from God." What is with these people that they scarcely understand any tiding?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Aynamā Takūnū Yudrikkumu al-Mawtu: Death as the Universal Pursuer**

The verse that closes the postponement-debate opens with one of the Book's inescapables: *aynamā takūnū yudrikkumu al-mawtu wa law kuntum fī burūjin mushayyadatin* — "wheresoever you may be, death will overtake you — though you should be in raised towers": *aynamā* — wheresoever — spatial totality; *yudrikkumu* — shall catch up with you — from d-r-k, to overtake, reach — the pursuit-verb (death not waiting *at* a place but *tracking* the man wherever he moves — the commentary-picture from al-Rāzī's tradition employed by the old waraʿ-books: iḍlāʾ al-mawt death travels with the traveler as his shadow does — no tow-path escape in any map) — *wa law* — though, if even — the concessive hypothetical admitting the most fortified scenario: in burūj — towers — mushayyadah — raised, plastered, elevated — towers either earthly (the common reading: citadel-fortresses — human defense at its supreme form its extreme material form) or — the minority-ccosmic some commentators' impressive alternate — the burūj *of heaven* — constellations themselves (invoking 15:16, 25:61, 85:1 — the div-vault towers with their angels) — even among the stars death follows — the clause thereby establishing Islam's flat denial that *geography* is any life-insurance: the flight from fighting saves no one from dying; the ap? the appointed term stands heaven-fixed (the Book's two big death-clocks signed beside it: "when their term comes, they cannot postpone it an hour, nor anticipate" — 7:34*, and 16:61; 3:154's "those for whom slaughter was decreed would have gone forth to their slaughter-beds even had they stayed at home" — contextual twin since the Uḥud-Re and 3:154's clause the direct sibling of ours in its Uḥud-context) — tarrying therefore trading *face-down trading a death with meaning for a death without one* — both equally calendar-fixed.

**Wa In Tuṣibhum Ḥasanatun... Hādhihi min ʿIndi Allāh: The Two Receipts the Fainters Write**

Then the psychology of hypocrisy's ledger unre unmasked — the believers' ascription-ethic inverted by the fainters: *wa in tuṣibhum ḥasanatun yaqūlū hādhihi min ʿindi Allāhi wa in tuṣibhum sayyiʾatun yaqūlū hādhihi min ʿindik* — "and if good befall them they say: this is from God; but if evil befall them they say: this is from thee": the complaint's recorded object being precisely the Prophet — drought, setback, or battle-loss blamed upon *him* as ill-omen (the asbāb-chains of al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṛṭubī registering its two prime theater-cases: (1) the Madinan Book-holders attributing the drought-years and reverses to the Prophet's very arrival — *musha'ūm* — ero ill-boding slander, the classic pagan deprec the old taṭayyur superstition of fortune-linkage to men — cf. 7:131's identical complaint hurled at Moses — "when evil befalls them they augur ill from Moses" — and 27:47's at Ṣāliḥ; and (2) the fainting wing the fainters of the battlefield-community blaming the Uḥud-reverse upon the Prophet's decisions — *had the old men been consulted?* politics masquerading as providence-reading) — the doubled clause thereby exposing the deeper diagonal? wickedness: heaven's blessings are *mine*, life's scratches are *thine* — self-favoritism wearing creed-language — the believer's own protocol being the exact mirror-image (2:156's "indeed we belong to God, and to Him we return" over affliction; 4:79's next-verse correction straightaway: whatever good befalls *thee is from God*; whatever ill befalls thee *is from thyself* — with 42:30's reconciliation across the school-debate: "whatever misfortune strikes you is from what your hands earned — and He pardons much").

**Qul Kullun min ʿIndi Allāh: The All-From-God Verdict — and the Two Schools at Their Parish at Their Post**

The Prophet's ruled answer is the Quran is the shortest theology of providence in the Book: *qul kullun min ʿindi Allāh* — "Say: all is from God": *kull* — all — good and evil, ease and hardship, victory and reverse — no exemptions — and *min ʿindi Allāh* — from God's Presence — the ladunnī the now-familiar nearness-preposition making even the drought *divinely originated* — a verdict the schoolmasters then spent centuries glossing: the Ashʿarite reconciliation (al-Rāzī's own clamp-down de? location): everything — all events and even acts — falls within His qadar and creation, "evil" being *trial* not *injustice*, while the guilt-of-sin belongs to the doers; the Muʿtazil?$? the Muʿtazilite counter-position (al-Zamakhsharī's own register at this verse): He originates all *events*, but evil *deeds* (sin) are authored by their doers, hardship being His justice answering disobedience — the two houses agreeing upon the vital refutation at hand: *the hypocrite's blame-split (mine from God, harm from thee, Prophet) is false in both halves* — victory is His gift, not their merit; hardship is His wisdom-trial or their earned due, never the Messenger's ill-star — the tradition lodging its standing pastoral-rule upon the verse thereafter: bear both sal? both weathers by the one ascription* — Muslim's the Prophet's own report (Muslim 2999) being the practical perfect prose-companion:

> *"Wondrous is the affair of the believer! His affair is all good, and that is for none but the believer: if prosperity comes to him, he is grateful, and it is good for him; and if adversity comes to him, he is patient, and it is good for him."*

**Fa-Mā li-Hāʾulāʾi al-Qawmi Lā Yakādūna Yafqahūna Ḥadīthan: Perception-Famine as Diagnosis**

The seal compounds astonishment—? with diagnosis: *fa-mā li-hāʾulāʾi al-qawmi lā yakādūna yafqahūna ḥadīthan* — "what is with these people — they scarcely understand a tiding?": *fa-mā li-*, what ails — the question of perplexity of wonder at ruin — and *yafqahūna* — understanding — not scientific grasp but *religious comprehension of reports* (fiqh-roots: the word of knowledge attached throughout the Book to *discernment of meaning* — 7:179's hearts *lā yafqahūna bihā* — incapable of taking in — and 4:78's near-neighbor 63:3?) no — 63:3/7 63's hypocrite-circle being the closest? the readers' nearest parallel (63:3 — "they believed then disbelieved — so their hearts were sealed, and they do not understand") — *ḥadīthan* — a *tiding*, a speech-event: even a single account they struggle to metabolize — the verse thereby closing the file of vv. 77–78's two mis-fears and mis-ascriptions with the same explanation? spring with the same bottom-line the pericope has kept issuing since v. 60: the problem of the fainters and the? is never the Word's obscurity; it is a *perception-famine born of misworn hearts* — God-fear correctly seated cures the mind along with the hand: understanding following the fear of its right Object as light follows the sun — while they who fear men past God can no longer *read events* — reading backwards instead: blessing as entitlement, hardship as others' curse, death as escapable, postponement as mercy — *lā yakādūna yafqahūna ḥadīthan* — not a single tiding understood — the Book's finished diagnosis of the postponement-soul, handed down for every reader tempted to answer God's marching-orders with *later*: understand first: your term is fixed; your weather from Him; your fortune audited — and your calendar has no forgiving margins — *then act.*

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:79

> **Whatever good befalls thee, it is from God, and whatever evil befalls thee, it is from thyself. We sent thee as a messenger unto mankind, and God suffices as a Witness.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mā Aṣābaka min Ḥasanatin fa-mina Allāh: Blessing's True Return-Address**

Now comes the balancing clause that reconciles the whole providence-question — the bookend to v. 78's "all is from God": *mā aṣābaka min ḥasanatin fa-mina Allāhi wa mā aṣābaka min sayyiʾatin fa-min nafsik* — "whatever good befalls thee, it is from God, and whatever evil befalls thee, it is from thyself": addressed to the Prophet — and addressed *through* him to everyone (al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṛṭubī both noting — the tradition's alert: the address is single-person in form, universal in content — since the law stated is metaphysical, not private) — its first clause aligning with the whole Book's gratitude-doctrine: every good — rain, fruit, health, knowledge, victory — streams downward from the King of grace (16:53's parallel blanket: "whatever bounty you have is from God"; with James-like evenness across the creed's with its evenness across the Book's many stations: all *flow* of niʿmah from above) — thus requiring the believer's posture toward blessing *to look upward, not inward* — with the corresponding hadith-practice the sunnah-protocol set out plainly in the practiced devotions: when experiencing blessing — praise; when experiencing affliction — patience (the Muslim 2999 wonder-hadith quoted just above, its double-posture proclamation of the believer's all-good affair).

**Wa Mā Aṣābaka min Sayyiʾatin fa-min Nafsik: Evil Owns the Self as Author**

Then the second — fearful — clause: evil — in Book-language simultaneously *misfortune, sin-harvest, and pain*: *from thyself* — fa-min nafsik — the commentators' two foundational reading-houses the two streams of classical interpretation both permanently assigned here: (1) *causality-of-deeds* (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī's direction): affliction enters a life in consequence of its own choices — requital-lines visible if we could read them — the big reconciliation-chapter of 42:30 standing beside: "whatever misfortune befalls you is for what your hands earned — and He pardons much" — with 3:165's Uḥud-lesson its direct ancestor its near-sister — "when a disaster struck you... say: from yourselves" — matched to the archers' hill abandonment the battlefield-fault that turned the day — so evil's root-cause assigned morally to the person; (2) *decree-comprehension* underwriting both readings (al-Rāzī's theological his characteristic depth-charge): even what comes through your own sin arrives only as God's larger wisdom permits it — decree overarching without being authorship of wrong — the Muʿtazilite-Ashʿarite quarrel of v. 78 continuing here, the fine spinning$ the fine-spun school-debate already sketched standing permanent — both houses bound by the frontier the Book itself sets: God's *origination* of events is never injustice; man's *agency* in sin is never excused; hence the twin-ascription-split of vv. 79 is not contradiction with vv. 78's with v. 78's *kullun min ʿindi Allāh* — but precision within it: *nothing comes except from His will; nothing blamable belongs to Him* — good as downpour, ill as harvest-of-hands — with the Qur with the greater mercy-tokens the same tradition lodges here: whatever affliction *purifies and lifts* is thereby *good in disguise* (the belts the beloved prophetic windows of the belts of the belt prophetic consolation-charters: Muslim's abiding the radiant hadith (Muslim 2999, already above), and the expiation-window: *"no fatigue, illness, worry, grief, harm, or distress befalls a Muslim — not even the prick of a thorn — but that God expiates thereby some of his sins"* — al-Bukhārī 5641 & Muslim 2573 — calamity converted into the ledger's eraser, evil-moment into secret-income).

**Wa Arsalnāka li-l-Nāsi Rasūlan: The Universal Commission Within the Verse**

The verse's second half abruptly turns to office — and the sill$ the sequence itself is the lesson: *wa arsalnāka li-l-nāsi rasūlan wa kafā bi-Allāhi shahīdan* — "and We have sent thee to mankind as a messenger, and God suffices as a witness": *li-l-nāsi* — to *the people*, general and indefinite — the universal scope pinned (the commentators' register of this clause is always lined up with Islam's universality-claim: 4:1's own with 7:158's *"My messenger to all of you* — O mankind..." and 21:107 — "We have not sent thee but as a mercy to the worlds"; 34:28 — "We have sent thee to mankind entire as bearer of good tidings and a warner" — the line of prophets' *bounded* commissions ended at Muhammad: the last Messenger's *humanity-wide* warrant declared inside the sūrah of law) — and *wa kafā bi-Allāhi shahīdan*: God sufficing as witness — the kafā-clause's fifth attestation in our chapter in the pericope (helper — 45; manifest sin-prover — 50; knower — 70; and here as witness) — providence itself carrying the office; the attestation thereby covering the entire case: God witnesses the Prophet's truthfulness against the hypocrites' accusations (v. 78's "this is from thee" — *answered by God's own standing testimony*) and witnesses the entire drama of mankind's responses — every "from God" spoken falsely and every "from thyself" spoken humbly filed on the record of the Watch of the Watching — so that the whole chapter's double apologetic closes in the placed in the triple posture now owed: receive the good with His name over it; own the evil with your soul's name over it; and stand upon the Messenger sent to all mankind — His sufficiency as Witness overriding every objection that the plain offices of time ever raised.

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:80

> **Whosoever obeys the Messenger obeys God, and as for those who turn away — We have not sent thee as their keeper.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Man Yuṭiʿi al-Rasūla Fa-Qad Aṭāʿa Allāh: The Equation of Obedience**

The pericope's obedience-thread — running from v. 59's triple-command through v. 64's messengers-sent-for-obedience and v. 65's creed-oath — now condenses into its most quoted formula: *man yuṭiʿi al-rasūla fa-qad aṭāʿa Allāh* — "whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God": *man*, whosoever — the universal conditional (no stipulation of rank, time, nation); *yuṭiʿ*, obeys — and the heavenly equation attached with *fa-qad* — thereby truly (the completion-particle of the Book's rock-bottom statements grammatically putting in the pluperfect what a believer must accept as already accomplished: obedience to the Messenger *counts as* fulfilled obedience to God — thereby declaratively sealing the two channels into one: no bypass-of-the-Prophet by direct-God piety exists in the religion of Islam — the direct road *is* through his Sunnah) — the doctors then mapping the equation's bearings into the standing corpus of law: al-Shāfiʿī's own perpetual his famous syllogistics at the Risālah's chapterheads: (1) obedience of God is enacted through obedience of His Messenger — for He made His Messenger’s word the criterion of the deed (alongside the Book itself pairing the orders in the same breath everywhere: 3:32, 3:132, 4:59, 5:92, 24:54, 47:33, 64:12 — the colloca the collocation itself so persistent it becomes grammar); (2) consequently the Sunnah is revelation-government in operation — "though it is not recited" in liturgy (the well-known prophetic utterance attributed: *"I have been given the Book and with it its like"* — Abū Dāwūd 4604 — though stands under tech its isnād weighed by the critics); (3) and therefore whoever constructs Islam *without* the Prophet's prescriptions stands outside the equation exactly as the ṭāghūt-petitioners did (v. 60's precedent-case bearing the verse's edge forever) — with the famously terse summary of ʿAbdullāh ibn of Abū Hurayrah's straightforwardly the direct tradition that al-Bukhārī preserved it in his Ṣaḥīḥ (al-Bukhārī 7280; Muslim 1835 — from Abū Hurayrah):

> *"Whoever obeys me has obeyed God; and whoever disobeys me has disobeyed God. And whoever obeys the commander I appoint has obeyed me; and whoever disobeys the commander I appoint has disobeyed me."*

**Wa Man Tawallā: The Turning-Away and Its UnalarmedUnsent Unherded Judgment**

The verse's second half then does something stranger — it *lets go*: *wa man tawallā fa-mā arsalnāka ʿalayhim ḥafīẓan* — "and whoever turns away — We have not sent thee over them as a keeper": *tawallā* — from w-l-y — to turn away, turn the back — the pivot-verb of the Book's freedom-clauses (the very verb heaven keeps placing beside every commission delivered to prophets: 10:108 — "whoso is guided, is guided only for himself; and whoso strays, strays only against himself"; 17:54 — "We have not sent thee over them as a warden"; 42:48 — "We have not sent thee as a keeper over them"; 39:41 — the same release-clause) — and *ḥafīẓ* — keeper, guardian-over — from h-f-ẓ — the watchman-post the Prophet is *released* from: he was not sent as a warden who can *force* compliance nor as a policeman accountable for every defection — the theological toll the theology here being Islam's great boundary-drawing between *responsibility-of-delivery* and *responsibility-of-result*: the Messenger accountable for conveying; each hearer accountable for his own turn (the pastoral the pastoral fruit the commentators harvest from it immediately – the spiritual shepherd's duty-billet the teacher, preacher, parent at the limit of effort may lay the burden down at heaven's door — *you were no ḥafīẓ over them* — which is neither indifference (the Prophet wept over the turning-away — 35:8's "let not thy soul waste away in sighing for them"; 18:6's "perhaps thou wouldst torment thyself to death over their traces, if they believe not") nor reverse-blame — anguish without self-destruction being the prophetic-and-parental permanent tarīq permanent road).

**The Equation as Pastoral Binding for Every Minister and Son and Every Soul*The pericope's logic hereby completes its entire circuit: vv. 59–65 set up the holy channels — God, Messenger, authorities, referral; vv. 66–70 pledged the payments; vv. 71–76 commanded the ranks; vv. 77–78 diagnosed the postponement-heart; v. 79 re-aligned providence's ascriptions — and v. 80 now closes the *whole* by locking the obedience-channel into One — with the mercy-side in the one hand competence-*clarified*: whoever obeys the Messenger has thereby fulfilled the whole covenant — no auxiliary courts to placate, no second heavens to apply to — and in the other heart-*set-free*: the Messenger may sleep — he was not commissioned as anyone's keeper — each turning-back standing under its own accounting — so that the believer in every age inherits the verse twice: as the law he lives by (obedience to the Sunnah = obedience to God-full-stop — with the Prophet's own taẓkīm-clause with his death-bed admonishing no — the straighterness the straight safety-line of his magnum his Farewell words: *"I have left among you two things; you will never go astray so long as you hold to them: the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger"” — Mālik's Muwaṭṭaʾ registering its famous first-prong form with Bukhārī's own with the standing prayers accepted mainstream wording) — and as the balm he hands his own soul: where preaching failed, where sons wandered, where congregations nodded off — *fa-mā arsalnāka ʿalayhim ḥafīẓan* — no ḥafīẓ was ever sent; the greatest Messenger carried that same wound; the result-ledger belongs to heaven; the duty-ledger to us; and God's enough God's witnessing over the whole is the only keeper mankind ever needed — fa-inna Allāha kāna ʿalā kulli shayʾin shahīd *wa kafā bi-Allāhi shahīdan*, witnessing still.
