3:123's Badr-address — "you were lowly, and He supported you"; and 2:267 8:26 — "remember when you were few, deemed weak in the land") — *fa-manna Allāhu ʿalaykum* — *but God conferred grace* — mann-word (the Book's own verb for the gracious-bestowal that arriveth down that uplifts the lower without demeaning — it is also the word of every prophetic biography — 28:86 God favored Moses with messengership; 49:17's "He favored you by guiding you to faith") — and then the closing of the whole counter-file: *fa-tabayyanū inna Allāha kāna bimā taʿmalūna khabīrā* — "so discern — God is ever Aware of whatsoever you do": *khabīr* — Aware through-and-through (the audit-attribute returning the sūrah's own pericope — v. 35's khabīr-seal above; the internal-edges the engine that counts even impulse) — the war-law thereby closing on the same ground it opened upon at 4:84-86: an army under God audits its own trigger-hands triggers — because the treasury of true gains is with God, the motive of every strike must be so too — and from this one verse the tradition drew its standing military ethics: presumption of brotherhood upon peace-cry; audit of suspicion before strike; spoils regarded as God's own estate; and the believer-warrior remembering *once you were the low man at the roadside too*.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:95

> **Those who stay behind among the believers — except for the disadvantaged — and those who strive in the way of God with their goods and lives are not equal. God favors those who strive with their goods and their lives a degree above those who stay behind. Unto both God has promised that which is most beautiful. But He favors those who strive with a great reward above those who stay behind.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lā Yastawī al-Qāʿidūna min al-Muʾminīna Ghayru Ulī al-Ḍarar: The Sitters and the Strivers Weighed**

The long battle-scroll (vv. 71–94) closes its first arch with the ummah's most sobering comparative: *lā yastawī al-qāʿidūna mina al-muʾminīna ghayru ulī al-ḍarar* — "those who stay seated among the believers — except the disadvantaged — and those who strive in the way of God with their goods and their selves are not equal": *qāʿidūn* — sitters — from q-ʿ-d — to remain seated (the word chosen for those who stay across the Book's whole across the Book's whole jihād-code: 9:83's "sit, then, with those who sit"; 9:90's muʿadhdhirūn coming to sit-with-sitters — the physical posture itself turned moral diagnosis: while God summons men to *go forth*, these *sit*) — and the key-exception inserted mid-verse: *ghayru ulī al-ḍarar* — save those with *ḍarar* — affliction, disadvantage, constraint (the asbāb for the exception being one of the Book's tender scenes: al-Ṭabarī's, al-Zamakhsharī's and al-Qurṛṭubī's roll: the blind Companions — the account leads with ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm of the tradition, or Ibn its standing name ibn Umm Maktūm — coming to the Prophet grieving that blindness kept him from the field — and the Prophet falling silent beneath the descent of the exception-clause; the verse arriving with its exemption sewn into the judgment itself) — *ḍarar* interpreted across the generations as blindness, lameness, chronic illness — and extended (in al-Rāzī's widening) to the man lacking mount, provision, or weapon — the equipment-poverty counting as bonafide affliction (cf. 9:91 — "no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, when they are sincere to God and His Messenger"; and 9:92's tear-streaked band who came seeking mounts and were turned away *crying because they could find nothing* — the Book mourning them instead of blaming them — the Quran's own canon of the weeping-exempt).

**Faḍḍala Allāhu al-Mujāhidīna... Darajatan: The Degree Word and the Two Promises**

Then the verse's royal equality-clause and its qualification — the sūrah of sun's justice of calibrated justice: *faḍḍala Allāhu al-mujāhidīna bi-amwālihim wa anfusihim ʿalā al-qāʿidīna darajatan* — "God favors the strivers with their goods and their selves over the sitters — by a degree": *darajah* — step, rank (the Book's own step-vocabulary — 6:132's "unto all are degrees according to what they have done"; 9:20's "those who believe, and migrate, and strive... are greater in rank with God"; 58:11's "God raises those among you who believe and those given knowledge by degrees") — *darajatan* left indefinite, which the classical commentators (al-Rāzī's own musing) deliberate as deliberately open: a degree — or *degrees* — for how many grades the singular-indefinite may stand plural (and the next verse's own plural *darajāt* at 4:96 answering the question immediately: not one step but *steps-many* — single darajah in this world, layered darajāt in the next) — then the ummah-consoling clause that prevents the elite from breaking the community: *wa kullan waʿada Allāhu al-ḥusnā* — "to both He has promised the Most Beautiful": *kullan* — each — the sitters *as believers* and the strivers — both are sworn to al-ḥusnā (Paradise definitive — the Book's short-form name for the Garden — with the faqīh al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's summary that God has not created has not made the believing sitter God-forsaken: promise-lines only differ in ranking, not in truth) — and *wa faḍḍala Allāhu al-mujāhidīna ʿalā al-qāʿidīna ajran ʿaẓīman* — "yet He favors the strivers over the sitters with a mighty wage": the schema of Islamic spiritual sociology the doctors keep citing — promise common, *rank differentiated*: fard-kifāyah logic at its root (jihād not upon every neck individually — the ummah honored by its band going forth and by its body conferring legitimacy upon it — upon both groups the promise, but upon the ransomed ones — the degree) — al-Rāzī's spiritual-diagnosis placing its permanent counter-question against every Muslim: do you belong to the band that *travels toward the rank*? or to the company that merely sits within the promise?

**Striving With Goods and Selves: The Two-Currency Striving**

The verse's war-canon set its double standard of sacrifice — *bi-amwālihim wa anfusihim* — with their wealth and their selves — giving to jihād the two classical tracks which the Sunnah then parades in hadith-roll: the wealth-striver equipping fighters (cf. the Prophet's own definition at Muslim 1884 — *"whoever equips a fighter in the way of God has himself fought; and whoever looks after his family in his absence has himself fought"*) and the self-striver himself in the saddle (with 61:11's plenary formula — "believe in God and His Messenger and strive in the way of God with your wealth and your selves — that is better for you, did you but know") — the commentators cherishing the *order* — amwāl first, anfus second — noting thereby that property-sacrifice is the cheaper gate, becoming often the preparation the established training for self-sacrifice (the soul practiced first at carrying lighter burdens, then heavier) — and the Book's standing summation phrase for this entire twofold code provided by the very sūrah by the End by 9:111's: "God has bought from the believers their selves and their wealth, that the Garden may be theirs" — the metaphysical sale-contract jurisprudence underneath every page of it: *God the Purchaser of lives-and-wealth offered at His path* — the sūrah's war-canon run through at last as one great sale-agreement — with the sitters left sitting upon unsold goods (save the afflicted, whom God exempted from the auction without penalty), and the strivers collecting their first payment tranche already: *ajran ʿaẓīman* — the mighty wage.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:96

> **Degrees conferred by Him, and forgiveness and mercy. Surely God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Darajātin Minhu: The Plural Above the Singular**

A terse seven-syllable verse — the sūrah in its most economical gear — yet the commentators unfold from it an entire ladder of rank: *darajātin minhu* — "degrees from Him": the plural *darajāt* deliberately stepping beyond v. 95's single *darajah* (the stepped-jurisprudence the classical line savors: if the world enjoys one badge-of-favor — victory and ghanīmah — the next world discloses *many graded rungs*: al-Rāzī standing here with the two interpretations the tafsīr-houses pass through — either (1) the mujāhid is favored by *one* degree in this world (his spoils-wage) but by *many* in the Hereafter, or (2) by one degree over the legitimate excused over the legitimately excused sitter — and by layered degrees over the sitter without excuse — and a third reading mounted as Ibn ʿAjībah's register keeps it: the degrees counting also the soul's own station-scales — rising nearness-to-God gained through the very acts of striving) — and the standing hadith seals the arithmetic (Ibn Kathīr's citation — and across the Sahīh al-Bukhārī 2790 Bukhārī 2790 confirm the exact wording: *"in Paradise are a hundred degrees that God has prepared for those who strive in His path — what is between the two degrees is as what is between the heaven and the earth"* — the Paradise-pagan the mujāhid's vertical estate carved out by heaven's own surveyor — one stair of it spanning creation-dimensions).

**Wa Maghfiratan wa Raḥmatan: The Two Soft Companions of the Striver**

Then the provision of the death-threshold with its twin attendants: *wa maghfiratan wa raḥmatan* — "and forgiveness and mercy": the standing two-guardian procession of the Book's eschatological doors (forgiveness erasing the trail behind; mercy flooding the road ahead — cf. 3:157's "and if you are slain in the way of God or die, surely forgiveness from God and mercy are better than whatever they amass"; 3:158's "and if you die or are slain, it is unto God that you shall be gathered"; and the sūrah's own earlier sūrah's own paired recycle at 4:100's *wa ghafūran raḥīmā* ahead) — al-Rāzī's annotation picking up its placement: the striver lives with fear chained to his back (no man walks to battle spiritually spotless — intention warps, taunts slip, spoils glitter) — God's *maghfirah* answers exactly the striver's hidden deformity: the cover-over of his partial failures; and *raḥmah* pays him beyond all desert beyond desert: degrees traded by grace, not invoice — hence the Prophet's own standing report upon the striver's two doors: (Bukhārī the sahīh phrase: "he who fights so that God's word may be supreme — that is God's path" — Bukhārī 2810 above — matched now by Tirmidhī 1637's list of the martyr's six privileges — "forgiven at the first blood-drop; shown his seat in Paradise..." — the maghfirah arriving *at the wound's first instant*, not at Judgment's end).

**Inna Allāha Kāna Ghafūran Raḥīmā: The Double Forgiving-Merciful Seal**

The verse closes in the Book's most beloved attribute-couplet: *inna Allāha kāna ghafūran raḥīman* — "God is ever Forgiving, Merciful": Ghafūr — repeated-Forgiver (gh-f-r — cover-conceal-root — the verb of the helmet and the shield of the covering that takes the blame-wound off sight) — and Raḥīm — ever-Merciful (the sūrah's own recurrent seal — vv. 16, 23, 24, 25, 26, 29... its cadence stitching every legal chapter to its maternal underside) — the commentators' note upon its siting upon its placement just *after* the two-step of degrees-and-wages: lest any fighter misconstrue the Garden as a renting as a paid estate he earned — God signs the roll with the forgiveness-couplet: *all merit you collect stands first under My covering, then under My awarding: your darajāt are Minhu — from Him* — with the sūrah's war-wages chapter thereby ending on the doctrine every spiritual tradition must labor to keep alive: wages real — and mercy prior — the deeds of the striver *counted* because God first *forgave the warping within them* — after which the very next verse scrolls the warning back: to the souls who won't move, won't rise, won't strive nor even migrate — the angels of death asking them, at the door, "in what state were you?" — degrees all being behind them, nothing ahead.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:97

> **When the angels take the souls of those who were wronging themselves, [the angels] say, "In what state were you?" They say, "We were weak and oppressed in the land." [The angels] say, "Was not God's earth vast enough that you might have migrated therein?" These shall have their refuge in Hell — what an evil journey's end!**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Inna Alladhīna Tawaffāhumu al-Malāʾikatu Ẓālimī Anfusihim: The Soul-Taking of the Self-Wrongers**

The sūrah's war-canon now opens its sternest single-scene chapter — the hijrah-judgment: *inna alladhīna tawaffāhumu al-malāʾikatu ẓālimī anfusihim* — "those whom the angels take in death, while they were wronging themselves": *tawaffā* — the Book's standard word for soul-collection (from w-f-y — to receive-in-full, take-up-a-debt — the angels as heaven's appointed receiv heaven's appointed receivers — cf. 6:61 — "He is the Irresistible over His servants, and sends guardians over you, until death comes to one of you, and Our messengers take him, and they neglect not"; 32:11 — "the Angel of Death who has been entrusted with you will take you") — the Book's commentators fixing at once the identity of the taken: professing Muslims who *stayed in Makkah under the idolaters' dominion*, refusing the migration to Madinah (the historical band of the first ummah — caught between faith and family — wealth-anchored by estates, or by the dread of road-and-enmity) — but the Book naming their state with the merciless term: *ẓālimī anfusihim* — *wrongers of their own souls* (the standing Quranic reframing of slavery-and-fear upon soul-docket upon soul-ledger: to remain where Islam cannot be lived, from motives of comfort, estate, or lineage, is not neutral staying-put — it is *ẓulm* against one's self — the harm-word the Book habitually reserves for objective wrong — 4:110's plenary — "whosoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks God's forgiveness, shall find God Forgiving, Merciful"; 65:1's "whosoever transgresses the limits of God, has wronged his own soul").

**Qālū Fīma Kuntum Qālū Kunnā Mustaḍʿafīna fī al-Arḍ: The Deathbed Cross-Examination**

The soul-taking arrives as interrogation — one of the most chilling forensic scenes in the Revelation: *qālū fīma kuntum* — "they say: in what state were you?" — the angels asking in the moment of extraction (with its structural twin-texts in the Book: 6:130's — "O company of jinn and men — did there not come to you messengers from among yourselves recounting to you My signs and warning you of this Day they say: we bear witness against ourselves"; 39:71's — "till, when they come to it, its gates are opened, and its keepers say to them..." — and 16:28-32's paired angel-scenes — the array of the death-interrogations; the tradition hadithologizing the Sunnah itself deepening the scene in the famous grave-cross in the famous grave-questions — "who is your Lord what is your religion who is your Prophet?" — Tirmidhī 1071's hadith in the funeral-registers) — and the captured answering with the plea that has excused every settler in history: *qālū kunnā mustaḍʿafīna fī al-arḍ* — "they say: we were weak in the land": the mustaḍʿaf-defence — the *we were powerless* — the commentators noting its authentic ring parfa its ring of ancient usage (the very word of v. 75's oppressed plea — *rabbana akhrijnā* — now turned inside-out as a self-acquit as self-acquittal) — and the counter-answer heaven hands the angels: *qālū alam takun arḍu Allāhi wāsiʿatan fa-tuhājirū fīhā* — "they say: was God's earth not vast — that you might have migrated in it?": the rebuttal-sentence — earth as vast-escape-route: *wāsiʿah* — spacious (the Book's standing birthing standing adjective of the of earth's generous capacity — 29:56 — "O My servants who believe — My earth is vast; so worship Me") — the angels' logic exact, merciless: the condition of weakness was *portable* — a man's feet were also part of his faith — the crushed soul was never commanded to *stay crushed*; the Divine instruction was *route-around was even then: walk* (cf. the standing two-fold hadith on the hijrah-aged on the migration-class: "hijrah shall not cease until repentance ceases; and repentance shall not cease until the sun rises from the west" — Abū Dāwūd 2479, Aḥmad's own canonical roll — expanding with it the migration-concept from geography to spiritual emigration forever — and its pairing at the Prophet's Makkah-conquest question — "what will you do with a believer who remains in the land of shirk?" — the tradition now erecting its standing doctrine: the professing soul that does not *move when it can* is answerable for its own captivity).

**Ulāʾika Maʾwāhum Jahannamu wa Sāʾat Maṣīrā: The Journey's-End of the Non-Movers**

Then the verdict — one of the sūrah's harshest, delivered with its terrible finality: *ulāʾika maʾwāhum jahannamu wa sāʾat maṣīrā* — "these — their refuge is Hell, and an evil journey's end": *maʾwā* — refuge — from a-w-y — shelter (the word the Book uses for permanent lodging — cf. 3:151's "their refuge is the Fire; evil is the abode of the wrongdoers"; 3:162's ladder 47:12-13's comparative refuges) — and *maṣīr* — destination — from ṣ-y-r — to become-arrive (the Book's own canar its standing journey—end word — and the darker-toned phrase *wa sāʾat maṣīrā* — "widow evil it is as journey's end" — exceptionally one of the Revelation's judgment-nomenclature formulas against categories of men — 2:126 its pivot against Abraham's prayer; 3:162 the destination—it destination-word of the wayward — all rolled now onto the *non-migrant*) — the commentators of the classical canon bearing up beneath the judgment's severity — al-Rāzī's ruling where the tradition stands: hijrah was, for the Makkan Muslims who *could*, a personal obligation of the covenant — fard ʿayn, not communal prayer of covenant-migration obligation — tied to the very construction: Islam was still propertyless except where it was embodied — Madinah as Islam's first live territory — so remaining behind meant strengthening shirk by one's presence-and-labor — hence the severity — (with its standing nuance: the verse judged those *who could* migrate — not the truly impotent, whom v. 98 immediately absolves — the entire infra-structure laid out as the four-class mapping by the commentators: (1) able who migrated — the veneration-class; (2) able who stayed and flunked stayed *despite* — v. 97's verdict-class; (3) unable — v. 98's excused; (4) the utterly resourceless — v. 98b's hoped-for-forgiven) — and behind all of it the sūrah's deepest life-law unfolding: Islam's claim upon the soul includes a claim upon the soul's *geography* — a believer must be able to say where his feet stand — the wide-earth argument having never been retired since — in every century, in every land where truth is unsafe, the Divine question stands: *if your soul is unsafe there, what is immovable about your boots?* — and the only acquittal is proven impossibility — not preference, not property, not the familiar chains of a well-furnished captivity.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:98

> **But not so the [truly] weak and oppressed among the men, women, and children, who neither have access to any means nor are guided to any way.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Illā al-Mustaḍʿafīna min al-Rijāli wa al-Nisāʾi wa al-Wildān: The Genuine Weak**

The angels' withering cross-examination of v. 97 receives its mercy-counterweight immediately: *illā al-mustaḍʿafīna mina al-rijāli wa al-nisāʾi wa al-wildān* — "except the weak and oppressed among the men, and the women, and the children": the *illā* — except — opening an acquittal-clause straight against the Hell-verdict of its predecessor (the Book's own juristic architecture: the *exception* — istithnāʾ — mooring the grave decree into its own true scope) — *al-mustaḍʿafīna* — the weakened-ones — from ḍ-ʿ-f — weakness (the exhaustive demographic then spelled out — men AND women AND children — wildān — young ones — the tradition’s honoring syntax: the excuse spreads beyond the warrior-class into the entire non-combatant household — the standing practice which the Prophet himself certified from Madinah onward in al-Ṭabarī’s record: after the sūrah’s verdicts he never missed a prayer without supplicating by name for the mustaḍʿafīn of Makkah — his standing plea being: “O God, deliver the weak among the believers from among the idolaters”) — the commentators' own roll of faces standing behind the clause: Ibn ʿAbbās's own testimony — *"I and my mother were among the mustaḍʿafīn; I was among the children, and my mother among the women"* (al-Ṭabarī's register) — the mother-and-child class of Makkah's trapped — whom no campaign, earthly or theological, could ever indict.

**Lā Yastaṭīʿūna Ḥīlatan wa Lā Yahtadūna Sabīlā: The Two-Fold Incapacity**

The acquittal's exact conditions are then filed with juridical precision: *lā yastaṭīʿūna ḥīlatan wa lā yahtadūna sabīlā* — "who have no means (of migration) — and are not guided to a way": *ḥīlah* — device, means, resource (from ḥ-w-l — turning-about capacity — the standing root-name of every moving-device: the man who lacks *ḥīlah* lacks the very leverage of motion — money, mount, guard, kin-network — the material instruments of departure) — note what al-Rāzī and al-Qurṛṭubī make of its order: where the truly-bound cannot *engineer* the escape, they are free — where they *could* but chose not, they belong to v. 97's class (with al-Rāzī's standing moral cautionary at once: a man must not waive himself into mustaḍʿaf-status on grounds of *hardship* — hardship is not incapacity — every hijrah that ever occurred was hardship-through — the exemption-word of God operates only where the capacity-dispatch is truly zero) — and second, *wa lā yahtadūna sabīlā* — "and are not guided to a way": even if they found means, they cannot find the road — the non-initiated — the slave under locked-quarters, the woman in a tribal roof with no counsel of migration-knowledge (their lack of *hudā al-sabīl* — route-guidance — being honored as the second exemption-arm: heaven counts *knowledge-of-direction* among the preconditions of obligation — no duty falls where the way-out was invisible) — the two rooted arms thereby filing (the fuqahāʾ-paragraphing: obligations-at-strong law are only upon the engine-ended and route-lit) — and the tradition then tells its own chapter of that same trapped column — the standing Sīrah accounts of the Makkan-escapees who attempted the road and were hauled back, pictured across the sīrah-pages for the whole ummah — with the Book's own commentary upon them at 29:10 — *"and among men is he who says: we believe — yet when he is tormented in God, he takes men's persecution as if it were God's own punishment"* — and its merciful resolution at 16:110 — *"then your Lord — for those who emigrated after they were persecuted, then strove and were patient — surely your Lord thereafter is Forgiving, Merciful"* — showing how the canonical verses braid mercy upon mercy around every trapped man who *tried* even once — while at the same time the sūrah locks up the catalogue of excuses at its two terms alone: no means, no way.

**The Demography of Oppression**

And there is one further grandeur in this short verse deserving its own slow reading: the Book's count of the *whole family* within the excused — men, women, children — in that order — the standing tafsir-note being its paradoxical strength: the ḍarar-exempt of v. 95 were those *physically* blocked; the ḥīlah-exempt here are those *practically* blocked — together tracing Islam's dual honesty toward powerlessness: body-blocked and means-blocked stand both before God as exonerated from the door-threshold obligations (with its simultaneous doctrine-rider: neither class thereby drops below the others in basic Islam-accountability — they are exempt from *hijrah and combat*, never from faith itself — for faith needs no camel and no escort-clan — intention and tongue suffice the trapped) — and Ibn ʿAjībah's inward reading again finds its counterpart — the soul's own trapped moments — seasons in life where the spirit genuinely *cannot break through* — no ḥīlah, no sabīl — where the only work left is the held-fastness itself — for the Lawgiver has excused not only the blocked body but the blocked route — the believer in his worst spiritual captivity being taught by the very exemption-structure: stay true where you stand; work your legs only when God opens your road.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:99

> **As for such, it may be that God will pardon them, for God is Pardoning, Forgiving.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Fa-Ulāʾika ʿAsā Allāhu an Yaʿfuwa ʿAnhum: Hope Deferred to Heaven's Pardon**

The exception of v. 98 blossoms into v. 99's own word of hope — among the gentlest sentences in the whole sūrah: *fa-ulāʾika ʿasā Allāhu an yaʿfuwa ʿanhum* — "as for such — it may be that God will pardon them": *ulāʾika* — *these* — the pointing-pronoun singling out the trapped column for mention as their own class (the Book's standing protocol after verdict-passages: the indicted named with indictment-points; the excused named with mercy-points) — and *ʿasā* — it may be — the commentators at once reviving v. 84's theology-of-hope: God's *perchance* in the mouth of the Revelation meaning not contingency but *royal understatement* — a hope-word God chooses when He wills the spirits to *wait in expectation rather than in mere relief* (the standing parallel-rolls of the Book's ʿasā-stations: 17:79's — "perhaps your Lord will raise you to a praised station"; 28:67's "perhaps he will be among the rightly guided"; 66:5's "perhaps his Lord, if he should divorce you, will give him better wives than you") — with the imprisonment-trapped receiving certainty-under-poetics (so al-Rāzī: the ʿasā of God lies beyond anything of the human maybe-order: a word that grants hope and withholds complacency) — and *yaʿfuwa* — pardon-wipe — from ʿ-f-w — to efface, to pass over (the pardon-verb the commentators savored for its image: the ʿafw not merely abstaining from punishment but *erasing the trail of the sin itself* from the ledger — the trail swept off the sand by the wind — cf. the Prophet’s own standing night-invocation — “Allāhumma innaka ʿAfūwwun tuḥibbu al-ʿafwa faʿfu ʿannī — O God, Thou art Pardoning and lovest pardon, so pardon me” — al-Tirmidhī 3513; Ibn Mājah 3850 — the report closing with the standing formula: “He loves pardon — so ask Him for it”) — effacement disbursed to men whose crime was nothing worse than being chained where they could do no more.

**Wa Kāna Allāhu ʿAfūwwan Ghafūrā: The Double-Forgiving Seal**

The verse closes with the attribute pairing: *wa kāna Allāhu ʿafūwwan ghafūrā* — "and God is Pardoning, Forgiving": *ʿAfūww* — the intensive-pardoner (the intensive pattern of ʿafw — its tones multiplied — the One who effaces *again and again and again*) — and *Ghafūr* — the cover-Forgiver (again the helmet-and-concealment root — gh-f-r — the Coverer of the record) — the two divine names being deliberately paired at this precise joint for one standing reason, al-Rāzī's summary among the classical commentators: *ʿafw* answers the *charge* — the excuse-case (ʿudhr) itself erased as if no voice of accusation ever spoke; *maghfirah* answers the *blemish* — whatever of hesitation, of faltering at road's edge, or of sloth remains within the faithful trapped (no trapped man crosses even a long road-test spiritually spotless — intention wavers, and tears shed under coercion have their moments of bargaining weakness) — so the double pardon-gate matches the two defects of the trapped: the first door knocking down the case against them, the second cleansing the soul within them.

**The Standing Pastoral Law of the Mustaḍʿaf-Verdict**

And the tradition from then on has read vv. 97–99 together as Islam's complete charter of *spiritual incapacity* — the full sequence so exact that the fuqahāʾ formalized it into the standing code of obligation (the able unpardoned — the able's decree; the genuinely-blocked uncharged — v. 98/99's pardon) — with its horizons broadening through the centuries into every pastoral dispensation of the religion: the ignorant excused (the man to whom the route of knowledge never reached) the coerced protected (the 16:106-clause — *"save him who is forced, while his heart is at rest in faith"*) — the materially-blocked relieved of every costly charge (hajj being only upon *man istaṭāʿa ilayhi sabīlā* — 3:97's standing formula — the very pattern of v. 98's *lā yastaṭīʿūna... wa lā yahtadūna sabīlā* threading itself through Islam's pillar-law) — with the upshot given by Ibn Taymiyyah's master principle, preserved in his standing maxims: *God's obligation upon any soul never rises higher than the ceiling of its own God-given capacity* — lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan illā wusʿahā (2:286) — and every duty carried beyond reach is, by this pair of verses, laid beneath God's own prefunded mercy — so that the theology of the sūrah's hijrah-arc is in the end wholly merciful: zeal must *pay* at Madinah — but the chained sleep clean under the double lamp of ʿAfūww and Ghafūr.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:100

> **Whosoever migrates in the way of God will find upon the earth many a refuge and abundance, and whosoever forsakes his home, emigrating unto God and His Messenger, and death overtakes him, his reward has fallen upon God, and God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Man Yuhājir fī Sabīli Allāhi Yajid fī al-Arḍi Murāghaman Kathīran wa Saʿah: The Wide-Earth Promise, Kept**

The sūrah's hijrah-arc (vv. 97–100) now receives its own triumphant counter-hymn — God's direct travel-agency contract with the emigrant: *wa man yuhājiru fī sabīli Allāhi yajid fī al-arḍi murāghaman kathīran wa saʿatan* — "whosoever migrates in the way of God finds in the earth many a refuge — and abundance": *murāgham* — from r-gh-m — the root of *rughm* — “despite” (the commentators' classical glosses branching among its spacious lands: a refuge to which the emigrant can turn and be secure from his persecutors — al-Ṭabarī; wide open country for roaming — breadth of land; even many alternatives of dwelling — each of the language-doctors piling upon its amplitude) — *kathīran* — much, many — the multiplication-particle; and *wa saʿah* — and amplitude — from w-s-ʿ — spreading room, plenty (its Book-rooting: 2:261's — "God is Ample, Knowing"; 4:97's objections its twin answer at 4:97 for the angel-question — *was God's earth not vast?* — the earth-amplitude named first there as an argument — here as a *promise* — the wide-amplitude this time guaranteed to the migrant himself: out-accommodated, out-abundant, out-rich — the very text becoming a standing mercy-axiom: God matches every abandoned hectare with wider ground) — with the Sīrah's two great exempla beneath: the Prophet's own emigration (beds whispered of; swords ringed about) — became Makkah conquered in eight years, Madinah the world's capital-of-revelation; and the Companions' exoduses — Bilāl from torture-ground to his honored station as the muʾadhdhin of Madinah; and Ṣuhayb al-Rūmī trading his whole fortune for road-freedom against his pursuers — Ibn Hishām’s standing story: Ṣuhayb detained by the Makkans, striking the ransom-bargain, telling them where his money lay hidden so they would let him pass — and arriving before the Prophet, who called out to him: “the sale has profited, Abū Yaḥyā!”)

**Wa Man Yakhruju min Baytihi Muhājiran ilā Allāhi wa Rasūlihi: Death Mid-Road, Full Wage**

Then the crown-miracle clause of the arc — the verse that turned hijrah into a wager with no losing ticket: *wa man yakhruju min baytihi muhājiran ilā Allāhi wa rasūlihi thumma yudrikhu al-mawtu* — "whosoever leaves his house, migrating to God and His Messenger — then death overtakes him — his reward has fallen due upon God": *thumma yudrikhu al-mawt* — *then death catches him up* (yudrik from d-r-k — the standing catchword from v. 78's towers — the same verb here swung from terror to destiny swung now into mercy-valor: the feared death upon the road, when it comes, is exactly *the clause of full payment*) — *faqad waqaʿa ajruhu ʿalā Allāh* — "his reward has fallen due *upon God*": waqaʿa — fallen-settled (the contractual form of covenant-due) — ʿalā — upon — the telling preposition making the Eternal the debtor in the emigrant's ledger: his wage not cancelled by his mid-road death but *charged upon God Himself* (the commentators' favorite doctrine of the whole of the whole war-and-travel canon: intention prevailing over completion — 4:100 in Bukhārī's titles al-Bukhārī's own classic hadith running its orthodox authentication — *"innamā al-aʿmālu bi'l-niyyāt — surely deeds are by intentions — and for every man only what he intended: he whose emigration was to God and His Messenger, his emigration is to God and His Messenger; he whose emigration was for for a worldly thing to acquire, or a woman to marry — his emigration is to that which he emigrated for"* — Bukhārī 1, Muslim 1907 — the Book of Revelation opening hadith of the whole canon) — and the sīrah-portrait beneath it — al-Ṭabarī's standing account of the aged emigrant who died on the road from Makkah, murmuring with his last breath: *lā ilāha illa Allāh* — and men of Madinah divided over whether his reward lapsed by incomplete arrival — whereupon this very verse descended: God Himself *assumed* his wage — (the Makkans mocking; the believers rejoicing; and heaven sealing: *the debtor in the emigrant's case is the Ever-Living, who can neither be defrauded nor default* — with the classical fuqahāʾ at once widening it into the whole destiny the whole doctrine of *religious death-in-transit* — the dying pilgrim, the sought-of the student perishing on the road of knowledge, the lettered the the emigrant of every century who leaves his city for faith's sake with his feet pointed Godward — each one standing beneath v. 100's underwritten clause — the wage-payer not the destination but the Sovereign — *faqad waqaʿa ajruhu ʿalā Allāh*) — and the two-attributes sealing once more — *wa kāna Allāhu ghafūran raḥīmā* — Forgiving, Merciful — the roll concluded with the pair that had recurred all the way from the sūrah's opening block, always arched over the faithful wherever they fall.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:101

> **And when you travel upon the earth, there is no blame upon you for shortening your prayers if you fear that the disbelievers may attack you; verily the disbelievers are unto you a manifest enemy.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Idhā Ḍarabtum fī al-Arḍi fa-Laysa ʿAlaykum Junāḥun an Taqṣurū mina al-Ṣalāh: The Road-and-Rukhsah Chapter**

After hijrah's estate hijrah's testament comes the traveler's rite — the sūrah now descending from emigration's life-stakes to the conduct of ordinary wayfaring: *wa idhā ḍarabtum fī al-arḍi fa-laysa ʿalaykum junāḥun an taqṣurū mina al-ṣalāh* — "and when you march-travel in the earth, there is no blame upon you that you shorten the prayer": *ḍarabtum* again — the road-threshing verb of v. 94 (the sūrah's standing lexicon pairing: traveling-as-striking — the journey written as blows upon the expanse beneath) — *junāḥ* — blame, sin-leaning crookedness (from j-n-ḥ — wing-side — the standing ethical image of the law: to slant lean over — yet here God declares the road shortening over unslanted); *taqṣurū* — from q-ṣ-r — shorten (the qasr-injunction — the four-unit prayer reduced to two — the canon-paired mercy: zuhr-ʿasr-ʿishāʾ halved for the wayfarer  — the Sunnah itself detailing its full conduct rules (the journey-measure, the settling-count, the joining-extensions) in the standing registers of al-Bukhārī 1090 and Muslim 686 — with the tradition’s standing classroom-question preserved beside them: the Companions asking why the road-traveler shortens his prayer yet keeps his fast — and the schools’ enduring answer rising from it: prayer is *compressed within itself*, while fasting requires day-wholeness — the two rukhsahs carrying different shapes) — and the sūrah’s key-clause following with its topic: *in khiftum an yaftinakum alladhīna kafarū* — “if you fear that the unbelievers may attack you”: *fitnah* here — assault-trial (the commentators' standing gloss: the fitnah of the war-road — ambush, sword, and capture) — and the standing debate-questions of the juristic tradition right that has followed this clause through four centuries of canon: does qaṣr shortening depend on *fear* or on *travel* itself the majority register (Ḥanafī except with the the standing positions: (1) the shortening upon all travel — the majority, on the Sunnah's custom the Sunnah's own general practice — the Prophet shortening *whenever* he journeyed, war or peace alike — ʿUmar's own reply to Ibn ʿUmar's when ʿUmar was asked why shortening continues though war-conditions have passed (Bukhārī Muslim 686's register): "I wondered at what you wonder at, so I asked the Messenger of God — and he said: *it is a ṣadaqah which God has given you — accept His ṣadaqah*" — the road-mercy being thereby not only fearwork but *giftwork* (ṣadaqah!) — charity from the road from the Lord of the road, handed to every rider of the ages); (2) the war-prayer's separate with v. 102 below descending laying the *salāt al-khawf* — the prayer-of-fear itself — as the *separate* fear-content statute, the present verse awarding two rukhsan topics at once: road-shortening plus battle-shortening both stacked across vv. 101–102 — fear-clause riding as a *readiness-condition* of the wild-road era more than as the license-condition for the rite (al-Rāzī's standing reconciliation: fear-pattern through the earliest practice — war-era journeys — then displayed again as habit codified — rukhsah of God covering all roads thereafter).

**Inna al-Kāfirīna Kānū Lakum ʿAduwwan Mubīnā: The Manifest-Enemy Clause**

The verse then closes by naming the strategic constant that had shaped these mercy-laws: *inna al-kāfirīna kānū lakum ʿaduwwan mubīnā* — "verily the unbelievers are unto you a manifest enemy": *ʿaduwwan mubīnā* — enemy *manifest, patent* (the Book's own attribute-standing applying mubīn to enmities: 2:168's — "Satan is to you a manifest enemy"; 12:5's — of Satan to man; 43:62's — of Satan to man again; now applied to the outward confeder to the external host the outward armed confederate to the armed unbelieving confederates at hand on the early roads) — the commentators' pastoral annotation: God names enemies *openly* so that the believers are taught *legally*: precaution is not cowardice (the warning ends the verse for a reason — shortening prayer on a dangerous road isn't worshipless convenience — it is *armed-sentry piety*: the same motive-line of v. 9's standing counsel upon leaving heirs of v. 9 — and of the tether-your-camel doctrine of v. 71 — taking protection *is itself part of the order of God*) — with the standing jurisprudential history delivering the pragmatic articulation: the early community traveled among amb through ambush-lands (raids, pursued envoys, hostile encirclement) — so the Road-Code of Islam was *hardened for war*: qasr of prayer (v. 101), joining of prayers (the Sunnah adding it), the prayer-of-fear in combat (v. 102), arms never laid down even during worship — and yet — the point the commentators keep returning to — the same Book that hardened the war-rite kept the peace-door open all through vv. 90–94 — the peace-offerer's hand, the constricted breast's immunity — the whole war-piece made in one breath: *march, pray shortened, hold your arms — and let every peace-token catch you ready*.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:102

> **When thou art with them and leadest them in prayer, let one group of them stand with thee in prayer, taking their arms with them. When they have performed their prostrations, let them withdraw to the rear, and let another group come that has not prayed and let them pray with thee, taking precaution and their arms. The disbelievers wish you to be heedless of your arms and your baggage that they might assault you all at once. There is no blame on you if you lay aside your arms when you are troubled by heavy rain or illness. But take your precaution. Surely God has prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Idhā Kunta Fīhim fa-Aqamta Lahumu al-Ṣalāh: Worship Under the Sword-Shadow**

The sūrah's war-rite descends now to its most riveting practical detail — a canonical prayer whose architecture is drawn for an active battlefield: *wa idhā kunta fīhim fa-aqamta lahumu al-ṣalāh* — "when thou art among them and dost establish the prayer for them": the address singular to the Prophet — imam under possible assault — and the standing asbāb the tradition preserves (al-Ṭabarī and al-Wāḥidī's rolls): the Prophet and his Companions facing the idolaters at ʿUsfān, the makkan corps under Khālid ibn al-Walīd — then still a champion of the opposition — when the enemy, spying the Muslims bowed in the midday prayer, plotted the rush — whereupon the verse descended between ẓuhr and ʿaṣr, and the battle-measure and the defensive prayer-order was installed in time for the afternoon prayer — the attack thereby misfired (the tradition's standing register of Khālid's own acknowledgement later, to the Prophet after his Islam: "we were prevented from it, by that which was revealed to you" — the war-rite itself counted in the victory-ledger).

**The Two-Shift Congregation: Prayer and Sentry as One Act**

Then the mechanics — Islam's most remarkable liturgical concession, the *ṣalāt al-khawf* proper: *fal-taqum ṭāʾifatun minhum maʿaka wa l-yaʾkhudhū asliḥatahum* — "let one band stand with thee, and let them take their arms": the congregation split into shifts — one company praying *armed*, the other holding the line (the formation schematics the fiqh-books preserve from the early generations: lines arranged so that prostration never leaves the whole host defenseless — at the sujūd one rank bows low with the imam while the rank behind stands guard, weapon in hand; when the first rank rises, the second prostrates alone — so that the imam completes his two rakʿahs and *each* rank has prostrated once with him and stood watch once against the enemy — with its standing alternative account, from Ṣāliḥ ibn Khawwāt's hadith in the Sunan (al-Tirmidhī Abū Dāwūd 1241; al-Nasāʾī 1532): one band prays a full rakʿah with the Prophet, departs; the second band comes, prays a rakʿah, departs; the Prophet completes the prayer — so that the leader has prayed the full measure the full prayer and each band has prayed its share — account upon account showing the flexibility of the concession: the unity of the ummah's worship kept *visible* even under fire, its posture distributed like a shield-line) — *wa l-yaʾkhudhū asliḥatahum* — *taking their arms with them* — the weapons clause never breaking the prayer's sanctity: the combatant-prostrater at once (the standing jurisprudence: arms may be borne through prayer in upon the fear-prayer — swords slung, bows carried, rifles or muskets across the centuries — the same law — worshippers holding steel between heaven and the front) — the commentators' philosophical annotation being the sūrah's own doctrine repeated at the liturgical level: *tawakkul does not cancel drawing-nigh-of-the-arm* (v. 71's ḥidhr; v. 101's mubīn-warning; here the armed sujūd — precaution invited into the very qiblah — the believer's security-work and his God-work fused into a single act — prayer not suspended by danger but *re-fitted* for it).

**Yawaddu Alladhīna Kafarū Law Taghfulūna ʿan Asliḥatikum: The Enemy's Heedlessness-Wish**

Then the verse's intelligence-brief — heaven naming the enemy's hope out loud: *yawaddu alladhīna kafarū law taghfulūna ʿan asliḥatikum wa amtiʿatikum fa-yamīlūna ʿalaykum maylatan wāḥidah* — "the unbelievers wish that you should be heedless of your arms and your baggage — that they might swoop upon you in one single attack": *yawaddu* — the wish-word of v. 89's levelers recurring — *taghfulūna* — from gh-f-l — heedlessness (its standing Sufi irony: the same ghaflah that the spirituals name the chamber-death of hearts is here the tactical death of camps — prayer is no opiate of vigilance; worship is designed not to lower the war-watch) — *amtiʿah* — baggage, travel-goods (the marching-train family of v. 94's ʿaraḍ-economy) — and *maylatan wāḥidah* — one swoop, one lapse one single mass-charge (m-y-l — the incline-word: the whole enemy weight tilting once, together, at the prayer-posture) — the commentators' standing note: heaven exposes the enemy's *strategic desire* so the believers may permanently invert it (the doctrine behind the standing hadith-couplet of war-ethics: preparation-together 8:60's "prepare against them what you can of force and tethered horses — by which you terrorize the enemy of God and your enemy" — the visible readiness itself deterring the swoop long before any clash).

**Fa-Laysa ʿAlaykum Junāḥun In Kāna Bikum Adhan min Maṭarin Aw Kuntum Marḍā: Mercy Even in the Armament-Rule**

Then the rukhsah inside the rukhsah — a concession within a concession: *fa-laysa ʿalaykum junāḥun an taḍaʿū asliḥatakum in kāna bikum adhan min maṭarin aw kuntum marḍā* — "no blame upon you that you lay aside your arms, if rain troubles you or you are sick": the armament-duty itself waived under weather-and-wound (the commentators' standing scene-setting: soaked fighters whose blades and straps became burden; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf's wounded-band named in the rolls as one of the occasions) — *junāḥ* returning from v. 101 (the slant-blame cancelled twice in two verses) — with the immediately-following command twined to the concession: *wa khudhū ḥidhrakum* — "yet take your precaution" (v. 71's very words — the ḥidhr-imperative ringing now for the third time in the war-canon — mercy never disabling vigilance; the rukhsah is a *loading-off*, not a *sleeping-sold not a sleep-at-post*) — and the whole verse sealed at last with its range-compressing threat: *inna Allāha aʿadda li'l-kāfirīna ʿadhāban muhīnā* — "surely God has prepared for the unbelievers a humiliating punishment": *ʿadhāban muhīnā* — degrading chastisement — from h-w-n — demeaning, debasing — the eschatological counter-value counter-measure of all the enemy's field-humiliations their battle-hopes (they hoped to humiliate the worshipper-host mid-sujūd; heaven reverses the entire axis — the prepared-in-advance — aʿadda — degradation filed for their account instead — the Book's own reversal-form running once more: you hold your ranks armed at prayer; their ranks will break unarmed at the Judgment) — thereby sealing the sūrah's war-liturgy: the ummah that prays *with swords* against a manifest-enemy never loses its spiritual posture thereby — mihrab and rampart become one wall — and the sweet by-product the tradition draws from its phrasing ever after (the Sufi schools the devotional commentators, al-Qushayrī's line: salāt al-khawf as the standing icon of the whole spiritual path: *the servant must serve — yet with arms* — dhikr and watchfulness never separating — the soldier-worshipper of Madinah re-embodied in every believer whose soul's ʿUsfān is the inner siege of his own ghaflah).

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:103

> **When you have completed the prayer, remember [and invoke] God, standing, sitting, or lying on your sides. Then when you are secure, observe proper prayer; for prayer at fixed hours is prescribed for the believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Fa-Idhā Qaḍaytumu al-Ṣalāta fa-Dhkurū Allāha Qiyāman wa Quʿūdan wa ʿalā Junūbikum: Remembrance in Every Posture**

The battle-prayer closes with the door that never closes — the dhikr-law: *fa-idhā qaḍaytumu al-ṣalāta fa-dhkurū Allāha qiyāman wa quʿūdan wa ʿalā junūbikum* — "when you have completed the prayer, remember God — standing, sitting, and upon your sides": *qaḍaytum* — completed, discharged (q-ḍ-y of settled-duty — the formal ṣalāt a defined act with a defined exit) — then the instruction swinging from *prescription* to *improvising remembrance*: with the rite discharged, the state persists — the believer never wanders from the hall from the hall of nearness merely because the form has ended (the three-posture specification the commentators love: *qiyāman* — standing; *quʿūdan* — sitting; *ʿalā junūbikum* — reclining on flanks — the whole body-c catalog of sustained postures — with its direct twin at 3:191 — "those who remember God standing and sitting and on their sides, and reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth: our Lord, Thou didst not create this in vain — glory be to Thee! Shield us from the punishment of the Fire" — the two verses meeting as the Revelation's paired charter: 3:191 linking dhikr with *contemplation-of-creation*; 4:103 linking it with the *aftermath of danger* — the two together delivering the inference of the whole dhikr-tradition: remembrance belongs to no single posture and no single hour — it is the ummah's breath) — with the field-setting itself instructive: a company that just prayed staggered-rakʿahs beside enemy cavalry now told — keep saying God's name, in every remaining position of your watches — the battlefield becomes monastery becomes prayer-mat in the widest sense (the comment tradition noting also the two senses of *udhkurū*: remember *in the heart* and invoke *with the tongue* — tasbīḥ, takbīr, personal pleading for victory — the war-dhikr authorized on the eve of clash — cf. 8:45's "O you who believe, when you meet a host, stand firm and remember God much, that you may prosper").

**Fa-Idhā iṭmaʾnantum fa-Aqīmū al-Ṣalāh: Security Restores the Form**

Then the answer-clause restoring the full mold: *fa-idhā iṭmaʾnantum fa-aqīmū al-ṣalāh* — "then when you are secure, establish the prayer": *iṭmaʾnana* — from ṭ-m-ʾ-n — descending-tran the deep settling-quiet (its Book-family: ṭumaʾnīnah — the serenity the ritual pause itself is commanded to contain — v. 102's armed communities now discharged at even now discharged at last into normality) — and the standing jurisprudence: the fear-rite is *exceptional*; the full canonical architecture returns when safety returns (never the concession becoming custom — rukhsahs are keyed to conditions — with the differing view in the earliest roll — some Companion-commentary taking "establish the prayer" to mean *repeat* or *complete* what was shortened; the majority reading being normative-restoration) — thereby as the classic case as the classical case-law sample for the entire uṣūl doctrine of *a condition-bound dispensation lapses with the condition* (ʿilla-zāla = rukhsa-zāla — the the war-prayer ceases at war's end).

**Inna al-Ṣalāta Kānat ʿalā al-Muʾminīna Kitāban Mawqūtan: The Fixed-Hour Prescription**

Then the verse's most formulaic declaration — recited through fifteen centuries at mosque-walls and minbar-ends: *inna al-ṣalāta kānat ʿalā al-muʾminīna kitāban mawqūtan* — "surely prayer is upon the believers a prescription *at appointed times*": *kitāb* here — written-injunction, binding decree (from k-t-b — the prescription-degree-word rather than the noun of the Book itself — with the comment-doctors listing its meaning-set: obligatory decree; well-ordered assignment; covenant-form) — and *mawqūtan* — time-bound — from w-q-t — appointed-hour (the tradition's greatest standing coat the clause the commentators single out as the Revelation's master-charter of time-obedient worship — with the Sunnah filling in its five daily stations — the Prophet's own complete r the miʿrāj-ledger of prescriptions (Bukhārī 349's standing roll the standing account of the fifty-prayers-reduced-to-five) — and the Prophet's time-table texts — "the likeness of the five prayers is as a river at your door in which he washes five times a day" — Muslim 667; "the best of deeds the most beloved deed to God is prayer at its time" — Bukhārī 527, Muslim 85 — the mawqūt-word stretching out thereafter over the ummah's whole architecture of life: mosques, muʾadhdhins, hours-glasses time calendars-of-prayer, the daily building the daily rhythm cohering around five bells-out-of-heaven) — with the verse's own placement being its silent sermon: in the very passage where heaven *most lavishly accommodates* the believers' prayers (shortened on the road, split under attack, dhikr-valid at every posture — the Book then clamps the axle: *nevertheless the set hour stands*: no rukhsah releases the time itself — prayer remains *kitāban mawqūtan* while walls fall — and the entire juridical machinery of qada-makeup, joining, and emergency-prayer exists precisely because the appointed hour is non-negotiable) — and Ibn ʿAjībah's, al-Qushayrī's inward register lifts the arc into the heart again: beyond the completed *outer* prayer, the heart's dhikr continues indefinitely — and when the heart *arrives* secure in the Presence (iṭmaʾn-an *inwardly*) — the very prayer of witnessing comes due — the ever-constant salāt of 70:23 — "those who persevere in their prayer" — posture, time, and weapon-shape now interiorized: qiyām as uprightness-of-covenant; quʿūd as the sitting of presence; junūb as the lying of humility — and the world-clock's five bells keeping the body in cadence with them all.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:104

> **Slacken not in the pursuit of these people. If you are suffering, verily they suffer even as you suffer, while you hope from God that for which they do not hope. Surely God is Knowing, Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lā Tahinū fī Ibtighāʾi al-Qawm: No Listlessness at the Chase**

The sūrah's Uḥud-cycle closes with the charge addressed to a wounded army: *lā tahinū fī ibtighāʾi al-qawm* — "grow not feeble in the pursuit of this people": *lā tahinū* — from w-h-n — slackness, losing-of-back languor (its battlefield lexicon the Book reserves for the aftermath-threshold: 3:146's own adjacent lesson — "how many a prophet with whom a mighty band fought — and they faint they flagged not for what struck them in the way of God, and they weakened not, neither did they humble themselves — and God loves the patient") — *ibtighāʾ* — seeking-pursuit (from b-gh-y — the track-and-reach of a quest — war-craft given the grammar-of-seeking: the enemy now run-analyze now objectively a target sought, not terror feared) — and *al-qawm* — *this* people — the demonstrative naming the particular foe (the standing asbāb the commentators preserve — al-Ṭabarī, al-Jaṣṣāṣ: after Uḥud's wounding, the Prophet urging the march in pursuit of Abū Sufyān's departing force — exhorted on foot himself, the surrounded the camp bruised, the loss-of-seventy fresh — and answering the murmur of fatigue with the doctrine spelled out below) — the Book's own syntax: pursuit not optional but *no-lahinī command lā-tahinū-command* — slackening at the moment of enemy withdrawal potentially breeding reversals (the sīrah-logic: the force that can re-chase can re-shape the peace-map — demoralized withdrawal unpursued teaches the enemy that your pain has overturned your will).

**In Takūnū Taʾlamūna Fa-Innahum Yaʾlamūna kamā Taʾlamūn: The Equal-Pain Equation**

Then the verse's celebrated therapy-of-suffering — its psychology spelled as logic: *in takūnū taʾlamūna fa-innahum yaʾlamūna kamā taʾlamūna* — "if you suffer pain — verily they suffer pain as you suffer pain": *taʾlamūna* — from a-l-m — pain (the Book's own verb repeated word-for-word on both sides — the symmetry itself the lesson) — and the object of the sūrah of the commentators' standing expansion: how the wounded at Uḥud bled — sword-cuts, broken teeth, slain comrades — while the Makkans withdrew believing themselves victors — heaven's ledger announcing: *they, too, left bodies upon your field — their wounds sting just as yours do — your after-shock was shared with them at close of strike* (with al-Qurṛṭubī's genuin al-Qurṛṭubī's standing reading among the justice-canon: no stroke lands upon your camp without its echo also landing upon theirs — the war-pain of one side never being the absolute proof of the other side's peace) — the verse thereby feeding the believers the first great counter-factual of spiritual military lore: *never measure the enemy's morale by your own aches* — pain is universally military; what divides camps is *what the pain is purchased for*.

**Wa Tarjūna mina Allāhi Mā Lā Yarjūn: The Hope-Advantage, the War's Decisive Commodity**

Then the asymmetrical counter the discrepancy that ends the argument: *wa tarjūna mina Allāhi mā lā yarjūna* — "while you hope from God that for which they do not hope": the sūrah's own earlier the tradition classifying it precisely: the believing army fights *expecting from God* three treasuries the enemy is incapable of even conceiving: (1) reward in the next world the other-home ledger: paradise upon the slain — 3:169's alive-with-their-Lord doctrine the doctrine at 3:169: "count not those slain in God's way as dead — nay — living with their Lord, provided for"; 3:157's "surely forgiveness from God and mercy are better than whatever they amass"; the renamed the same hope-treasury of v. 74's two-wage clause — and (2) victory-and-divine-support even in this world — the niṣrat-of-nasr the promised naṣr — Ibn Kathīr's own note: 24:55's "God has promised those who believe and work righteousness that He will make them successors in the land"; 61:13's "help from God and a near victory"; 110:1's "when the help of God comes, and the victory" — and (3) the standing engine the dignity-engine: strength through hope — the argued-from the hope-advantage itself announced by Ibn Kathīr and al-Jaṣṣāṣ as a field-advantage: *the fighting man with heaven to hope from is harder to break than the fighting man with only spoils to hope for* — the army whose paymaster is God keeps its edge whether the day ends in plunder or in graves (its classic counter-image being the idolater's: he fights for the world's ledger alone — when the ledger bleeds red he collapses) — and the seal lands with the twin-audits the attribute-seal closing the war-canon: *wa kāna Allāhu ʿalīman ḥakīmā* — "God is Knowing, Wise": Knowing — the One who gauges every drop of suffering (the Ledger-holder of both camps' pains); Wise — the One who proportions each campaign's outcome to its covenant-condition (the standing structure of the entire war-block — vv. 71–104 — finally summed at its last seal: precaution — obedience — referral of rumors — covenant — treaty — battle-order — travel-rites — war-prayer — and then this last field-psychology — *all of it authored by the Knowing, never by accident; all of it dispensed by the Wise, never by spite*) — with the tradition's own standing teacher-line upon v. 104 passed down since al- since al-Ṭabarī: *fatigue reverses nothing; pain is shared but hope divides — and the wise keep marching*.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:105

> **Verily We have sent down unto thee the Book in truth, that thou mightest judge between men according to what God has shown thee. So be not an advocate for those who betray their trust.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Innā Anzalnā Ilayka al-Kitāba bi'l-Ḥaqq: The Judgment-Charter Verse**

The war-scroll of vv. 71–104 finally rolls shut — and the sūrah returns to the great law-around law-aroundment of its governance-peric to the great law-frame of its governance-pericope (vv. 58–60's amānāt and referral) — with the verse the canon calls the charter of Prophetic adjudication: *innā anzalnā ilayka al-kitāba bi'l-ḥaqqi li-taḥkuma bayna al-nāsi bimā arāka Allāh* — "verily We have sent down to thee the Book in truth — that thou mightest judge between men by what God has shown thee": the Book *with-the-truth* again (its standing seal from 2:176 — "that is because God has sent down the Book in truth"; 3:3's parallel) — now aimed not merely at doctrine but at *court-bench* exercise: li-taḥkuma — that *thou judgest* (the singular-Prophet charged with the standing office — the standing legal-theory structure of Islam's judiciary: the Prophet's court the fountain-head; the ummah's qāḍīs thereafter inheriting procedure-and-ethic from his hand) — *bimā arāka Allāh* — "according to what God has shown thee" (arā — He caused to see — the magnificent phrasing the comment-doctors elaborate: judgment by *God's showing* — revelation plus proven-evidence plus the pointing the trained discernment God had granted the Prophet — with Ibn Taymiyyah's master-note: the shown truth spans both *revelation* and *manifest reality* — the qāḍī's two-texture sourcing: text plus plainest fact).

**Wa Lā Takun li'l-Khāʾinīna Khaṣīman: Thou Art Not the Treacherous' Advocate**

Then the constitutional ceiling of the whole office — the clause the canon marks as one of Islam's most absolute judicial restraints: *wa lā takun li'l-khāʾinīna khaṣīman* — "so be not for the betrayers an advocate": **khāʾinīn* — betrayers — treacherous breaches — from kh-w-n — breach-of-trust (the standing treachery-word (the same lexeme returning at v. 107: *"and plead not for those who betray themselves"*) — and *khaṣīm* — adversarial pleader — partisan advocate (from kh-ṣ-m — dispute — the standing litigant-word) — with the standing asbāb the canonical rolls deliver: al-Wāḥidī and al-Qurṛṭubī's registered account of Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq of Banū Ẓafar — accused of stealing a coat of mail and smuggling it into concealment with a Jewish neighbor — the stolen evidence planted upon the innocent man — Ṭuʿmah's his clan coming to plead with the Prophet on the slander-pretext that *their clansman* was wronged (clan-solidarity raised at court) — and the Prophet on the verge of exonerating him — until these very verses descended, staying his hand: *be not an advocate for the treacherous* (with the standing unveiling-sequence falling out in order: v. 105 the charter; 106 the seeking-of-forgiveness for the near-miss; 107–108 the verdict upon self-betrayers and their hidden plotting; 109 the rebuke to the pleaders; 111 the standing criminal jurisprudence — every crime upon its doer alone) — the account itself being the classical standing-symbol of rule-of-law's birth in Islam: the court's mercy for the *claimant's felt plight* — a clan hurt, a honor-invoked — versus the *evidenced wrong*: with the Book teaching thereafter the pure jurisprudential maxim — advocacy grounded not in kin-love but in justice (its epilogue remembered everywhere in the fiqh: Ṭuʿmah fled, apostatized, was crushed under a falling wall-mass under a fallen wall at Makkah — the comment-doctors recording the age the story rolls of the Sīrah).

**The Judge's Impartiality as Islam's Court-Foundation**

The commentators then extend the decree-consequence the verse's legal-transfers to the whole judicial office of the ummah — the rule coming down: no judgment on account of kinship, wealth, rank, or religious surface-dress: (1) the Prophet himself could be aimed-at by false pleaders — no human station is immune from the advocate-trap (the standing lesson: even the Messenger was given a revelation-check against clan-weighed outcry — with the accompanying hadith-register of his standing impartiality: the celebrated declaration, “were Fāṭimah the daughter of Muḥammad to steal, Muḥammad’s hand would cut hers” — recorded in al-Bukhārī 3475 and Muslim 1688); (2) advocacy belongs to the case-fact, not the clan-fact — judges and pleaders alike bound; and (3) the transfer to every believer: *never plead for the betrayer* — not your father, not your son, not your party, not your nation — with the Book's own further course at vv. 135 following right behind: "be persistently standing for justice, witnesses for God — even against yourselves — or parents — or kin — whether rich or poor — God is more worthy of both" — the whole judicial-block 4:105–112 + 135 being the Quran's standing rule-of-law cathedral — and the sūrah's architecture thus traceable: war-light cooled (v. 104) — judgment-authority built (v. 105) — itself anchored against the clan-form of treacherous pleading that was burning through the tribal life of pre-Islamic Arabia — so that Madinah's newly-born polity would stand not upon swords but upon *uncorrupted courts* — the first clause of which God addressed not to any vizier but to the judge-in-chief — the Prophet — as if to say: the law begins with *you*, and reaches downward.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:106

> **And seek forgiveness of God; surely God is Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa-staghfir Allāh: The Judge Asked to Seek Pardon**

Between the judicial charter of v. 105 and the deep exposure of treachery's nocturnal mechanism in vv. 107–108, the sūrah inserts a six-word command that would become one of the most theologically argued sentences of Madinah's first court-era: *wa-staghfir Allāh* — "and seek forgiveness of God": addressed in the singular, to the Prophet himself — and the immediate context is defined: he had been on the verge of accepting a clan's outcry and clearing a treacherous thief — pulled back mid-motion by the revelation of v. 105 — and now instructed to wash even the *nearness* of the misstep in istighfār (with the twin-attribute seal again attending: *inna Allāha kāna ghafūran raḥīman* — "God is Forgiving, Merciful" — the very mercy he was commanded to access, named so that the command itself be heard as invitation rather than disgrace).

**'Iṣmah and the Prophet's Near-Advocacy: The Canonical Debate**

The classical houses then take up the knot this verse forced upon theology: does the command imply the Prophet *sinned*? The tradition's answers, filed for all time: (1) al-Rāzī's standing defense — the report indicates the Prophet *considered* but decided nothing, awaiting Godward guidance; his istighfār was sought for that mere *inclination to hear their plea* — or, on the stronger r on the further reading, on behalf of *those who had sought to sway him*: the clan-pleaders themselves before whom the door of advocacy stood open (so the instruction reads distributively: "seek forgiveness — for them"); (2) the deep structure from the doctrine of ʿiṣmah — prophetic protection guarding the *delivery* of the message and the *outcomes* of the deeds — with the standing spiritual register of the Book as mercy-school the standing register reading such episodes as the prophets' own commissioned pedagogy: a prophet drawn to the edge of an error *so that the whole ummah thereafter learns the edge's position* (the parallel the commentators themselves preserve: Sulaymān's field of horses — 38:32–33 — with its Prophet-borne ag its owned subject: "until the sun was hidden in the veil; bring them back to me" — the Book allowing its prophets to approach the world's allure the ambush-edge so the lesson may complete); (3) the plainest reading — and the plainest school-reading honored across the majority: istighfār covers also *what is not sin at all* — the Prophet's own self-declared custom: "I seek God's forgiveness seventy times a day" — Bukhārī 6307 — and its plenary: "by God, I seek forgiveness of God and repent to Him more than seventy times daily" — that continuous istighfār being honor-completion, not repentance-of-crime — washing even the position-short-of-the-best washing even the inadvertent leanings toward kin toward clamor — which in lesser men never amounted even to a thought-crime) — the standing hadith completing the theology with the Prophet's own elevated measure: "people! repent " the hadith on istighfār's internalization the hadith of the heart's rust at Muslim 2322 at Bukhārī 7487: *"indeed a dimness a darkness til there descends upon my heart — and indeed I seek God's forgiveness a hundred times a day"* — Muslim 2702 — the descending-dimness (the yukhān — rust-tr the passing-covering that never became error) being exactly what the standing command at 4:106 polishes away.

**The Judge's Inward Discipline**

And the tradition thereafter drew from the verse its standing professional counsel for every occupant of every seat of judgment: the holder of authority over men should habitually *ask forgiveness after every court-session* — for authority itself is a gravity well — bent toward each session's plausibles, pressures, and partialities (the comment-doctors unfolding the practical syllabus: the judge's istighfār compensating his juristic fatigue — decisions between brother and stranger — between claimant's tears and cold evidence — between the clan's persistence and the innocent's innocence: each sitting leaving its spiritual residue — with the standing hadīth-grid the grid of the Prophetic practice echoing inside it: the Prophet's own instruction to judges in the Tirmidhī-rolls to beware their "inner voice after the standing Sunnah doctrine: reward for the mujtahid even when *mistaken* — Muslim 1716 — Bukhārī 7352 — when a judge strives and errs, one reward; when right, two — the whole systemic mercy thereby disclosed: heaven knows the seat winds the seat's warping-strings pull every mind off plumb — hence the command washes the office itself regularly) — so that the verse stands as the constitutional hygiene of Islam's entire court-theory: the law's holder being the first and most regular visitor of the fountain of pardon — *and seek God's forgiveness* — with the paired mercy of v. 106 awaiting every judge who, having judged, turns back toward God — thereby planting at the center of Islam's judiciary the standing doctrine: a court that does not wash itself daily becomes treacherous ground without knowing it — with the Prophet's own morning and evening istighfārs standing as the the standing precedent of the entire profession of judgment until the end of hours.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:107

> **And plead not on behalf of those who betray their own selves. Surely God loves not the one given to treachery and sin.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Lā Tujādil ʿan Alladhīna Yakhtānūna Anfusahum: No Advocacy for the Self-Betrayers**

The judicial-block turns from the Prophet's own washing (v. 106) to the deeper diagnosis of the accused: *wa lā tujādil ʿan alladhīna yakhtānūna anfusahum* — "and plead not on behalf of those who betray their own selves": *tujādil* — dispute-plead — from j-d-l — the standing contention-verb (the verse's own word-pairing now echoing v. 105's *khaṣīm* — advocate-adversary — with jidāl as the dispute's process-form: do not *carry their litigation* — do not *wield law-speech on their side*) — and the phrase that becomes the block's theological axis: *yakhtānūna anfusahum* — they betray *their own selves*: the standing pause-word of the tradition: theft framed as *self-theft*; the burglar's actual booty, measured in the last account, being nothing but a raiding of his own soul's credit — the classical commentary sharpening the Quranic ontology of sin in general (the Book's recurrent formula — *mā ẓalamnāhum wa lākin kānū anfusahum yaẓlimūn* — "We wronged them not, but they wronged themselves" — 2:57; 3:117; 9:70; 16:118; 29:40 — every wrong ultimately returning to its carrier like a missile reversed at its owner's chest) — the legal-block thereby uncovering the full picture of its lesson: the verdict of the verdict of courts, addressed outward, rests upon the ontology of inward accounts — every accepted plea on behalf of a self-betrayer is a second betrayal of his soul; and the Prophet's court, had it cleared Ṭuʿmah, would have compounded the man's inward ruin upon his outward one.

**Inna Allāha Lā Yuḥibbu man Kāna Khawwānan Athīman: The Trenchant-Name**

Then heaven's own verdict-profile: *inna Allāha lā yuḥibbu man kāna khawwānan athīman* — "surely God loves not the one habituated who is a treacherous sinner": *khawwān* — the intensive habit-form of kh-w-n — treachery raised to professional grade (its Book-roll being short and stern: 8:58's "if thou fearest treachery from a people, throw back their covenant to them equally — surely God loves not the treacherous"; 22:38's—"surely God defends those who believe — surely God loves not any treacherous ingrate"; and 4:107 here — the intensive *khawwān* meaning: the man who has *settled into* perfidy — whose breach has become his standing gait rather than his stumble); and *athīm* — steeped-in-sin (the ithm-word intensive — the standing paired-form the Book reserves for the steeped-in-guilt: "whoever earns a sin, earns it only against himself" — verse 111's own sequel clause below) — *lā yuḥibbu* — loves not — the stark non-love clause the commentators ring ever since with the Book's own register: God's *not-loving* of a soul being a verdict far more precise than mere wrath — wrath can pass; being unfavored being excluded from His love means being left without the inner sweetness that saves (the Sunnah confirming alongside — cf. 9:4–7; 2:195; 3:134 — God loving the God-fearing, the patient, the just, the benevolent — and the opposite — God's non-love going deliberately to the *character-classes*: the treacherous, the extravagant, the arrogant, the corrupt) — the seals behind v. 107 thus sealing the entire court-block's essence: it is not merely that judges may not *favor* the treacherous — the one who *pleads* treachery's case stakes himself against a Divine attribute-line against God's own declared non-love of the class — with the tradition's transpositions standing ever since: (1) the qāḍī's mercies may never cross into pleading the accused's *cause*; (2) the advocate catches the advocate must not manufacture *speech* on behalf of betrayers; (3) even sympathetic onlookers fall under the clause — the comment-doctors spreading the command *to all who hear of betrayal* — every man forbidding himself from becoming a mere *onlooker-lawyer* of the khawwān (the standing hadith-consequence in Bukhārī's rolls: *"whoever aids an oppressor in his injustice — God grants that oppressor mastery over him"* — Bukhārī 6953 — the standing rule: aid given to a treacherous cause *joins the cause*); and the canonical court-book thereafter knits the entire block into one standing charter: judges wash in istighfār (v. 106), plead no self-betrayers' case (v. 107), fear the muḥīṭ encompassing (v. 108), bar their clan-pleaders likewise (v. 109), and leave one door — the door of repentance — standing open at last for the self-betrayer himself (v. 110).

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:108

> **They seek to hide themselves from men, but they cannot hide from God. He is with them when they conspire by night with words displeasing to Him, and God encompasses whatsoever they do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Yastakhfūna mina al-Nāsi wa Lā Yastakhfūna mina Allāh: The Two Audiences of Shame**

The court-block's camera now moves from the plea-chamber to the thief's real operating room — the night-parlor: *yastakhfūna mina al-nāsi wa lā yastakhfūna mina Allāh* — "they conceal from men — and they do not conceal from God": *yastakhfūna* — they seek-hiding — from kh-f-y — concealment (its standing Book-roll grading the sinner's pathetic double-standing: shame *calibrated exactly to the wrong audience* — the sinner's whole caution-energy poured into deflecting human gaze while the One before Whom it must all be disclosed stands ignored — the commentators' standing formulation being this verse's own ratio the standing formulation: al-khafiyy cf. 13:10's — "equal are you in secrecy — he who conceals his speech and he who proclaims it, and he who hides by night and he who goes abroad by day"; 10:61's "not an atom's weight escapes your Lord"; 20:7's "He knows the secret and the more hidden"; and the sūrah's own paired piece at v. 81 — "they hide within their souls what they do not disclose to thee" — the paired spy-exposure of the whole pericope now completing itself across the two peric the two passages) — and the operational detail follows: the Prophet's the clan-plot itself running by night: evidence-smuggling plans, planted stolen armor, the protected innocence the framed alibi — the standing asbāb recalled here again as illustration of the single principle: every night-parlor operates beneath a lamp it cannot see.

**Wa Huwa Maʿahum Idh Yubayyitūna Mā Lā Yarḍā mina al-Qawl: The Third in Their Chamber**

Then the sūrah's most terrible of consolations — God's own attendance at their conspiracy: *wa huwa maʿahum idh yubayyitūna mā lā yarḍā mina al-qawl* — "He is *with* them when they night-plot with speech that displeases Him": *maʿahum* — with them (maʿiyyah — accompaniment — the theologians' standing care: the He-is-with-them the pronoun triggered the standing commentary-protocol on the verse (al-Rāzī, al-Qurṛṭubī, Ibn Taymiyyah): *with* here means *encompassing them in knowledge, hearing, sight, and recording* — not in approbation or spatial lest men read spatial-presence lest anyone ever imagine bodily presence — cf. the paired party the twin-text's own guard: 58:7 — "He is the fourth of three, and the sixth of five — with them wheresoever they may be" — always in knowledge; and the ummah's soul-care the soul-doctors deriving from their own nuance: God's *maʿiyyah* speaks double-tongue — comfort-thread comfort to the lonely believer ("fear not — He is with us") — woe to the conspirator ("He is the third listener of their whisper")) — and the deed described: *yubayyitūna* — night-scheming (from b-y-t by night — the same participle as v. 81's *yubayyitūna* — the sūrah's deliberate echo across its two dark-chambers: the hypocrite cabal slandering the Prophet's obedience — v. 81; the Ṭuʿmah-clan staging the planted evidence — v. 108 — God's authorial scheme returning the identical verb to brand *night-labor itself* as the standing engine of public injustice: false verdicts are *conceived by night*, in curtains behind curtains, long before they are pronounced under noon) — *mā lā yarḍā mina al-qawl* — *that of speech which displeases Him* — the phrasing's own finesse its standing academic note: not *displeasing-to-God* as mere synonym of *sinful* but framed around *qawl* — speech: the whole crime-engine runs through said-words — doctored testimony, rehearsed accusation, alibi-scripts (the standing modern echoing the standing lesson of the jurisprudes ever since: the conspiracy of a false case is a *literary* factory — its product being polished speeches designed to move courts — and heaven's note is simply that the critic above every other critic already gave His review) — and the seal lands with the impassable name: *wa kāna Allāhu bimā yaʿmalūna muḥīṭan* — "God is encompassing whatsoever they do": *muḥīṭ* — from ḥ-w-ṭ — to surround, encompass — the Book's standing ominous attribute (3:120's "God is encompassing of what they do"; 4:126's "God is encompassing of all things"; 8:47's; 11:92's; 41:54's; 85:20's "and God is, behind them, encompassing" — the classical roll of its uses being uniformly shadowed: the word visits only scenes of defiant wrongdoing of confident wrongdoing — as if the culprit had built his fortress of private space and heaven simply replies: *muḥīṭ* — fortresses themselves lie within His ring) — the verse thereby sealing the entire courtroom-block with its own epistemology-of-justice: no chamber of man is truly private — no plot-script unread; no staged no planted no planted costume-piece resting quietly where its planter laid it: the Encompassing One sees each coil before the court of morning even sits.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:109

> **There you are, pleading on their behalf concerning the life of this world! But who will plead with God on their behalf on the Day of Resurrection, or be a guardian for them?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Hāʾ Antum Hāʾulāʾi Jādaltum ʿAnhum fī al-Ḥayāti al-Dunyā: Mocked Advocates of Earth**
