Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr remark on the humility encoded in the grammar: although rulings could have issued through the Prophet in his own words, the Book teaches the questioners before teaching them the rule — the teaching being: fatwā is not opinion; it is transmission from the One who owns the estate of v. 126 — hence the verse then recites the actual content, beginning with the most arresting phrase: *wa mā yutlā ʿalaykum fī al-kitāb* — "and what has been recited to you in the Book."

**Wa Mā Yutlā ʿAlaykum fī al-Kitāb: The Recited-Again Ruling — Orphan-Girls and the Cheated Dowry**

*Wa mā yutlā ʿalaykum fī al-kitābi fī yatāmā al-nisāʾi allātī lā tuʾtūnahunna mā kutiba lahunna wa targhabūna an tankiḥūhunna* — "and what has been recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan-girls to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, while you desire to marry them": the commentators recognize the double-reference: (1) "what is recited to you in the Book" = the earlier passage of this very sūrah — vv. 2–3 above ("give the orphans their property... and if you fear you cannot deal justly with the orphans — then marry whom you please of women") — God ruling now by *pointing back* to His own prior ruling: the answer to the women's consultation is partly: *you have already been told* — reread vv. 2–3. And (2) the precise abuse identified: guardians of orphan-girls — controlling both the girl's property and her marriage — would either marry her themselves for her wealth, giving her less than her due dowry ("you do not give what is prescribed for them" — her proper mahr and her inheritance-share), or prevent her marriage to others so that her wealth might remain in the household, or marry her while having no true desire for her. The standing report of the first hearers' attitude — noted in the tradition of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and others: the Companions, hearing these verses, wished to leave off marrying orphan-girls altogether; and the Prophet — in Muslim's standing narration when asked about the orphan-girl verse — defined the target precisely: it is the guardian who, seeing her beauty and wealth, marries her for her money and does not treat her fairly in the dowry — injustice forbidden, not marriage itself.

**Raghiba: The Two Readings and the Two Abuses**

The pivot-word of the verse carries a celebrated double-reading: *wa targhabūna an tankiḥūhunna* — most read it "while you desire to marry them" (the guardian drawn to the dowered girl for her property) — and another standing transmission (reported from ʿĀʾishah's circle) reads with the implied negative understood from the context: that you are *averse* to marrying them — the guardian turning away from the plain or poor orphan-girl, yet neither marrying her fairly nor releasing her to others, holding her suspended while her property is consumed. Ibn Kathīr gathers both and remarks that the verse embraces both abuses: the greedy marriage that takes the girl without her rights, and the neglectful detention that takes her rights without the marriage — the word *raghiba* (from r-gh-b — inclining, desiring) covering the two directions in which desire, unmanaged by piety, wrongs the dependent: excessive desire that exploits, and withheld desire that abandons. Between them stands the only lawful posture: the marriage of fairness, or the release with kindness — the very alternatives Mercy continues to elaborate in vv. 128–130 below.

**Wa al-Mustaḍʿafīna min al-Wildān: From Orphan-Girls to the Oppressed Children**

The verse then enlarges its protectorate: *wa al-mustaḍʿafīna min al-wildān* — "and concerning the oppressed among the children": *mustaḍʿaf* — the passive-participle of al-ḍuʿf — weakness — the standing Qur'ānic category of the socially weakened (4:75's standing plea on behalf of "the oppressed men, women, and children crying: our Lord — take us out of this city of the wrongdoing people"; 4:98's excuse-boundary for "the oppressed among men, women, and children who can devise no plan and are not guided to a way"). The position — noted by the commentators — unfolds the sūrah's deepest logic: the child is here not a lineage-asset but a *trust*, and the law of the sūrah consistently locates holiness at the point of weakness: where a person is small, dependent, propertyless, and voiceless — there the Book posts its strongest guards: the orphan-girl first (the most defrauded of the vulnerable), then oppressed children generally, then — in the sweeping clause — *wa an taqūmū li-l-yatāmā bi-l-qisṭ* — "and that you stand firm for the orphans with justice": *qūmū* — standing — the posture of vigilance and service (the same verb that 4:135 will raise to its summit: "be standing-firm for justice — witnesses for God — even against yourselves") — and *qisṭ* — the portioning justice, equal shares without desert-distinctions. The entire verse is thus the sūrah's thesis restated as gerund: God has spoken — concerning women, the recited ruling; concerning orphan-girls, the full share; concerning children, protection; concerning orphans, standing justice — and then the closing assurance unseals everything: *wa mā tafʿalū min khayrin fa-inna Allāha kāna bihi ʿalīman* — "and whatever good you do — God is ever Knowing of it": khayr in the indefinite — *any* good — and the ʿalīm's knowledge the guarantor that no kindness shown to a voiceless dependent is ever spent where it cannot be recorded — the pattern the Book seals elsewhere with the same broad surety ("so whoever does an atom's weight of good shall see it" — 99:7; "God does not waste the wage of the good-doers" — 9:120; "whatever good you send before you for your souls — you shall find it with God — better and greater in reward" — 73:20): the family-law of heaven audited by the Knowing One Himself.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:128

> **And if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion, there is no sin upon them both that they make terms of peace between themselves with terms of peace — and peace is better. But greed is made present in the souls. And if you do good and keep from evil — then God is ever Aware of what you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Imini Raʾatun Khāfat min Baʿlihā Nushūzan: The Fear From the Other Side of the House**

The marriage-file continues, now from the wife's vantage — the sūrah's standing equity of address: as v. 34 regulated the husband's fear of *her* nushūz, so now: *wa imini raʾatun khāfat min baʿlihā nushūzan aw iʿrāḍan* — "and if a woman fears from her husband ill-treatment or aversion": *nushūz* — again (v. 34's standing word) — from n-sh-z — rising, elevation: here the husband's high-handedness — the rising of the stronger partner above the marriage-covenant in arrogance, harshness, or contempt; and *iʿrāḍ* — from ʿ-r-ḍ — turning the side, presenting the back: the cold withdrawal — the husband emotionally abandoning the marriage while legally remaining in it (the standing Book-file of the word: "who turns away from My reminder — his is a straitened life" — 20:124; "turn not away thy cheek from men" — 31:18). The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Qurṭubī) note that the Book here legislates from the *woman's perception* — *khāfat* — "she fears" — the same epistemic standard used for the husband in v. 34 ("whose nushūz you fear"): relational breakdown is adjudicated first at the level of what is sensed and reasonably feared, not only after public scandal — the law honors the interior weather of the house before the walls crack audibly.

**Lā Junāḥa ʿAlayhimā an Yuṣliḥā: Permission Before Permission Is Asked — The Primacy of Ṣulḥ**

The verse's central mercy opens a door neither side must be shamed for seeking: *lā junāḥa ʿalayhimā an yuṣliḥā baynahumā ṣulḥan — wa al-ṣulḥu khayr* — "there is no sin upon them both that they make terms of peace between themselves with terms of peace — and peace is better": *junāḥ* — from j-n-ḥ — the wing, the leaning side: hence sin as a *leaning from straightness* — and the Book removes the lean of shame from reconciliation: the couple that negotiates — she perhaps relinquishing some of her dowry or nights, he perhaps agreeing to reforms — commits no fault; the arrangement need not mimic the default pattern to be valid before God. Then comes one of the Book's most economical axioms — jurists and sages have made it a standing title of the law of settlement: *wa al-ṣulḥu khayr* — "and peace is better": four words in English, two in the Arabic, containing what al-Qurṭubī marveled at as a whole jurisprudence: not merely *permitted* but *better* — amendment preferred over adjudication, voluntary concession over compulsory verdict — its standing Book-kin: "and their case is consultation among them" — 42:38; "and reconciliation between brothers" — 49:9-10's standing command ("make peace between your two brothers"); and the celebrated Ḥasan-al-Baṣrī dictum quoted in this place by Ibn Kathīr: to give up a right for the sake of unity is itself worship. The Sabāb-gloss brings it to earth: ʿĀʾishah's standing report (Bukhārī's standing source — Bukhārī 5212; Muslim's companion-narration): Sawdah bint Zamʿah, fearing the Prophet's iʿrāḍ and wishing to remain his wife, gifted her night to ʿĀʾishah — and "in her case," the commentators report, the verse revealed its mercy: no fault upon them in the settlement they chose — the law ratifying the selfless generosity of the aging wife and the quiet acceptance of the Prophet, so that she remained among the Mothers of the Believers to her last day.

**Wa Uḥḍirati al-Anfusu al-Shuḥḥ: Greed Seated in the Soul Itself**

Then the sentence that commentators call the piercing X-ray of the human condition — *wa uḥḍirati al-anfusu al-shuḥḥa* — "but greed is made present in the souls": *shuḥḥ* — from sh-ḥ-ḥ — avarice of the clingy, comprehensive kind — deeper than bukhl (stinginess) and broader than ḥirṣ (eagerness): the soul's instinct to hoard its own allotment and eye its neighbor's. And the verb is the marvel: *uḥḍirati* — passive of iḥḍār — *is made present* — as though greed were a permanent attendee summoned to every human sitting, seated within the self rather than imported from outside: al-Rāzī pauses here to observe that the Book does not say greed *afflicts* souls from without but that it is *brought to sit inside* them — hence no spouse enters settlement-negotiations innocent of it, and hence the next clause's command. The Book's standing shuḥḥ-file is the standing commentary: 59:9 — "and they prefer others over themselves though poverty be theirs — and whoever is preserved from the greed of his soul — those are the successful"; 64:16 — "fear God as much as you are able... and whoever is preserved from the greed of his soul — those are the successful"; 3:180's standing warning to the miserly. In marriage the application is exact: both parties come to the ṣulḥ-table with a seated guest named Greed — he wants the whole dowry, she wants the whole schedule; he counts his provisions, she counts her concessions — and the Book, rather than pretending the guest absent, names him, so that his operations can be watched: the spiritual genius of the legislation being that it reforms the inward before adjudicating the outward.

**Wa In Tuḥsinū wa Tattaqū: The Two Wings of Every Settlement**

The verse then sets the flight-condition: *wa in tuḥsinū wa tattaqū fa-inna Allāha kāna bimā taʿmalūna khabīran* — "and if you do good and keep from evil — then God is ever Aware of what you do": iḥsān and taqwā — the standing Book-pair (2:195 — "do good — for God loves the good-doers"; 16:128 — "God is with those who keep from evil and those who are good-doers"; 5:93's doubled commendation) — here applied to marital settlement: do good — beyond the bare contract — and keep from evil — within the bare contract: taqwā as the floor and iḥsān as the ceiling of conduct between spouses. And the seal — *khabīr* — the Expert-Aware, the Intimately-Informed (v. 35's standing anticipation — "God is ever Knowing, Aware" — ʿalīm khabīr; 31:16's standing weightlessness of the mustard-seed under His awareness) — reminding the settling couple that no doled-out kindness within the settlement goes unaudited by heaven, and no buried resentment escapes its ledger. The tradition adds the standing price-tag for the path refused: the hadith in al-Tirmidhī's standing narration — "among the lawful things most odious to God is divorce" (its standing source: Abū Dāwūd 2178; the Prophet's standing caution balancing the concession-doctrine of this verse) — reconciliation exalted, dissolution demoted to last resort — and the sūrah will enforce the order in vv. 129–130 which follow.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:129

> **And you shall never be able to deal equally between wives, even if you should desire it; but do not incline with full inclination, so that you leave her as one suspended. And if you set things right and keep from evil — then God is ever Forgiving, Merciful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Lan Tastaṭīʿū an Taʿdilū: The Pronouncement That Closed One Door and Opened Another**

The sūrah now distinguishes two kinds of justice with a verdict that has echoed through every court of fiqh since: *wa lan tastaṭīʿū an taʿdilū bayna al-nisāʾi wa law ḥaraṣtum* — "and you shall never be able to deal equally between wives, even if you should desire it": *lan* — the negative particle of absolute perpetuity — never, not ever — a divine proclamation about human capacity itself; *taʿdilū* — from ʿ-d-l — the balancing of scales — equalizing; and *ḥaraṣtum* — from ḥ-r-ṣ — stretched-to-the-limit desire — you may strain every nerve of goodwill, and still the verdict stands: *lan tastaṭīʿū* — you shall not be able. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī with his standing chains; Ibn Kathīr; al-Qurṭubī) gather the interpretation into a two-story ruling: (1) justice in the *outward* — housing, maintenance, nights, expenditure — is commanded and enforceable, made the express condition of plural marriage earlier in the sūrah (v. 3: "then marry whom you please... but if you fear you cannot deal justly — then only one"); and (2) justice in the *inward* — equal love, equal attraction, equal gladness of the eyes — is declared impossible — God legislating against the pretense that hearts can be court-ordered. The Sabāb-material illustrates from the highest home: ʿĀʾishah's standing reports of the Prophet's scrupulous outward equality — and his candid inward confession, the standing duʿāʾ preserved in the Sunan (al-Tirmidhī 1140's standing register — and its parallels in Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah): "O God — this is my division in that which I control — so do not take me to task about that which You control and I do not" — outward apportionment owned as human duty, inward inclination handed back to its true Owner.

**Fa-Lā Tamīlū Kulla al-Mayl: The Prohibited Leaning**

If perfect balance is impossible, the verse does not therefore license surrender to imbalance; it draws instead the line of the *permissible tilt* versus the *prohibited leaning*: *fa-lā tamīlū kulla al-mayli fa-tadharūhā ka-al-muʿallaqah* — "but do not incline with full inclination, so that you leave her as one suspended": *mayl* — from m-y-l — the tilt, the lean (its standing Book-file: 27:10 — Moses' staff — "as though it inclined as a jinn" — and 68:9's standing warning — "they wish that you should incline — so that they might incline" — the moral lean of compromise); *kulla al-mayl* — the *whole* leaning — not every degree of preference (that the preceding clause has excused) but the total capitulation of conduct to preference, until the less-loved wife hangs *ka-al-muʿallaqah* — "as one suspended": the passive participle of ʿ-l-q — hanging — the woman neither married (enjoying the rights and companionship of marriage) nor divorced (free to seek another marriage) — hung on a hook between statuses. Al-Qurṭubī calls it among the most compressed social images in the Book: the verse forbids the husband to convert his inevitable inward inequality into a visible misery — to starve the less-favored wife of nights, conversation, and presence until she dangles. The standing prophetic arithmetic of that dangling: the celebrated warning (its standing source in the two Ṣaḥīḥs — Bukhārī's standing register 5214; Muslim 2921): "whoever has two wives and leans to one of them shall come on the Day of Resurrection with one side leaning — drooping" — the body's very posture displaying in the next world the tilt it concealed in this.

**The Muʿallaqah File: Suspension From This Verse to the Code of Law**

The juristic tradition built upon *ka-al-muʿallaqah* an entire branch of protective law: the wife whose husband absents himself endlessly, deserts without maintenance, or simply freezes her out — sits precisely in the suspended state this verse names — and the schools, from Mālik's standing opinion to the ḥanafī mechanism (the dissolution-route through the judge's authority), worked to ensure no woman must dangle: the Māliki four-year rule, the ijtiḥād of the late jurists extending dissolution-rights to the judge — all genealogies tracing back to this one simile. And the inward application — noted by the spiritually minded commentators — extends past households: any covenant-holder who keeps another soul *suspended* between acceptance and dismissal — the ignored employee, the half-welcomed convert, the relative confined to the cold periphery — practices small-scale the very suspension the verse forbids large-scale: the Book's standing ethic that human bonds must be honored or cleanly released (2:229's standing formula — "retention in kindness or release with goodness"; 65:2's echo) — never strung along in the limbo that serves only the suspender's convenience.

**Wa In Tuṣliḥū wa Tattaqū: Repair, Piety, and the Names That Answer Both**

The verse ends where every family-verse of the sūrah ends — in the doubled doorway of amendment and piety: *wa in tuṣliḥū wa tattaqū fa-inna Allāha kāna ghafūran raḥīman* — "and if you set things right and keep from evil — then God is ever Forgiving, Merciful": *iṣlāḥ* — the setting-right of what has warped (its standing Book-pair with taqwā appearing at 2:160; 2:182; 4:128 just above — "if you do good and keep from evil") — and the two Names sealing the syllable of hope: *ghafūr* — the Much-Forgiving (for the leaning already done, the nights already starved, the years already tilted — repentance opens before the guilty husband as before any other sinner) — and *raḥīm* — the Merciful (for the repair still fragile — the sūrah's standing Name-pair that has sounded through its family-file from v. 23 onward: "God is ever Forgiving, Merciful" — 4:23; 4:24; 4:96 — and the several standing stations of the sūrah itself). ʿĀʾishah's standing summary crowns the passage — her remark that in outward division nobody observed the Prophet exceeding fairness (Muslim's standing collections are full of her documentation of his rotation and provisioning) — yet even the best of homes required *kulla al-mayl* to remain a forbidden zone: the Book teaching thereby that the law does not demand the impossible (equal hearts — which it has just declared forever beyond reach) but absolutely demands the possible (equal nights, equal provision, the prohibition of the suspended wife) — the exact midpoint between utopia and license where all the sūrah's family-legislation stands.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:130

> **And if the two separate, God shall enrich each of them from His bounty; and God is ever All-Encompassing, All-Wise.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa In Yatafarraqā Yughni Allāhu Kullan min Saʿatih: The Divine Alimony-Guarantee**

The marriage-file of vv. 128–130 closes with a promise so gentle that commentators have prized it as the Book's own consolation to every ending household: *wa in yatafarraqā yughni Allāhu kullan min saʿatih* — "and if the two separate, God shall enrich each of them from His bounty": *yatafarraqā* — the dual of separation — should the reconciliation-attempts of v. 128 and the repair of v. 129 fail, and the marriage lawfully end — no disaster-note sounds; instead the verse assigns the aftermath to God Himself: *yughni Allāhu kullan* — "God shall enrich each" — the verb *yughni* from gh-n-y — sufficiency, the condition of needing no one — with God as its standing Name al-Ghanī — the Self-Sufficient (2:263's standing pairing "God is Self-Sufficient, Forbearing"; 6:133 — "your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, possessing mercy"; 35:15 — "O mankind — you are the poor unto God — and God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praised") — and its stunning grammatical placement here: not "perhaps He shall make them content" but the unqualified future-verb of divine undertaking — enrichment guaranteed *to each* — *kullan* — the singular pronoun deliberately individualizing: the husband and the wife, separately, severally, each one — the exalted pledge extending to the departing wife who may face the severest economic exposure of the separation, written as surely as to the husband. Al-Ṭabarī reads the clause as God's standing comfort against the fear that holds bad marriages frozen — the fear of destitution — and Ibn Kathīr marks its precise sense: God shall enrich the one with another spouse, with provision otherwise, with contentment itself — *min saʿatih* — "from His bounty" — *saʿah* from s-ʿ-w — width, amplitude — the bounty of God being the standing Qur'ānic superlative of resources ("God's earth is wide" — 29:56; "God is Possessor of great bounty" — 2:105; 3:174; 8:29; 57:21's standing *al-faḍl al-ʿaẓīm*) — the married pair having shared one household under God's width, each departs under that same width — the house dividable, the Provider undivided.

**The Consolation-File: When Endings Are Not Punishments**

The verse stands within a wider Book-comfort that the commentators fold together here: 65:2–3's standing promise — "and whoever keeps from evil — God makes for him a way out — and provides for him from whence he does not reckon" — revealed, the standing Sabāb-reading says, precisely in the wake of the divorce-legislation of Sūrah al-Ṭalāq; and 65:6's provision-duties framing the separated wife's maintenance. The practical wisdom is the standing pastoral point: the law permits divorce as last resort — "among the lawful things most odious to God" (v. 128's standing hadith-caution — Abū Dāwūd 2178's register) — yet once the door is walked through with iḥsān, God does not exit with the marriage; He remains as the Sponsor of both households that were formerly one. The tradition-level pastoral register adds the standing observation of the sages: how many a harmful union ended, and each party found in the years after — through new marriage, through livelihood, through sheer interior peace — the "enrichment" this verse promised, discovering that the feared door had been in fact two doors. And the psychological note deserves its own line: the verse re-narrates divorce theologically — removal from the ledger of shame to the ledger of divine providence — not celebrating separation (v. 128's *al-ṣulḥu khayr* still standing) but removing the terror-argument that freezes couples in cruelty: the breakable marriage a healthier institution than the unbreakable prison.

**Wa Kāna Allāhu Wāsiʿan Ḥakīman: The Two Names That Seal the Promise**

The verse seals with a Name-pair unique in the sūrah's family-file: *wa kāna Allāhu wāsiʿan ḥakīman* — "and God is ever All-Encompassing, All-Wise": *wāsiʿ* — the Vast, the Ample-Containing — a Name the Book folds around every constraint it loosens (its standing file: 2:115 — "whithersoever you turn — there is the face of God — God is All-Encompassing, Knowing"; 2:268 — "God promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty — and God is All-Encompassing, Knowing"; 5:54's standing "and God is All-Encompassing, Knowing"; 24:32 — the sūrah of marriage-regulation — "if they should be poor — God shall enrich them from His bounty — and God is All-Encompassing, Knowing") — the name itself the etymological match of *saʿatih* earlier in the verse: bounty wide because the Giver is Vast; His amplitude guarantees the amplitude of the promise. And *ḥakīm* — the All-Wise — seals the legislation's other flank: the permission of separation is no concession to chaos but the decree of Wisdom that saw what counselors and courts cannot — sometimes iṣlāḥ fails, sometimes the two plants grow only apart — and the Wise legislated release with dignity. The two Names together answer the two anxieties of the divorcing: the Wāsiʿ answers the economic fear ("how shall we each live?"), and the Ḥakīm answers the juridical-moral fear ("was this release itself lawful, wise, right?") — God Vast enough to enrich both, and Wise enough that His permission needs no apology. The marriage-file thus closes the way the sūrah's whole legal style closes — law folded into Names: the ordinance given, the anxiety named, the divine attribute posted as standing guarantee — and the reader exits the family-chapters as he entered them (4:1's standing exordium — "fear your Lord... God is ever over you a Watcher") — between taqwā at the threshold and bounty at the farewell. From here the sūrah will lift its gaze once more from households to the All (v. 131's standing crescendo: "unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and the earth... God is sufficient as a Guardian") — and the ownership-cadence of v. 126, planted deliberately above this family-file, now gathers it up: every household settled here was settled upon God's own estate, under the Encompassing — the Wāsiʿ — the Wise.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:131

> **Unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth. And We have charged those who were given the Book before you, and We charge you: be mindful of God. But if you disbelieve — then unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth. And God is ever Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Triple Ownership-Cadence: v. 126, v. 131, v. 132**

The Book now returns to its standing ownership-plaque — but in an unprecedented run: the sūrah, having posted the plaque at v. 126 ("unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth — and God encompasses all things"), posts it again here, and yet again at v. 132 — a threefold tolling inside seven verses that the commentators mark as among the sūrah's most deliberate structural monuments. Al-Rāzī suggests the flower of the placement: immediately before these declarations stood the verse of enrichment — v. 130's standing promise ("God shall enrich each of them from His bounty") — and the frightened hearts of separating spouses needed to know *whose* bounty was pledged: so the Book answers before the question is whispered — the heavens and the earth and all they hold are the estate of the Promiser — the guarantee of enrichment underwritten by universal ownership. The verse's own the standing comment-canon likewise observes the cadence's position *between* the family-file just closed (vv. 127–130) and the justice-summit opening below (v. 135): all earthly apportionment — dowries, inheritances, provisions — flows from the One to whom everything already belongs; human giving and receiving is but the internal accounting of His estate. Its standing Book-kin toll across the revelation — 2:284; 3:109; 3:129; 4:126 above; 10:55 ("lo — unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and the earth"); 14:2; 34:1 — but nowhere in the Book do the tolls sound so clustered as here: the sūrah of the household pausing thrice to remind the householders whose house the universe is.

**Wa Laqad Waṣṣaynā... An Ittaqū Allāha: The One Command Common to Every Community**

The verse then reaches across the borders of every religious civilization with the standing charge of all revelation: *wa laqad waṣṣaynā alladhīna ūtū al-kitāba min qablikum wa iyyākum an ittaqū Allāh* — "and We have charged those who were given the Book before you, and We charge you: be mindful of God": *waṣṣaynā* — from w-ṣ-y — the solemn bequest-charge, the covenant-instruction deposited with trustees (its standing Book-file: 2:125 — the charge to Abraham and Ishmael to purify the House; 2:132 — "and Abraham charged his sons with it — and Jacob: my sons — God has chosen the religion for you"; 6:151–153's standing ten-charge compendium; 42:13 — "He has ordained for you of the religion what He charged Noah with — and what We revealed to thee — and what We charged Abraham and Moses and Jesus: establish the religion and scatter not therein"). Al-Rāzī draws the standing doctrine the verse's syntax plainly teaches: taqwā — the mindfulness-reverence toward God — is the one *sharīʿah common to all religious communities* — rituals vary, laws differ, calendars diverge, but the inner command laid upon "those who were given the Book before you" and upon "you" is one command, grammatically shared in a single predicate: *an ittaqū Allāh* — the universal constitution under all particular codes. The standing scholastic register (from al-Ṭabarī's chains through Ibn Kathīr's summary) designates taqwā the "comprehensive counsel" — al-waṣiyyah al-jāmiʿah — of every prophet to every people: the command containing obedience in whole, for the God-fearing cannot persist in any known wrong. And its placement after the ownership-declaration is itself exegesis: because all belongs to Him, all owe Him; the deed of universal possession grounding the universal duty — property and piety bound in one verse.

**Wa In Takfurū: The Freedom of Refusal Announced Inside the Command**

Then the verse performs the standing dramatic movement of Qur'ānic legislation — command, then the announcement of the command's violation, then the announcement of the violation's costlessness-for-God: *wa in takfurū fa-inna li-llāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — "but if you disbelieve — then lo: unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth": the ownership-plaque tolling a second time — now not as comfort to the separating but as indifference-adjacent majesty to the refusing: your disbelief removes nothing from the estate; your refusal of the King does not depose the King; you disbelieve *inside* His property, breathing His air, standing His ground — the standing irony the Book presses everywhere (its standing parallels: 3:10 — "as for those who disbelieve — neither their wealth nor their children shall avail them aught against God"; 2:6 — "it is all one upon them whether thou warnest them or warnest them not"; 36:10's identical formula). Ibn Taymiyyah's standing distinction orders the scene: the command of taqwā is God's *religious-law will* — what He loves and demands; the outcome of disbelief falls under God's *creative will* — which permits what it forbids — so that the disbeliever defies the command yet never escapes the decree: he remains a tenant of the heavens and earth he denies having a Landlord.

**Wa Kāna Allāhu Ghaniyyan Ḥamīdan: Self-Sufficiency and the Praise That Owes Nothing to Its Debtors**

The verse seals with the Name-pair that answers the deepest question the disbeliever could think to ask — *what does God lose by my loss?*: *wa kāna Allāhu ghaniyyan ḥamīdan* — "and God is ever Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy": *ghanī* — from gh-n-y — not mere wealth but complete independence — freedom from need in every direction (v. 130 had spent His enrichment on spouses; here His standing note — al-Rāzī's standing scholastic formulation — He is *neither increased by obedience nor diminished by disobedience*: worship does not fatten Him, rebellion does not wound Him; the hadith qudsī in Muslim's standing register 2577 — "O My servants — were the first of you and the last of you, the human of you and the jinn of you, to be as pious as the most pious heart of any one man of you — that would not increase My kingdom in anything... and were they to be as wicked as the most wicked heart — that would not decrease My kingdom in anything") — and *ḥamīd* — the Praiseworthy — the Name of intrinsic, creditor-free praiseworthiness: praised not because creatures happen to praise (their praise is charity they receive, not tribute He needs) but because praise inheres in His very attributes — the standing Name-pair appearing at 2:267's giving-verse ("God is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy"), 14:8 (Moses' proclamation: "if you disbelieve — you and whoever is on earth altogether — then lo, God is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy"), 22:64, 31:12 (Luqmān's counsel), 31:26, 35:15 ("you are the poor unto God — and God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praised"), 57:24, 60:6. The sūrah of orphans, wives, and dowries thus ends this charge with the reverse-view mirror: the Creator needs nothing in His creation — every obligation He lays is benefit laid upon the obliged, every gift He gives is loss He never feels — the Self-Sufficient Praiseworthy One legislating taqwā not as tribute-collection but as the standing open door through which impoverished tenants may walk into the width of v. 130's bounty — while the horizon of v. 133 now darkens just ahead: the Self-Sufficient who can enrich any household He chooses can also, if He wills, replace entire peoples who decline the tenancy-terms — "if He so wills, He can remove you, O mankind — and bring others."

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:132

> **Unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth, and God suffices as a Guardian.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Third Toll: Ownership Sounded Until the Hearing Settles**

The cadence tolls a third time: *wa li-llāhi mā fī al-samāwāti wa mā fī al-arḍ* — "unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth" — and with this the sūrah completes its densest repetition-cluster: v. 126 (with *muḥīṭ* — Encompassing), v. 131 (with *ghanī ḥamīd* — Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy), and now v. 132 — three tolls in seven verses, each sealed with a different Name, as though the Book were fastening the household-legislation of the sūrah with three separate nails. The commentators' standing structural note (al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī both pausing over the clustering) reads the sequence as graded comfort and warning: the first toll (v. 126) universal — the Frame around everything; the second (v. 131) covenantal — ownership as the ground of the taqwā-charge laid on every community; the third (v. 132) fiduciary — ownership as the ground of trusting God alone as Trustee. The soul, having heard the estate belongs to God three times, may finally do what the second half of this verse commands: stop trying to be its own guardian.

**Wa Kafā Bi-llāhi Wakīlan: The Sufficiency-Formula at Its Summit**

Then the Name that draws the practical deduction: *wa kafā bi-llāhi wakīlan* — "and God suffices as a Guardian-Trustee": the standing sufficiency-formula — *kafā bi-llāhi...* — the Book's own architecture for adequacy, a formula of which the commentators note there is none more beloved in the spiritual curriculum: the servant places some task — provision, protection, vindication, guidance — in divine custody, and the Book replies with this standing declaration: *suffices* — God alone fills the entire post; no adjunct-trustee is required, no co-signer needed (its standing register inside this very formula: 3:173 — "God suffices us — an excellent Guardian" — ḥasbunā Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl — the cry of the believers when told "the people have gathered against you — so fear them," and the sentence increasing them only in faith; 4:45 — "God knows best your enemies — and God suffices as an Ally — and God suffices as a Helper"; 4:81 — "trust in God — and God suffices as a Guardian"; 17:96 — "He suffices as Knowing of His servants' sins — Seeing"; 33:3 — "trust in God — and God suffices as a Guardian"; 33:48; 39:38; 65:3 — "whoever trusts in God — He is sufficient for him"; 73:9). *Wakīl* — from w-k-l — to entrust affairs to another: the one appointed to manage what the appointer cannot manage himself — the law-term lifted into theology: the jurists' wakālah-contract (power of attorney) simply mirrors at human scale the standing relation the word announces: the believer is the principal who delegates; God is the Trustee who never errs, never sleeps, never embezzles, never dies — the standing devotional verse sealing the matter at 39:62: "God is the Creator of all things — and He is Guardian over all things."

**Tawakkul: The Trustee-Doctrine in Its Full Register**

Around this Name the tradition built its entire science of reliance — *tawakkul* — the verbal noun of the same root (w-k-l): the deliberate entrusting of outcomes to God while the limbs work their assigned parts. The standing hadith-definitions cluster here as the commentators cite them beneath this verse: the Prophet's standing spectacle-definition in al-Tirmidhī's register (Tirmidhī 2344): "were you to trust in God with the trust due to Him, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds — they set out in the morning with empty bellies and return full" — the birds deploying their wings fully (work) while the emptiness and fullness belong to Another (trust); and its standing complement — the hadith of the camel (Tirmidhī 2517): "tie her and trust" — iʿqilhā wa tawakkal — the Prophet refusing the dichotomy of diligence versus reliance, legislating the both-and by which the law of custody operates: bind the camel, then entrust its staying. Ibn al-Qayyim's standing taxonomy (his celebrated chapter on tawakkul's degrees) reads the present verse as the doctrine's ground-floor: tawakkul is only rational where the Trustee is (1) owner of everything — hence the verse's first half; (2) sufficient for everything — hence its second; the two clauses together composing the intellectual warrant of reliance: *because all is His, and because He suffices as Guardian — entrust*. And the practical register of the sūrah's context keeps the doctrine from floating: the preceding family-file involved precisely the anxieties where tawakkul is strained — divorce-settlements, orphan-estates, dowries, the economics of the suspended wife — the Book answering with the standing fiduciary announcement: the estate is God's; the Guardian post is God's; the tenants may therefore act with justice inside their littleness without terror of the ledger, since the Keeper of the estate is sufficient for every aftermath (65:3's standing promise coupling tawakkul with the divorce-legislation itself: "whoever trusts in God — He is sufficient for him — God shall bring His command to pass; God has set a measure for every thing"). The verse, in six Arabic words, thus converts three verses of celestial title-deed into the emotionally livable conclusion: since the heavens and the earth are the possession — and the possessor suffices as the guardian — no orphan, no separating spouse, no guardian-worn believer of the sūrah's audience is ever actually *unguarded*: they are only ever between appointments of their one sufficient Trustee.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:133

> **If He wills, He shall remove you, O mankind, and bring others; and God is ever Able to do that.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**In Yashaʾ Yudhhibkum Ayyuhā al-Nās: The Replaceability Announcement**

From the sufficiency of God as Guardian, the verse turns to the dark-mirror doctrine that only the Self-Sufficient can safely announce: *in yashaʾ yudhhibkum ayyuhā al-nāsu wa yaʾti bi-ākharīn* — "if He wills, He shall remove you, O mankind, and bring others": *yudhhibkum* — from dh-h-b — take away, cause to depart — removal entire; *wa yaʾti bi-ākharīn* — "and bring others" — the verb of arrival bringing a replacement-creation to stand where the removed stood. The address — *ayyuhā al-nās* — "O mankind" — is the Book's universal vocative (its standing stations: 2:21 — "O mankind — worship your Lord"; 4:1 — the sūrah's opening exordium; 22:1 — "O mankind — be mindful of your Lord"; 35:15 — "O mankind — you are the poor unto God") — and its placement here universalizes the warning deliberately: commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr) note the verse is not aimed at one clan or one era but at the species-standing assumption that the current tenants are indispensable — nearly all the early commentators reading the removal comprehensively: God can remove *existing human beings altogether* and bring others — or, as al-Qurṭubī adds the wider possibility, another kind of creation entirely who might serve Him better than the disobedient. The verse therefore stands as the negative pedal of v. 131's charge: taqwā had been commanded; disbelief had been announced as possible; and now the cost — not to God (He is Ghanī, v. 131) but to the disbelieving tenants — replacement.

**The Substitute-Peoples Register: The Book's Standing File of Removal-and-Succession**

The commentators gather here the Book's whole standing file on divine substitution — a file the sūrah has already drawn upon and will draw upon again: 6:133 — "your Lord is the Self-Sufficient, Possessor of Mercy — if He wills, He shall remove you and appoint successors after you whomsoever He wills — as He raised you up from the posterity of another people" — the standing parallel whose coupling of Ghanī with removal the present passage mirrors (v. 131's Ghanī → v. 133's removal; 6:133's Ghanī → removal); 5:54 — already the sūrah's own standing anticipation — "O you who believe — whoever of you turns back from his religion — God shall bring a people He loves and who love Him..." — replacement-by-better-love; 14:19–20 — "have you not seen that God created the heavens and the earth in truth — if He wills, He shall remove you and bring a new creation — nor is that aught difficult for God" — the removal announced with its standing shrug; 47:38 — "and if you turn away, He shall substitute another people for you — and they shall not be the likes of you" — replacement specified as *improvement* for God, not loss; 70:40–41 — "We are able to substitute better than they"; 76:28 — "We created them and strengthened their frames — and when We will, We shall substitute their likes for them, substitution entire"; 9:39 — the march-or-perish verse — "if you march not forth, He shall punish you with a painful punishment and shall substitute a people other than you — nor shall you harm Him at all" — the standing formula *wa lā taḍurruhū shayʾan* annihilating any delusion that stubbornness injures heaven. The register, laid end to end, composes what Ibn Taymiyyah calls the law of divine disposability-of-nations: history contains no irreplaceable people.

**Salmān's Back: The Standing Report of Identification**

The verse carries one of the most remarked identification-anecdotes in the whole tafsīr corpus: the standing report (al-Qurṭubī and al-Zamakhsharī's standing citation — and its transmission-lines through Muqātil's and others' tafsīr-matān) that when this verse came down — or its sister-text 47:38 ("if you turn away, He shall substitute another people...") — and the Prophet was asked "who are those who would be brought?" — he placed his hand upon the back or shoulder of Salmān al-Fārsī — Salmān the Persian, the Companion whose search for truth had carried him from Zoroastrian Isfahan to Christian Syria to the bondage of a Jewish household in Yathrib and finally to the Prophet — and said: "this man and his people" — meaning the Persians — and in some transmissions he added words that made the point entire: "were faith suspended at the Pleiades — *law kāna al-īmān muʿallaqan bi-al-thurayyā* — men from among them would surely reach it." The commentators unfold the anecdote's standing lessons in several directions: (1) ethnicity is no tenure — the *ākharūn* — the "others" of the verse — may come from a nation the first audience considered marginal: the Persian stranger serving as prophetic emblem of God's freedom to re-appoint the bearers of His religion; (2) the replacement may already stand inside the congregation unrecognized — Salmān sitting in the Prophet's own circle while the question was asked, the future of the ummah leaning unsuspected on a foreigner's back; (3) and the standing historical reading — ventured by the historians of tafsīr — that the Muslim eastward expansions, the Persian scholarly flowerings (the compilers of the Six Books themselves largely of Persian origin: al-Bukhārī of Bukhārā; Muslim of Nishapur; al-Tirmidhī; al-Nasāʾī; Abū Dāwūd of Sijistān; Ibn Mājah of Qazvin), read to many later commentators as the long echo of the Prophet's gesture: God had indeed brought "others" — and their service had indeed sounded the heights.

**Wa Kāna Allāhu ʿAlā Dhālika Qadīran: Power Appended to Threat**

The seal converts warning to certainty: *wa kāna Allāhu ʿalā dhālika qadīran* — "and God is ever Able to do that": *qadīr* — from q-d-r — power, capacity, the standing attribute-name of omnipotence (2:20 — "God is over all things Able"; 2:148; 3:26's standing roll; 11:4; 18:45; 29:20; 33:27 — the sūrah-flanked "and God is ever over all things Able"; 46:33's question-answer — "is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them — surely — and He is the Creator, the Knowing"; 67:1's closing tribute) — the attribute here appearing in its deliberate grammatical posture: *ʿalā dhālika* — "over *that*" — the demonstrative pointing back at the very act just announced (removal-and-replacement), as if to nail the power-statement to this specific threat lest any hearer file it under impossibilities. Al-Rāzī's standing scholastic observation closes the sequence: v. 131 established God's independence (Ghanī) — needing no people; v. 132 established His adequacy (Kafā) — needing no partners; v. 133 establishes His capability (Qadīr) — needing no tenants; so that the whole triad composes one standing lesson for every community, then and now: the heavens and the earth run at full divine sufficiency, and humanity's lease remains as contingent as its reverence — the Owner, Guardian, and Powerful One being at every moment able to sign other names into the tenancy.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:134

> **Whosoever desires the reward of this world — with God is the reward of this world and the Hereafter; and God is ever Hearing, Seeing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Man Kāna Yurīdu Thawāba al-Dunyā: The World-Seeker Addressed Without Insult**

After the replacement-warning of v. 133, the Book turns to the motives that drive its hearers — and does so with a striking gentleness: *man kāna yurīdu thawāba al-dunyā fa-ʿinda Allāhi thawābu al-dunyā wa al-ākhirah* — "whosoever desires the reward of this world — with God is the reward of this world and the Hereafter": *thawāb* — from th-w-b — returning, recompense: the reward conceived as what *comes back* upon the doer of deeds (its standing Book-file: 3:148 — "God gave them the reward of this world and the best reward of the Hereafter"; 3:195 — "their Lord answered them: I shall not waste the work of any worker among you"); and the syntax carries the commentators' standing wonder: the verse does not scold the world-desire but *redirects it to the right supplier* — you want this world's reward? Then seek it *from God* — for both this world's distribution and the next's are stocked in His one treasury. Al-Zamakhsharī marks the positive reading explicitly: those who struggle sincerely for religion may receive the reward of both worlds — the Book's own standing double-reward file confirming: 12:56–57 — Joseph "established in the land" in this world, then "and the reward of the Hereafter is best"; 3:146–148 — the patient fighters beside the prophets given "the reward of this world and the best reward of the Hereafter — and God loves the good-doers"; 29:27 — Abraham given his reward in this world, "and in the Hereafter he shall surely be among the righteous"; 28:14 — Moses at maturity granted wisdom and knowledge — reward arriving mid-biography, "thus do We reward the good-doers."

**The Ominous Side: Ṭuʿmah's Advocates and the Ironic Thawāb**

Al-Ṭabarī, however, records the reading that darkens the verse — and its plausibility anchors itself in the sūrah's own recent history: the file of Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq (vv. 105–115), whose advocates within Madīnah had displayed belief outwardly in order to gather the *world's* reward — the booty of fighting alongside the Prophet and the general protection that Muslim identity conferred in the city. For such, the verse reads as standing irony: they pursued thawāb al-dunyā and obtained it — and "the reward of this world and the Hereafter" becomes, in their case, an ominous double-entry: this world paying its wage in full, and the Hereafter holding its own recompense for the hypocrisy — the counter-position the Book runs in its standing contrasts ("whoever desires the harvest of the Hereafter — We increase him in his harvest; and whoever desires the harvest of this world — We give him of it — but in the Hereafter he has no portion" — 42:20; "whosoever desires the fleeting life — We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We will — then We appoint for him hell" — 17:18; 3:145; 33:28–29 — the Prophet's wives asked to choose between the good of this world and God and His Messenger and the Abode of the Hereafter). The tradition adds its standing intention-verdict — the celebrated hadith (Bukhārī 1; Muslim 1907): "actions are but by intentions, and every man shall have only what he intended — so whoever's migration was for the sake of worldly benefit or for a woman he marries — his migration is for that to which he migrated": the Hijrah itself — the glory-act of the community — convertible into mere commerce by its inner aim.

**The Standing Prayer of the Middle Position**

Yet the Book's mercy builds a bridge between the two readings — and the commentators (beginning with al-Zamakhsharī's note) direct the reader to the standing prayer that resolves the verse's tension: 2:201 — "but among them are those who say: our Lord — give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter — and shield us from the punishment of the Fire" — the ḥasanah-in-both-worlds petition, which the Prophet and the community made the standing daily supplication of the ummah (the tradition recording that the most frequent of the Prophet's supplications was precisely this verse — its standing register in Bukhārī and Muslim's ḥadīth-collections of his most-repeated prayers — "our Lord — give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter"). The verse before us thus legislates the honest middle position between world-contempt and world-idolatry: this world's reward is not denounced — it is *located*: *fa-ʿinda Allāhi* — "with God is..." — the preposition of presence and custody — the seeker directed to the shelf where both treasuries stand side by side. To desire the world's good *from God* is commerce with heaven; to desire it *instead of* God is the Ṭuʿmah-file; and to desire it *for* God — as means for worship, family, charity — stands among the standing marks of the prophetic life itself.

**Wa Kāna Allāhu Samīʿan Baṣīran: The Two Names That Audit Desire**

The seal posts the two auditors of intention: *wa kāna Allāhu samīʿan baṣīran* — "and God is ever Hearing, Seeing": the standing Name-pair of perception (its stations: 4:58 above — "God is ever Hearing, Seeing"; 17:1's standing exordium; 22:61; 22:75; 31:28; 40:20; 40:56; 42:11 — "nothing is as His likeness — and He is the Hearing, the Seeing"; 58:1) — and its fittingness here exact: the verse concerns *desires* — the innermost cargo of the heart — and so its audit requires precisely these two Names: the Samīʿ who hears the world's-reward asked aloud and the bargain whispered inwardly, and the Baṣīr who sees the intention beneath the migration, the aim beneath the action — the standing pair guarding the standing verse so that no hearer mistakes the gentleness of "with God is the reward of this world" for blindness about *why* the reward was sought. Between v. 133's Qadīr (power to replace peoples) and v. 135's imminent justice-summit, the Samīʿ-Baṣīr seal keeps the examination intimate: the Book having warned the community as a mass now addresses the single desiring heart — you who desire the world's reward — the One holding both worlds hears your asking and sees your aim: ask, therefore, carefully — and ask for both.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:135

> **O you who believe — be ever upstanding in equity, witnesses for God, even though it be against yourselves, or parents, or kindred. Whether one be rich or poor — God is worthier of them both. So follow not caprice, lest you swerve. And if you twist or turn away — then God is ever Aware of whatsoever you do.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Kūnū Qawwāmīna bi-l-Qisṭ: The Standing-Posture of the Whole Religion**

The sūrah now arrives at one of the one of the load-bearing walls of the entire Qur'ānic ethic — a verse the community's jurists, preachers, and reformers have quoted without pause: *kūnū qawwāmīna bi-l-qisṭi shuhadāʾa li-llāhi wa law ʿalā anfusikum* — "be ever upstanding in equity, witnesses for God, even though it be against yourselves": *qawwāmīn* — the intensive plural of qāʾim — those who stand, remain standing, stand to maintain: not occasional dispensers of justice but its standing custodians — the intensive form (faʿʿāl) carrying constancy through difficulty — and it is the very posture the Book attributes to God Himself: 3:18's standing predicate — "God — bearing witness that there is no god but He — and the angels and those possessed of knowledge — *qāʾiman bi-l-qisṭ* — standing-firm in equity" (and 5:8's standing twin: "be upstanding for God, witnesses in equity — and let not hatred of a people move you to be unjust — be just — that is nearer to mindfulness"). *Qisṭ* — the portion-justice, the apportioning of each his exact due (v. 127's standing station — "that you stand firm for the orphans with qisṭ") — versus *ʿadl* — the rectification-justice: the two words of the Book's justice-vocabulary meeting here in the community's standing charter. The commentators remark on the command's economy: *kūnū* — "be" — not "do" — justice demanded as a state of being, an identity, before it is demanded as an act; the ummah called to *be* upstanders the way it is called to *be* believers.

**Shuhadāʾa Li-llāhi: Testimony as Property of God**

Then the phrase that converts every courtroom into a sanctuary: *shuhadāʾa li-llāh* — "witnesses for God": the testimony belongs to God before it belongs to the plaintiff — al-Ṭabarī's standing paraphrase fixing the meaning: "uphold justice for the sake of God when you bear witness" — and the standing mystical commentary of Rūzbihān al-Baqlī deepening it: "the spirit of tawḥīd will not take root in a person's heart so long as God holds upon him a claim he has not fulfilled" — truthful witnessing being precisely one of those standing claims, a debt owed to God that speech must discharge. The standing witness-file of the Book stands behind the phrase: testimony required for commercial writing (2:282's standing ordinance — "and bring witnesses when you transact"); for the orphan's inheritance-handover (4:6 above — "when you deliver to them their property — take witnesses over them"); for the gravest criminal charges (4:15's standing four-witness rule; 24:2–9's liʿān machinery) — the whole legal order resting on human throats that tell the truth — and 22:78's standing honor-title — "that the Messenger may be a witness over you, and you may be witnesses over mankind" — showing the courtroom-duty to be the local form of the ummah's cosmic vocation. Hence the verse's terrifying pronoun: *li-llāh* — *for God* — not for the clan, not for the co-religionist, not for the poor against the rich nor the rich against the poor: the witness serves a third Party who is present at every testimony — and 25:72’s standing praise of "those who do not bear false witness" marking the counterfeit as the standing disqualification.

**Wa Law ʿAlā Anfusikum: The Hardest Direction First**

The test-cases then proceed in ascending order of cost: *wa law ʿalā anfusikum awi al-wālidayni wa al-aqrabīn* — "even though it be against yourselves, or parents, or kindred": the self named *first* — the commentators (Ibn Kathīr's standing summary) noting the order as deliberate pedagogy: whoever will testify against his own interest has inoculated himself against the subtler corruptions; and parents and kindred placed next because kinship is the oldest pressure-chamber of false witness — the Ṭuʿmah episode of vv. 105–115 being the sūrah's own standing illustration (a clan rallying to defend its guilty kinsman against the innocent Jew — al-Ṭabarī's standing Sabāb-file, which the commentators fold back under this verse: had Ṭuʿmah's clan lived by v. 135, the whole affair would have ended in a confession instead of an apostasy). The standing duty-priority established: the deference owed to parents (17:23's standing ordinance — the very next-nearest command in the Book's ethics) does not extend to shielding them from truthful testimony — kindness to parents operates everywhere *except* inside the witness-box; there, only God is parent. The hadith-register preserves the standing report of the Prophet's own calibration — asked to do justice in the case of a poor reported in connection with this verse: an incident in which the Prophet inclined in judgment toward a poor man, thinking him incapable of truly wronging the wealthier, whereupon the reminder descended: wealth and poverty are both false objects of tilt — *immā yakun ghaniyyan aw faqīran fa-Allāhu awlā bihimā* — "whether one be rich or poor — God is worthier of them both": *awlā* — nearer, worthier, more entitled — the poor man's advocacy belongs to God, not to the sentimental witness; the rich man's customary immunity likewise belongs to God, not to the bought witness — judge neither *for* the wallet nor *against* it: the arbitration of the classes already assigned to the Court above, which (the commentators add, folding v. 130 back in) has promised to enrich *both* from His bounty.

**Fa-Lā Tattabiʿū al-Hawā an Taʿdilū: Caprice — the One Banned Advocate**

The verse then names the only counsel excluded from the bar: *fa-lā tattabiʿū al-hawā an taʿdilū* — "so follow not caprice, lest you swerve": *hawā* — from h-w-y — falling, then the falling-desire, caprice (its standing book-file: 2:120; 2:145; 5:48–49's standing triple-warning to the Prophet himself — "judge between them by what God has revealed — and follow not their caprices"; 6:150; 18:28 — "obey not him whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows his caprice"; 23:71 — "had the truth followed their caprices — the heavens and the earth and whosoever is in them had been corrupted"; 38:26 — "David — We have made you a vicegerent in the earth — so judge between the people in truth and follow not caprice — for it shall lead you astray from God's way"; 45:23; 53:3's standing exemption — "nor does he speak from caprice" — of the Prophet alone; 79:40–41) — and the Book's standing double-reading of *taʿdilū*: the verb from ʿ-d-l meaning both "to act justly" and — by a celebrated lexical fork noted by al-Rāzī and al-Bayḍāwī — "to swerve aside": so the clause reads equally "follow not caprice *that you may be just*" (caprice the enemy of justice) or "follow not caprice *lest you swerve*" (caprice the author of deviation) — and the commentators remark that the two senses compose one counsel: justice is precisely the straight line from which caprice bends the witness. The verse's own book-kin finish the inventory of banned bends: 5:8's standing twin ("let not hatred of a people move you not to be just"); 24:2's standing flogging-verse ("let not pity for them seize you concerning the religion of God") — hatred banned in one verse, pity in another, self-interest and kinship in this one — the Book having by now fenced the witness-stand against every affection, noble or base.

**Wa In Talwū aw Tuʿriḍū: The Twist and the Turn, and the Khabīr Who Sees Both**

The ending names the two failings of the actual witness and hands both to the Expert-Aware: *wa in talwū aw tuʿriḍū fa-inna Allāha kāna bimā taʿmalūna khabīran* — "and if you twist or turn away — then God is ever Aware of whatsoever you do": *talwū* — from l-w-y — twisting — the standing term for distorting testimony or scripture alike (its standing file: 3:78 — "they twist their tongues with the Book that you may suppose it from the Book"; 2:75’s men "who heard the speech of God then tampered with it"; the very shape of the tampering witness: the words turned on the tongue until they face falsehood's direction); *tuʿriḍū* — turning away (v. 80's standing word — v. 128's iʿrāḍ) — the sin of silence: withholding the testimony altogether, declining the witness-duty when it is owed (its standing prohibition: 2:283 — "let not the witness refuse when he is called"; and 2:282's terminal warning — "he who conceals it — his heart is sinful") — so that the verse covers the whole crime-spectrum of the compromised witness: active distortion and passive refusal. And over both: *khabīr* — the Expert-Aware — the standing auditor-Name of the sūrah (v. 35 — "God is ever Knowing, Aware"; v. 94's standing seal; v. 128's station just above) — here placed with alchemical precision: a witness can twist words past the whole courtroom and the whole press of Madīnah, and turn away from the whole bench — but the Khabīr's expertise is precisely in interiors, in the grain of intentions under the grain of words: the verse sealing thereby the sūrah's longest-running lesson — from v. 86's greeting-judgment through the Ṭuʿmah-file and the family-file — that the community which would stand for equity must stand first before the Aware One who reads the standing posture itself.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:136

> **O you who believe! Believe in God and His Messenger, and in the Book which He has sent down upon His Messenger, and in the Book which He sent down aforetime. And whosoever disbelieves in God, and in His angels, and in His books, and in His messengers, and in the Last Day, has indeed gone far astray.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Yā Ayyuhā Alladhīna Āmanū... Āminū: "Believe, You Who Believe" — The Command to Be What You Are**

The verse opens with one of the Book's most dislocating vocatives: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū — āminū* — "O you who believe! — Believe": those already named believers are commanded to believe — an address-form the commentators have pondered from the beginning. Al-Ṭabarī records the first reading historically: the primary addressees were those among the People of the Book of Madīnah who had come to believe in their own prophet(s) but had not yet borne full witness to Muḥammad and his Book — the Book calling them "you who believe" by the belief they legitimately held, and then ordering them to complete the act: believe *in God and His Messenger* — the second belief not a repetition but an arrival: faith's fulfillment in the bearer God now actually addresses them through. Yet the commentators extend the form to every hearer in every generation — al-Rāzī's register gathering the enduring expositions: the command to the believing is the command to *increase* in belief — moving from belief-by-report to belief-by-investigation, from outer assent to the settled certainty the tradition elsewhere names (ʿĀʾishah's standing theology-of-certainty preserved in the tafsīr-collections: her celebrated remark in the tafsīr-collections: "if you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much" — certainty arriving as knowledge increases); or — as others phrase it — the command to *hold fast* to belief, renewing it as the standing devotional formula commands: the Prophet's standing exhortation recorded in the Sunan (its standing register in Aḥmad's Musnad and the ḥadīth-collections generally): "renew your faith" — asked, "how do we renew it, O Messenger of God?" — answered: "increase in saying: lā ilāha illā Allāh." Faith in this register is not a past event but a standing ordinance: the believer lives under a present-tense command to keep being what his name declares.

**The Five-Point Archipelago: The Verse's Own Creed-List**

Then the verse erects the five-point schema of īmān — the positive command of two articles (God and His Messenger) doubled into a negative inventory of five: *wa man yakfur bi-llāhi wa malāʾikatihi wa kutubihi wa rusulihi wa al-yawmi al-ākhiri* — "and whosoever disbelieves in God, and His angels, and His books, and His messengers, and the Last Day": the commentators immediately note the architecture — the command names two (God, Messenger) because in them are contained all five, and then the forensic clause enumerates the five because in them sits the definition of kufr — disbelief not as a vague posture but as a breach at enumerated points. The standing Book-register of the list is its own commentary: 2:285 — "the Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord — and the believers: each one believes in God and His angels and His books and His messengers — we make no distinction between any of His messengers"; 2:177 — the sūrah of the Cow's standing creed-verse ("righteousness is not that you turn your faces to the east and west, but righteousness is: whoever believes in God and the Last Day and the angels and the Book and the prophets — and gives of his wealth..."); and the sūrah's own later row — 4:150–151 below — where those who "disbelieve in God and His messengers, and wish to make a distinction between God and His messengers, saying: we believe in some and disbelieve in some" are declared "the disbelievers in truth" — the archipelago-principle standing: the articles are inseparable — a broken link voids the chain.

**Al-Wāḥid li-l-Jamīʿ: Gabriel's Question as the Standing Gloss**

The tradition's master-text for this entire lexical territory is the celebrated hadith of Gabriel — the standing source in the two Ṣaḥīḥs (Bukhārī 50; Muslim 8): the stranger with intensely white garments and intensely black hair, sitting knee-to-knee with the Prophet before the Companions, asking: "tell me about faith" — and the Prophet answering with the sixfold formula that glosses this verse forever: "that you believe in God, and His angels, and His meeting, and His messengers, and the Last Day, and that you believe in the decree — its good and its evil" — the present verse's five enlarged to six by the meeting-decree pair, the whole tradition's catechism of islām-īmān-iḥsān descending from that single sitting. The mufassirūn (Ibn Kathīr here as elsewhere) treat the hadith as the verse's living exegesis: belief as *taṣdīq* — inward assent-attestation — not merely lip-service; and belief as one seamless fabric — the angel-belief because the angels are the couriers of revelation; the book-belief because the books are its cargo; the messenger-belief because the messengers are its bearers; the Last Day because it is its horizon — God at the origin and the End, the entire middle furnished by His envoys and their texts.

**Fa-Qad Ḍalla Ḍalālan Baʿīdan: The Far Error and Its Register**

The verse closes with the standing verdict-form for total apostasy: *fa-qad ḍalla ḍalālan baʿīdan* — "has indeed gone far astray": *ḍalāl* — from ḍ-l-l — losing the way, error — with its standing superlative-doublet *baʿīd* — far, remote: error measured by distance from the Road (its standing register: 2:108 — "whosoever exchanges belief for disbelief has strayed from the evenness of the way"; 4:60 above — Satan desiring "to lead them far astray" — ḍalālan baʿīdan — the identical phrase there in Satan's wish, here in its realized state; 4:116 — "whoever associates partners with God has gone far astray"; 4:167 — "those who disbelieve and bar from God's way have gone far astray"; 14:18; 22:12; 34:8; 42:18); and the doubled cognate-accusative (*ḍalla ḍalālan*) intensifying as Arabic intensifies — the act named and then its cognate object naming its kind: not a stumble but an *error-of-the-far-kind*. Ibn Taymiyyah's standing principle orders the scene: since īmān is the condition of every deed's acceptance and every promise's arrival, the public loss announced here is not one item among others but the dissolution of the contract itself — the far error being precisely the stepping outside the archipelago within which alone meaning, covenant, and hope are legally alive. And the verse's zoom-structure teaches its own lesson: the sūrah of the household and the court of justice (vv. 127–135) now anchors both in eternal geography — spouses and orphans, witnesses and judges, all acting inside an īmān whose poles are God and the Last Day — the family-law of the sūrah fenced at each end by the two worlds in which it is lived.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:137

> **Verily those who believe, then disbelieve, then believe, then disbelieve, and then increase in disbelief — God was not one to forgive them nor to guide them unto a way.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Inna Alladhīna Āmanū Thumma Kafarū: The Oscillation-Diagnosis**

The archipelago-verse of v. 136 having defined what belief must hold, the Book now diagnoses the heart that cannot hold it: *inna alladhīna āmanū thumma kafarū thumma āmanū thumma kafarū thumma izdādū kufran* — "verily those who believe, then disbelieve, then believe, then disbelieve, and then increase in disbelief": a four-step oscillation crowned by a fifth movement that is different in kind — *izdādū* — from z-y-d — increase: the state graduating from alternation into a settled momentum. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī gathering the earliest readings) localize the pattern: most likely the hypocrites of Madīnah, whose outward-inward oscillation the coming verses (vv. 138–146) will anatomize at length — the structural argument being decisive: this verse forms the heading of that entire hypocrisy-file, so its referent must be the wavering-in-sincerity rather than those who never claimed Islam at all. Others among the early reading-traditions localized it in those among the People of the Book who believed in their own scriptures, disbelieved in what came after, "believed" outwardly in the Prophet's presence, disbelieved in his absence, and increased thereby in a compound estrangement (3:72's standing stratagem-file: "a faction of the People of the Book said: believe in what was sent down upon the believers at the day's opening — and disbelieve at its end — perhaps they will turn back"); early Shīʿī tafsīr applied it to those who manifested faith in the Prophet's lifetime then refused ʿAlī's authority; but the flow of context — the hypocrisy-chapter opening here and running to v. 146 — anchors the first reading as the standing one.

**The Threefold Repentance-Question: A Door the Verse Both Opens and Narrows**

Yet the verse's most debated legacy lives in its own grammar: disbelief is mentioned after belief *twice* — and then the increase — before the warning is issued. Al-Ṭabarī records the juristic corollary drawn by some early authorities: since the pattern allows two returns before the hardening, some held the repentance of an apostate might be accepted a limited number of times — "three" being the count some derived. But the standing majority — al-Ṭabarī himself leading — held the door of repentance never legislated shut in this life: the verse acknowledges, by its very alternation-clause, the *possibility of return* — communal and legal acceptance of one who leaves and repents — while warning that each oscillation *diminishes* the likelihood of a final return, because the heart is being trained in reversibility: al-Zamakhsharī's psychological note — each relapse engraves the soul's facility in sliding — and al-Rāzī's corresponding note: wavering of this depth indicates belief was never rooted at all. The closing-clause is thus read not as a juristic count but as an x-ray of trajectory — the danger named is not the number of falls but the *direction of the sum*: *thumma izdādū kufran* — the checkbook of alternation ending in deficit-increase.

**Lam Yakuni Allāhu Li-Yaghfira Lahum: The Rare Negative Will**

The verdict that follows belongs to the Book's rarest register — explicit divine non-forgiveness announced in the past-continuous form: *lam yakuni Allāhu li-yaghfira lahum wa lā li-yahdiyahum sabīlan* — "God was not one to forgive them nor to guide them unto a way": *lam yakun* with the following imperfect — "He was never of a disposition to..." — and the commentators' standing boundary-drawing: (1) the majority — forgiveness is closed for the one who *dies* upon the increase — death-in-kufr being the seal that ends the repentance-window (its standing Book-kin: 4:18 — "repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until death attends one of them, and he says: now I repent"; 3:90 — "those who disbelieve after their belief then increase in disbelief — their repentance shall not be accepted — and those are the astray" — the nearly word-for-word parallel); (2) the standing theological schools' glosses: the Muʿtazilite reading — God "will not guide them" in the Hereafter to the Garden, guidance forfeited when the state was sealed by death; or His guidance removed in this very life as standing punishment; the Ashʿarite rejoinder — a plain assertion that God does not guide disbelievers in this life itself, with the "increase" clause standing for them as proof that faith and disbelief have real degrees — obedience and sin genuinely increasing or diminishing them (the Ashʿarite locus classicus in the faith-debate). And v. 145–146 below frames the hope-window precisely: the lowest depth belongs to the hypocrites — "*except those who repent and make amends*" — the Book itself reopening, four verses on, the door it seems here to close — confirming the majority reading: the closure is not upon the repentant but upon the state-in-which-one-dies.

**The Standing Tremor-Application: Oscillation as a Soul-Disease**

The psychological filing of the verse — the standing register from the spiritual commentators inward — universalizes the pattern without shrinking its severity: oscillation between commitment and betrayal is a disease with a trajectory — and trajectories, not single points, judge lives. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd's standing dictum (its standing register in the moral literature) gathers the point: "the believer sees his sins as a mountain beneath which he sits, fearing it will fall upon him; the profligate sees his sins as a fly that passes across his nose, and he flicks it away" — the difference between the two being precisely the presence or absence of one-directional increase. The verse stands as the heading of the sūrah's hypocrisy-dossier: first the oscillation diagnosed (v. 137), then the ironic announcement (v. 138), then the false alliances exposed (v. 139), then the sitting-with-mockers forbidden (v. 140) — an anatomy of the two-faced soul that will close, at vv. 145–146, with both its depth and its escape: "verily the hypocrites are in the lowest depth of the Fire... save those who repent and make amends and hold fast to God and make their religion sincere for God." The sūrah of social justice thus pauses its courtroom to examine the hiddenest courtroom of all — the heart before its Lord — where belief must either increase or it will, by the physics of the soul, decline.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:138

> **Give glad tidings to the hypocrites that theirs shall be a painful punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Bashshiri al-Munāfiqīna: The Glad Tidings That Are Not Glad**

The hypocrisy-dossier's second verse delivers one of the Book's most chilling rhetorical strokes: *bashshiri al-munāfiqīna bi-anna lahum ʿadhāban alīman* — "give glad tidings to the hypocrites that theirs shall be a painful punishment": *bashshir* — the imperative of b-sh-r — the very verb of Gospel good-news (its own standing register across the Book: "We give thee glad tidings of a boy" — 3:45; "give glad tidings to the patient" — 2:155; the word *bushrā* being the standing name of prophetic gladness) — here commandeered into its exact opposite: news of punishment announced in the vocabulary of joy. The commentators recognize the device instantly — the standing Qur'ānic register of ironic mockery: 3:21 — "give those who disbelieve in God's signs and slay the prophets... glad tidings of a painful punishment"; 9:3 — "give glad tidings of a painful punishment to those who disbelieve"; 9:34 — to the gold-and-silver hoarders "give them glad tidings of a painful punishment"; 31:7; 45:8; 84:24 — each time the annunciation-vocabulary announcing doom, as though the Book were saying: you traded the true glad tidings; here are the only tidings your conduct has purchased. Al-Zamakhsharī's literary note marks the sting's exact location: the irony lands hardest on *munāfiqīn* — the hypocrites — because their entire career had been the pursuit of advantageous appearances; in contempt of appearance-worship the Book dresses their doom in their favorite costume: outward good-news wrapping inward ruin — the mirror-image of their lives, which wrapped inward ruin in outward good-news. And the double-edge of the vocative itself: the Prophet is commanded to pronounce the sentence — making the exposure public, stripping the concealment they labored to maintain; the very announcement a punishment before the punishment.

**The Inversion-Logic: Joy-Vocabulary as Final Sarcasm**

The Book elsewhere explains why the guilty receive no glad tidings at all: 25:22 — "the day they see the angels — no glad tidings that day for the guilty" — the Day's joy-vocabulary entirely reserved for the upright; the hypocrites, by contrast, are addressed *in this life* with the glad-word precisely because in the next there is none for them: the wardrobe of celebration lent one final time, parodically, before being closed forever. And the counter-note the commentators add (16:58–59 carrying the standing parallel of impious grief): the pre-Islamic Arabs, receiving the "glad tidings" of a newborn daughter, had their faces darken — the Book wielding the same joy-word to shame the joyless; here the hypocrites, who considered themselves the cleverest joy-brokers of Madīnah, receive their last headlines in the style they always craved — *bashshir* — and the content undoes the word. Al-Biqāʿī's rhetorical tradition gathers the device under standing irony (the standing register of the rhetoricians: the "announcement-irony" — *al-tabshīr al-tahakkumī* — mockery through the form of felicitation).

**ʿAdhābun Alīm: The Painful Punishment**

The content of the faux-tidings is stated plainly: *ʿadhāban alīman* — "a painful punishment": *alīm* — from ʾ-l-m — pain: the standing punishment-adjective across the Book (its register in this sūrah alone: 4:18; 4:161 below; the several standing stations throughout) — and its descriptive minimalism deliberate: no detail of kind or duration — the darkness of the unspecified letting the horror do its own work, the standing method of the Book's briefest doom-verses. Yet the commentators locate its reality precisely within this sūrah's own map: v. 145 below will name the destination — "verily the hypocrites are in the lowest depth of the Fire" — *al-dark al-asfal* — the basement-basement beneath even the open disbelievers — the hypocrites outranked in punishment by those they privately agreed with, because they added to unbelief the artistry of pretense.
