And the place of all this within the chapter-structure: v. 137 diagnosed the oscillation; v. 138 announces the wages; v. 139 will expose the false alliances that the hypocritical heart arranges as insurance — taking disbelievers as protectors "instead of the believers" — the glad tidings of v. 138 therefore read as the answer to the insurance-policy of v. 139 before it is even described: insure yourself with whomever you like — your underwriter has already announced His settlement. The spiritual commentators (Ibn ʿAjībah's standing inward register) extend the application to every pretense-managing heart: every soul that maintains a public face in commerce with God while banking a private face against Him lives inside this verse's irony — receiving good news daily (health, provision, reputation) while the account being settled is of another kind. The verse, six words long, thereby stands as one of the Book's purest exhibitions of style-as-judgment: the sentence itself is the sentence.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:139

> **Those who take the disbelievers as protectors instead of the believers — do they seek might through them? Nay — might belongs to God altogether.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Alladhīna Yattakhidhūna al-Kāfirīna Awliyāʾa: The Insurance-Policy of the Two-Faced**

The dossier now names the hypocrites' characteristic foreign policy: *alladhīna yattakhidhūna al-kāfirīna awliyāʾa min dūni al-muʾminīn* — "those who take the disbelievers as protectors instead of the believers": *awliyāʾ* — the plural of *walī* — the protector-patron-ally (from w-l-y — nearness) — a word the commentators insist carried, in the tribal climate of Arabia, the weight of a *total* bond: mutual defense, shared fortune, absolute loyalty — walāyah being the social cement of pre-Islamic allegiance, which the Book does not abolish but consecrates-redirects: God the believers' ultimate Walī (2:257 — "God is the Protector of those who believe — He brings them out of darkness into the light"; 2:107; 3:68; 4:45's standing within this very sūrah; 5:55 — "your Protector is but God and His Messenger and those who believe — those who keep the prayer and give the alms, bowing down"; 6:14; 7:196; 9:116), fellow believers one another's true awliyāʾ (8:72; 9:71 — "the believing men and believing women are protectors one of another"), and the counterfeit patronages exposed: the idolaters' vanity-shrines (13:16), the disbelievers' Satanward lean (7:30; 16:100 — "his patronage is over those who take him as protector"), the disbelievers one another's closed guild (8:73 — "those who disbelieve are protectors one of another — unless you do this, there will be tribulation in the land and great corruption"). The standing comment-canon localizes the act here: the Madīnan hypocrites cultivating secretly the Jewish clans (al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī's reading) or the Meccan idolaters (other reports) as a hedge — an insurance-policy against the possibility that the Prophet's enterprise fail — "instead of the believers" carrying its precise sting: not *alongside* them but in *preference* to them, the heart's first loyalty already transferred to the enemy camp that the tongue publicly opposes.

**Min Dūni al-Muʾminīn: The Loyalty-Migration as Perfidy**

The commentators draw the verse's standing legal-sociological line: the Book prohibits not neighborliness, trade, covenants, or kindness with non-believers (60:8's standing balance — "God does not forbid you, regarding those who have not fought you over religion and have not expelled you from your homes, from being righteous toward them and dealing justly with them — God loves the just") but precisely *yattakhidhūna awliyāʾa min dūn* — the adoption of the outside camp as one's *protector-fraternity of first resort*: the transfer of ultimate reliance. Its standing prohibition-file: 3:28 — "let not the believers take the disbelievers as protectors instead of the believers — whoever does that has nothing from God"; 4:89 above (regarding those who turn back); 4:144 below — the verse's own near-repeat in this dossier ("O you who believe — take not the disbelievers as protectors instead of the believers — do you wish to give God a clear warrant against you?"); 5:51 — "take not the Jews and Christians as protectors — they are protectors one of another — and whoever of you takes them as protectors is surely one of them"; 5:80-81's standing rebuke; and the extreme case — 9:23 — even family members, where loyalty to them means standing against faith. The perfidy-diagnosis stands triple: such alliance (1) betrays the community's trust, (2) reveals opportunism — hedges placed with two bookmakers at once, and (3) — the point of the verse's second half — manifests a *theological* misjudgment: distrust in the sufficiency of God's protection, as though the guarantee of 4:132 above ("God suffices as a Guardian") were inadequate collateral.

**A-Yabtaghūna ʿIndahumu al-ʿIzzah: Might Sought at the Wrong Address**

Then the withering question: *a-yabtaghūna ʿindahumu al-ʿizzah — fa-inna al-ʿizzata li-llāhi jamīʿan* — "do they seek might through them? Nay — might belongs to God altogether": *ʿizzah* — from ʿ-z-z — might, power, dignity, invincibility — the withstanding-strength that cannot be subdued — and the interrogative framed as exposure: your secret alliance with the disbelievers is, at bottom, a *quest for might* — prestige, safety, backup in the day things go wrong — conducted at the false address. The Book's standing ʿizzah-file pronounces the asset's true registry: 63:8 — the Medīnan-surah's standing counter-claim, spoken against the very words of the arch-hypocrite Ibn Ubayy himself ("might belongs to God and His Messenger and the believers — but the hypocrites know not"); 10:65 — "let not their speech grieve thee — verily might belongs to God altogether — He is the Hearing, the Knowing"; 35:10 — "whoever desires might — to God belongs might altogether"; and 29:41’s standing parable concluding the search forever: "the parable of those who take protectors apart from God is that of the spider that makes a house — and verily the frailest of houses is the spider's house — if they but knew": the hedger's web of secret alliances, woven strand by strand, hangs exactly there — in air, adhesive only to itself. And *jamīʿan* — "altogether" — sealing the totality: not a majority-share but the whole asset class — every quantum of might concentrated in one Owner, who distributes derivatives to His believers as He wills (63:8's standing assignment) and leaves the false address permanently unfunded. The practical register descends to every age's version of the same hedge: alliances with the powerful against one's own community out of fear that God's promise is slow; prestige sought through disavowal; the quiet trimming of loyalties to keep every door open — the verse detecting in each the identical theological error: a census of might that omitted its only Holder. The hypocrites of Madīnah sought ʿizzah with Quraysh and the clans; the clans dissolved, Quraysh surrendered, Ibn Ubayy died chewing his bitterness at Khaybar's aftermath — and 4:141 below will complete the portrait: waiting "with you" in the days of victory, claiming "were we not with you?" when the spoil is divided — might having migrated, as it always does, to the Side that never needed it.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:140

> **He has already sent down upon you in the Book that when you hear the signs of God being disbelieved in and mocked at, do not sit with them until they engage in some other discourse — else you are indeed like them. Verily God will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers in Hell all together —**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Wa Qad Nazzala ʿAlaykum fī al-Kitāb: The Citation of an Earlier Ruling — Legislating by Quotation**

The dossier's fourth verse takes an extraordinary legislative step: it *quotes the Book itself as precedent*: *wa qad nazzala ʿalaykum fī al-kitāb* — "He has already sent down upon you in the Book": the commentators (al-Ṭabarī with his standing chains; Ibn Kathīr citing the consensus) identify the referent nearly unanimously: 6:68 — revealed in the Meccan period, years earlier — "and when thou seest those who engage in vain discourse concerning Our signs, turn away from them until they engage in some other discourse — and if Satan should make thee forget, then do not sit, after the reminding, with the wrongdoing people" (and its standing companion 6:69 — "those who fear God are in no way accountable for them — but a reminder, that perhaps they may fear"). The Medīnan verse thus does not merely repeat the Meccan ruling; it *files the earlier verse as standing law* — the act itself a standing lesson in Qur'ānic legal method: earlier revelation is not a draft but an accumulating corpus; each new sūrah builds with the already-built. Al-Qurṭubī dwells on the legal significance: the prohibition is thereby doubly anchored — revealed once about Meccan mockers of the revelation, reactivated here about the Madīnan mockers in the hypocrite-majlis — the same ruling governing two capitals and two calendars: the Book's own demonstration that its rulings are not occasion-bound fossils.

**Fa-Lā Taqʿudū Maʿahum: The Seat as a Vote — The Sociology of Complicity**

The ruling itself is of disarming simplicity — and therefore of unending force: *idhā samiʿtum āyāti Allāhi yukfaru bihā wa yustahzaʾu bihā fa-lā taqʿudū maʿahum ḥattā yakhūḍū fī ḥadīthin ghayrihi — innakum idhan mithluhum* — "when you hear the signs of God being disbelieved in and mocked at, do not sit with them until they engage in some other discourse — else you are indeed like them": the command drills into the sociology of presence — *taqʿudū* — sitting — the most passive of acts — legislated as though it were speech: because presence is broadcast. Al-Zamakhsharī's standing gloss distills it: it is not enough to abstain from mocking and disbelieving oneself; sitting passively in the mocking-circle *lends silent support and tacit approval* — the absent counter-signature registering as consent. The jurists built the standing analogy-architecture upon it: attendance is endorsement in matters of communal boundaries (the principle echoing through rulings on gatherings of open sin — the standing maxim that the silent occupant of the wrong assembly shares its classification — grounded precisely in *innakum idhan mithluhum* — "else you are indeed like them": the threat of *equation* — the witness of the mockery classified by the Book with the mocker, though he never mocked: guilt-by-assembly formalized in revelation). Yet the exit-clause is equally deliberate: *ḥattā yakhūḍū fī ḥadīthin ghayrihi* — "until they engage in some other discourse" — the boycott conditional and conversational, not absolute and social — when the topic moves, the seat may return: the Book regulating boundaries without abolishing society, displeasure expressed as temporary standing-to-one's-feet rather than as permanent excommunication. And the *kh-w-ḍ* root of *yakhūḍū* — wading — the standing Book-word for plunging into discourse (its register: 6:68’s twin usage; 9:65; 43:83; 52:12; 74:45 — "we used to wade with the waders") — paints the mockery-session as people splashing in shallows they mistake for depths: the believer is forbidden to wade with them, not to converse with them.

**The Hypocrisy-Barometer: Association as Revelation of Identity**

Al-Zamakhsharī's standing note — gathered with approval in the later literature — generalizes the verse into a barometer of the heart: the sincerity of one's faith, indeed one's true religious identity, is revealed not only by one's own words and deeds but by *the character of the company one keeps when truth is being dishonored*. With v. 139's false-protector taking, this sitting-with-mockers forms the two behaviors by which the hypocrite outs himself: the alliance he contracts in fear, and the majlis he keeps in comfort — outward profession untouched in both, inner allegiance exposed in both. Ibn Kathīr adds the standing delimitation that balances the ruling: the prohibition targets the gathering *where the mockery occurs and continues* — 6:68's own forgetfulness-clause ("if Satan should make thee forget, then do not sit, after the reminding" — the accidental attender purified by immediate rising) — the law legislating for the living, not for perfection's mannequins: memory returns, and the feet follow.

**Inna Allāha Jāmiʿu al-Munāfiqīna wa al-Kāfirīna: The Assembly Where Assemblies Are Judged**

The verse seals with its standing eschatological gathering-threat: *inna Allāha jāmiʿu al-munāfiqīna wa al-kāfirīna fī jahannama jamīʿan* — "verily God will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers in Hell all together": *jāmiʿ* — the Gatherer (its standing register: 4:87 above — "God — there is no god but He — He shall surely gather you to the Day of Resurrection"; and 3:9 — "our Lord — Thou shalt surely gather mankind unto a Day about which there is no doubt") — and the classification it enforces the exact inverse of the sitting it forbids: you feared to be *unlike* the mockers by rising from their majlis; beware instead being *like* them in the final majlis — for *innakum idhan mithluhum* finds its eschatological twin here: the sitten-with and the sat-with are gathered *jamīʿan* — all together — one assembly sealing all assemblies. The sūrah's own earlier audience-principle of 4:87 (gathering as certainty) now specialized: every human circle is practice for the final Circle; choosing one's sitting-room is choosing one's Resurrection-neighborhood. The dossier will continue below (v. 141's wavering watchers: "those who lie in wait for you — if a victory comes to you from God, they say: were we not with you?") — but v. 140 has already delivered its permanent legislation across the centuries: the rule of the seat — hear revelation mocked, and the body must file the soul's dissent with its feet — seven Arabic verbs containing a whole jurisprudence of protest without violence, withdrawal without severance, and testimony without a word spoken.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:141

> **Those who lie in wait concerning you: if a victory comes to you from God, they say, "Were we not with you?" And if the disbelievers have some share, they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you, and defend you from the believers?" God shall judge between you on the Day of Resurrection, and God shall never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Alladhīna Yatarabbaṣū Bikum: The Watchers at the Fence**

The dossier's fifth verse paints the hypocrites' characteristic posture in a single participle: *alladhīna yatarabbaṣū bikum* — "those who lie in wait concerning you": *yatarabbaṣū* — from r-b-ṣ — to wait-and-watch, to lurk in observation of an outcome before committing (its standing Book-file: 9:52's standing challenge — "say: do you await for us aught save one of the two best while we await for you that God afflict you"; 9:98 — "among the Bedouin are those who take what they spend as a loss, and await the turns of fortune against you"; 57:14 — "they await nay" — the full register of tarabbuṣ as the creed of the calculator who will not pledge until the ledger settles). The sūrah had already sketched these watchers mid-battle (vv. 72–73 above: "among you is he who would surely tarry — then if a calamity befalls you he says: God has blessed me, in that I was not present with them — but if a bounty comes to you from God, he says — as if there were no affection between you and him — would that I had been with them, then I would have attained a great triumph"); v. 141 now adds the decisive detail al-Ṭabarī's chains record: their watchfulness is not mere cowardice — it is *double bookkeeping with both armies*: the verse will show them corresponding openly with the Muslim side in victory and with the enemy side in defeat — hypocrisy mature into active intelligence-trading.

**Alam Nakun Maʿakum: The Share-Claim of the Absent**

When the banner swings Muslim-ward: *fa-in kāna lakum fatḥun min Allāhi qālū alam nakun maʿakum* — "if a victory comes to you from God, they say: were we not with you?": *fatḥ* — the opening-victory (its standing register: 8:10; 48:1 — "verily We have opened for thee a clear opening"; 110:1) — and the claim-form itself the standing signature of the opportunist: the rhetorical *alam* — "did we not...?" — a question that presumes assent, designed to harvest the spoils of Badr and the booty of every victory while the claimer had kept himself, in Ibn Kathīr's standing phrase, safe behind the walls. The commentators note the delicate duplicity of the word *maʿakum* — "with you" — true in geography (many did march reluctantly, 9:46-47's standing diagnosis of their disruptive presence), false in allegiance: proximity of bodies cited as proof of union of hearts — the exact confusion of association-vocabulary with loyalty-reality that vv. 139–140 have just disassembled.

**Alam Naḥūl ʿAlaykum wa Namnaʿkum min al-Muʾminīn: The Betrayal-Invoice**

When the tide swings the other way, the invoice switches creditor: *wa in kāna li-l-kāfirīna naṣībun qālū alam naḥūl ʿalaykum wa namnaʿkum min al-muʾminīn* — "if the disbelievers have some share, they say: did we not gain mastery over you, and defend you from the believers?": *naṣīb* — the assigned portion (the standing word of lots and shares across the sūrah's inheritance-file, now grimly repurposed: a "portion" of victory) — and the two verbs itemize the treason-bill: *naḥūl* — from ḥ-w-l — to gain control, to maneuver into mastery — "we out-maneuvered you (O disbelievers) for you" — and *namnaʿkum min al-muʾminīn* — "and we kept the believers off you": the hypocrites presenting their *absence* from the Muslim ranks as a service rendered to the enemy — their treacherous non-participation invoiced as intercession, their withheld swords billed to the account of military protection. Al-Ṭabarī notes the historical resonance: at Uḥud, when three hundred turned back with Ibn Ubayy at the field's edge (3:166-167's standing file), the withdrawal functioned materially as aid to Quraysh — and the hypocrites' subsequent whispering with the Meccans dressed it as deliberate strategy in their favor. The word *al-muʾminīn* — "from the believers" — slipping from their mouths as a third-party designation — the hypocrites, claiming Islam before the Muslims, speaking of the believers to the enemy as *them*: the pronoun betraying what the testimony-of-faith conceals.

**Allāhu Yaḥkumu Baynakum: The Judgment Reserved, and the Way Denied**

Then the verdict that closes every chapter of this dossier: *Allāhu yaḥkumu baynakum yawma al-qiyāmati* — "God shall judge between you on the Day of Resurrection": the standing deferral-formula (its register: 2:113 — "God shall judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they differed"; 3:55; 10:93; 16:124; 22:17; 32:25; 39:3; 39:46) — the Book's standing answer to unprovable inner treachery: since the hypocrite's real allegiance cannot be subpoenaed in this world, the case is assigned to the only court where hearts testify — the deferral itself a mercy (the community spared endless loyalty-inquisitions) and a threat (the deferred verdict inescapable). And then the standing charter-clause that jurists and theologians both quarry: *wa lan yajʿala Allāhu li-l-kāfirīna ʿalā al-muʾminīna sabīlan* — "and God shall never grant the disbelievers a way over the believers": *lan* — the never of perpetuity — with *sabīl* — a way — glossed in the standing readings as either a *proof/warrant* on the Day of Judgment (no argument by which the disbeliever can prevail over the believer before God) or — al-Qurṭubī's and Ibn Kathīr's community-reading — a promise concerning *this world's ultimate outcome*: the community of the believers never finally subjugated: the juristic tradition famously deriving from this clause the ruling that a disbeliever may not hold a Muslim slave — such ownership a "way over" a believer that the law forbids, a convert in a non-Muslim's ownership requiring sale or emancipation — Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī both registering the derivation as the clause's standing legal life. The verse thereby seals the fence-sitters' file: their vigilance-for-profit yields them neither camp's trust, and the Resurrection's docket will sort by allegiances the tongue never uttered but the feet always showed — *God shall judge between you* — while the ummah, promised that the disbelievers hold no ultimate way over it, is taught to watch its own fence-line: not every claim of *alam nakun maʿakum* — "were we not with you?" — survives the audit of the Watching One who saw who awaited whom.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:142

> **Verily the hypocrites would deceive God, but it is He who deceives them. And when they stand for the prayer, they stand lazily — to be seen of men — and they remember God only a little —**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Inna al-Munāfiqīna Yukhādiʿūna Allāh: The Fraud Attempted Upward — and the Counter-Fraud**

The dossier descends now from posture to essence: *inna al-munāfiqīna yukhādiʿūna Allāha wa huwa khādiʿuhum* — "verily the hypocrites would deceive God, but it is He who deceives them": *yukhādiʿūna* — Form III of kh-d-ʿ — the interactive fraud, deception attempted *upon* a counterpart (its standing register: 2:9 — "they would deceive God and those who believe — but they deceive none save themselves, though they perceive not") — the base absurdity stated in the attempt's very object: deception addressed to the All-Knowing, camouflage worn before the All-Seeing — the commentators (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī) explaining the *counter-deception* clause with precision: God's "deceiving" them is His *requital in kind* — He lets their outward Islam function fully in this world: their lives protected, their marriages valid, their inheritances honored, their persons unmolested — the hypocrite enjoying every legal fruit of a belief he does not hold, and thereby lulled into supposing the fraud succeeded: a mercy-like arrangement functioning as a snare. The standing eschatological picture completes the counter-stroke — al-Suddī's celebrated reading with 57:13's standing scene: "on the Day when the hypocrite men and hypocrite women will say to those who believe: wait for us, that we may borrow from your light — it shall be said: turn back and seek a light — and a wall shall be struck between them with a gate — its inner side mercy, its outer side punishment": the hypocrites given a light on the Bridge — brief, matching the brief public Islam of their lifetimes — then the light suddenly plucked away mid-crossing (2:17's standing parable registering: "God took away their light and left them in darkness, not seeing") — the outward-to-light correspondence exact: they had borrowed the believers' outward forms in the world; on the Bridge they borrow the believers' outward glow — and both loans are recalled at the same hour.

**Wa Idhā Qāmū ilā al-Ṣalāti Qāmū Kusālā: Laziness as the Liturgy of the False**

Then the anatomical detail — the tell by which the physicians of the heart recognize the disease: *wa idhā qāmū ilā al-ṣalāti qāmū kusālā yurāʾūna al-nāsa* — "and when they stand for the prayer, they stand lazily — to be seen of men": *kusālā* — the plural of *kaslān* — sluggish, heavy-limbed, reluctantly hauled upright — the body's manifesto where the tongue's is disbelieved: the prayer they perform they perform as conscripts, not as lovers. The commentators enumerate the standing marks (al-Ṭabarī's chains and al-Rāzī's glosses): prayer without *niyyah* of nearness — no intention of drawing close to God; or "reluctantly, without hope of reward or fear of punishment" — the interior of the act hollow, its shell retained for the audience named in the second clause: *yurāʾūna al-nāsa* — "to be seen of men" — *riyāʾ* — the standing vice-word (from r-ʾ-y — seeing): performance for spectators. The Book's standing riyāʾ-file assembles itself around them: 107:4–7 — "woe unto those who pray — those who are of their prayer heedless — those who make a show — and withhold small kindnesses"; 4:38 above — the spenders "who spend their wealth to be seen of men"; 2:264 — the charity voided by reminder and injury; 8:47 — "be not like those who went forth from their homes boastfully, to be seen of men and barring from God's way." Ibn Kathīr registers the tradition's standing severity here: the riyāʾ-poisoning of worship stands in the Prophet's celebrated taxonomy as the hidden shirk — its standing register in Aḥmad's Musnad and Ibn Mājah: "the thing I fear most for you is the lesser idolatry" — "and what is the lesser idolatry, O Messenger of God?" — "al-riyāʾ."

**Wa Lā Yadhkurūna Allāha illā Qalīlan: The Dhikr-Deficit as the Final Signature**

The verse's closing clause hands the community its standing diagnostic: *wa lā yadhkurūna Allāha illā qalīlan* — "and they remember God only a little": dhikr — the remembrance-invocation of God — standing in the devotional curriculum as the believer's standing atmosphere ("remember God with much remembrance" — 33:41; "the remembrance of God is greater" — 29:45; "those who remember God standing and sitting and on their sides" — 3:191) — and the hypocrite's deficit measurable in the commentators' standing inventory: (1) the invocation-formulas rarely or never upon their tongues except as camouflage; (2) — since prayer itself is named remembrance (20:14 — "keep up the prayer for My remembrance") — their "little remembrance" reads as: prayer in public only, never alone — al-Rāzī's and al-Zamakhsharī's standing observation that the hypocrite prays where eyes are and skips where eyes are not: the closet-prayer — which the tradition makes the standing hallmark of sincerity (the Prophet's standing description of the seven shaded on the Day when there is no shade but His: among them "a man who remembers God in solitude and his eyes overflow" — Bukhārī's standing register 6479; Muslim 1031) — entirely absent from their ledger; (3) even within the public prayer, the silent interior invocations unattended — the motions performed, the meanings skipped. The whole verse thus assembles the hypocrite's worship-profile: fraud at the fountainhead (deceiving God), lethargy in the limbs (standing lazily), theater in the intention (seen of men), famine in the heart (little remembrance) — four signatures one biography. And the tradition's standing pastoral counsel to every sincere reader is the fear these verses reliably induce: the Companion-generation wept over such passages, auditing their own prayers by the kusālā-rubric — ʿUmar's standing attitude before the hypocrisy-verses legendized in the story of his asking Ḥudhayfah (keeper of the Prophet's hypocrite-list) whether his own name stood anywhere upon it — the sūrah's anatomy of the false thus functioning in every age as the sincere community's mirror: not an invitation to accuse, but a summons to self-indictment — because the only person whose riyāʾ you can subpoena is your own.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:143

> **Wavering between this and that — belonging neither to these nor to those. And whomsoever God leads astray, thou shalt never find for him a way.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mudhabdhabīna Bayna Dhālika: The Physics of the Wavering Self**

The anatomy of the hypocrite's posture receives its definitive word — one of the rarest and most expressive in the Book: *mudhabdhabīna bayna dhālika lā ilā hāʾulāʾi wa lā ilā hāʾulāʾ* — "wavering between this and that — belonging neither to these nor to those": *mudhabdhab* — from the quadriliteral root dh-b-dh-b — a reduplicated formation whose very sound enacts its meaning: the dithering, seesawing back-and-forth of something that cannot settle — a word-form the linguists note is nearly onomatopoeic, the doubled syllable swinging like the pendulum it describes (its standing uniqueness in the Book: the root appears nowhere else in the Qur'ān — reserved as the one-word portrait of the hypocrite's inner weather). *Bayna dhālika* — "between this and that" — the occupant of the middle claimed by neither side: *lā ilā hāʾulāʾi* — not toward these (the believers), *wa lā ilā hāʾulāʾ* — nor toward those (the disbelievers). Al-Zamakhsharī's standing gloss: they waver between faith and unbelief under the sway of Satan and their own passions — belonging fully to no covenant, and therefore owned fully by no community: the standing existential penalty of the hedged life — to be the trusted native of no country. The commentators mark the diagnostic precision: the verse does not call them disbelievers (the sharīʿah must continue treating them by their profession) nor believers (reality refuses the title) — but names them by their *motion*: dhabdhabah — the standing theological category for those whose religion is an instrument panel of readings rather than a settled direction. Al-Rāzī, surveying the surah-dossier of these passages, registered the standing judgment that flows from the whole anatomy: hypocrisy is a state more evil than bare disbelief — the liar compounding unbelief with fraud, espionage, and belittling — the moral instinct the tradition knows from every community: the open adversary may yet be honored; the smiling saboteur can only be mourned — and the Book itself will ratify the comparative verdict at v. 145: the *lowest* depth for the waverers.

**Wa Man Yuḍlili Allāhu: The Leading-Astray of God and Its Schools**

Then the phrase that anchors one of the standing debates of Muslim theology: *wa man yuḍlili Allāhu fa-lan tajida lahu sabīlan* — "and whomsoever God leads astray, thou shalt never find for him a way": iḍlāl — leading astray — attributed to God Himself, in a verse-cluster the commentators treat with admitted gravity (its standing register: 4:88 above in this very dossier — "would you guide him whom God has led astray?"; 7:186 — "whomsoever God leads astray, no guide has he — and He leaves them in their insolence, wandering blind"; 13:33 — "whomsoever God leads astray has no guide"; 39:23; 39:36; 40:33 — "whomsoever God leads astray has no guide"; 42:46 — "whomsoever God leads astray has no way"; 18:17 — "whomsoever God guides is the guided — and whomsoever He leads astray, thou shalt never find for him a guiding protector"; 2:7's standing seal-passage: "God has sealed their hearts"); and the standing school-readings: the Muʿtazilite position — iḍlāl as God's *withdrawal of favor* (luṭf) and active guidance, a withholding imposed *as punishment* upon prior disobedience: God abandons the obstinate to the waywardness they chose — astray-labels marking the consequence, not the cause; the Ashʿarite position — affirming this punitive withholding while also upholding God's sovereign freedom to mislead whom He wills, guidance and misguidance alike lying within divine creation (16:93's standing statement — "God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills" — alongside 14:4 — "He leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills — and He is the Mighty, the Wise"); and the eschatological gloss — some readings locating the "leading astray" of the confirmed hard-hearted in the Hereafter itself (17:72’s standing: "whosoever was blind in this life shall be blind in the Hereafter and further astray from the way"). Ibn Taymiyyah's standing reconciliation-order across the Book's register: the Book never says God misleads the *seeker* — every "leading-astray" verse lands upon one who first sold his way (2:16 — "those are the ones who purchased error at the price of guidance — so their commerce profited not"); divine iḍlāl is the sealing of a human purchase, never the prevention of a human request — the standing rule the commentators distill: man chooses the direction; God authors the consequence.

**Fa-Lan Tajida Lahu Sabīlan: The Prophet's Helplessness as the Verdict's Seal**

The closing clause turns to the Prophet himself — *fa-lan tajida lahu sabīlan* — "thou shalt never find for him a way": *lan* — never — and the addressee the most powerful intercessor of the community: if even the Messenger cannot unseal the sealed heart — cannot locate a road back for the fixed waverer — then the verdict is not social (excommunication by men) but providential (a closure enacted above the sky of every advocate). Its standing Book-kin gathers the theme: 28:56 — "thou guidest not whom thou lovest — but God guides whom He wills"; 4:88 above — "would you guide whom God leads astray?"; 7:186; 13:33's register. The pastoral point the commentators draw for the community: the wavering-state is not static; the dhabdhabah-pendulum, given time, slows toward the heavier side — and the side it settles upon is the side the soul keeps feeding. Hence the dossier's exact placement of hope: vv. 145–146 below will announce the lowest depth — and immediately legislate the exception: "save those who repent and make amends and hold fast to God and devote their religion entirely to God" — the pendulum, while the heart still beats, retains the freedom to swing *toward* the side it has so far only visited. The dhabdhabah-portrait thereby closes its own file with the standing admonition the spiritual commentators inscribe beneath it: lukewarmness is not innocence; it is a direction — and every direction, continued, arrives.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:144

> **O you who believe! Do not take the disbelievers as protectors instead of the believers. Do you wish to give God a clear warrant against you?**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Repetition That Is Not Mere Repetition: v. 144 After v. 139**

The Book now formally reissues, in direct vocative, the prohibition it stated descriptively five verses earlier: *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū lā tattakhidhū al-kāfirīna awliyāʾa min dūni al-muʾminīn* — "O you who believe! Do not take the disbelievers as protectors instead of the believers": v. 139 having exposed the *hypocrites* for this very act in third-person diagnosis, v. 144 turns to *the believers* in second-person command — the standing Qur'ānic method of transmuting others' pathology into the community's immunization: you have seen what the waverers do; now you — the addressed, the professionally believing — are bound by name never to do it. The commentators mark the rhetorical architecture (al-Qurṭubī noting the reinforcement-purpose of the repetition): between the two statements stand vv. 140–143 — the sitting-with-mockers file, the watching-for-outcomes file, the deceiving-God file, the wavering-pendulum file — so that when the prohibition returns in v. 144, it returns *loaded*: no longer an abstract rule of alliance but the seal of a completed anatomy. The believer has been shown the whole career of the false heart: it hedges, it sits, it watches, it prays lazily, it oscillates — and at each station the enabling act is the same — taking its ultimate reliance outside the household of faith. Hence the command's return, now as standing law: **lā tattakhidhū** — take not.

**Min Dūni al-Muʾminīn: The "Instead-of" Clause as the Line Itself**

The boundary-phrase deserves its renewed dwelling — *min dūni al-muʾminīn* — "instead of the believers": the sin located not in contact but in *substitution* — the disbelieving party admitted into the precise slot the Book reserves for God (5:55: "your Protector is but God and His Messenger and those who believe") and for the fraternity it welds (9:71: "the believing men and the believing women are protectors one of another"). The standing legal ethic — reaffirmed at every commentary-generation — keeps the verse from brutal application: dealings, treaties, neighborliness, commerce, and kindness stand lawful with all peaceful people (60:8's standing injunction balancing the prohibition-file); what stands forbidden is the walāyah-transfer — the heart's own embassy moved to a foreign capital: protection sought there first, secrets deposited there first, futures wagered there first. The tradition's standing counsel-name for this posture: "whoever resembles a people is one of them" (the standing register in Abū Dāwūd 4031's hadith-collection) — resemblance not of dress but of ultimate reliance — the believer's signature being precisely *where* he deposits his back-up plan (4:132's standing fiduciary clause hovering above the entire dossier: "God suffices as a Guardian").

**A-Turīdūna an Tajʿalū Li-llāhi ʿAlaykum Sulṭānan Mubīnan: Handing God the Brief Against Oneself**

Then the verse's formidable second half — its interrogative thunderclap: *a-turīdūna an tajʿalū li-llāhi ʿalaykum sulṭānan mubīnan* — "do you wish to give God a clear warrant against you?": *sulṭān* — from s-l-ṭ — authority, warrant, power-of-proof: the word the Book uses for a *demonstrated authorization* — an open-and-shut evidentiary warrant (its standing register: 4:91 above — "against them We have given you a clear warrant"; 6:81; 14:10 — "have you brought us a clear warrant?"; 27:21; 37:156; 52:38); and *mubīn* — manifest, self-evidencing — the sulṭān that needs no elaboration because the record itself speaks. The rhetorical shape of the phrase the commentators (al-Rāzī dwelling on the horror of its logic) unfold: ordinarily, the accused before God might plead complicated circumstances, mixed motives, partial innocence — the standing hope of every defendant; but the believer who *knowingly, covenantedly* transfers his reliance to the enemies of his faith, while bearing the name of believer, has done something juridically unique — he has *prepared and handed over the prosecution's complete brief*: his conduct itself becomes God's sulṭān mubīn against him — a warrant so clear no cross-examination is needed. The image is courtroom-reversed: the defendant furnishing the court its decisive evidence — and the question *a-turīdūna* — "do you *wish* this?" — exposing the act's voluntariness: nobody sleepwalks into this warrant; it is signed. The standing spiritual application generalizes its discipline: every deliberate sin performed open-eyed after knowledge is, in miniature, the furnishing of a sulṭān — the tradition's standing counsels of concealment and repentance (v. 148 below; the Prophet's standing word in Muslim's register 2990: "all my community shall be pardoned except those who sin openly") arranged precisely to keep the believer from ever converting his falls into *warrants* — which is why the dossier's next verse, announcing the lowest depth, hurries to add its exception-clause: the door of repentance the only legal instrument that voids a sulṭān already issued.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:145

> **Verily the hypocrites shall be in the lowest depth of the Fire, and thou shalt never find for them a helper —**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Inna al-Munāfiqīna fī al-Darki al-Asfali min al-Nār: The Basement of the Basement**

The dossier now delivers its sentence of location — among the most fearful half-dozen words in the entire Book: *inna al-munāfiqīna fī al-darki al-asfali min al-nār* — "verily the hypocrites shall be in the lowest depth of the Fire": *dark* — a depth, a level-bottom — a word whose morphology (its standing lexical note: from d-r-k — to reach the bottom, to overtake) already carries descent; and *al-asfal* — the superlative of *sāfil* — low — *the lowest* — grammar announcing that the Fire itself is terraced, and that beneath its levels for the merely disbelieving yawns another level — the *sub-basement* reserved for the false. The commentators from al-Ṭabarī forward read the comparative precisely: the hypocrites outrank in punishment those whose creed they privately shared — the open idolater of Mecca graded *above* the secret traitor of Madīnah — and the standing reasons gathered across the literature (al-Bayḍāwī, al-Rāzī, al-Zamakhsharī): (1) hypocrisy compounds unbelief with *lying* — the whole apparatus of fabricated testimony ("we bear witness that thou art indeed the Messenger of God — and God knows that thou art His Messenger — and God bears witness that the hypocrites are liars" — 63:1); (2) it adds *contempt* — belittling the religion it publicly wears; (3) it functions as *espionage* — the hypocrite's position inside the community converting his unbelief into active sabotage: spying, demoralizing, secrets traded to the enemy (v. 141's invoice-file above) — the internal enemy more destructive than ten external ones; and (4) — the sealing reason — it *mocks the remedial arrangement itself*: the door of repentance exists exactly where the hypocrite pretends to stand — inside the community, inside the prayer-line — so his refusal of it is more deliberate than any outsider's distance. Al-Rāzī's standing judgment summarizes the dossier's cumulative force: hypocrisy is a state more evil than disbelief.

**The Terraced Fire and the Standing Fear of the Companions**

The tradition's reception of this verse is itself part of its exegesis — for the verse's most documented effect was not upon the hypocrites but upon the *sincere*: Ibn Abī Mulaykah's standing report (its standing register in the tafsīr-collections and the Ṣaḥīḥ-tradition of al-Bukhārī's Book of Tafsīr): "I met thirty of the Companions of the Prophet — every one of them feared hypocrisy for himself — none of them said he had the faith of Gabriel and Michael." Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's standing formulation orders the psychology: "no one fears it but a believer, and no one feels secure from it but a hypocrite" — the mark of the disease being precisely the confidence that one does not have it. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's standing scene with Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān — the Prophet's confidant to whom the secret names of the hypocrites had been entrusted — remains the standing icon: the Caliph of Islam, at whose approach Satan was said to flee (Bukhārī's standing register 3683: "whenever you take a path, Satan takes a path other than yours"), asking privately: *am I, by God, among them?* — and Ḥudhayfah's "no" treasured by the tradition as reassurance — yet the asking itself installed as the standing spiritual discipline of the ummah: only those who audit their worship by the kusālā-rubric of v. 142 — lazy standing, little remembrance — keep the basement-door locked against themselves.

**Wa Lan Tajida Lahum Naṣīran: The Court Without Appeal or Counsel**

The verdict doubles itself with its standing annihilation-clause: *wa lan tajida lahum naṣīran* — "and thou shalt never find for them a helper": *lan* — the perpetual never — addressed again to the Prophet, the community's supreme advocate: the verse of v. 143's structure repeated from abyss-side: no way (v. 143) and now no helper (v. 145) — the hypocrite's file closing with the two absences of eschatological bankruptcy: no road and no intercessor. Its standing Book-register gathers the form: 4:52 above — "those are the ones whom God has cursed — and whomsoever God curses, thou shalt find no helper for him"; 3:56 — "as for those who disbelieve, I shall punish them with a terrible punishment in this world and the Hereafter — and they shall have no helpers"; 2:86, 2:270, 3:192, 9:74's own 33:17; the several standing the register of *lā naṣīr* as the Book's standing signature of total estrangement (3:22; 3:126; 5:72; 9:113; 29:22). And the commentators note the justice of the symmetries: the hypocrites had spent their careers amassing helpers — the clans of v. 139, the Meccan connections of v. 141 — as substitutes for the one Helper; the lowest depth is precisely the territory where substitute-helpers are administratively impossible: every alliance of the fence-sitters dissolving at the horizon where it was purchased to operate.

**The Exception Coming: Verse 146's Door in the Wall**

Yet the Book, which has now descended lower than any other verse of the Qur'ān reaches — *the lowest depth* — reserves for the very next verse its standing reversal: "save those who repent and make amends, and hold fast to God, and devote their religion entirely to God — those are with the believers, and God shall grant the believers a great reward." The commentators insist the juxtaposition is the dossier's whole pedagogy: the severity of v. 145 is not the abolition of hope but its *pricing* — the deep cell announced so that the exit-terms, when they arrive, shine with their true value: the same Book that assigns the hypocrite the absolute bottom assigns the repentant hypocrite — one verse later — *maʿa al-muʾminīn* — "with the believers" — the association he never truly occupied in life restored to him in the Hereafter through the medicine of v. 137's own diagnosis: while breath remains, the pendulum of v. 143's dhabdhabah can still be swung, not merely watched. The lowest depth then functions in the economy of Mercy as what the standing tradition calls a *burden of warning* — its standing register in the Prophet's counsels: the Fire described in detail not to extinguish hope but to make the exit-legible — 4:145 the pit, 4:146 the ladder, both verses one rope.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:146

> **Save those who repent, and make amends, and hold fast to God, and make their religion sincere for God — those are with the believers — and God shall grant the believers a great reward.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Illā Alladhīna Tābū: The Exception That Reopens the Sky**

Directly beneath the deepest floor of the Fire, the Book opens a door: *illā alladhīna tābū* — "save those who repent": the exception-particle (*illā*) performing here one of its grandest rescues in the Qur'ān — reaching down into *al-dark al-asfal* (v. 145) and legislating an exit from the Book's own absolute bottom. The commentators (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr) set the verse in the dossier's standing pattern of sealed-state versus open-state: v. 137's "God was not one to forgive them" held for those who *die* in increase-of-disbelief; here stands the standing counter-promise for those who *return* in life — the Qur'ān's grammar of damnation always including this parenthesis, its sentences of doom written with an exception-hinge built into the lintel (39:53's standing summit: "say: O My servants who have transgressed against their souls — despair not of God's mercy — verily God forgives all sins — verily He is the Forgiving, the Merciful"). Not even the *munāfiq* — the Qur'ān's most condemned figure, out-punished beneath the pagan — is marooned beyond repair: the repentance-door swings even at the basement level — and its terms are the verse's next three clauses.

**Wa Aṣlaḥū: Amendment — the Outward Half of the Cure**

The first condition after return: *wa aṣlaḥū* — "and make amends": *iṣlāḥ* — the setting-right (from ṣ-l-ḥ) — the standing pairing with repentance across the Book (2:160; 5:39; 6:54; 16:119; 25:70-71; 28:67; 42:25 — "He it is who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons evils") — amendment as verification: the tongue's return validated by the hand's repair — the broken congregation-practices rejoined, the leaked confidences stanched, the spoils-claims renounced. Yet the commentators note the ordering's wisdom for *this* case: for the hypocrite, visible amendment alone is the *easy* half — his whole career had been outward appearance excellently managed — so the Book immediately legislates deeper.

**Wa Iʿtaṣamū bi-llāh: Holding Fast — the Refuge-Clause**

The second condition: *wa iʿtaṣamū bi-llāh* — "and hold fast to God": *iʿtiṣām* — from ʿ-ṣ-m — protection, inviolability: to grip God as one's safeguard — the standing covenant-vocabulary (3:101 — "whoever holds fast to God has been guided to a straight path"; 3:103's standing rope-command — "hold fast all together to the rope of God and divide not"; 22:78 — "hold fast to God — He is your Protector — an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper") — the commentators glossing the "rope" and the holding-fast variously as the Qur'ān, the covenant, the dīn itself. For the former hypocrite the clause has its exact bite: his original disease was *reliance-migration* (v. 139 — taking the disbelievers as protectors); the cure is not merely to stop doing so but to *positively* transfer the grip — iʿtiṣām not as the leaving of false anchors but as the seizing of the true one.

**Wa Akhlaṣū Dīnahum Li-llāh: Sincerity — the Heart's Own Repentance**

Then the condition beneath all conditions: *wa akhlaṣū dīnahum li-llāh* — "and make their religion sincere for God": *ikhlāṣ* — from kh-l-ṣ — to render pure, unmixed (its standing register: 7:32; 39:2-3 — "verily We sent down the Book upon thee in truth — so worship God, making religion sincere for Him — lo, to God belongs pure religion"; 40:14; 98:5 — "they were commanded only to worship God, making religion sincere for Him, as men of pure faith"; 112:1-4's standing sūrah named after it). Al-Ṭabrisī's standing observation decodes why this clause — and not the others — forms the actual *term* of the hypocrite's cure: **hypocrisy is a sin of the heart, so repentance from it must be a repentance *of* the heart** — an outward renovation leaving the inward directorate untouched is merely improved hypocrisy: the riyāʾ-machine (v. 142's "to be seen of men") repainted. Ikhlāṣ alone reaches the basement — religion rededicated to its one Audience, the deeds re-motored from spectators to the Face of God (2:272 — "you give only seeking the Face of God"; 13:22; 92:20 — "seeking only the Face of his Lord Most High"). The commentators name the interiority of this station precisely: the former hypocrite's exit-visa is not a new schedule but a new *address* — every act reposted from the gallery to God.

**Ulāʾika Maʿa al-Muʾminīn: With the Believers — the Restoration-Formula**

Then the standing restoration-verdict that repays all four conditions in one phrase: *ulāʾika maʿa al-muʾminīn* — "those are with the believers": *maʿa* — "with" — the preposition of full association: the one who never truly sat in the believers' majlis though his body attended it (v. 140's sitting-file) now recorded *with them* by divine decree — the commentators noting the phrase's two registers: legal-communal *now* (their repentance reinstates them fully — no probationary half-membership in the law) and eschatological *then* (gathered with the believers at the Resurrection instead of to the hypocrite-basement). And the verse closes by widening its own aperture: *wa sawfa yuʾti Allāhu al-muʾminīna ajran ʿaẓīman* — "and God shall grant the believers a great reward": the *great reward* promised not to the repenters alone but to *the believers* collectively — al-Rāzī's standing reading of the syntax: the repentant hypocrites, having been just named "with the believers," are folded within this promise's pronoun — the sentence's movement mirroring the community's own: the returned son counted in the family-inheritance without remainder. The dossier of vv. 137–146 thereby completes its arc: oscillation (137), ironic announcement (138), false protectors (139), mocking majlis (140), watchful waiting (141), deceptive prayer (142), pendulum-wavering (143), the warrant against oneself (144), the lowest depth (145) — and then, at the end of the Book's darkest corridor: tābū, aṣlaḥū, iʿtaṣamū, akhlaṣū — a four-step staircase built straight up from the basement floor to *with the believers* and *a great reward* — the sūrah of justice proving, in its hypocrisy-chapter, that its God keeps the sentence of doom and the deed of pardon in adjacent verses, lest the condemned despair or the comfortable presume.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:147

> **What would God do with your punishment, if you give thanks and believe? And God is ever Thankful, Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Mā Yafʿalu Allāhu bi-ʿAdhābikum: Punishment as Divine Non-Interest**

The dossier of doom ends in a question of pure mercy — one of the Book's most tender confrontations of human math with divine purpose: *mā yafʿalu Allāhu bi-ʿadhābikum in shakartum wa āmantum* — "what would God do with your punishment, if you give thanks and believe?": the question-form here not interrogative but *expulsive* — a standing rhetorical figure of removal: punishment imagined as a commodity God has no *use* for — the commentators (al-Ṭabarī; al-Rāzī records the standing formulation: God has no need of punishing you; your punishment gives Him nothing; your pleasure and gratitude give you everything) — the doctrine sealed by the standing Name-pair of v. 131's file (*ghanī ḥamīd* — Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy): the Self-Sufficient gains nothing from torturing His creatures, and therefore punishment enters the divine economy only as justice's response to refusal — never as divine appetite. Its standing Book-kin gathers the same expulsive-shape: its register of divine disinterest in the sinner's ruin: 39:7 — "if you disbelieve — lo, God is free of need of you — though He is not pleased with disbelief for His servants — but if you give thanks, He is pleased with it for you" — the near-twin of our verse's logic (His pleasure registered upon gratitude, His displeasure upon refusal — need never entering the account); 14:7’s standing covenant ("if you give thanks I shall surely increase you"); 4:131-132 above ("unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens..."); and the standing qudsī-complement in Muslim's register 2577 (the long hadith of divine absolutes: "righteousness does not increase My kingdom, nor wickedness decrease it"). The question thus legislates a theology of divine freedom: punishment is never God's *project*; it is only ever His *correspondence* to human refusal — correspondence that evaporates the moment its addressee corrects his own address.

**In Shakartum wa Āmantum: Gratitude and Belief as the Standing Antidote-Pair**

The condition is two-stemmed and beautiful in its ordering: *in shakartum wa āmantum* — "if you give thanks and believe": *shakara* — to give thanks — placed *before* īmān — a syntactic surprise the commentators savor (al-Zamakhsharī's standing note exploring the inversion): gratitude as the very *door* of belief — the thankful heart already bowing toward its Benefactor before its creed completes; and in immediate context the precise cure-codeword for the dossier's patients: the hypocrite's standing disease had been riyāʾ (v. 142 — performance for observers) — the religion of audience-seeking — and *shukr* is its exact pharmacological opposite: religion of Benefactor-facing — thanks directed not at the witnesses but at the Source. The tradition's standing gratitude-file assembles beside the verse: 14:7 — "your Lord proclaimed: if you give thanks, I shall surely increase you; but if you disbelieve — verily My punishment is severe"; 31:12 — Luqmān's standing "whoever gives thanks gives thanks for his own soul"; 34:13 — "work, O house of David, in thanks — and few of My servants are the thankful"; 39:7 above; 54:35; and the Prophet's standing embodiment — ʿĀʾishah's celebrated night-report (Bukhārī's standing register 4836; Muslim 2820): he prayed until his feet split — "shall I not be a thankful servant?" — gratitude named not as the minimum of religion but as its summit-occupation.

**Wa Kāna Allāhu Shākiran ʿAlīman: The Thankful God — the Semantic Miracle of the Pair**

Then the verse performs its standing linguistic wonder — the Name the commentators treat as among the Book's most astonishing revelations of the divine character: *wa kāna Allāhu shākiran ʿalīman* — "and God is ever Thankful, Knowing": *shākir* — the Thankful One — God named by the very predicate the verse asks of His creatures: *shakartum* — *you* thank — answered by *shākir* — *He* thanks — the semantic correspondence the commentators (the standing note from the earliest language-commentaries forward) call the verse's built-in music: the same root sounded from both parties within a few words — human gratitude echoing upward, divine Gratitude answering downward — an audible reconciliation after the dossier's nine verses of descending darkness. The commentators unfold *al-Shākir* with its standing doctrine: God's "thanks" are His *acceptance and recompense* — His counting little obedience as much, His praising the servant for what He Himself granted ("He thanks them for what they do — and increases them of His bounty" — 35:30; its standing register: 2:158 — "whoever does good of his own accord — verily God is Thankful, Knowing"; 9:121 — "nor do they spend any outlay... but it is recorded to them, that God may repay them the best of what they did"; 64:17 — "if you lend God a goodly loan — He shall double it for you and forgive you — and God is Thankful, Forbearing"; 42:23). And *ʿalīm* — Knowing — closing the audit: thankfulness is known even when unwitnessed (its standing complement: gratitude-hidden recorded as surely as gratitude-proclaimed — the riyāʾ-poisoned dossier thereby answered in full: the only Spectator who matters keeps the only record that counts). The hypocrisy-dossier (vv. 137–147) thus ends not in the basement of v. 145 but in this sweet expulsion-question — *what would God do with your punishment?* — the divine answer being: nothing at all, if only gratitude and belief make punishment obsolete — and the Name of the Thankful One standing over the closed file as its seal: the God who thanks the thankful, and knows.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:148

> **God loves not the open speaking of evil — save on behalf of one who has been wronged. And God is ever Hearing, Knowing.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Lā Yuḥibbu Allāhu al-Jahra bi-al-Sūʾi min al-Qawl: Speech as Moral Dignity's Frontier**

Immediately after the dossier's mercy-floodgate, the Book legislates the ethics of the tongue: *lā yuḥibbu Allāhu al-jahra bi-al-sūʾi min al-qawl illā man ẓulim* — "God loves not the open speaking of evil — save on behalf of one who has been wronged": *jahr* — from j-h-r — audible publicness (its standing register: 6:3 — "He knows the secret and the open"; 13:10 — "he who whispers speech and he who proclaims it"; 21:110 — "He knows what is proclaimed of speech and what you conceal"; 87:7) — the sin located not in the thought but in its *broadcast*: the Book granting that resentment, anger, even condemnation may arise in the chest, but forbidding the mouth's conversion of them into public currency. The commentators register the verse's twin-context: (1) its local occasion in the dossier — the repentance of the former hypocrites (v. 146): once returned, their past falseness is no longer open-season for public mention — according to al-Rāzī's contextual reading: the repentant are not to be vilified by reminders of their former hypocrisy — the community forbidden from keeping old files open on souls God has newly sealed into the believing register — the standing ethic that public memory must obey divine amnesty; (2) its universal scope — the standing principle of Islamic ethics that faults — others' and even one's own — are to be *concealed*, not merchandised: the tradition's standing hadith-cluster (Muslim's register 2990: "all my ummah shall be pardoned except those who sin openly — and among open sinning is that a man does a deed by night, God covers him, and in the morning he says: O so-and-so — last night I did such-and-such — his Lord having veiled him through the night, and by morning he removes God's own veil from himself") — the veil of God over the night-sinner being treated as a divine courtesy the dawn-confessor criminally declines: public evil-speech unwinding God's own covering. Exceptions the commentators carefully hold: the witness summoned in justice (v. 135's standing command — witnesses for God even against the self), the warning against genuine harm (the hadith-sciences' own public impeachment of unreliable transmitters), and the ruling-clause the verse itself immediately legislates.

**Illā Man Ẓulim: The Wronged One's Licensed Complaint**

The exception stands in a single compressed relative clause — *illā man ẓulim* — "save one who has been wronged": the verb passive — *he was wronged* — and the license belongs to the wronged as such: the victim may speak the evil *against* the wrongdoer — publicly accusing, complaining, redress-seeking — this publicness reclassified from slander to claim-of-right. Al-Ṭabarī chains the standing glosses: the wronged may invoke against the oppressor (the duʿāʾ of the maẓlūm being the tradition's most feared projectile — Bukhārī's standing register 2448: "fear the supplication of the wronged — for between it and God there is no veil"), may report him to authority, may publicize his conduct to obtain justice or protection — 42:41 standing as the Book's own parallel license: "whoever defends himself after being wronged — upon those there is no way." The jurists built the verse's standing legal compartments: complaint-filing, the petitioner's description of injuries, and the standing boundary that the license is measured by its purpose — redress, not relish: the wronged one who converts his license into a banquet of defamation overshoots the exceptional warrant (al-Qurṭubī's standing boundary-notes gathering the early cautions).

**The Abū Bakr Scene: The Angel, Satan, and the Gathering**

Al-Rāzī transmits the occasion-report that fixes the verse in lived memory: a man abused Abū Bakr in the Prophet's presence; Abū Bakr sat silent — once, twice — then began to answer; and the Prophet rose to leave. Abū Bakr followed him out asking: you sat while I was abused, yet rose when I and the Prophet's standing reply (its standing register in Abū Dāwūd 4896 and Aḥmad's Musnad): "an angel was answering on your behalf — but when you began to answer him back, Satan entered — and I do not sit in a gathering where Satan enters" — and the verse, the report concludes, descended: the subtlest of calibrations — the *silent* wronged one defended by heaven itself (the angel rebutting in his stead), the *answering* wronged one descending from angelic custody into the quarrel's own arena — permission undenied (the exception-clause granted) yet the higher path marked: concealment-with-dignity outranking licensed retaliation. Its standing Book-kin gathers the same gradation: 42:40-43 — "the recompense of an evil is an evil like it — but whoever pardons and makes amends — his wage falls upon God... and whoever is patient and forgives — verily that is of the firmness-of-purpose of affairs"; 23:96 — "repel evil with that which is better"; 13:22; 28:54 — "they shall be given their reward twice over for that they were patient, and they repel evil with good"; 41:34 — "repel with that which is better — and lo, the one between whom and you is enmity becomes as a bosom-friend" — the ethic of *supersession* standing as the sūrah's own moral sky above the license's floor.

**Wa Kāna Allāhu Samīʿan ʿAlīman: The Two Names That Settle Every Silence**

The verse seals with the two perceiver-Names — *wa kāna Allāhu samīʿan ʿalīman* — "and God is ever Hearing, Knowing": the Samīʿ as the wronged one's standing solicitor: whatever he does not broadcast, the Hearing One has already heard — silence therefore never a forfeiture of evidence; the broadcast withheld is not data lost but data *deposited* — and the ʿAlīm as the abuser's standing dossier: the open speaker of evil building a record in a court he forgets is sitting. The two Names thereby adjudicate both the command and the exception: you may conceal (He hears anyway), and you may complain (He knows it is true) — the ethics of the tongue in the sūrah of justice resting finally, like all its ethics, upon the standing doctrine that freedom of concealment is freedom's loan against an audit already complete (6:3; 21:110; 87:7's standing confirmations: concealed and proclaimed alike known). The hypocrisy-dossier of vv. 137–148 thereby closes where it always intended to: after the anatomy of those who *performed* religion before men, the Book legislates the community's own speech: no merchandising of faults, no archival cruelty toward the repentant, no banquet of scandal — save the cry of the wronged, which heaven itself hears before it reaches a human ear — the sūrah of the Watcher (4:1) proving to the end that its deepest laws are about who is doing the listening: God, always God — Samīʿan ʿAlīman.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:149

> **If you do good openly or conceal it, or pardon an evil — God is ever Pardoning, Powerful.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**In Tubdū Khayran aw Tukhfūhu: Goodness Despotic Over Its Own Broadcast**

The speech-ethic of v. 148 — which forbade the open speaking of *evil* — now receives its counterpart governing the open display of *good*: *in tubdū khayran aw tukhfūhu* — "if you do good openly or conceal it": the verse's plain architecture (the standing note of the commentators from al-Zamakhsharī's register forward): where evil-speech is *licensed only by exception* (the wronged one's complaint), good-action is *free in both modes* — display and concealment equally lawful, the Book declining to criminalize the open good — for the open charity builds the social fabric it depicts (the standing hadith-balance: "secret charity extinguishes the Lord's anger" — al-Ṭabarānī's standing register — set beside the public charity that commands the standing blessing of 2:271: "if you make the alms public — excellent — and if you hide them and give them to the poor — that is better for you — and it shall expiate for you some of your sins" — concealment named *better*, display never named *sin*) — the hypocrisy-dossier above having made the true line unmistakable: the question is never the act's visibility but its *address* (v. 142's riyāʾ-file visibly in the background: laziness in solitude, display for the gallery — there the visibility was the offense because the address was the audience; here, where God is the address, visibility varies freely).

**Aw Taʿfū ʿan Sūʾin: Pardon as the Verse's Own Pinnacle**

Then the verse's own moral peak — and its connection to the exception-clause of the preceding verse is the commentators' standing insight: v. 148 had licensed the wronged to complain publicly; v. 149 immediately builds the higher road: *aw taʿfū ʿan sūʾ* — "or pardon an evil": *taʿfū* — from ʿ-f-w — to efface, to leave behind, to pardon so that the trace itself dissolves (the root's own image in the standing lexical notes: the wind effacing the footprints) — the pardon that *erases* rather than merely suspends. Al-Zamakhsharī's standing framing: having permitted the redress-seeker's outcry, the Book now points to the nobler option — ʿafw as the emulated divine attribute — the standing Book-file of pardon exalted: 5:13 — "pardon and overlook — do you not love that God should forgive you?" (its twin 24:22 — to the well-dowered believers regarding their poor kinsfolk — "let them pardon and overlook — do you not love that God should forgive you?" — the standing formula binding human pardon to hope of divine); 42:40 — "whoever pardons and makes amends — his wage falls upon God"; 42:43 — "whoever is patient and forgives — verily that is of the firmness of purpose"; 3:134 — "the restrainers of anger and the pardoners of men — and God loves the good-doers"; 7:199 — "take to pardon, and enjoin what is right, and turn from the ignorant"; 15:85; 45:14 — "tell those who believe to forgive those who hope not for the days of God"; 2:237; 64:14. The wronged soul of v. 148 thereby faces the sūrah's standing staircase of options: conceal (commended), complain (licensed), pardon (exalted) — the last rung introducing the two Names that explain why it is the highest.

**Fa-Inna Allāha Kāna ʿAfūwwan Qadīran: Pardon From Power, Not From Weakness**

The seal joins two Names that commentators (al-Qurṭubī leading the standing note) treat as a deliberate jurisprudence of pardon: *fa-inna Allāha kāna ʿafūwwan qadīran* — "God is ever Pardoning, Powerful": *ʿafūw* — the standing intensive of pardon — He whose erasure of sins is overwhelming, habitual, unceasing (its standing register: 4:43 above — "God is ever Pardoning, Forgiving"; 4:99 — "God is ever Pardoning, Forgiving"; 22:60; 58:2 — "God is ever Pardoning, Forgiving"; the Prophet's standing supplication-formula of the Ramadan nights — ʿĀʾishah's celebrated question: if I know the Night of Decree, what shall I "say: O God, Thou art Pardoning and lovest pardon — so pardon me" — Tirmidhī's standing register 3513); and *qadīr* — the All-Powerful — and the pairing's exact pedagogic point (al-Qurṭubī's standing note now a standing talisman of the whole ethic): God pardons *from power* — vengeance perfectly within His grasp, pardon perfectly within His choice — and this is the model pardon the verse teaches: **to forgo retaliation when retaliation is available** — pardon from a position of strength approximating the divine attribute; pardon from weakness, by contrast, being merely helplessness wearing a halo. The tradition's standing virtue-file confirms the measurement: the Prophet's celebrated testimony about the man who adds to his affairs nothing but increase — Muslim's standing register 2588: "charity does not decrease wealth; and God does not increase the servant who pardons except in might (ʿizzan); and no one humbles himself for God's sake but that God raises him" — the pardoners' ʿizzah — remember v. 139's hypocrites seeking might at false addresses — arriving by precisely the opposite road: not alliance-acquisition but injury-effacement. The hypocrisy-dossier's two closing verses (148–149) thereby make a single counsel: control your tongue about others' evil, open your hand in goodness, and where you have been wronged — climb: silence, complaint if needed, pardon if able — and the Names stand over the staircase as its guarantors: the Hearing-Knowing audit of v. 148, and here the Pardoning-Powerful — the God whose own pardon from unlimited power writes the standing template for every wronged believer standing over an offense with a writ already licensed and a hand that can rise above it.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:150

> **Verily those who disbelieve in God and His messengers, and wish to make a distinction between God and His messengers, and say: "We believe in some and disbelieve in some" — and wish to take a way between —**

**Expanded Commentary**

**The Turn From Hypocrites to Selective Believers: The Dossier Changes Hands**

The sūrah's long hypocrisy-file (vv. 137–149) now closes, and the Book opens the final movement of the chapter — the address to the People of the Book that will run to the sūrah's end: *inna alladhīna yakfurūna bi-llāhi wa rusulih* — "verily those who disbelieve in God and His messengers": the commentators mark the structural shift (the standing note that the rest of the sūrah addresses the scriptural communities): the internal fifth column having been anatomized, the Book turns to the neighboring communities whose problem is not secret unbelief but *selective* belief — a taxonomy of partial assent. The verse's architecture compiles the four motions of this partiality in cumulative succession: (1) disbelieving in God and His messengers — the baseline charge; (2) *wa yurīdūna an yufarriqū bayna Allāhi wa rusulih* — "and wish to make a distinction between God and His messengers" — the severing of the Sender from the sent; (3) *wa yaqūlūna nuʾminu bi-baʿḍin wa nakfuru bi-baʿḍ* — "and say: we believe in some and disbelieve in some" — the fragmentation of the messengers themselves into accepted and refused lists; (4) *wa yurīdūna an yattakhidhū bayna dhālika sabīlan* — "and wish to take a way between" — the intention to construct a middle-road between belief and disbelief — the standing résumé of every cafeteria-religion: the menu-approach to revelation.

**Yufarriqūna Bayna Allāhi wa Rusulih: Severing the Sender From the Sent**

The second clause names a severance whose logic the commentators dissect from its two directions. The first: believing in God while refusing His messengers — the deist-minimum, the "we need no intermediaries" position — which the Book treats not as surplus-piety but as *separation of God from His own government*: the messengers are God's standing plenipotentiaries; to recognize the King while refusing His ambassador is to refuse the King's choice of administration — 3:31-32's standing linkage formula: "say: if you love God, follow me — God will love you... say: obey God and the Messenger — but if they turn away — verily God loves not the disbelievers." The second direction — accepted by some early readings — is the severing *among* the messengers: affirming this prophet and denying that one — acknowledgment made tribal rather than theological: "we accept our own" (2:91's standing exposure: 2:91 — "when it is said to them: believe in what God has sent down — they say: we believe in what was sent down to us — and they disbelieve in what is beyond it — though it is the truth confirming what is with them"; 2:87's chronicle — "whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire — you waxed arrogant — some you denied and some you slew"). Both directions meet at the standing counter-command — the creed-verse of 2:285 — "we make no distinction between any of His messengers" — *lā nufarriqu bayna aḥadin min rusulih* — the believers' self-description written precisely as the negative of this verse's charge; with its standing companions 2:136 ("say: we believe in God and in what was sent down to us and in what was sent down to Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac and Jacob and the Tribes... we make no distinction between any of them") and 3:84 — the archipelago of v. 136 above re-anchored: the articles of faith admit no partial subscription.

**A Way Between: The Middle That Does Not Exist**

The fourth clause names the aspiration and thereby exposes the illusion: *wa yurīdūna an yattakhidhū bayna dhālika sabīlan* — "and wish to take a way between": *bayna dhālika* — between that — between belief and disbelief — a middle-road sought where the Book will announce, in the next verse, that there is no such territory: the terrain between īmān and kufr being not a third country but a mirage (al-Zamakhsharī's standing note: the "way between" is in truth *within* the realm of disbelief — the middle position collapsing on audit into one of the two it straddles). The commentators connect the verse's anatomy to its standing historical referents — most prominently the Jewish and Christian communities of the Prophet's horizon who acknowledged their own prophets while refusing Muḥammad — though the phrases stand deliberately general (al-Rāzī's standing principle: the ruling follows the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion): the selective subscriber exists in every age — the believer in "God" who declines prophets, the devotee of one messenger who resents another, the modern who keeps revelation's ethics while returning its cosmology. The verse's unfinished syntax — the sentence breaking off mid-relative-clause, its *verdict* withheld until v. 151 ("it is they who are truly disbelievers") — forms its own pedagogics: the description of the selective believer left hanging incomplete across the verse-break, imitating structurally the incompleteness of his creed — the sentence itself partial until God's own completion arrives: *ulāʾika humu al-kāfirūna ḥaqqan* — the Book demonstrating in its very grammar that a partial faith, like a partial verse, waits upon completion — and receives, from the other side of the period, the completion it did not hope for.

---

## Sūrah al-Nisāʾ 4:151

> **It is they who are the disbelievers in truth, and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment.**

**Expanded Commentary**

**Ulāʾika Humu al-Kāfirūna Ḥaqqan: The Caption That Closes the Case**

The verse that completes the sentence broken off at v. 150 issues the Book's standing definition-verdict, one of its most emphatic grammatical forms: *ulāʾika humu al-kāfirūna ḥaqqan* — "it is they who are the disbelievers in truth": the pronoun-of-separation (*faṣl*) *hum* between subject and predicate locking the equation — *they*, and no others — plus *ḥaqqan* — the accusative of emphasis, "in truth, veritably": the selective believers officially registered as *real* disbelievers — the word *ḥaqqan* doing the devastating work: their creed may be partial, but their classification is complete. The commentators (al-Zamakhsharī's standing note most quoted) unfold the verdict's logic: what they sought was "a way between" belief and disbelief — and the Book's answer is that **there is no between in this matter**: the articles of faith are an indivisible constitution; to strike one article is to annul the document — the principle the creed-verses had already installed (2:285 — "we make no distinction between any of His messengers") and that this verdict now enforces with a definitional hammer: *partial* assent is not a lesser īmān but a form of kufr — because the object of faith is not only God and messengers severally but God's own *choice* of His messengers — His wisdom in sending *whom He sends* (6:124's standing counter-assertion of the principle: "God knows best where He places His message"). To veto the Sender's selection is to sit in judgment over the Sender — the standing theological point: they who believed "in some" believed not in God-as-Disposer but in their own inherited roster: their god, on audit, their preference; and preference is not faith.

**The Reference-Range: People of the Book — and Every Partial Subscriber After Them**

The standing comment-canon localizes the announcement's first address — most of the early readings: the Jews and Christians of the Prophet's horizon, who received their own scriptures sincerely and drew their line of refusal at Muḥammad (2:91's standing dossier of the refusal-logic: "we believe in what was sent down to us" — tribal acknowledgment masquerading as fidelity); some early reports surname the verse's sabab to delegations who came professing Mūsā and ʿĪsā while declining the Paraclete-claimed Prophet (its standing discussions in al-Ṭabarī's chains). Yet the wording's breadth — *inna alladhīna...* — the demonstrative-universal "those who" — keeps the verdict permanently open for occupation: al-Rāzī's standing hermeneutic maxim ("the lesson is in the generality of the expression, not the specificity of the cause") assigning every generation's selective subscriber to the same registry: the believer-in-God-only, the prophet-cafeteria of the comparative-religionist, the internal Muslim position that accepts this verse and "has reservations" about that one (2:85's standing internal warning within the Ummah itself: "do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in the wage of such among you shall be but disgrace in the life of this world — and on the Day of Resurrection they shall be driven to the severest punishment").

**Wa Aʿtadnā li-l-Kāfirīna ʿAdhāban Muhīnan: The Prepared Humiliation**

The sentence closes with the standing preparation-formula of the Book's penal register: *wa aʿtadnā li-l-kāfirīna ʿadhāban muhīnan* — "and We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment": *aʿtadnā* — from ʿ-t-d — to hold ready, to prepare in advance (its standing register: 4:18 — "We have prepared for them a painful punishment"; 4:37; 4:93; 4:102; 4:161 below; 17:10; 33:8; 48:6 — the Book's own penal-inventory: a punishment pre-fabricated, waiting, as the guests of v. 122's counter-file had their Gardens pre-prepared — 4:57 — *uʿiddat*) — and the qualifier chosen for this dossier's penalty: *muhīn* — from h-w-n — humbling, disgracing: the humiliation-punishment (its standing file: 4:14 — "a humiliating punishment" for transgressing the inheritance-limits; 4:37; 4:102; 22:57; 58:5 — "the disbelievers shall have a humiliating punishment").
